# NICHOLAS CO-
## PERNICUS OF TORUŃ
### ON THE REVOLUTIONS OF THE 
### heavenly spheres, in **VI** Books.

---

->You have in this work, now newly born and published,<-
->diligent reader, the movements of the stars, both fixed<-
->and wandering <note>original Latin: "erraticarum." This refers to the planets, which appear to "wander" across the sky compared to the "fixed" stars.</note>, restored from both ancient<-
->and also recent observations: and further<-
->adorned with new and wonderful hypotheses.<-

<meta>This page follows the title page of the 1543 first edition. It contains the famous (and at the time, unsigned) preface by Andreas Osiander, which sought to present Copernicus’s heliocentric theory as a mathematical tool rather than a literal physical reality to avoid controversy. The catchword at the bottom "gis rea" indicates the start of the word "magis realem" on the following page.</meta>

# TO THE READER REGARDING THE HYPO-
## THESES OF THIS WORK.

I do not doubt that certain learned men, now that the report of the novelty of the hypotheses <note>In this context, "hypotheses" refers to the underlying mathematical assumptions or models used to explain planetary motion.</note> of this work has spread—which establishes that the Earth moves and that the Sun remains immobile in the center of the universe—will be greatly offended, and think that the liberal arts, which were correctly established long ago, ought not to be thrown into confusion. But if they are willing to weigh the matter exactly, they will find that the author of this work has committed nothing that deserves blame. For it is the duty of an astronomer to collect the history of celestial motions through diligent and skillful observation. Then, he must conceive and devise causes for these motions, or hypotheses—since he cannot by any means reach the true causes—of such a kind that, if they are assumed, these same motions can be correctly calculated from the principles of geometry, both for the future and for the past. This craftsman <note>Referring to Copernicus.</note> has performed both of these tasks exceptionally well. For it is not necessary that these hypotheses be true, nor even likely; this one thing is sufficient: that they provide a calculation consistent with observations. Unless, perhaps, someone is so ignorant of geometry and optics that he considers the epicycle <note>term: epicycle. A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in ancient astronomy to explain the complex paths of planets.</note> of Venus to be likely, or believes it to be the reason why Venus sometimes precedes and sometimes follows the Sun by forty degrees and more. For who does not see that, if this is assumed, it necessarily follows that the diameter of the star <note>The author uses "star" here to refer to the planet Venus.</note> would appear more than four times larger, and the body itself more than sixteen times larger, at perigee <note>original Greek: "περιγειῳ" (perigeio). The point in an orbit where the planet is closest to the Earth.</note> than at apogee <note>original Greek: "απογειῳ" (apogeio). The point in an orbit where the planet is furthest from the Earth.</note>? Yet the experience of every age contradicts this. There are other things in this discipline no less absurd, which there is no need to examine at present. For it is clear enough that this art is completely and simply ignorant of the causes of the apparent unequal motions. And if it devises any by imagination—as it certainly devises many—it does not devise them to persuade anyone that it is so, but only so that they may establish a correct calculation. Moreover, since various hypotheses sometimes offer themselves for one and the same motion (as in the movement of the Sun: eccentricity and the epicycle), the astronomer will seize that one which is easiest to grasp. The philosopher, perhaps, [will seek] more for likelihood... <note>The text ends mid-sentence here; the catchword "gis rea" suggests the next page continues with "magis realem" (more real).</note>

<meta>catchword: gis rea</meta>

<summary>This preface, written by Andreas Osiander, argues that Copernicus's heliocentric model should be viewed as a mathematical convenience for calculation rather than a physical claim about the universe's actual structure. It defends the work against potential critics by distinguishing the role of the astronomer (who models) from the philosopher (who seeks truth).</summary>
<keywords>Andreas Osiander, hypotheses, astronomical calculation, Venus, epicycle, perigee, apogee, heliocentrism, geometry, celestial motions</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes the anonymous preface by Andreas Osiander and presents a supportive letter from Cardinal Nicholas Schönberg, which serves as an official endorsement of Copernicus's work, written seven years before its publication.</meta>

[will] require more <note>The text continues from the previous page: "magis requirēt" (will require more [certainty]).</note>, yet neither will grasp or teach anything for certain unless it has been divinely revealed to him. Therefore, let us allow these new hypotheses to become known alongside the ancient ones, being no less plausible, especially since they are both admirable and easy to use, and bring with them a vast treasury of highly learned observations. As far as hypotheses are concerned, let no one expect anything certain from astronomy, since it can provide nothing of the kind; otherwise, if he takes as true that which was constructed for another purpose, he will depart from this discipline more of a fool than when he arrived. Farewell.

### NICHOLAS SCHÖNBERG, CAR-
### dinal of Capua, to Nicolaus Copernicus, Greetings.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'C' illustrating a figure (possibly a scholar or cleric) seated at a desk, surrounded by elaborate floral and architectural scrollwork.</image-desc>

Since reports of your excellence, through the constant talk of everyone, reached me several years ago, I began at that time to hold you in high regard and even to congratulate our countrymen among whom you flourished with such great glory. For I had understood that you were not only exceptionally skilled in the discoveries of the ancient mathematicians, but had also established a new system of the world. In this system, you teach that the Earth moves; that the Sun occupies the lowest <note>original: "imum"; in the cosmological language of the time, the "lowest" point often referred to the center of the universe.</note>, and therefore the central place of the world; that the eighth sphere <term>eighth sphere. The sphere of the "fixed stars," which in traditional geocentric cosmology was the outermost part of the universe; here, it is described as immobile.</term> remains forever immobile and fixed; and that the Moon, together with the elements included within its sphere, situated between the heavens of Mars and Venus, revolves in an annual course around the Sun. I have also learned that you have completed commentaries <note>Referring to the manuscript of the work itself.</note> on this whole system of astronomy and have compiled the motions of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>, calculated and set into tables, to the greatest admiration of everyone. Therefore, most learned man, unless I am being a burden to you, I beg you again and again most earnestly to communicate this discovery of yours to scholars, and to send to me at the earliest possible moment your nightly labors <note>original: "lucubrationes"; a term for scholarly work produced by the light of a lamp, implying diligent study.</note> concerning the sphere of the world, together with the tables and whatever else you have pertaining to this same subject. I have, moreover, given the task to Theodoric von Reden <note>A colleague of Copernicus and a clerical official in Rome.</note> that everything should be copied there at my expense and brought to me. If you grant me this favor, you will realize that you have dealt with a man who is concerned for your name and eager to do justice to such great virtue. Farewell. Rome, the Kalends of November, in the year 1536.

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the introductory materials—including Osiander's anonymous foreword and Cardinal Schönberg’s encouraging letter—to the actual author’s preface. Copernicus now addresses the Pope directly to justify the publication of his controversial heliocentric theory.</meta>

# TO THE MOST HOLY
## LORD POPE PAUL
### THE THIRD, SUPREME PONTIFF,
#### The Preface of Nicolaus Copernicus to the Books
##### of the Revolutions.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial letter 'S' featuring two men in scholarly robes standing in an outdoor setting with a building in the background; they appear to be engaged in a serious intellectual discussion.</image-desc>

I can well enough imagine, Most Holy Father, that as soon as certain people hear that in these books of mine, which I have written about the Revolutions of the spheres of the universe, I attribute certain motions to the terrestrial globe, they will immediately shout that I and such an opinion should be hissed off the stage <note>original: "explodendum"; a theatrical term meaning to be driven off the stage by booing or clapping.</note>. For my own works do not please me so much that I do not weigh what others will judge of them. And although I know that the thoughts of a philosopher are far removed from the judgment of the common people—because it is his endeavor to seek the truth in all things, as far as God has permitted to human reason—nevertheless, I consider that opinions entirely alien to the truth must be avoided.

And so, when I considered with myself how absurd a "thing to hear" <note>original Greek: ἀκρόαμα (*akroama*); referring to a lecture or a doctrine intended for a private audience.</note> they would judge it—those who know that the judgment of many centuries has confirmed the opinion that the Earth is placed motionless in the middle of the heavens as its center—if I, on the contrary, were to assert that the Earth moves; I hesitated for a long time whether I should bring to light my commentaries written to demonstrate its motion, or whether it would be better to follow the example of the <term>Pythagoreans: followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras who often kept their advanced mathematical and philosophical teachings secret from the general public</term> and some others, who were accustomed to hand down the mysteries of philosophy not through writing, but only from hand to hand to their relatives and friends. As the letter of Lysis to Hipparchus testifies. 

And indeed, they seem to me to have done this, not as some think from a certain envy of sharing their teachings, but so that these most beautiful things, investigated with much effort by great men, should not be held in contempt by those who either find it a nuisance to devote any honest labor to literature unless it is profitable, or who, even if they are stirred to the liberal study of philosophy by the encouragement and example of others, are nevertheless of such dull-wittedness...

<summary>Copernicus begins his formal dedication to Pope Paul III, acknowledging that his theory of the Earth's motion will be seen as absurd and explaining his long hesitation to publish for fear of ridicule.</summary>
<keywords>Nicolaus Copernicus, Pope Paul III, Heliocentrism, Earth's motion, Pythagorean secrecy, scientific publishing, philosophy vs. public opinion</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s letter to Pope Paul III. He explains that his fear of being ridiculed for his "absurd" ideas—the Earth moving—initially kept him from publishing, but the encouragement of high-ranking friends and the evident confusion in existing astronomical models finally persuaded him to share his work.</meta>

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

...their own stupidity among philosophers, moving about like drones among bees. When I weighed these things in my mind, the contempt I feared because of the novelty and apparent absurdity of my opinion nearly drove me to abandon the work I had begun.

But my friends, while I delayed and even resisted, drew me back. Among them first was Nikolaus von Schönberg, Cardinal of Capua, renowned in every field of learning. Next to him was a man who loves me dearly, Tiedemann Giese, Bishop of Kulm <note>Original: "episcopus Culmensis"; modern Chełmno, Poland.</note>, a devoted student of sacred and all good literature. For he frequently exhorted me, and sometimes even with added reproaches, demanded that I publish this book and finally allow it to come into the light—a book which had remained hidden with me not just for nine years, but already into its fourth nine-year period <note>Copernicus refers to the Roman poet Horace’s advice to keep a manuscript for nine years before publishing; he notes he has kept his for thirty-six years (4 x 9).</note>. Many other eminent and learned men did the same, urging me not to refuse my labor any longer for the common benefit of mathematical studies despite my fear. They argued that the more absurd my doctrine about the motion of the Earth appeared to most people now, the more admiration and gratitude it would earn after the publication of my writings, once the haze of absurdity was seen to be removed by the clearest demonstrations. Persuaded by these advisers and led by that hope, I finally allowed my friends to proceed with the publication they had long requested.

But perhaps Your Holiness will not be so surprised that I dared to bring these "night-studies" <note>original: "lucubrationes"; refers to scholarly work performed by candlelight late into the night.</note> of mine to light—after having put so much effort into elaborating them that I did not hesitate to commit my thoughts on the motion of the Earth to writing—but will rather expect to hear from me what came into my mind that I dared to imagine some motion of the Earth, contrary to the accepted opinion of mathematicians and almost contrary to common sense. Therefore, I do not want it to be hidden from Your Holiness that nothing else moved me to think of a different way of calculating the motions of the spheres of the universe than the fact that I realized mathematicians are not consistent with themselves in investigating them. First, they are so uncertain about the motion of the Sun and Moon that they cannot even [determine the length of] the returning year...

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s dedication to Pope Paul III. Having just mentioned how his friends persuaded him to publish, he now explains the scientific motivation for his work: the chaotic and "monstrous" state of existing astronomical theories (Ptolemaic and Aristotelian), which failed to provide a unified or accurate system for the heavens.</meta>

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

...so that they might be able to demonstrate and observe your greatness. Next, in establishing the motions of these, as well as the other five <term>wandering stars</term> <note>Original: "errantium stellarum," the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, they do not use the same principles and assumptions, nor the same demonstrations of their apparent revolutions and motions. For some use only <term>homocentric circles</term> <note>Circles sharing a single center, usually the Earth; the Aristotelian model.</note>, others use <term>eccentrics and epicycles</term> <note>Complex geometric models where circles are offset from the center or move upon other circles; the Ptolemaic model.</note>, yet they do not fully achieve what they seek with these. For those who relied on homocentrics, although they demonstrated that several diverse motions could be composed from them, they were unable to establish anything certain from them that clearly corresponded to the <term>phenomena</term> <note>Observed events in the sky.</note>. Those, however, who devised eccentrics, even if they seem for the most part to have accounted for the apparent motions with matching numbers, nevertheless admitted many things in the process that seem to contradict the first principles regarding the uniformity of motion. They were also unable to find or deduce from these the most important thing: the shape of the world and the definite <term>symmetry</term> <note>Proportionality and structural harmony.</note> of its parts. 

But it happened to them just as if someone took hands, feet, a head, and other limbs from different places—drawn excellently indeed, but not in relation to a single body—so that they did not match each other at all, and a monster rather than a human was composed from them. Thus in the process of demonstration, which they call a <note>Greek: "methodon"</note> **method**, they are found to have either omitted something necessary or admitted something foreign and completely irrelevant to the matter. This would least of all have happened to them if they had followed certain, fixed principles. For if the hypotheses they assumed were not fallacious, everything following from them would undoubtedly be verified. Although these things I am saying now are obscure, they will become clearer in their proper place.

When I had turned over in my mind for a long time this uncertainty of the mathematical traditions regarding the calculation of the motions of the world's spheres, I began to be annoyed that no more certain explanation of the movements of the <term>mechanism of the world</term> <note>Original: "machinae mundi," a common metaphor for the universe as a designed structure.</note>—which was built for us by the best and most orderly Craftsman of all—was agreed upon by philosophers, who otherwise examine the most minute things regarding this world so exquisitely. Therefore, I took this task upon myself: to reread the books of all the philosophers I could obtain, to investigate whether anyone had ever thought that there were other motions...

<summary>Copernicus criticizes contemporary astronomers for their inconsistent and "monstrous" models of the universe, which fail to reflect a unified divine design. This frustration leads him to research ancient alternative theories about the motion of the spheres.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, homocentric circles, eccentrics, epicycles, symmetry of the world, mechanism of the world, scientific method, planetary motion</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus’s preface to Pope Paul III. After describing the fragmented and "monstrous" state of existing astronomical models, Copernicus now explains how he turned to ancient authors to see if anyone had ever proposed that the Earth moves, finding the intellectual justification to begin his own investigation.</meta>

# AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

...the motions of the spheres of the world than those had proposed who profess Mathematics in the schools. And indeed, I first found in Cicero that Nicetus <note>Likely Hicetas of Syracuse, a 4th-century BCE philosopher.</note> had perceived that the Earth moves. Later, I also found in Plutarch that others were of the same opinion. I have decided to set down his words here, so that they may be available to everyone: 

<note>original: "οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι μένειν τὴν γῆν, Φιλόλαος δὲ Πυθαγόρειος κύκλῳ περιφέρεσθαι περὶ τὸ πῦρ κατὰ κύκλου λοξοῦ ὁμοιοτρόπως ἡλίῳ καὶ σελήνῃ. Ἡρακλείδης ὁ Ποντικὸς καὶ Ἔκφαντος ὁ Πυθαγόρειος κινοῦσι μὲν τὴν γῆν οὐ μήν γε μεταβατικῶς, τροχοῦ δίκην ἐνισμένοις ἀπὸ δυσμῶν ἐπὶ ἀνατολὰς, περὶ τὸ ἴδιον αὐτῆς κέντρον."</note>

*Others say that the Earth stands still, but Philolaus the Pythagorean says that it moves around the central fire <note>The Pythagoreans believed in a "Central Fire" distinct from the Sun, around which all celestial bodies revolved.</note> in an oblique circle, just like the Sun and the Moon. Heraclides of Pontus and Ecphantus the Pythagorean move the Earth, not through space, but like a wheel fixed on an axle, turning from west to east around its own center.*

Taking this opportunity, I too began to think about the mobility of the Earth. And although the opinion seemed absurd, yet because I knew that others before me had been granted this liberty—to imagine whatever circles they pleased to demonstrate the <term>phenomena</term> <note>Visible celestial events or appearances.</note> of the stars—I thought it would be easily permitted for me as well to test whether, by assuming some motion of the Earth, more firm demonstrations than those of the others could be found in the revolution of the heavenly spheres.

And so, having assumed the motions which I attribute to the Earth later in this work, I finally found, through much and long observation, that if the motions of the rest of the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>The planets.</note> are compared to the Earth’s circulation and calculated for the revolution of each star, not only do their phenomena follow from this, but the orders and magnitudes of all the stars and spheres, and even heaven itself, are so interconnected that in no part of it can anything be moved without the confusion of the remaining parts and of the whole universe. 

Accordingly, in the progress of the work, I have followed this order: in the first book, I describe all the positions of the spheres, together with the motions I attribute to the Earth, so that this book contains, as it were, the general <term>constitution of the universe</term> <note>The physical layout and structural laws of the cosmos.</note>. In the remaining books, I then compare the motions of the rest of the stars and all the spheres with the mobility of the Earth, so that it may be gathered from this to what extent the motions and appearances of the rest of the stars and spheres can be <term>saved</term> <note>From the phrase "saving the appearances" (sozein ta phainomena); to provide a mathematical explanation that matches what we see.</note> if they are compared to the Earth’s motions. Nor do I doubt that ingenious and learned Mathematicians will agree with me, if what...

<sig>iiij</sig>
<meta>catchword: philoso</meta>

<summary>Copernicus cites ancient Greek and Roman authorities who first suggested the Earth's motion, justifying his own mathematical experiments with a heliocentric model. He claims this model creates a perfectly interconnected universe where no part can be changed without disrupting the whole.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Author's Preface" (the dedication to Pope Paul III). In the previous section, Copernicus explained how he was inspired by ancient philosophers who believed the Earth moved. He now argues that his work, though potentially controversial, is intended for a learned audience and serves the practical needs of the Church, such as calendar reform.</meta>

...philosophy especially requires, [that they] will wish to know and weigh, not in passing, but deeply, those things which are brought forward by me in this work for the demonstration of these matters. But in order that the learned and unlearned alike might see that I avoid the judgment of no one at all, I preferred to dedicate these my night-labors <note>original: "lucubrationes"; this term refers to scholarly work performed by candlelight late into the night.</note> to your Holiness, rather than to anyone else, because even in this most remote corner of the earth in which I live <note>Copernicus lived in Frombork (Frauenburg), on the northern edge of Poland, far from the centers of the Italian Renaissance.</note>, you are held to be most eminent in the dignity of your rank and in your love of all letters and even Mathematics, so that you might easily be able by your authority and judgment to restrain the bites of slanderers—even though the proverb says there is no remedy against the bite of a sycophant.

If perhaps there will be idle talkers <note>original Greek: "ματαιόλογοι" (mataiológoi); literally "speakers of vanity" or "babblers."</note> who, although they are ignorant of all Mathematics, yet take it upon themselves to judge them, and because of some passage of scripture, badly distorted for their own purpose, dare to reprehend and attack this my undertaking: I do not care for them, to the extent that I even despise their judgment as rash. For it is not hidden that Lactantius <note>Lactantius (c. 250–325 AD) was an early Christian advisor to Constantine who famously mocked the idea of a spherical Earth and the existence of people on the other side of the world (antipodes).</note>, an otherwise famous writer but little a mathematician, speaks quite childishly about the shape of the earth when he mocks those who have declared that the earth has the form of a globe. Therefore, it ought not to seem strange to students if some such people mock us also. 

Mathematics is written for mathematicians <note>original: "Mathemata mathematicis scribuntur." This is one of Copernicus's most famous defenses of his work, arguing that only those trained in the science are qualified to judge it.</note>, to whom these my labors, if I am not mistaken in my opinion, will also seem to contribute something to the ecclesiastical Commonwealth, over which your Holiness now holds the leadership. For not so long ago, under Leo X, when the question of reforming the Church Calendar was being discussed in the Lateran Council <note>The Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517). The Church was struggling to fix the date of Easter because the Julian calendar no longer matched the solar year.</note>, it remained undecided then for the sole reason that the lengths of years and months, and the motions of the Sun and Moon, were not yet considered to be sufficiently measured. From which time onward, I have directed my mind to observing these things more accurately, being encouraged by that most distinguished man, Lord Paul, Bishop of Fossombrone <note>original: "Semproniensi." Paul of Middelburg (1446–1534) was a scientist and bishop who led the papal commission on calendar reform.</note>, who then presided over that business. What I have achieved in that matter, I leave to the judgment of your Holiness especially, and of all other learned Mathematicians; and lest I seem to your Holiness to promise more regarding the utility of the work than I can perform, I now pass to the undertaking.

<meta>catchword: INDEX</meta>

<summary>Copernicus defends his heliocentric theory against potential religious critics by citing the need for better mathematical data for Church calendar reform and dedicating the work to the Pope. He famously asserts that "mathematics is written for mathematicians," dismissing non-expert scriptural objections as "idle talk."</summary>

<meta>This page follows the conclusion of Copernicus's dedicatory preface to Pope Paul III. Having justified his work as a scholarly pursuit intended for the improvement of the Church's calendar and the advancement of mathematical truth, he now provides a table of contents for the first two of the six books that comprise "De revolutionibus."</meta>

# INDEX OF THE CONTENTS
## IN EACH OF THE CHAPTERS, OF THE SIX
### books of Nicolaus Copernicus, concerning the revolutions of the heavenly
### spheres.

### BOOK ONE.

1. That the world is spherical.
2. That the earth is also spherical.
3. How the earth with the water forms one globe.
4. That the movement of the heavenly bodies is uniform and circular, perpetual, or composed of circular movements.
5. Whether a circular movement belongs to the earth, and concerning its location.
6. Concerning the immensity of the heaven relative to the size of the earth.
7. Why the ancients thought that the earth rested in the middle of the world, as a center.
8. The resolution of the aforementioned reasons, and their insufficiency.
9. Whether several movements can be attributed to the earth, and concerning the center of the world.
10. Concerning the order of the heavenly spheres.
11. Demonstration of the threefold movement of the earth.
12. Concerning the magnitude of straight lines in a circle. <note>In modern geometry, these are known as "chords." Copernicus uses them to build his trigonometric tables.</note>
13. Concerning the sides and angles of plane rectilinear triangles.
14. Concerning spherical triangles.

### BOOK TWO.

1. Concerning circles and their names.
2. Concerning the obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer," the circle of the zodiac.</note> and the distance between the tropics, and how they are determined.
3. Concerning the arcs and angles of the intersecting circles: the equinoctial, the zodiac, and the meridian, from which declination and right ascension are derived, and concerning their calculation.
4. How also for any star positioned outside the circle that is through the middle of the signs <note>The ecliptic.</note>, provided its latitude and longitude are known, its declination and right ascension may be revealed, and with which degree of the zodiac it reaches the middle of the sky <note>original: "caelum mediat"; this refers to the star's culmination or meridian transit.</note>.
5. Concerning the sections of the horizon <note>original: "finitoris"; a classical term for the horizon as the "limiter" of sight.</note>.
6. What the differences of the midday shadows are.
7. The longest day, the latitude of sunrise, and the inclination of the sphere; how they are demonstrated from one another, and concerning the remaining differences of the days.
8. Concerning the hours and parts of the day and night.
9. Concerning the oblique ascension of the parts of the zodiac, and how for any rising degree, the degree that is at the middle of the sky is also given.
10. Concerning the angle of intersection of the zodiac with the horizon.
11. Concerning the use of these tables.
12. Concerning the angles and arcs of those circles which flow through the poles of the horizon to the same circle of the signs <note>These are the vertical circles or circles of altitude used in spherical astronomy.</note>.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
## ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK ONE.

#### Chapter 1: That the universe is spherical.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within an ornate frame of foliage.</image-desc>
In the first place, we must observe that the universe is spherical. This is either because this shape is the most perfect of all, requiring no joins and being complete in itself; or because it is the most spacious of figures, which most suits that which is to contain and preserve all things; or even because the most perfectly finished parts of the universe—I mean the Sun, the Moon, and the stars—are seen in this shape; or because all things strive to be bounded by this form, as is apparent in drops of water and other liquid bodies, when they seek to be bounded by themselves. <note>Copernicus is referencing the natural tendency of liquids to form droplets (surface tension) as an analogy for the "natural" shape of the cosmos.</note> Therefore, no one should doubt that such a shape has been assigned to the heavenly bodies.

#### Chapter 2: That the Earth is also spherical.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a figure and architectural elements surrounded by floral patterns.</image-desc>
The Earth is also spherical, since from every side it rests upon its center. <note>In the physics of this era, the "center" was the point toward which all heavy things naturally fell.</note> Although a perfect sphere is not immediately apparent because of the great height of mountains and the depth of valleys, these do not significantly alter the overall roundness of the Earth. This is manifest for the following reasons: for those traveling North from any location, the pole of the daily revolution <note>The celestial pole around which the stars appear to rotate.</note> gradually rises, while the opposite pole sinks by the same amount, and more stars in the North are seen not to set, while in the South, some stars no longer rise. Thus, Italy does not see Canopus, which is visible in Egypt. And Italy sees the last star of the River <note>original: "fluuij stellam"; referring to the constellation Eridanus, which stretches far into the southern sky.</note>, which the colder climate of our region <note>Copernicus is writing from Frombork (Frauenburg) in modern-day Poland.</note> does not know. Conversely, for those traveling South, those stars rise higher, while those that are high for us sink down. Furthermore, the inclinations of the poles have everywhere the same ratio to the distances measured on the Earth, which...

<summary>In these opening chapters, Copernicus argues that the universe and the Earth must be spherical, citing the perfection of the shape and observational evidence from star positions at different latitudes.</summary>
<keywords>spherical universe, roundness of the Earth, celestial poles, Canopus, Eridanus, stellar observation, Nicolaus Copernicus</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the text of Book One, Chapter 2, providing empirical evidence for the Earth's sphericity based on celestial observations and maritime perspective, before beginning Chapter 3 which discusses the relationship between land and sea volumes.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

occurs in no other than a spherical figure. From which it is clear that the Earth is also enclosed by poles and is therefore globular. Add also that evening eclipses <note>original: "defectus"</note> of the Sun and Moon are not perceived by those living in the East, nor morning ones by those living in the West; while those in the middle see them—the former later, the latter earlier. Sailors also observe that the waters lean upon this same form, since land which is not visible from the deck of a ship is often seen from the top of the mast. Conversely, if something shining is placed at the top of the mast, as the ship moves away from the land, it seems to those remaining on the shore to gradually descend, until finally it is hidden as if setting. It is also established that waters, flowing by their own nature, always seek lower places—just like the earth—nor do they press further from the shore than the Earth's convexity <note>The curvature of the globe.</note> allows. Therefore, the land must be that much higher, wherever it rises out of the Ocean.

### How the earth and water form one globe. Chapter III.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or author, in a classical or architectural setting.</image-desc>
Here, therefore, the surrounding Ocean, pouring forth the seas everywhere, fills its deeper descents. Thus it was necessary that there be less water than land, lest the water absorb the entire earth—since both strive toward the same center by their weight—but rather that it might leave some parts of the land for the safety of living creatures, and so many islands open here and there. For what else is the continent itself, and the whole world of land, but an island larger than the others? Nor should certain Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, which dominated medieval science.</note> be listened to, who have claimed that the whole of the water is ten times larger than the whole earth. They take this conjecture from the fact that in the transformation of elements, they say ten parts of water are made from one part of earth during dissolution. They say the earth protrudes to some extent because it is cavernous and not balanced everywhere according to its weight, and that the center of gravity is one thing, and the center of magnitude another. But they are deceived by ignorance of the art of Geometry. They do not know that water cannot even be seven times greater if any part of the earth were to be dry, unless the earth completely vacated the center of gravity and gave place to the waters as being heavier than itself. For spheres are to each other in the triple ratio of their diameters <note>Copernicus refers to the geometric rule that the volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube of its diameter.</note>. If, therefore, the earth were one part to seven parts of water...

<meta>catchword: but (original: set)</meta>

<summary>Copernicus provides evidence for Earth's sphericity through observations of eclipses and ships at sea, then begins a geometric refutation of the Aristotelian theory that water is ten times more abundant than land.</summary>
<keywords>sphericity of Earth, eclipses, maritime observations, center of gravity, Peripatetics, geometry of spheres, volume of oceans</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from Chapter III, moving from a theoretical discussion of the volume of the oceans to empirical evidence provided by modern exploration and the geometry of shadows.</meta>

## ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK I.

if it were even an eighth part <note>Copernicus is refuting the traditional Aristotelian view that the volume of water was ten times that of land.</note>, its diameter could not be greater than the distance from the center to the surface of the waters; it is far from being ten times greater than the land. That there is also no difference between the center of gravity of the earth and the center of its magnitude can be understood from this: that the convexity of the earth spreading out from the ocean does not continuously swell as it recedes; otherwise, it would push back the sea waters as much as possible and would in no way allow inland seas or such vast gulfs to break through. Furthermore, the depth of the abyss would never cease to increase from the shore of the ocean, so that no island, nor rock, nor any piece of land would be encountered by sailors as they progressed further. Now, however, it is well known that between the Egyptian sea and the Arabian gulf <note>The Isthmus of Suez.</note> there remains barely fifteen <term>stadia</term> <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of length, roughly 185 meters; Copernicus’s figure here is notably smaller than the actual distance, likely following ancient sources.</note> in the very middle of the world. Conversely, Ptolemy in his *Cosmography* <note>original: "Coſmographia"; today known as Ptolemy’s *Geography*.</note> extended the habitable land to the middle circle, leaving beyond it unknown land where more recent explorers have added <term>Cathay</term> <note>Northern China.</note> and vast regions as far as 60 degrees of longitude. Thus, the land is now inhabited over a greater longitude than what remains for the ocean.

This will be even clearer if we add the islands found in our time under the Princes of Spain and Portugal, and especially **America**, named after its discoverer, the master of ships <note>A reference to Amerigo Vespucci.</note>. Because of its size, which is still not fully determined, they think it is another world, besides many other islands previously unknown. We should therefore not be surprised that there are <term>Antipodes</term> <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe.</note> or **Antichthones** <note>original: "Antichthones"; a Greek term for "those on the opposite earth."</note>. For geometric reasoning forces us to believe that America itself is situated diametrically opposite to India on the Ganges. From all these things, I think it is manifest that land and water together lean upon one center of gravity, and that there is no other center of magnitude for the earth; and since the earth is heavier, its gaping parts are filled with water. Therefore, there is a small amount of water in comparison with the earth, even if on the surface more water perhaps appears.

For it is necessary that the earth, with its surrounding waters, have the same shape that its shadow reveals; for it produces the darkening of the Moon by the circumferences of a perfect circle. Therefore, the earth is not flat, as **Empedocles** and **Anaximenes** thought; nor drum-shaped, as **Leucippus** held; nor boat-shaped, as **Heraclitus** believed; nor hollow in any other way, as **Democritus** suggested. Nor is it cylindrical, as **Anaximander** claimed; nor infinite in its thickness downward from its lower part, as **Xenophanes** supposed; but it is of absolute roundness, as the Philosophers believe.

<summary>Copernicus argues that land and water share a single center of gravity, citing recent Spanish and Portuguese discoveries—including America—to prove that landmasses are more extensive than ancient geographers like Ptolemy believed. He concludes by affirming the Earth's absolute sphericity, refuting various ancient theories of its shape based on the evidence of lunar eclipses.</summary>

### That the motion of celestial bodies is uniform, circular, and perpetual, or composed of circular motions. Chapter IV.

After this, we shall recall that the motion of celestial bodies is circular. For the mobility of a sphere is to be turned in a circle; by this very act, it expresses its own form in the simplest of bodies, where one cannot find a beginning or an end, nor distinguish one part from another, as it moves through the same points back into itself. There are, however, several motions belonging to the multitude of the orbs. The most obvious of all is the daily revolution, which the Greeks call <term>nychthemeron</term> <note>original: "νυχθήμερον"; a period of 24 hours comprising both day and night.</note>, that is, the space of a day and a night. By this motion, the whole universe is thought to glide from the east to the west, with the Earth alone excepted <note>Copernicus is carefully framing this from the perspective of traditional appearance before he fully argues for the Earth's motion.</note>. This is understood as the common measure of all motions, since we measure time itself primarily by the number of days. Then we see other revolutions that are, as it were, acting in opposition—that is, from west to east—namely those of the Sun, the Moon, and the five "wanderers" <note>original: "errantium"; the planets Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. Thus the Sun dispenses the year to us, and the Moon the months, which are the most common divisions of time; likewise, each of the other five planets makes its own circuit. Yet they differ in many ways. First, they do not revolve around the same poles as that primary daily motion, but instead travel through the obliquity of the <term>Zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"; literally "the standard-bearer," a common Latin term for the circle of the zodiac constellations.</note>. Second, in their own circuits, they do not appear to be carried uniformly; for the Sun and Moon are found to be sometimes slow and at other times faster in their course. As for the other five wandering stars, we perceive them sometimes even to move backward <note>Known as retrograde motion.</note> and to come to a "station" <note>A point where a planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction.</note> here and there. And while the Sun always proceeds on its own direct path, the planets wander in various ways, straying sometimes toward the South and sometimes toward the North, which is why they are called "planets" <note>From the Greek *planētēs*, meaning "wanderer."</note>. Add to this also that sometimes they become closer to the Earth, called <term>Perigee</term>, and at other times further away, called <term>Apogee</term>. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that their motions are circular, or composed of several circles, because these irregularities observe a fixed law and return at established periods; this could not happen if the motions were not circular. For only a circle can bring back what has already passed; just as, for example, the Sun, through a motion composed of circles, brings back to us the inequality of days and nights and the four seasons of the year...

<summary>Copernicus argues that celestial motions must be circular or composed of circles because they are repetitive and follow predictable laws. He notes the various apparent irregularities of the planets—such as changing speeds and retrograde motion—which he intends to explain through geometry.</summary>
<keywords>circular motion, nychthemeron, zodiac, planets, retrograde motion, perigee, apogee, celestial spheres</keywords>

# THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK I.

->NICHOLAS COPERNICUS<-

it brings them back <note>original: "bis reducit"; completing the sentence from the previous page regarding the return of planets to their starting positions.</note>, in which several motions are understood. Since it is impossible that a simple celestial body should move irregularly in a single orbit. For that would have to happen either because of an inconstancy in the moving power <note>original: "uirtutis mouentis"; the internal or external force believed to drive the spheres.</note>—whether that power be an external force or part of its inner nature—or because of some unevenness in the revolving body. Since the mind recoils from both these ideas, and it is unworthy to suppose such a thing exists in those things which are established in the best order, it is reasonable to conclude that their uniform motions appear irregular to us. This happens either because the circles in which they revolve have different poles, or because the Earth is not at the center of the circles in which they move. To us, viewing them from the Earth, the passing of these stars appears irregular because of their unequal distances; those that are closer seem larger than those further away (as is demonstrated in the study of optics). Thus, even on equal sections of an orbit, the motions will appear unequal in equal amounts of time because of the varying distance from our line of sight. For this reason, I think it is necessary above all else that we carefully observe the relationship of the Earth to the heavens, lest while we wish to investigate the loftiest things, we remain ignorant of those closest to us, and by the same error attribute to the celestial bodies things that belong to the Earth.

### Whether a circular motion belongs to the Earth, and concerning its location. Chapter V.

Now, since it has been demonstrated that the Earth also has the form of a globe, I think we must see whether a motion also follows from its form, and what place it holds in the universe; without these, it is impossible to find a certain explanation for the appearances in the heavens. Although authors generally agree that the Earth remains at rest in the center of the universe, so much so that they think the contrary view is unthinkable and even ridiculous, if we consider the matter more carefully, it will appear that this question is not yet settled, and therefore should by no means be disregarded. For every change in place that is seen is due either to the motion of the object being watched, or of the observer, or certainly to a differing movement of both. For between things moved equally in the same direction, motion is not perceived—I mean between the thing seen and the one seeing it. Now, the Earth is the place from which that celestial circuit is viewed and reproduced for our sight. If, therefore, some motion of the Earth...

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought that if a motion</meta> is assigned [to the Earth], the very same motion will appear in all things which are outside of it, but in the opposite direction, as if they were passing by. This is especially true of the daily revolution. For this <term>daily revolution</term> <note>The perceived 24-hour rotation of the stars around the Earth.</note> seems to carry along the entire universe, except for the Earth and those things around it. However, if you were to grant that the heavens have no part in this motion, but that the Earth rotates from west to east, you would find—if you considered the matter seriously—that this is indeed the case regarding the apparent rising and setting of the Sun, Moon, and stars.

And since the sky is that which contains and covers all things, the common place of the universe, it is not immediately obvious why motion should not be attributed to the thing contained rather than to the container, or to the thing located rather than to the one that provides the location. Indeed, this was the opinion of Heraclides and Ecphantus the Pythagoreans, as well as Nicetas of Syracuse (as mentioned in Cicero), who envisioned the Earth rotating in the center of the universe. They believed that the stars "set" because they were blocked by the Earth, and "rose" because the Earth moved away from them.

Once this is assumed, there follows another no less serious doubt concerning the location of the Earth, even though almost everyone has now accepted and believed that the Earth is the center of the universe. For if someone were to deny that the Earth occupies the middle or center of the universe, yet did not believe the distance was so great that it could be compared to the sphere of the <term>fixed stars</term> <note>The distant stars that do not change their positions relative to one another, unlike planets.</note>, but was significant and evident relative to the orbits of the Sun and other stars; and if he thought that for this reason their motion appeared different—as if they were regulated by a center other than the center of the Earth—he might perhaps be able to provide a sound reason for their apparent diverse motion. For the fact that the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>original: "errantia sidera"; refers to the planets.</note> are seen closer to the Earth at one time and further away at another, necessarily proves that the center of the Earth is not the center of their orbits. Thus it is not even certain whether the Earth moves toward and away from them, or they move toward and away from the Earth.

It would not be so surprising if someone, in addition to that daily revolution, should imagine some other motion for the Earth. Indeed, the Pythagorean Philolaus—a mathematician of no ordinary skill—is said to have believed that the Earth rotates and even wanders through space with several motions, being "one of the stars." Those who have written the life of Plato record that Plato did not hesitate to travel to Italy specifically for the sake of visiting him.

Many, however, have believed it could be demonstrated by geometric reasoning that the Earth is in the center of the universe, and that compared to the vastness of the heavens it is like a point, occupying the place of a center, and is for that reason immobile, because when the universe moves, the center <meta>catchword: "maneat" (remains/stays)</meta>

<summary>In this passage, Copernicus explores the possibility of Earth's rotation and displacement from the center of the universe, citing ancient Pythagorean philosophers to support his hypothesis. He argues that the apparent motion of the heavens could be explained by the Earth's own movement, noting that planets change their distance from us, which suggests Earth is not their orbital center.</summary>

## On the Immensity of the Heavens Compared to the Size of the Earth. Chapter VI.

That such a massive weight as the Earth has no significant proportion <note>original: *aestimationem*; here meaning a measurable ratio or value</note> to the magnitude of the heavens can be understood from this: the <term>boundary circles</term> <note>original: *finitores circuli*</note> (for this is how the Greeks interpret <term>horizons</term> <note>original: *horizontas* (ὁρίζοντας)</note>) divide the entire sphere of the heavens into two equal halves. This could not happen if the size of the Earth were significant compared to the heavens, or if its distance from the center of the world were notable. For a circle that cuts a sphere into two equal halves must pass through the center of that sphere, and it is the largest circle that can be circumscribed upon it. 

Let the circle ABCD be the horizon, and let the Earth, from which our vision originates, be E. This E is also the center of the horizon, which defines the boundary between what is visible and what is hidden. Suppose we observe through a <term>dioptra</term> <note>A portable sighting instrument used by ancient astronomers to measure positions of stars.</note>, a <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: *horoscopium*; here referring to an instrument for observing the time or the position of the stars, not a modern astrological chart.</note>, or a <term>chorobates</term> <note>A long wooden level used for surveying and astronomical alignment.</note> placed at point E. We see the beginning of Cancer rising at point C, and at that very moment, the beginning of Capricorn is seen setting at point A. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a circle representing the celestial sphere. Two diameters, labeled AEC and BED, intersect at the center point E. Point E represents the Earth or the observer’s eye. The points A, B, C, and D are marked on the outer circle, representing the rising and setting points of zodiac signs. Small markers outside the circle indicate the orientation of these sightings.</image-desc>

Since A, E, and C are found to be in a straight line according to the sighting instrument, it is clear that this line is the <term>diameter</term> <note>original: *dimetientem*</note> of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*, literally "the sign-bearer."</note>, because six signs of the zodiac constitute a semicircle, and the center E is the same as the center of the horizon. Again, when the revolution has changed so that the beginning of Capricorn rises at point B, the setting of Cancer will then be seen at point D. The line BED will also be a straight line and a diameter of the zodiac. Since it has already been shown that AEC is also a diameter of that same circle, it is clear that the center is at their intersection, point E. 

Thus, the horizon circle always divides the zodiac—which is the greatest circle of the sphere—into two equal parts. In a sphere, if a circle cuts any of the "great circles" through the middle, the cutting circle itself must also be a great circle. Therefore, the horizon is one of the great circles, and its center is seen to be the same as the center of the zodiac. Nevertheless, a line of sight from the surface of the Earth must necessarily be different from one starting at the Earth's center. But because of the immense distance of the heavens compared to the Earth, these lines become effectively like parallel lines. Due to the extreme distance of their destination, they appear to be a single line, since the space that [contains]...

He argues that because the horizon always bisects the heavens, the Earth must be situated at the center of the celestial sphere, or so close to it that its size is negligible.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the text of Chapter VI, where Copernicus argues that the observed immensity of the universe compared to the Earth does not necessitate that the Earth is stationary at the center.</meta>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

...occupies a space that, compared to their length, is rendered incomparable to the senses, in the manner demonstrated in the *Optics* <note>Referring to the mathematical study of light and perspective, likely referencing the works of Euclid or Ptolemy.</note>. By this argument, it is clear enough that the heavens are immense in comparison to the Earth and present the appearance of an infinite magnitude; but by the estimation of the senses, the Earth is to the heavens as a point is to a body, and as the finite is to the infinite in magnitude. Nothing else seems to have been demonstrated.

Nor does it follow that the Earth must rest in the middle of the universe. Indeed, we should wonder even more if such a vast world revolved in the space of twenty-four hours rather than its smallest part, which is the Earth.

For as they say the center is immobile and the things closest to the center move the least, this does not prove that the Earth rests in the middle of the universe. It is no different than if you were to say that the sky turns while the poles rest, and the things closest to the poles move the least. Just as **Cynosura** <note>The constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Bear), often used to refer to the North Star.</note> is seen to move much slower than **Aquila** <note>The Eagle constellation.</note> or **Canicula** <note>The "Little Dog" star (Procyon) or sometimes the "Dog Star" (Sirius).</note> because it describes a smaller circle near the pole, since they all belong to a single sphere. The mobility of that sphere, which fades away at its axis, does not allow all its parts an equal motion; yet the revolution of the whole brings them back in an equality of time, though not in an equality of distance.

The logic of the argument rests on this: as if the Earth were a part of the celestial sphere, sharing its nature and motion, so that being close to the center, it would move very little. Therefore, as a body itself and not the center, it will also move, covering similar celestial arcs as the heavens in the same time, though they be smaller.

How false this is, is clearer than light. For it would be necessary for it to be noon always in one place and midnight in another, so that daily sunrises and sunsets could not occur, since the motion of the whole and the part would be one and inseparable.

But for those things which are distinguished by a difference in nature, the logic is far different; things enclosed in a smaller circuit revolve faster than those tracing a larger circle. Thus, **Saturn**, the highest of the <term>wandering stars</term> <note>planets</note>, completes its revolution in thirty years, and the **Moon**, which is undoubtedly closest to the Earth, completes its circuit in a month. Finally, the Earth itself will be thought to circle through the space of a day and a night.

Thus, the same doubt about the daily revolution arises again. Moreover, its location is still sought and remains even less certain from the things said above. For that demonstration provides nothing other than the indefinite magnitude of the heavens relative to the Earth. But how far this immensity extends is not at all clear.

He challenges the traditional geocentric view by suggesting that the Earth, like other celestial bodies, moves at a speed relative to its nature and position.</summary>

## Why the ancients thought the Earth rests in the middle of the universe as its center. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap letter Q. The interior of the letter contains a figure, likely a scholar or astronomer, seated in a study with books or instruments, surrounded by ornate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>For this reason, the ancient philosophers tried to assert by various other arguments that the Earth stands still in the middle of the universe. They cite as the most powerful cause the nature of **heaviness** and **lightness** <note>In Aristotelian physics, "gravity" (heaviness) and "levity" (lightness) were inherent qualities of elements—the tendency to move toward or away from the center—rather than a force of attraction between masses.</note>. The element of Earth is indeed the heaviest, and all weighted things are carried toward it, striving toward its innermost center. Since the Earth is spherical, heavy objects are carried from all directions naturally at right angles to its surface; unless they were held back by the surface itself, they would fall into its center. A straight line that meets the boundary plane—where it touches the sphere—at right angles leads to the center. It follows, then, that things carried toward the middle seem to come to rest there. Therefore, the whole Earth will rest even more firmly in the center, and as it receives all falling things into itself, it will remain immobile by its own weight.

In the same way, they strive to prove this by the logic of motion and its nature. Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) established the physical framework that dominated Western science for nearly 2,000 years.</note> says that the motion of a single and simple body is simple; of simple motions, one is straight and the other is circular. Of straight motions, one is upward and the other is downward. Consequently, every simple motion is either toward the center (downward), away from the center (upward), or around the center (circular). Now, it is fitting for earth and water—which are considered heavy—to be carried downward, which is to seek the center. Air and fire, however, which are endowed with lightness, move upward and away from the center. It seems consistent to grant straight motion to these four elements, but to the celestial bodies, it is to be turned in a circle around the center. These are the views of Aristotle. 

If, therefore, says Ptolemy of Alexandria <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the most influential astronomer of antiquity, whose Geocentric (Earth-centered) model Copernicus is challenging.</note>, the Earth were to rotate, at least with a daily revolution, the opposite of what was said above would have to happen. For that motion would have to be exceedingly swift, and its speed insurmountable, to carry the entire circumference of the Earth around in twenty-four hours. Things that are stirred by a sudden rotation seem entirely unfit for gathering together; rather, things already united are scattered, unless they are held together by some firm bond. And long ago, he says, the dissipated Earth would have [passed into] the heavens themselves (which is quite ridicu-

### Resolution of the stated arguments, and their insufficiency. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral and foliate motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
For these and similar reasons, they say that the Earth rests at the center of the world, and there is no doubt that this is how they hold it to be. However, if someone were to believe that the Earth moves, they would surely say that such motion is **natural**, not **violent** <note>In the Aristotelian physics of Copernicus's time, "natural motion" was the inherent, effortless movement of an object toward its natural place (like a stone falling), whereas "violent motion" was forced and required constant external energy to overcome an object's nature.</note>. Now, things that occur according to nature produce the opposite effects of those produced by violence. For things that are subjected to force or an external impulse must necessarily be destroyed and cannot last long; but things that happen by nature are well-ordered and preserved in their optimal composition. 

Therefore, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the influential Greco-Egyptian astronomer who codified the geocentric (Earth-centered) model.</note> fears without reason that the Earth and all terrestrial things would be scattered in a revolution made by the power of nature, which is quite different from artifice <note>original: "artis"</note> or what can be attained by human intellect. But why does he not suspect the same even more regarding the universe, whose motion must be as much swifter as the heavens are larger than the Earth? Or have the heavens become so immense because they are pulled away from the center by an ineffable violence of motion, destined to collapse otherwise if they stood still? 

Certainly, if this logic held, the magnitude of the heavens would also extend to infinity. For the more the motion itself is carried upward by its own force, the faster the motion will be, because of the ever-increasing circumference which must be traversed in the space of 24 hours; and in turn, as the motion increases, the immensity of the heavens would increase. Thus, velocity would promote magnitude, and magnitude would promote velocity, unto infinity. But according to that physical axiom <note>A fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics stating that an infinite body cannot have motion because there is no way to "complete" a path that has no end.</note>, what is infinite cannot be traversed, nor moved by any means; the heavens will necessarily stand still.

Yet they say that outside the heavens there is no body, no place, no vacuum, and absolutely nothing, and therefore there is nowhere the heavens could expand into; then it is truly strange if something can be restrained by nothing. But if the heavens were infinite, and finite only in their interior concavity, it might perhaps be more true that there is nothing outside the heavens, since everything

Whether the world is finite or infinite, let us leave to the debates of the <term>physiologists</term> <note>Copernicus uses the term "physiologists" in the classical sense to mean natural philosophers or those who study the physical laws of nature.</note>; we hold this much as certain: that the Earth, enclosed within its poles, is bounded by a spherical surface. Why do we not admit that the appearance of this daily revolution belongs to the heavens, but the reality belongs to the Earth? This situation is just as if Virgil’s Aeneas were saying:

> We set sail from the port, and lands and cities recede.
<note>original: "Prouehimur portu, terræq; urbesq; recedunt." From Virgil's Aeneid, Book III, line 72. Copernicus uses this literary reference to explain the concept of relative motion.</note>

For when a ship floats along in calm water, everything outside is seen by the sailors to move in the likeness of the ship's motion, while they conversely think they are at rest along with everything they have with them. In the same way, it can certainly happen with the motion of the Earth that the whole world is thought to revolve. What then should we say of the clouds and other things hanging in the air in any way, or sinking, or rising back to the heights? Only that not only the Earth moves with the watery element joined to it, but also a significant part of the air, and whatever has a kinship with the Earth in the same way. This may be because the nearby air, mixed with earthy or watery matter, follows the same nature as the Earth, or because the motion of the air is an "acquired" motion, which it shares with the Earth through proximity in perpetual revolution and without resistance. Conversely, with no less wonder, they say the highest region of the air follows the celestial motion, as indicated by those sudden stars—I mean Comets and what the Greeks call <term>Pogonias</term> <note>Literally "bearded stars," a term used in antiquity to describe a specific appearance of a comet’s tail.</note>—for they assign that region as the place where they are generated, and they rise and set just like other stars. We can say that the part of the air is deprived of that terrestrial motion due to its great distance from the Earth. Therefore, the air nearest to the Earth will appear calm, along with things suspended in it, unless it is tossed back and forth by wind or some other force, as happens. For what else is wind in the air but a wave in the sea? We must admit that the motion of things falling and rising is twofold in comparison to the world, being entirely composed of both straight and circular motion. Since things which by their weight...

He argues that straight motion is a sign of a system out of balance, whereas circular motion represents the natural, harmonious state of a whole body.</meta>

### NICOLAI COPERNICI

...sinking <note>This sentence completes the thought from the previous page regarding why heavy objects fall.</note>, since they are essentially earthy, there is no doubt that the parts preserve the same nature as their whole. The same reasoning applies to those things which are swept into the heights by the force of fire. For even this terrestrial fire is fed primarily by earthy matter, and philosophers define a flame as nothing other than burning smoke. Now, it is the property of fire to expand whatever it has entered, and it does this with such force that it cannot be restrained by any means or machines from breaking its prison and completing its work. 

Expansionary motion moves from the center toward the circumference; accordingly, if any earthy part is set on fire, it is carried away from the middle toward the heights. Therefore, when they say that a <term>simple body</term> <note>In the physics of the time, "simple bodies" were the pure elements (earth, water, air, fire) which were thought to have a single, natural direction of motion.</note> has a simple motion, this is verified primarily regarding circular motion—provided that the simple body remains in its natural place and in its unity. For while in its place, the motion is none other than circular, which remains entirely within itself, much like a body at rest. 

But straight motion comes upon those things that wander from their natural place, or are thrust out of it, or are in any way outside of it. Nothing is so contrary to the order of the whole and the form of the world as being out of place. Therefore, straight motion only happens to things that are not "behaving correctly," <note>original: "non recte se habentibus"</note> nor are they perfect according to their nature, since they are separated from their whole and abandon its unity. 

Furthermore, those things that move up and down, even apart from circular motion, do not perform a simple, uniform, and equal motion. For they cannot be regulated by their lightness or the impulse of their own weight. Whatever falls begins with a slow motion and increases its velocity as it falls. Conversely, we see this terrestrial fire (for we see no other) swept into the heights and immediately grow weak, as if acknowledging that the cause of this violence is the earthy matter. 

Circular motion, however, always revolves equally, for it has an unfailing cause. But other motions hasten toward a conclusion; once they have reached their destination, they cease to be heavy or light, and that motion stops. Since, therefore, circular motion belongs to the whole, while straight motion belongs to the parts, we can say that circular motion remains present along with the straight, just as "life" remains present in a sick animal. 

Certainly, even this point—that Aristotle distributed simple motion into three types: away from the center, toward the center, and around the center—will be regarded merely as an act of reason. In the same way, we distinguish a line, a point, and a surface, even though one cannot exist without the other, and none of them...

I would add also that it seems quite absurd to attribute motion to the container or the space-provider, and not rather to the thing contained and located, which is the Earth. It is necessary, therefore, to take a more general view of motion around a center, and it is enough that each motion remains attached to its own center. You see, then, that from all these arguments, the mobility of the Earth is more probable than its rest, especially regarding the daily revolution, which is most characteristic of the Earth.

### Whether multiple motions can be attributed to the Earth, and concerning the center of the universe. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'C' featuring a robed figure, likely an astronomer or scholar, holding a navigational or astronomical instrument, possibly a cross-staff.</image-desc>
Since, therefore, nothing prevents the mobility of the Earth, I think we must now see whether several motions might belong to it, so that it could be considered one of the wandering stars. For the fact that the Earth is not the center of all revolutions is proven by the apparent unequal motion of the planets and their variable distances from the Earth, which cannot be understood as circles <term>homocentric</term> <note>Having the same center. Copernicus argues that if the Earth were the center of everything, planetary paths would be perfectly circular and uniform relative to us, which they are not.</note> with the Earth. Since there are many centers, one might not without reason doubt whether the center of the universe is the center of terrestrial gravity or something else. For my part, I believe that **gravity** is nothing other than a certain natural appetite <note>A "natural desire" or inherent tendency</note> implanted in the parts by the divine providence of the Creator of all things, so that they might combine themselves into their own unity and integrity by coming together in the form of a globe. It is credible that this affection is present also in the Sun, the Moon, and the other shining planets, so that by its power they remain in that roundness in which they present themselves, while nonetheless performing their circuits in many ways. If, therefore, the Earth also performs other motions—for example, around a center—it will be necessary that these are the motions which appear similarly in many external phenomena, among which we find the annual circuit. For if this motion were transferred from the Sun to the Earth, and the Sun were granted immobility,

All these things are taught to us by the principle of order in which they succeed one another, and by the harmony of the whole universe, if only we look at the matter with "both eyes," as the saying goes.

### On the order of the celestial spheres. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring a scholar or figure seated at a desk with a celestial globe.</image-desc>
I see that no one doubts that the highest of all visible things is the heaven of the fixed stars. We see that the ancient philosophers wished to determine the sequence of the <term>wandering stars</term> according to the magnitude of their revolutions <note>The time it takes to complete one orbit</note>, adopting the principle that among objects carried with equal speed, those further away appear to move more slowly, as is demonstrated in Euclid’s *Optics*. Therefore, they think that the Moon completes its circuit in the shortest space of time because, being closest to the Earth, it revolves in the smallest circle. Saturn, truly, is the highest, which completes the greatest circuit in the longest time. Beneath it is Jupiter. After this, Mars.

Concerning Venus and Mercury, however, differing opinions are found, because they do not range away from the Sun in every direction as the others do. For this reason, some place them above the Sun, as in Plato's *Timaeus*, while others place them below it, as Ptolemy and a large part of the moderns do. <term>Alpetragius</term> <note>original: "Alpetragius"; referring to Al-Bitruji, a 12th-century Spanish-Arabian astronomer</note> makes Venus higher than the Sun and Mercury lower. Therefore, those who follow Plato—since they think all stars, being otherwise dark bodies, shine with light received from the Sun—believe that if these planets were below the Sun, they would be seen as half-circles or certainly less than full due to their proximity to it. For they would reflect the light they receive mostly upwards, that is, toward the Sun, as we see in the new or waning Moon. Furthermore, they say that by their interposition, the Sun would sometimes be blocked, and its light would fail according to their size; since this never appears, they think these planets never go beneath the Sun. On the other hand, those who place Venus and Mercury below the Sun claim their reasoning from the vastness of the space found between the Sun and the Moon.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 10 regarding the order and distances of the celestial spheres. The opening "tion" completes the word "revolution" (revolutionem) from the previous page, referring to the time it takes for planets to complete their orbits.</meta>

->BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

revolution. <note>original: "tionem"</note> For they found that the maximum distance of the Moon from the Earth—which is sixty-four and one-sixth parts, where the radius of the Earth is one—is contained nearly eighteen times in the minimum distance of the Sun, which consists of 1,160 of those same parts. Between the Sun and the Moon, therefore, there are 1,096 parts. Consequently, so that such a vast void should not remain empty, they calculate from the intervals of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit farthest from or closest to the center of motion</note> by which they reason out the thickness of those spheres, and they find that these numbers nearly match: the highest point of the Moon is followed by the lowest point of Mercury, and the highest point of Mercury is followed by the lowest point of Venus, which finally, at its highest <term>apsis</term>, reaches almost to the lowest point of the Sun. For they calculate about 177 ½ of the aforementioned parts between the apsides of Mercury, and then they find the remaining space is nearly filled by the interval of Venus, which is 910 parts.

Therefore, they do not admit that there is any opacity in the stars similar to that of the Moon; rather, they believe the planets shine either by their own light or are saturated throughout their entire bodies with solar light, and for that reason, the Sun is not obstructed. It is a very rare occurrence for them to be positioned directly between our sight and the Sun, as they usually deviate in latitude <note>They usually pass above or below the Sun's disk from our perspective</note>. Furthermore, because their bodies are small in comparison to the Sun—since even Venus, being larger than Mercury, can scarcely cover a hundredth part of the Sun, according to <term>Al-Battani</term> <note>original: "Machometus Aracensis," a 9th-century Arab astronomer</note>, who estimates the diameter of the Sun to be ten times larger—they argue it is not easy to see such a tiny spot in the midst of that most brilliant light. Nevertheless, <term>Averroes</term> <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and polymath</note> mentions in his paraphrase of Ptolemy that he saw "a certain blackish thing" <note>original: "nigricãs quiddam"</note> when he found the <term>conjunction</term> <note>When two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky</note> of the Sun and Mercury indicated by the calculations. Thus, they decree that these two stars move beneath the solar circle.

But how weak and uncertain this reasoning is, is made manifest by the fact that, although according to <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>The 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is challenging</note> there are 38 parts from the center of the Earth to the surface of the nearest Moon, according to a truer estimation it is more than 52 parts (as will be shown below). Yet, in all that great space, we know of nothing being contained except air and, if you like, also what they call the <term>element of fire</term> <note>In the traditional Aristotelian view, the region between the Earth and the Moon was filled with spheres of air and fire</note>. Furthermore, the diameter of the circle of Venus, through which it wanders about 45 degrees more or less away from the Sun on either side, must be six times larger than the distance from the center of the Earth to its lowest apsis, as will be demonstrated in its proper place. What then will they say is contained in all that space, which is so much larger than what would be needed to hold the Earth, the air, the ether, the Moon, and Mercury, and moreover that...
