# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...that vast <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the old system, a small circle on which a planet moves, while that circle itself moves along a larger one</note> of Venus would occupy, if it revolved around a stationary earth. Also, Ptolemy’s argument—that the Sun must be carried in the middle between those planets that move away from it in every direction <note>referring to the outer planets like Mars or Jupiter</note> and those that do not move away <note>referring to Mercury and Venus, which always appear near the Sun</note>—is shown to be unconvincing by the fact that the Moon, which also moves away from the Sun in every direction, proves its falsity. 

Truly, what reason will those people give—who place Venus below the Sun, then Mercury, or separate them in some other order—for why they do not make their circuits separate and distinct from the Sun, like the other wandering stars <note>planets</note>, if indeed the rule of speed and slowness does not fail the order? <note>Copernicus refers to the principle that planets further from the center should move more slowly.</note> Therefore, it must be either that the earth is not the center to which the order of the stars and spheres is referred, or certainly that there is no logic to the order, and it is not clear why a higher place should be owed to Saturn rather than to Jupiter or any other planet.

For this reason, I think we should by no means disregard the view that Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author who wrote a famous encyclopedia of the liberal arts</note>, and indeed others among the Latin authors, have mastered. For they believe that Venus and Mercury run around the Sun, which exists in the middle; and for that reason they think these planets do not move further away from the Sun than the curvature of their spheres allows, since they do not circle the earth like the others, but have their <term>apsides</term> <note>the high and low points of an orbit</note> turned elsewhere. What else do they mean to signify, except that the center of those spheres is around the Sun? 

Thus, truly, the sphere of Mercury will be enclosed within that of Venus (which is agreed to be more than twice as large), and it will occupy a place within that expanse sufficient for itself. Taking this opportunity, if anyone should also relate Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars to that same center, provided they understand the size of those spheres to be such that they contain and surround the earth along with those others, he will not be mistaken, as the mathematical <note>original: "Canonica"</note> rule of their motions declares. 

For it is well known that they are always closer to the earth around their "evening rising"—that is, when they are opposite the Sun, with the earth between them and the Sun. Conversely, they are farthest from the earth at their "evening setting," when they are hidden near the Sun, namely when we have the Sun between them and the earth. These things sufficiently indicate that their center belongs more to the Sun, and is the same center to which Venus and Mercury also direct their revolutions. But truly, since all these planets rely on a single middle point, it is necessary that the space left between the convex sphere of Venus and the concave sphere of Mars also be recognized as a sphere...

### BOOK I OF THE REVOLUTIONS

...or a sphere distinguished from them sharing a common center <note>homocentric</note> along both its surfaces, which would contain the Earth together with its attendant, the Moon, and everything contained beneath the lunar globe. For we can in no way separate the Moon from the Earth—as the Moon is unquestionably closest to it—especially since we find a quite suitable and ample space for it in that area. Therefore, we are not ashamed to confess that this entire system encompassed by the Moon, along with the center of the Earth, travels through that **great orb** <note>The Earth's orbit</note> among the other **wandering stars** <note>The planets; from the Greek 'planētēs', meaning 'wanderer'</note> in an annual revolution around the Sun; and that the Sun is the center of the universe. Moreover, with the Sun remaining immobile, whatever motion appears to belong to the Sun is instead more truly attributed to the mobility of the Earth. 

The magnitude of the world is so great that, while the Earth’s distance from the Sun has a size quite evident relative to the orbs of the other wandering stars in proportion to their breadth, this distance is as nothing when compared to the sphere of the **fixed stars**. I think this is easier to concede than to allow the intellect to be distracted by an almost infinite multitude of spheres—which those who kept the Earth in the middle of the world were forced to do. Instead, the wisdom of nature is more to be followed: just as she has been most careful not to produce anything superfluous or useless, she has instead often enriched a single thing with many effects.

Though all these things are difficult and almost unbelievable—certainly contrary to the opinion of many—yet, with God’s favor, we will make them clearer than the Sun itself in the following pages, at least for those who are not ignorant of the **mathematical art**. Therefore, while the first principle remains safe—for no one will suggest one more suitable—namely, that the duration of time measures the size of the orbs, the order of the spheres follows in this manner, beginning from the highest:

The first and highest of all is the sphere of the fixed stars, containing itself and all things, and therefore immobile; it is indeed the place of the universe to which the motion and position of all other stars are compared. For as to why some think it also changes in some way: we shall assign another cause for why it appears so in our deduction of the Earth’s motion. Saturn, the first of the wandering stars, follows, completing its circuit in 30 years. After this is Jupiter, moving in a twelve-year revolution. Then Mars, which circles in two years. <meta>catchword: [of] stars,</meta>

In this arrangement, we find an admirable symmetry of the universe and a certain bond of harmony between the motion and the size of the spheres, such as cannot be found in any other way. For here the attentive observer may notice why the forward and backward movement <note>This refers to "retrograde motion," where planets appear to move backward in the sky from our perspective on Earth.</note> appears larger in **Jupiter** than in **Saturn**, and smaller than in **Mars**; and again larger in **Venus** than in **Mercury**. And why such a reversal appears more frequent in **Saturn** than in **Jupiter**, yet rarer in **Mars** and in **Venus** than in **Mercury**. Furthermore, it explains why **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**, when they are <term>visible all night</term> <note>original: "acronycti"; a Greek-derived term referring to a planet being in "opposition," meaning it is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, making it visible all night and at its closest point to us.</note>, are closer to the Earth than when they are near their disappearance and reappearance <note>Referring to when they are lost in the Sun's glare.</note>. Indeed, **Mars**, when it is visible all night, appears to equal **Jupiter** in size, distinguished only by its reddish color; yet elsewhere it is barely found among stars of the second magnitude, recognized only by those who track it with diligent observation. All these phenomena proceed from the same cause: the motion of the Earth. However, the fact that none of these movements appear in the fixed stars proves their immense height, which causes even the circle of the annual motion, or its image, to vanish from our sight. For every visible object has a certain limit of distance beyond which it is no longer seen, as is demonstrated in the science of **Optics**. That there is still a vast distance from **Saturn**, the highest of the planets, to the sphere of the fixed stars, is demonstrated by their twinkling lights. By this sign they are most especially distinguished from the planets, for it was necessary that there be a very great difference between the moving and the non-moving. So great, indeed, is this divine workshop of **God, the Best and Greatest** <note>original: "Opt. Max.", an abbreviation for "Optimus Maximus."</note>.

## Demonstration of the Triple Motion of the Earth. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
Since, therefore, so many and such great testimonies from the wandering stars agree with the mobility of the Earth, we shall now explain the motion itself in general, insofar as the appearances are demonstrated by it as a hypothesis. We must admit three distinct motions entirely. The first is what we said the Greeks call the <term>day-and-night</term> <note>original: "νυχθήμερον" (nychthēmeron); the 24-hour period of one full rotation.</note> cycle, which is the Earth's own rotation around its axis, turning from west to east. Because of this, the universe is thought to be carried in the opposite direction, describing the **equinoctial** circle, which some call the <term>equidial</term> <note>original: "æquidialem"; literally "equal-day," a synonym for the equator.</note>, imitating the meaning of the Greek

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

stars, among whom it <note>original: ἰσημέρινος (*isēmerinos*); the Greek word for 'equinoctial' or 'equator'</note> is called the **equator**. The second motion is the **annual motion of the center**, which describes the circle of the signs <note>The Zodiac</note> around the **Sun**, proceeding from west to east—that is, in the order of the signs—positioned between **Venus** and **Mars**, as we have said, along with those things that depend upon it. From this it happens that the **Sun** itself appears to pass through the zodiac with a similar motion. For example, when the center of the Earth passes through **Capricorn**, the **Sun** appears to pass through **Cancer**; when the Earth is in **Aquarius**, the **Sun** appears in **Leo**, and so on, as we have described. Regarding this circle—which passes through the middle of the signs—and its plane, one must understand that the **equinoctial circle** and the Earth's axis have a shifting inclination. For if they remained fixed and simply followed the motion of the center, no inequality of days and nights would appear. Instead, it would always be the solstice, or the winter solstice, or the equinox, or summer, or winter; or whatever the quality of the season was, it would remain exactly the same.

Therefore, a third motion follows: the **motion of declination**, also in an annual revolution, but moving in "precedence"—that is, reflecting back against the motion of the center <note>This "third motion" was Copernicus's way of explaining why the Earth's axis always points toward the same spot in the sky (the North Star), keeping the seasons consistent even as the Earth orbits the Sun.</note>. Thus, with both motions being nearly equal and moving in opposite directions, it results in the Earth's axis and the **equator** (the greatest of the parallel circles) pointing toward nearly the same part of the universe, just as if they remained immobile. In the meantime, the **Sun** is perceived to move through the tilt of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi"; literally "the sign-bearer," a common term for the zodiac belt</note> by that same motion which carries the center of the Earth; it is no different than if the Sun itself were the center of the world, provided you remember that the distance between the Sun and the Earth has already been eclipsed by our perspective on the sphere of the fixed stars. 

Since these matters are such that they demand to be placed before the eyes rather than merely spoken of, let us describe the circle **A B C D**, which represents the annual circuit of the Earth's center in the plane of the zodiac, and let **E** near its center be the **Sun**. I shall divide this circle into four parts using the intersecting diameters **A E C** and **B E D**. Let point **A** hold the beginning of **Cancer**, **B** of **Libra**, **C** of **Capricorn**, and **D** of **Aries**. Now, let us place the center of the Earth first at **A**, upon which I shall designate the Earth's **equator F G H I**, though not in the same plane, except that the diameter **G A I** is the common section of the circles—that is, of the equator and the zodiac. With the diameter **F A H** also drawn at right angles to **G A I**, let **F** be the limit of the greatest declination toward the South, and **H** toward the North. With these things thus proposed, those on Earth will see the **Sun** near the center **E** under **Capricorn**, making the winter solstice, at which time the maximum...

Alternatively: Let there likewise be a diameter AEC in the underlying plane, which is also the common section of the circle erected perpendicular to that plane. Or to put it more correctly: that motion around the axis, from the perspective of AE, traces a conical surface <term>conical surface|a cone-shaped path traced by the Earth's axis due to its fixed tilt during the annual orbit</term>, having its apex at the center of the Earth, and its base a circle parallel to the **equator**; in the opposite sign, everything happens in an equal manner, but reversed. It is therefore clear how these two motions—that of the center [the orbit] and that of the inclination [the axial tilt]—interacting with each other, force the Earth's axis to remain in the same steady alignment <note>original: "libramento"</note> and in a consistent position, making everything appear as if these were motions of the **Sun**. However, we were saying that the annual revolutions of the center and of the declination are nearly equal; for if they were exactly equal, the **equinox** and **solstice** points, as well as the entire obliquity of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi"</note> under the sphere of the fixed stars, would not change at all. ...this difference, growing larger only with time, has become manifest: from the time of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is challenging.</note> down to our own, it amounts to nearly 21 degrees, by which the equinoxes now precede. For this reason, some believed that the sphere of the fixed stars also moves, and therefore they favored a superior **ninth sphere**. When this was not enough, more recent thinkers added a **tenth**; and yet they have not reached the goal, which we hope to attain through the **motion of the earth**. We shall use this as a principle and hypothesis in the demonstrations of other matters.

## On the magnitude of straight lines in a circle. Chapter 12.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'Q' containing a circular portrait of a bearded man in scholarly attire, surrounded by decorative floral patterns.</image-desc> Since the proofs which we shall use in almost the entire work deal with straight lines and arcs, and with plane and spherical <note>original: "conuexis" - literally 'convex' or 'curved', referring here to triangles mapped onto the surface of a sphere</note> triangles, concerning which many things are already clear from **Euclid's Elements**, they nevertheless do not contain what is most sought here: how sides can be obtained from angles, and angles from sides. Since an angle does not measure a subtending straight line <note>A "subtending line" is a chord—a straight line connecting two points on a curve.</note>—just as the line does not measure the angle—but rather the arc does. For this reason, a method was discovered by which the lines subtending any arc may be known; with their aid, we can obtain the arc corresponding to an angle and, conversely, the straight line which subtends the angle through the arc. Therefore, it seems appropriate to treat these lines. Also regarding the sides and angles of both plane and spherical triangles, which **Ptolemy** handed down separately and through examples, so that they may be settled here once and for all, and thereafter what we are about to present may become clearer. 

By the common consensus of mathematicians, we divide the circle into 360 parts. The ancients assigned 120 parts to the diameter. But later writers, to avoid the entanglement of fractions <note>original: "scrupulorum" - literally 'scruples', used here to mean small, difficult fractional units</note> in the multiplication and division of numbers concerning these lines—which are for the most part <term>incommensurable</term> <note>Lines that cannot be expressed as a simple ratio of whole numbers, such as the relationship between a diameter and a circumference.</note> in length, and often even in power—established a rational diameter, some at 1,200,000, others at 2,000,000, others differently, from the time when Indian numerical figures <note>Referring to the arrival of "Arabic" numerals in Europe, which made complex calculations much easier than Roman numerals.</note> came into use. This number [exceeds] any other, whether Greek or Latin, with a certain unique...

### Theorem I.

**G**iven the diameter of a circle, the sides of the triangle, square, hexagon, pentagon, and decagon inscribed in that same circle are also given. Since the line from the center <note>The radius.</note>, being half the diameter, is equal to the side of the hexagon. Furthermore, the square of the side of the triangle is three times, and the square of the side of the square <term>tetragon</term> <note>From the Greek 'tetragonon', meaning a four-sided figure or square.</note> is two times, the square of the side of the hexagon, as has been demonstrated in **Euclid’s Elements**. Therefore, the side of the hexagon is given in length as 100,000 parts; the square as 141,422 parts; and the triangle as 173,205 parts. Now, let the side of the hexagon be <term>AB</term>, which, according to the 11th [proposition] of the second book, or the 30th of the sixth book of Euclid, is cut in "extreme and mean ratio" <note>This refers to the Golden Ratio, a mathematical proportion where the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</note> at point <term>C</term>, and let the larger segment be <term>CB</term>, to which an equal length

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment marked with five points from left to right: A, C, E, B, and D. Point C and E are positioned closely together in the left half of the segment AB.</image-desc>

<term>BD</term> is added. Therefore, the whole line <term>ABD</term> will also be cut in extreme and mean ratio, and the added smaller segment [BD] will be the side of a decagon inscribed in a circle in which <term>AB</term> was the side of the hexagon. This is manifest from the 5th and 9th [propositions] of Euclid’s 13th book. Now, <term>BD</term> itself will be given in this way: let <term>AB</term> be bisected <note>Cut exactly in half.</note> at <term>E</term>. It is clear from the 3rd [proposition] of the same book of Euclid that the square of <term>EBD</term> is five times the square of <term>EB</term>. But <term>EB</term> is given in length as 50,000 parts; from this, its five-fold square is given, and <term>EBD</term> itself is 111,803 parts in length. If the 50,000 parts of <term>EB</term> are subtracted from this, there remains <term>BD</term> at 61,803 parts, the sought-after side of the decagon. The side of the pentagon, the square of which is equal to the squares of the sides of the hexagon and decagon combined, is given as 117,557 parts. Thus, given the diameter of a circle, the sides of the triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and decagon inscribable in that same circle are given, which was to be demonstrated.

->Theorem Second.<-

If a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle, the rectangle contained by the diagonals is equal to those rectangles contained by the opposite sides. For let the quadrilateral ABCD be inscribed in a circle; I say that the [product] contained by the diagonals AC and DB is equal to the sum of those contained by AB with CD, and by AD with BC. proportional sides; just as BC is to BD, so is EC to AD, and the [rectangle] produced by EC and BD is equal to that produced by BC and AD. Again, AB is to BD as AE is to CD, and the [rectangle] produced by AB and CD is equal to that produced by AE and BD. But it has already been declared that the product of AD and BC is as much as the product of BD and EC. # THE WORKS OF NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

On the diameter **AD**, let **AB** and **AC** be the chords of the given unequal arcs. Since we wish to find the chord **BC**, the chords of the remaining arcs of the semicircle, **BD** and **CD**, are provided from the calculations mentioned above. These form the quadrilateral **ABCD** within the semicircle.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a semicircle with diameter AD. Inscribed within the semicircle is a quadrilateral ABCD, with diagonals AC and BD drawn.</image-desc>

The diagonals of this quadrilateral, **AC** and **BD**, are known, along with three of its sides, **AB**, **AD**, and **CD**. In such a figure, as has already been demonstrated, the product of the diagonals **AC** and **BD** is equal to the sum of the products of the opposite sides: **AB** times **CD**, and **AD** times **BC**. Therefore, if the product of **AB** and **CD** is subtracted from the product of **AC** and **BD**, the remainder will be the product of **AD** and **BC**. Thus, by using the diameter **AD** as a divisor, the value of the sought-after chord **BC** is calculated as accurately as possible. Furthermore, since the lengths of the sides of the pentagon and hexagon are known from the previous sections, this method allows us to find the chord subtending 12 degrees (the difference between the arc of a pentagon, 72°, and a hexagon, 60°). This chord is found to be 20,905 parts <note>Copernicus uses a standard radius or diameter of 100,000 or 200,000 units to avoid working with fractions, a precursor to decimal trigonometry.</note>.

### Theorem Fourth.

**G**iven a chord subtending any arc, the chord subtending half of that arc is also given. Let us describe a circle **ABC** with diameter **AC**, and let **BC** be the arc of a known chord. From the center **E**, let the line **EF** intersect **BC** at right angles; this line, 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a full circle with center E and diameter AC. A chord BC is shown, which is bisected at a right angle at point F by a radius originating from center E and extending to point D on the circumference. Chords AB and BD are drawn. A line extends from D through center E to point G on the opposite side of the circle, forming diameter DG, and chord BG is also drawn.</image-desc>

according to the third proposition of Euclid's third book <note>original: "tertiam tertij Euclidis". This refers to the theorem stating that a radius perpendicular to a chord bisects that chord.</note>, will bisect the chord **BC** at point **F**, and when extended, will bisect the arc at point **D**. Let chords **AB** and **BD** also be drawn. Since the triangles **ABC** and **EFC** are both right-angled and share the angle **ECF**, they are similar triangles. Therefore, just as **CF** is half of **BC**, **EF** is half of **AB**. Since **AB** (which subtends the rest of the semicircle) is already known, **EF** is also known, as is the remaining segment **DF** (the difference between the radius and **EF**). Let the diameter be completed as **DEG**, and let **BG** be joined. In the triangle **BDG**, a perpendicular line **BF** drops from the right angle **B** to the base. Consequently, the product of **GD** and **DF** is equal to the square of **BD** <note>This uses the geometric mean theorem: in a right triangle, the altitude to the hypotenuse squared equals the product of the two segments of the hypotenuse.</note>. Thus, the length of **BD** is found, which subtends half of the arc **BDC**. Since we already determined the chord for 12 degrees, we now find the chord for 6 degrees to be 10,467 parts; for 3 degrees, 5,235 parts; for one and a half degrees, 2,618 parts; and for three-quarters of a degree <term>dodrans<gloss>three-quarters</gloss></term>, 1,309 parts.

## Fifth Theorem.

Furthermore, when the chords of two arcs have been given, the chord that subtends the arc composed of the sum of those two is also given. Let the given chords in a circle be **AB** and **BC**; I say that the chord of the whole arc **ABC** is also given. For, by drawing the diameters <term>AFD</term> and <term>BFE</term> <note>Copernicus uses the term "dimetientibus" for diameters</note>, let the straight lines **BD** and **CE** also be subtended. These are provided from the preceding theorems because **AB** and **BC** are given; and **DE** is equal to **AB**. By connecting **CD**, a quadrilateral **BCDE** is formed, whose diagonals **BD** and **CE**, along with three sides **BC**, **DE**, and **BE**, are known. The remaining side **CD** will also be given by the Second Theorem <note>original: "per secundum Theorema"; this refers to Ptolemy's Theorem regarding the products of the diagonals and sides of an inscribed quadrilateral</note>. Consequently, **CA** is given as the chord subtending the remainder of the semicircle, and it is the chord of the whole arc **ABC**, which was sought.

Furthermore, since we have so far found the straight lines that subtend three degrees, one and a half degrees, and three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem," meaning 3/4</note> of a degree, anyone could construct a table <term>canon</term> with the most exact logic using these intervals. However, if one wishes to proceed degree by degree, and join one to another, either by halves or by some other method, they might rightly doubt the chords of those parts. This is because the geometric methods <note>original: "graphicæ rationes"</note> for demonstrating them are lacking to us. Yet nothing prevents us from achieving this by another method, without an error noticeable to the senses and without any discrepancy in the assumed numbers. This is exactly what Ptolemy sought regarding the chords of one degree and a half degree, first giving us a warning.

## Sixth Theorem.

The ratio of arcs is greater than the ratio of the straight chords of the greater arc to the smaller. Let there be two unequal arcs joined in a circle, **AB** and **BC**, and let **BC** be the greater. I say that the ratio of arc **BC** to **AB** is greater than the ratio of the chords **BC** to **AB**. These chords form angle **B**, which is divided into two equal parts <note>bisected</note> by the line **BD**. Let **AC** be joined, intersecting **BD** at point **E**. Similarly join **AD** and **CD**, which are equal because they are subtended by equal arcs. Therefore, since in triangle **ABC** the line that bisects the angle also cuts **AC**...

<meta>This page continues the proof of Theorem 6, which establishes a fundamental geometric inequality: that the ratio of two arcs in a circle is greater than the ratio of their corresponding chords. This theorem is crucial for Copernicus to justify the interpolation of values in his mathematical tables, allowing him to calculate the chords of very small angles like one degree or half a degree.</meta>

# NICOLAI COPERNICI
<meta>catchword: AB cir (original catchword referring to the arc AB)</meta>

in **B**, the segments of the base will be **BC** to **AB**, as **CB** to **AB**, and since **BC** is greater than **AB**, **BC** is also greater than **BA**. Let **DF** be drawn perpendicular to **AC**, which will bisect **AC** at point **F**, a point which must necessarily be found within the larger segment **BC**. And since

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram featuring a circle with points A, B, C, and D on its circumference. D is positioned at the bottom, and B at the top. AC is a horizontal chord with points E and F marked on it. Lines connect D to points A, B, C, E, and F. DF is perpendicular to AC. A partial arc with its center at D and radius DB is drawn, intersecting line AD at point H and the extension of line DF at point I.</image-desc>

in every triangle, the larger angle is subtended by the larger side, in triangle **DBF**, the side **DB** is greater than **DF**, and furthermore **AD** is greater than **DE**. For this reason, with center **D** and radius **DB**, let an arc be described; it will intersect **AD** and pass through **DF**. Let it intersect **AD** at **H**, and let it be extended into the straight line **DFI**. Since, therefore, the sector **DBI** is greater than triangle **BDF**, while triangle **DEA** is greater than sector **DEH**, the triangle **DEF** will have a smaller ratio to triangle **DEA** than sector **DBI** has to sector **DEH**. But sectors are proportional to their arcs or the angles at the center, while triangles sharing the same vertex are proportional to their bases. Therefore, there is a greater ratio of the angles **BDF** to **ADB** than of the bases **BF** to **AE**. Thus, by addition <note>original: "coniunctim," referring to the Euclidean method of combining ratios</note>, the angle **FDA** has a greater ratio to **ADB** than **AF** has to **AE**. In the same way, the ratio of **CDA** to **ADE** is greater than that of **AC** to **AE**. And by subtraction <note>original: "diuisim"</note>, the ratio of **CDB** to **EDA** is also greater than **CB** to **EA**. However, the angles **CDB** and **EDA** are in the same ratio as the arcs **CB** and **AB**. Furthermore, the ratio of the base **CB** to **AE** is as the chord **CB** is to the chord **AB**. Therefore, the ratio of the arc **CB** to the arc **AB** is greater than the ratio of the chord **BC** to the chord **AB**, which was to be demonstrated.

### Problem.

But since an arc is always greater than its subtending straight line <note>the chord</note>, given that a straight line is the shortest distance between two points, this inequality nevertheless tends toward equality as we move from larger to smaller sections of the circle, so that finally, at the point of contact with the circle <note>the limit of the ratio</note>, the straight line and the curved arc exit together. It is necessary, therefore, that before reaching that point, they should differ from one another by no discernible amount. For example, let arc **AB** be 3 degrees and arc **AC** be 1.5 degrees <note>original: "I. S." where S stands for 'semis,' meaning one half</note>. The chord subtending **AB** has been shown to be 5235 parts where the diameter is 200,000, and chord **AC** is 2618 of those same parts. And since the arc is double the other...

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book I.

the <term>arc</term><note>Latin: *circumferentia*. Copernicus uses this to mean the curved length along the circle's edge.</note> **AB** to **AC**, however, the <term>chord</term><note>Latin: *subtensa*, literally "stretched under." A straight line connecting two points on a curve.</note> **AB** is less than double the chord **AC**, which adds only a single unit to the 2617. Since, therefore, we see that we have reached a point where the difference between the straight and the curved line completely escapes the senses, as if they had become a single line, we do not hesitate to apply the same ratio of 1309 for that three-quarters of a degree to the full degree and the remaining parts. Thus, by adding a quarter to the three parts, we establish one degree at 1745 units, a half-degree at 872½ units, and a <term>third</term><note>Latin: *trientis*, a Roman unit for one-third.</note> of a part at approximately 582 units.

By this shortcut, we can compress into a single quadrant what would otherwise need to be spread across a semicircle. This is especially useful because these halves are used more frequently in demonstrations and calculations than the whole chords. We have presented the table increased by <term>sixths</term><note>Latin: *sextantes*, meaning intervals of 10 minutes (since 1/6 of a 60-minute degree is 10 minutes).</note> of a degree, having three columns. In the first are the degrees (or parts of the circumference) and their sixths. The second contains the numerical value of the half-line subtending double the arc. The third holds the difference between these numbers occurring at each degree, from which one may proportionally add what fits the individual <term>minutes</term><note>Latin: *scrupulis*, literally "small stones," used here for the 60th-parts of a degree.</note> of the degrees.

NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

## On the sides and angles of plane rectilinear triangles. Chapter XIII.

### I.

<image-desc>A circular diagram with an inscribed triangle. The vertices are labeled A, B, and C. Point A is on the left, B is at the top, and C is on the right of the circle.</image-desc>

If the angles of a triangle are given, the sides are given. Let there be, I say, a triangle ABC, around which a circle is circumscribed according to the fifth problem of the fourth book of <term>Euclid<note>Copernicus refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, a foundational Greek mathematical text. Book IV, Proposition 5 describes how to draw a circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle.</note></term>. Therefore, the <term>arcs<note>original: "circumferentiæ"</note></term> AB, BC, and CA will be given in the manner where 360 parts are equal to two right angles <note>In modern terms, the sum of the angles in a triangle is 180 degrees, which corresponds to the arc of a semicircle.</note>. When the arcs are given, the sides of the triangle inscribed in the circle are also given as <term>chords<note>original: "subtensæ," meaning the straight line "stretched under" an arc.</note></term> through the published <term>Table<note>original: "Canonem." This refers to the Table of Chords/Sines Copernicus calculated in the previous sections.</note></term>, in those parts where the <term>diameter<note>original: "dimetiens"</note></term> is assumed to be 200,000.

### II.

If, however, two sides of the triangle are given along with one of the angles, the remaining side and the remaining angles will be known. For either the given sides are equal, or they are unequal. Moreover, the given angle is either right, acute, or obtuse. Furthermore, the given sides either enclose the given angle, or they do not enclose it.

<image-desc>A diagram of an acute triangle with vertex A at the top, B at the bottom left, and C at the bottom right.</image-desc>

Let there be first, therefore, in triangle ABC, two given equal sides, AB and AC, which enclose the given angle A. Therefore, the remaining angles at the base BC, since they are equal, are also given as half of the remainder of angle A subtracted from two right angles <note>Since the sum of angles is 180°, if you know angle A, the other two angles in an isosceles triangle are (180 - A) / 2.</note>. And if an angle around the base was the one originally given, its peer is immediately given, and from these, the remainder of the two right angles is found. But when the angles of the triangle are given, the sides are given; and the base BC itself is given from the Table in parts where AB or AC (as if from a center) would be 100,000 parts, or the diameter 200,000 parts.

### III.

<image-desc>A diagram of a right-angled triangle with vertex A at the top-left (the right angle), B at the bottom-left, and C at the bottom-right.</image-desc>

But if the angle BAC is a right angle enclosed by the given sides, the same result will follow. For it is most clear that the <term>squares<note>original: "quadrata"</note></term> produced from AB and AC are equal to the square of the side

## IIII.

Now let the acute angle ABC be given, along with the given sides AB and BC which enclose it. From point A, let a perpendicular line AD descend to the base BC (extended if necessary, depending on whether it falls inside or outside the triangle). By this perpendicular, two right-angled triangles, ABD and ADC, are distinguished. Since the angles in ABD are given—for D is a right angle and B is given by <term>hypothesis<note>In geometry, the "hypothesis" refers to the initial conditions or known values we start with.</note></term>—therefore, AD and BD are given as the chords subtending angles A and B in those parts where AB (the diameter of the circle) is 200,000 according to the Table. And by the same ratio by which the length of AB was given, AD and BD are similarly given; CD is also given, by which BC and BD differ from each other. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle ADC, with the sides AD and CD being given, the sought-after side AC and the angle ACD are given through the preceding demonstration.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing triangle ABC with a perpendicular line AD dropped from vertex A to the base BC. Point D lies on the segment BC. Vertex A is at the apex, B at the bottom left, and C at the bottom right.</image-desc>

## V.

It will happen no differently if the angle B were obtuse. From point A, a perpendicular line AD is drawn to the straight line BC (extended), which creates a triangle ABD of known angles. For the exterior angle ABD is given from [the known] ABC, and D is a right angle; therefore BD and AD are given in those parts where AB would be 200,000. And since AB and BC have a given ratio to each other, AB is therefore given in the same parts as BD and the whole line CBD. Therefore, in the right-angled triangle ADC, since two sides AD and CD are given, the sought-after side AC is also given, along with the angle BAC and the remaining angle ACB, which was sought.

Now let either of the two given sides be the one subtending the given angle...

### VII.

When all the sides of a triangle are given, the angles are also given. Regarding an <term>equilateral triangle<note>original: "Isopleuro." From the Greek words for "equal sides."</note></term>, it is too well known to need stating that each of its angles is one-third of two right angles <note>In modern terms, 180 degrees divided by 3, which is 60 degrees.</note>. In <term>isosceles triangles<note>triangles with two equal sides</note></term> it is also clear. For the ratio of the equal sides to the third side is as the ratio of the radius <note>original: "dimidia diametri," literally "half of the diameter."</note> to the chord subtending the arc. By this, the angle enclosed by the equal sides is found from the Table (where 360 degrees <note>original: "partium CCCLX"</note> around the center are equal to four right angles); then the remaining angles at the base are also given as half of the remainder of two right angles. 

It remains now to demonstrate this in <term>scalene triangles<note>triangles where all three sides have different lengths</note></term>, which we shall similarly divide into right-angled triangles. Let there be, therefore, a scalene triangle of given sides <term>ABC</term>, and from the vertex to the side that is longest—let us say <term>BC</term>—let the perpendicular line <term>AD</term> descend. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a scalene triangle ABC. Vertex A is at the top, B at the bottom left, and C at the bottom right. A perpendicular line (altitude) is dropped from vertex A to a point D on the base line BC, creating two right-angled triangles, ABD and ADC.</image-desc>

Now, the thirteenth proposition of the second book of <term>Euclid<note>Euclid of Alexandria, the Greek mathematician whose "Elements" served as the primary textbook for geometry for 2,000 years.</note></term> reminds us that the side <term>AB</term>, which subtends an acute angle, is less in <term>power<note>original: "potestate." In classical geometry, the "power" of a line refers to the area of the square built upon it. This is a precursor to the Law of Cosines.</note></term> than the other two sides by twice the rectangle contained under <term>BC</term> and <term>CD</term>. For angle <term>C</term> must be acute; otherwise, side <term>AB</term> would happen to be the longest side, contrary to our hypothesis, as may be observed from Euclid’s seventeenth proposition of the first book and the two following it. Therefore, <term>BD</term> and <term>DC</term> are given, and there will be <term>right-angled triangles<note>original: "orthogonia"</note></term> <term>ABD</term> and <term>ADC</term> with given sides and angles—as has already been repeated often—by which the angles of the sought triangle <term>ABC</term> are also established.

**Alternatively.**

The same thing might perhaps be shown more conveniently by the penultimate proposition of Euclid’s third book: if we describe a circle using the shorter side <term>BC</term> as the radius (with <term>C</term> as the center), which will cut both remaining sides, or at least one of them. Let it cut both: <term>AB</term> at point <term>E</term>, and <term>AC</term> at point <term>D</term>, with the line <term>ADC</term> extended to point <term>F</term> to complete the diameter <term>DEF</term>. With these things thus constructed, it is clear from that Euclidean rule: Since the rectangle under <term>FAD</term> is equal to...

And let these remarks on <term>rectilinear triangles<note>triangles made of straight lines on a flat plane</note></term> suffice, in which a great part of <term>geodesy<note>original: "Geodesiæ," the science of measuring land and the Earth's surface</note></term> consists. Now let us turn to spherical triangles.

### On Spherical Triangles. Chapter 14.

In this context, we define a <term>convex triangle<note>a spherical triangle</note></term> as that which is contained by the arcs of three <term>great circles<note>original: "maximorum circulorum," circles that share the same center and diameter as the sphere itself</note></term> on the surface of a sphere. The difference and magnitude of the angles, however, are determined by the arc of a great circle which is described using the point of intersection as its pole—specifically, that arc which is intercepted by the <term>quadrants<note>quarter-circles of 90 degrees</note></term> of the circles forming the angle. For as the arc thus intercepted is to the entire circumference, so is the angle of the intersection to four right angles (which we have said contain 360 equal parts).

<meta>This page transitions from plane geometry to the foundations of spherical trigonometry. ->NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

# I.

If there are three arcs of <term>great circles<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, such as the equator or meridians on Earth.</note></term> of a sphere, any two of which added together are longer than the third, it is evident that a spherical triangle can be formed from them. For what is proposed here regarding arcs, Euclid demonstrates in the 24th proposition of his eleventh book regarding angles; since the ratio of angles and arcs is the same, and great circles are those which pass through the center of the sphere, it is clear that those three sectors of the circles, to which the arcs belong, form a <term>solid angle<note>An angle formed by three or more planes meeting at a single point (the center of the sphere).</note></term> at the center of the sphere. Therefore, what was proposed is manifest.

# II.

Any arc of a triangle must be less than a <term>semicircle<note>original: "hemicyclio"</note></term>. For a semicircle forms no angle at the center, but falls into a straight line. But the remaining two angles, to which the arcs belong, cannot enclose a solid at the center, and consequently cannot form a spherical triangle. And I judge this to have been the reason why <term>Ptolemy<note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Roman astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is revising.</note></term>, in his explanation of this kind of triangle—especially regarding the figure of the spherical sector—insists that the chosen arcs should not be greater than a semicircle.

# III.

In spherical triangles having a right angle, the <term>chord<note>Latin: "subtendens," literally "stretching under." In this period, mathematicians used the lengths of chords of double arcs, which is mathematically equivalent to the modern sine function.</note></term> of double the side opposite the right angle is to the chord of double one of the sides enclosing the right angle, as the diameter of the sphere is to the chord of double the angle enclosed by the remaining side and the first side on a great circle of the sphere.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating spherical trigonometry. It depicts a segment of a sphere with its center at point F. A spherical triangle ABC is shown on the surface, with various lines and planes originating from the center F and passing through the vertices and arcs. Additional points labeled D, E, G, H, I, K represent auxiliary constructions for the geometric proof.</image-desc>

For let there be a spherical triangle *ABC*, in which angle *C* is a right angle. I say that the chord of double *AB* is to the chord of double *BC*, as the diameter of the sphere is to the chord which, on a great circle, subtends double the angle *BAC*. With *A* as the <term>pole<note>The point on the sphere 90 degrees away from every point on the circle being described.</note></term>, let the arc of a great circle *DE* be described, and let the quadrants of the circles *ABD* and *ACE* be completed. From the center of the sphere *F*, let the common sections of the circles be drawn: *FA* for circles *ABD* and *ACE*, [and for...]

...while [the line] of A C B and D E is F E, and F D is the [line] of A B D and D E. Furthermore, [let] F G [be the line] of the circles A C and B C. Then, let B G be drawn at right angles to F A, B I to F C, and D K to F E; and let G I be joined.
Since, therefore, if a circle intersects another circle through its poles, it intersects it at right angles, the angle comprised under A E D will be a right angle; and A C B is also a right angle by hypothesis; and each plane E D F and B C F is perpendicular to the plane A E F. Therefore, if a straight line were raised at right angles from the point in the common segment F K E in the underlying plane, it will also comprise a right angle with K D, according to the definition of mutually perpendicular planes. For which reason, K D is also perpendicular to A E F, according to the <term>fourth proposition of Euclid’s eleventh book<note>Euclid's *Elements*, Book XI, Proposition 4 states that if a straight line is set up at right angles to two intersecting straight lines at their point of intersection, it will be at right angles to the plane containing them.</note></term>. By the same reasoning, B I is erected perpendicular to the same plane; and therefore D K and B I are parallel to each other according to the sixth proposition of the same book. Moreover, G B is also [perpendicular] to F D, because the angles F G B and G F D are right angles; thus, by the tenth proposition of Euclid’s eleventh book, angle F D K will be equal to G B I. But the angle at F K D is a right angle, as is G I B, by the definition of an erected line. Therefore, the sides of similar triangles are proportional: as D F is to B G, so D K is to B I.
But B I is <term>half the chord of double the arc C B<note>Copernicus uses the "chord of the double arc" (subtendens duplum), which is mathematically equivalent to the modern sine function: sin(θ) = 1/2 chord(2θ).</note></term>, since it is at a right angle to the line from the center F. By the same reasoning, B G is half the chord of double the side B A, and D K is half the chord of double D E (or of the double angle A), and D F is the half-diameter (radius) of the sphere. It is clear, therefore, that the chord of double arc A B is to the chord of double arc B C as the diameter is to the chord of double angle A (or the intercepted arc D E), which was the appropriate thing to demonstrate.

But three are already given—D E, A B, and E B (from the quadrant of the circle)—therefore, the fourth, the chord of twice C B, is given, and the side C B itself is found. And since the chords of the doubles of C B are to C A as those of B F are to E F (because the ratios of both are as the diameter of the sphere to the chord of twice the angle C B A), and because things which have the same ratio to a single thing are the same as each other: with three now given (B F, E F, and C B), the fourth, C A, is given, which is the third side of the triangle A B C.

Again, by permutation, the chord of twice C A will have the same ratio to the chord of twice C B as the chord of twice angle A B C has to the diameter; from this, side C B is given, and the remaining arcs A D and B E are found from the quadrants of the circles. Therefore, arc B F is given, as is the remaining side A B. By similar reasoning as in the preceding parts, from the chords of the doubles of B C, A B, and F B E, the chord of twice D E is given, which is the remaining angle C. Furthermore, if B C were taken as given, A C will again be given as before, and the remaining A D and B E, through which the chords...

### XI.

Every triangle, of which two sides have been given along with any angle, results in the remaining angles and sides being known. Therefore, by the fourth theorem of this book, the triangle **adf** will have its angles and sides known.

### XII.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a spherical triangle on a segment of a globe. Points are labeled A, B, C, D, E, and F, with arcs connecting them to illustrate trigonometric properties and relationships between angles and sides on a curved surface.</image-desc>

Furthermore, if two angles are given in any way along with any side, the same results follow. Maintaining the construction of the previous figure, let the angles **ACB** and **BAC** of triangle **ABC** be given, along with side **AC**, which lies between both angles. Moreover, if either of the given angles had been a right angle, all other parts could be reached by reasoning through the preceding fourth theorem. Therefore, **AD** will be the remainder of a <term>quadrant<note>A quadrant is one-quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees.</note></term> subtracted from angle **CAD**, and the angle under **BAD** will be the residue of angle **BAC** out of two right angles, while angle **D** is a right angle. And through the given angle, the arc **DE** is given, as is the remainder **EF**, and angle **BEF** is a right angle, while angle **F** is common to both triangles. Likewise, through the fourth theorem, **BE** and **BF** are given, by which the other sought-after sides **AB** and **BC** will be established. 

Furthermore, if one of the given angles was opposite to the given side—for example, if angle **ABC** is given instead of **ACB**, while the others remain—it will be established by the same demonstration that the entire triangle **ADF** is given in its angles and sides, and similarly the particular triangle **BEF**. This is because, on account of angle **F** being common to both, and **EBF** (which is at the vertex) being given, and **E** being a right angle, it was demonstrated in the preceding sections that all its sides are also given; from these, finally, the same things follow as we have said. For all these things are always linked by a mutual and perpetual connection, as befits the form of a globe.

as it happens that such lines become nearer to or further from the center through the 15th proposition of Euclid's third book. Then, let **FG** be drawn parallel to **BE**, which cuts **BD** (the common section of the circular planes) at point **G**, and let **CG** be connected. It is clear then that angle **EFG** is a right angle, namely equal to **AEB**; and **EFC** is also a right angle, since **CF** is the half-chord of double **AC**. Therefore, **CFG** will be the angle of the section of circles **AB** and **AC**, which we therefore also obtain. For **DF** is to **FG** as **DE** is to **EB**, since triangles **DFG** and **DEB** are similar. Therefore, **FG** is given in the same units in which **FC** is also given. But in the same ratio is also **DG** to **DB**; thus **DG** will also be given in the units in which **DC** is 100,000 <note>Copernicus uses a standard radius of 100,000 for his calculations, providing five decimal places of precision in modern terms.</note>. Furthermore, the angle **GDC** is given by the arc **BC**. Therefore, through the second proposition of plane triangles, side **GC** is given in the same units as the other sides of the plane triangle **GFC**. Therefore, by the final proposition of plane triangles, we will have angle **GFC**, which is the sought-after spherical angle **BAC**, and then we will perceive the remaining angles through the 11th theorem of spherical triangles.

[If the ratio] was given, the circumferences of the segments themselves will also be given.

For let circumference **ABC** be given about center **D**, which is cut in any way at point **B**, provided however that the segments are smaller than a semicircle. Let the ratio of the <term>half-chord of double arc<note>original: *dimidiæ sub duplo*; Copernicus is using the chord-based system that preceded modern trigonometry. This phrase refers to what we now call the sine of the angle.</note></term> **AB** to the half-chord of double **BC** be given in length in some way; I say that circumferences **AB** and **BC** are also given. For let the straight line **AC** be subtended <note>A "subtended" line is a straight chord connecting two points on a curve.</note>, which the diameter cuts at point **E**. From the endpoints **A** and **C**, let perpendiculars fall to that diameter, which are **AF** and **CG**; these must be the half-chords of double **AB** and **BC**. Therefore, in the right-angled triangles **AEF** and **CEG**, the angles at vertex **E** are equal, and because of this, the triangles themselves are equiangular and similar; they have proportional sides corresponding to the equal angles. As **AF** is to **CG**, so **AE** is to **EC**. <note>The OCR reads "AB ad BC," but the geometric logic of the similar triangles AEF and CEG requires the segments of the chord, AE and EC.</note> Therefore, by whatever numbers **AF** or **GC** were given, we will have **AE** and **EC** in those same numbers, and from these the whole **AC** will be given in the same units. 

But the chord subtending circumference **ABC** itself is given in the parts in which the radius **DEB** is given; in these same parts, the half **AK** of **AC**, and the remainder **EK**, are also given. Let **DA** and **DK** be joined; these will also be given in the same parts as **DB**, as the half-chord subtending the remaining segment of **ABC** from the semicircle, contained under angle **DAK**. Therefore, angle **ADK** is given, which contains half the circumference of **ABC**. But with two sides of triangle **EDK** given, and the angle **EKD** being a right angle, [angle] **EDK** will also be given; hence the whole angle **EDA**, which contains circumference **AB**, will be known. By this, the remaining circumference **CB** will also be established, the demonstration of which was sought.

**When all the angles of a triangle are given, even if none is a right angle, all the sides are given.**

# NICOLAUS COPER-
## NICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK TWO.

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial 'C' depicting a scholar in robes standing in a study and pointing towards an armillary sphere or celestial globe.</image-desc>

Since in the preceding book we have summarized the three motions of the Earth, by which we promised to demonstrate all the appearances of the stars <note>In Renaissance Latin, *stella* or *syderum* often refers generally to all celestial bodies, including planets and the Sun.</note>, we shall henceforth do this by examining each part individually and investigating them to the best of our ability. We shall begin, moreover, with the most well-known revolution of all: the cycle of day and night. This we said is called a <term>nychthemeron<note>original: νυχθήμερον; a Greek term for a full 24-hour period of one night and one day.</note></term> by the Greeks. We have taken this period to be most especially and directly attributed to the terrestrial globe, because from this unit of time the months, years, and other time-periods of many names arise, just as numbers arise from the number one. 

Therefore, regarding the inequality of days and nights, the rising and setting of the Sun, the parts of the <term>zodiac<note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, marking the path of the Sun and planets.</note></term> and its signs, and other such things that follow from this revolution, we shall say a few things. We do this especially because many others have written quite abundantly about these matters; their writings, however, support and agree with our own findings. It makes no difference if, where they demonstrate something by assuming a stationary Earth and a spinning universe, we—looking at it from the opposite perspective—arrive at the same goal. This is because in matters which are relative to one another, it happens that they mutually agree with each other. Nevertheless, we shall omit nothing that is necessary. 

But let no one be surprised if we still speak simply of the "rising" and "setting" of the Sun and stars, and similar things. Let them know that we are speaking in the accustomed manner, which can be understood by everyone, while always bearing in mind that:

> -> As we are carried by the Earth, the Sun and Moon pass by us, <-
> -> And the stars’ turns return and then recede. <note>Copernicus is here paraphrasing the poet Virgil (*Aeneid* III, 72: "We are carried out from the port, and the lands and cities recede"), adapting the classical verse to describe the Earth moving through space.</note> <-

the circle of signs <note>The zodiac.</note>, under which the center of the Earth itself travels in its annual revolution. But since the <term>zodiac<note>The belt of the heavens extending approximately 8 degrees on either side of the ecliptic, the Sun's apparent path.</note></term> is oblique <note>Tilted.</note> to the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>, according to the degree of the Earth's axial tilt relative to it, the Earth describes two circles through its daily revolution that touch each other on both sides. These are the extreme limits of its tilt, which are called the **Tropics**. For the Sun appears to make its *tropas* <note>original: "tropas"; from the Greek *tropos*, meaning 'a turn'.</note>—that is, its turnings—at these points, specifically at the winter and summer points. Hence, they have become accustomed to calling the northern one the **Solstitial Tropic** <note>The Tropic of Cancer.</note> and the other toward the south the **Brumal Tropic** <note>The Tropic of Capricorn; "Brumal" refers to the winter solstice.</note>, just as was explained above in the summary account of the Earth's revolutions.

Next follows the circle called the **Horizon**, which the Latins call the *Finitor* <note>Literally "the finisher" or "the limiter".</note>; for it defines for us the visible part of the world from the part that is hidden. On this circle, all things that set appear to rise again. It has its center on the surface of the Earth and its pole at our zenith <note>The point directly overhead.</note>. But since the Earth is incomparable to the immensity of the heavens—especially because even this whole space between the Sun and the Moon, according to our hypothesis, cannot be compared to the magnitude of the heavens—the circle of the horizon appears to bisect the heavens into two equal parts as if through the center of the universe, as we demonstrated from the beginning. 

However far the horizon is tilted relative to the equinoctial, it also touches two parallel circles on either side: a northern one consisting of those stars always visible, and a southern one of those always hidden. These are named **Arctic** and **Antarctic** by <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose work on the "Sphere" was a standard astronomical textbook in the Renaissance.</note> Proclus and nearly all the Greeks. These circles become larger or smaller according to the degree of the horizon's tilt or the elevation of the celestial pole.

There remains the **Meridian**, which passes through the poles of the horizon and also through the poles of the equinoctial circle, and is therefore perpendicular to both circles. When the Sun reaches this circle, it marks midday and midnight. But these two circles having their center on the surface of the Earth—I mean the Horizon and the Meridian—entirely follow the motion of the Earth and our own sight. For wherever the eye is, it assumes for itself the center of a sphere of all things visible around it. Hence, all circles traced upon the Earth project their own similar images of circles into the heavens, as is demonstrated more clearly in <term>cosmography<note>The science that maps the general features of the universe, combining elements of geography and astronomy.</note></term> and in works concerning the dimensions of the Earth. And these indeed are the circles that have their own names, whereas others could be designated in infinite ways and names.

## On the obliquity of the zodiac, the distance of the tropics, and 
### how they are measured. Chapter II.

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap woodcut initial 'S' depicting a landscape with a building and rolling hills under a sky with clouds.</image-desc>
Since the circle of signs <note>The zodiac; original: "Signifer".</note>, therefore, proceeds obliquely between the tropics and the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>, I now judge it necessary that we investigate the distance between these tropics, and likewise the size of the angle of intersection between the equinoctial and zodiacal circles. To perceive this, one must rely on the senses and the skill of instruments. For this purpose, let a wooden square be prepared, or preferably one made of a more solid material such as stone or metal—lest perhaps the wood, being unstable due to changes in the air, might deceive the practitioner. Let one of its surfaces be most exactly smoothed, and let it have a width sufficient to admit the required divisions, such as three or four cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–20 inches.</note>. 

Taking one of the corners as a center, a quadrant of a circle is drawn according to the capacity of that space and divided into 90 equal parts <note>Degrees.</note>, which are likewise subdivided into 60 minutes <note>original: "scrupula"; literally 'small stones', used here for the 60th parts of a degree.</note>, or into as many as the space can receive. Then, a gnomon <note>The part of a sundial or instrument that casts a shadow.</note> is fixed to the center, a <term>Cylindroides<note>A cylindrical-shaped rod.</note></term> perfectly turned on a lathe; it should be set perpendicular to that surface and project slightly, perhaps by the width of a finger or less.

Once this instrument is so prepared, it is appropriate to lay out a meridian line on a floor paved to the level of the horizon, which has been leveled as diligently as possible by means of a <term>Hydroscope<note>An instrument using water to determine a level surface.</note></term> or a <term>Chorobates<note>A long wooden level used by Roman engineers, described by Vitruvius.</note></term>, so that it does not slope in any direction. Upon this floor, a circle is described, and at its center, a gnomon is erected. We shall observe and mark where the extremity of the shadow touches the circumference of the circle at some time before noon. We shall do the same after noon, and then bisect the arc of the circle lying between the two marks already noted. In this way, a straight line drawn from the center through the point of bisection will infallibly indicate for us the North and South <note>original: "meridiem & Septentrionem".</note>.

Upon this line, as a base, the surface of the instrument is erected and fixed perpendicularly, with its center turned toward the south. A plumb line descending from the center should correspond exactly at right angles to the meridian line. It happens in this way that the surface of the instrument contains the meridian circle. From here, on the days of the Summer Solstice and the Winter Solstice <note>original: "Solsticiij & Brumæ".</note>, the midday shadows of the Sun are

...observed through that index or Cylinder falling from the center, using some device placed around the underlying circumference of the quadrant: so that the position of the shadow may be held more surely, and we will note as accurately as possible the middle of the shadow in degrees and minutes <note>original: "scrupulis"; literally 'small sharp stones', used here for the 60th parts of a degree.</note>. For if we do this, the arc which is marked between the two shadows found—the Summer Solstitial and the Winter <note>original: "Brumalem"; the winter solstice.</note>—will show us the distance between the tropics and the total obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the 'sign-bearer' or ecliptic circle.</note>. Taking half of this, we will have the distance of the tropics themselves from the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and the size of the angle of inclination of the equinoctial to that circle which is through the middle of the signs <note>The ecliptic, the sun's apparent path.</note> will be made manifest.

Ptolemy, therefore, found this interval between the aforementioned Northern and Southern limits to be 47 degrees, 42 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum primorum"; 'first small parts' or minutes.</note>, and 40 seconds, of which the circle is 360. This is just as he found it observed before his time by Hipparchus and Eratosthenes. These are the 11 parts of which the whole circle is 83 <note>A ratio used by ancient Greek astronomers to express the obliquity (11/83 of 360° is roughly 47° 42' 39").</note>. From this, the half-difference, which is 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds, proved the distance of the tropics from the equinoctial circle (where the circle is 360 degrees) and the angle of intersection with the zodiac.

Ptolemy therefore thought that these values remained invariably in this state and would always remain so. But from that time, these values are found to have continually decreased down to our own day. For it has now been found by us and some others of our contemporaries that the distance of the tropics is no more than 46 degrees and almost 58 minutes, and the angle of intersection is 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and two-fifths of one <note>23° 28' 24".</note>. Thus it is now sufficiently clear that the obliquity of the zodiac is also mobile. We shall speak more of this below, where we will also show by a fairly probable conjecture that it was never greater than 23 degrees and 52 minutes, nor will it ever be less than 23 degrees and 28 minutes.

We shall proceed in other cases as we have done in this example. 

However, one must not be unaware that the meridian circle cuts the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferum"; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic circle where the zodiac constellations are located.</note> at right angles at those signs where it touches the tropics. For as we said, it then passes through the poles of the zodiac itself. But at the equinoctial points, it makes an angle as much smaller than a right angle as the zodiac declines from a right angle, so that according to the minimum inclination it is 66 degrees and 32 minutes. 

It should also be noticed that for equal arcs of the zodiac taken from the equinoctial or tropic points, the angles and sides of the triangles result in being equal. For instance, if we describe the equinoctial arc **ABC** and the zodiac **DBE**,

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a celestial sphere showing the intersection of the equinoctial arc A-B-C and the zodiacal/ecliptic arc D-B-E at point B. A vertical axis connects poles K and H. Spherical triangles F L B and B M G are marked, illustrating geometric symmetry relative to the equinox.</image-desc>

intersecting each other at point **B** (where the equinox is located), and we take equal arcs **FB** and **BG**, and through the poles of the daily rotation we draw two quadrants of circles **KFL** and **HGM**, there will be two triangles, **FLB** and **BMG**. In these, the sides **BF** and **BG** are equal, the angles at the vertex **B** are equal, and those at **L** and **M** are right angles. Therefore, by the sixth [proposition] of the *Spherics* <note>Referring to the "Sphaerica," a foundational ancient Greek textbook on spherical geometry, most likely that of Theodosius of Bithynia.</note>, the triangles have equal sides and angles. Thus the **declinations** **FL** and **MG** are equal, as are the **right ascensions** **LB** and **BM**, and the remaining angle **F** is equal to the remaining angle **G**. 

In the same way, the proof will be clear for equal arcs taken from a tropic point. For example, when **AB** and **BC** are equal on either side of the tropic contact at **B**: if we draw quadrants **DA** and **DB** from the pole **D** of the equinoctial circle, 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a spherical triangle. A curved base line spans from A to C with a midpoint B. Point D is positioned above B as an apex. Arcs connect D to points A, B, and C, dividing the structure into two symmetric spherical triangles, A B D and D B C.</image-desc>

there will similarly be two triangles, **ABD** and **DBC**. Their bases **AB** and **BC** are equal, and the side **BD** is common to both, and the angles at **B** are right angles. By the eighth [proposition] of the *Spherics*, it will be demonstrated that these triangles have equal sides and angles. By this, it is manifest that the angles and arcs laid out for one quadrant of the zodiac are the same for the remaining [quadrants] of the whole...

<meta>catchword: Table</meta>

...they will agree with the quadrants of the whole circle. For this reason, we shall provide an example of a **Table** <note>original: "Canonicæ"; refers to a set of astronomical tables used for calculation.</note> below. In the first column, the parts of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi"; the path of the sun through the heavens.</note> will be placed. In the following place will be the **declinations** <note>The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator.</note> corresponding to those parts. In the third column will be the **minutes** <note>original: "scrupula"; literally "small stones," used here for sixtieths of a degree.</note> by which the specific declinations differ and exceed those that occur under the maximum **obliquity** <note>The angle of the tilt of the Earth’s axis relative to its orbit.</note> of the zodiac, the sum of which is 24 minutes. We shall do the same in the table of ascensions and angles. For it is necessary that when the obliquity of the zodiac changes, everything else that follows it must change as well.

Furthermore, in **right ascension** <note>The distance measured eastward along the celestial equator.</note>, the difference is found to be very small, such that it does not exceed a tenth part of one "time" <note>A unit equivalent to one degree on the celestial equator.</note>, and in an hour of time it accounts for only one one-hundred-and-fiftieth part. Indeed, the ancients called the parts of the equinoctial circle **times** <note>original: "tempora"</note>, which rise together with the parts of the zodiac. There are 360 of these in the circle, as we have often said; but to distinguish between them, most have named the parts of the zodiac **degrees** <note>original: "gradus"</note> and the parts of the equinoctial "times." We shall also follow this practice from now on. Since this difference is so small that it might rightly be ignored, it was not a burden for us to include it here as well.

From these tables, the same values will be evident for any other obliquity of the zodiac, provided that for each part, a similar proportion is taken from the ratio of the increase from the minimum to the maximum obliquity. For example, if the obliquity is 23 degrees and 34 minutes, and I wish to know the declination for 30 degrees of the zodiac measured from the equinox: I find in the **Table** <note>original: "Canone"</note> 11 degrees and 29 minutes, and a difference of 11 minutes. This difference would be added in its entirety if the zodiac were at its maximum obliquity, which, as we said, was 23 degrees and 52 minutes. But now the tilt is set at 23 degrees and 34 minutes, which I say is 6 minutes greater than the minimum tilt <note>Copernicus is using 23 degrees and 28 minutes as his minimum tilt value.</note>. Those 6 minutes are one-fourth of the 24 minutes by which the maximum obliquity exceeds the minimum. Following that same ratio, one-fourth of the 11-minute difference is nearly 3 minutes. When I add these to the 11 degrees and 29 minutes, I will have 11 degrees and 32 minutes, which is the declination of those 30 degrees of the zodiac from the equinox at that time. One may do the same for angles and right ascensions, except that for the latter one must always subtract the difference, while for the former one must always add it, so that all calculations for a given time may emerge more accurately.

### How the declination and right ascension of any star located outside the zodiac, whose latitude and longitude are established, may also be made clear, and with which degree of the zodiac it reaches the meridian. Chapter 4. <note>original: "signiferi" (the zodiac or ecliptic) and "caelum mediat" (reaches the meridian or the middle of the sky).</note>

These things have been explained concerning the <term>zodiac</term><note>The "signifer" or "standard-bearer," the path of the zodiac.</note>, the <term>equator</term><note>The "equinoctial circle," the projection of Earth's equator into space.</note>, and the meridian circle, and their mutual intersections. However, for the purpose of the daily revolution, it is not only important to know what appears through the zodiac itself—by which the causes of solar appearances alone are revealed—but also to demonstrate the declination from the equator and the right ascension in a similar way for those stars that are outside of it, whether they be fixed or wandering stars, provided their longitude and latitude have been given.

<image-desc>A celestial coordinate diagram showing a circle ABCD representing the sphere. Arcs AEC (equator) and BED (zodiac/ecliptic) intersect at point E. Points F and G represent the poles of these two circles. A star is located at point H on arc GHKL. Another arc FHMN descends from the diurnal pole F through the star's position. Various points are labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, K, L, M, N.</image-desc>

Therefore, let a circle ABCD be drawn through the poles of the equator and the zodiac; let AEC be the semicircle of the equator around pole F, and BED the semicircle of the zodiac around pole G, with the intersection of the equator at point E. From pole G, let the arc GHKL be drawn through the star; let the given position of the star be at point H, through which the quadrant of a circle FHMN descends from the pole of the daily motion <insert>the diurnal pole F</insert>. It is then clear that the star which exists at H reaches the meridian at the same time as the two points M and N, and the arc HMN itself is the declination of the star from the equator, and EN is the right ascension in the <term>right sphere</term><note>The "sphæra recta," where the celestial equator is perpendicular to the horizon.</note>, which are what we are seeking. 

Since, therefore, in triangle KEL, the side KE is given, and angle KEL and the right angle EKL are given, the sides KL and EL are therefore given by the fourth theorem on spherical triangles, along with the remaining angle KLE; thus the whole arc HKL is given. And for that reason, in triangle HLN, two angles are given, HLN and the right angle LNH, along with side HL; therefore, by the same fourth theorem on spherical triangles, the remaining sides are given: HN, the declination of the star, and LN, which leaves NE as the right ascension, by which the sphere is changed from the equinox to the star. Or in another way: if from the preceding sections you take the arc KE of the zodiac as the right ascension of LE itself, LE itself will be given in reverse from the <term>Table of Right Ascensions</term><note>original: "Canone ascensionum rectarum."</note>, and LK as the declination corresponding to LE,
