### On the sections of the horizon. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'H' depicting a scholar or astronomer sitting at a desk with a book and a globe, framed by an architectural border.</image-desc>The horizon circle is one thing in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The view from the Earth's equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon and the equator passes directly overhead.</note> and another in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>The view from any latitude between the equator and the poles, where the celestial equator is tilted relative to the horizon.</note>. For it is called the horizon of a right sphere when the equator is perpendicular to it, or rather, when it passes through the poles of the equator. However, we call it an oblique sphere when the equator is tilted toward the horizon. Therefore, in a right sphere, all stars rise and set, and the days are always equal to the nights. This is because the horizon bisects all the <term>parallel circles</term><note>The circles of daily rotation (diurnal circles) followed by stars as the Earth rotates.</note> described by the daily motion, specifically through the poles, and those things occur there which we have already explained regarding the meridian. Truly, we define "day" here as the time from the rising of the Sun to its setting, not in the common sense of "from light to darkness"—which is from dawn to the first torchlight—about which we shall say more when discussing the rising and setting of the zodiacal signs. Conversely, where the axis of the earth is perpendicular to the horizon <note>This refers to the North or South Poles.</note>, nothing rises or sets, but everything is turned in a circuit and is either always visible or always hidden, unless another movement should bring it forth—such as the annual motion around the Sun. Because of this annual motion, it follows that a continuous day lasts for a six-month space, with night lasting for the remaining time; there is no distinction other than between winter and summer, because the equator coincides with the horizon in that place. Furthermore, in an oblique sphere, some stars rise and set, while others are always visible or always hidden, and in the meantime, the days and nights become unequal. In this case, where the oblique horizon touches two parallel circles according to the degree of its inclination, the one toward the visible pole defines the stars that are always visible, and conversely, the one toward the hidden pole defines those that are always hidden. Therefore, as the horizon moves through the entire latitude between these limits, it cuts all the parallel circles in the middle into unequal arcs, except for the equator, which is the greatest of the parallels; and great circles always bisect each other. Therefore, the oblique horizon itself divides the greater arcs of the parallels in the upper hemisphere toward the visible pole from those toward the southern and hidden

pole, and conversely in the hidden hemisphere, in which the Sun, appearing in its daily motion, causes the inequality of days and nights.

### On the differences of noon shadows. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with foliate patterns within a square border.</image-desc>There are also differences in noon shadows, according to which some people are called **Periscii**, others **Amphiscii**, and others **Heteroscii**. The **Periscii** <note>literally "around-shadowed"</note> are indeed those whom we can call "circular-shadowed," because they receive the Sun’s shadow from all sides. These are the people whose zenith <note>original: "vertex sive polus horizontis"</note> is distant from the pole of the Earth by an amount less than, or no more than, the distance of the tropic from the equator <note>original: "aequinoctiali"</note>. For in those places, the parallels of latitude which the horizon touches—marking the boundaries of stars that are always visible or always hidden—are greater than or equal to the tropics. Consequently, the summer Sun, rising high among the stars that never set, casts the shadows of <term>gnomons</term><note>A gnomon is the vertical rod or pillar of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> in every direction during that time. But where the horizon touches the tropic circles, these circles themselves become the boundaries of the always-visible and always-hidden stars. Therefore, at the <term>solstice</term><note>original: "solstitio"</note>, the Sun is seen to graze the earth at midnight, at which moment the entire <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signifer circulus"</note> coincides with the horizon; immediately, six signs of the zodiac rise together, while the opposite six set at the same time, and the pole of the zodiac coincides with the pole of the horizon.

The **Amphiscii** <note>literally "both-way shadowed"</note>, who cast their noon shadows toward both sides <note>North and South</note>, are those living between the two tropics. This is the region which the ancients call the Middle Zone <note>the Torrid Zone or Tropics</note>. And since throughout that entire tract the zodiac circle passes twice directly overhead <note>original: "bis rectus insistit"</note>—as is demonstrated in the second theorem of Euclid’s *Phaenomena*—the shadows of the gnomons disappear twice there. As the Sun moves from one side to the other, the gnomons cast their shadows sometimes toward the South <note>original: "Austrum"</note> and sometimes toward the North <note>original: "Boream"</note>.

The rest of us, who live between these two groups, are **Heteroscii** <note>literally "one-way shadowed"</note>, because we cast our noon shadows in only one direction, namely toward the North. The ancient mathematicians were accustomed to divide the Earth into seven <term>climates</term><note>In ancient geography, "climates" (climata) were zones of latitude defined by the length of the longest day, rather than weather patterns.</note>, such as through Meroë, Syene, Alexandria, Rhodes, the Hellespont, the middle of the Black Sea, the Borysthenes, Byzantium, and others through individual parallels, according to the variation and increase of the longest days. They also used gnomons to observe the length of shadows at noon during the equinoxes and both <term>solstices</term><note>original: "solis conversionibus"</note>, and...

<meta>catchword: ...and [the positions]</meta>

<summary>Copernicus classifies the inhabitants of Earth into three groups—Periscii, Amphiscii, and Heteroscii—based on the behavior of their noon shadows, which is determined by their latitudinal distance from the equator and tropics. He also mentions the ancient geographical system of "climates" or latitudinal zones defined by solar observations.</summary>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK II.

...the elevation of the pole, or the latitude of each segment. These things, having changed somewhat over time, are not exactly the same as they were in the past, because of the changing obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"</note>, as we have said, which was unknown to the ancients; or to put it more correctly, because of the varying inclination of the equatorial circle toward the plane of the zodiac, upon which those things depend.

But the elevations of the pole, or the latitudes of places, and the equinoctial shadows agree with those recorded in ancient times: which was bound to happen, since the equatorial circle follows the pole of the terrestrial globe. Therefore, those segments are not defined or designated with enough precision by the various occurrences of shadows and days, but more correctly by their distances from the equatorial circle, which remain constant. However, that change in the tropics, although very small, allows for a slight variation of days and shadows in southern regions, which becomes more evident as one moves toward the North. 

Regarding the shadows of <term>gnomons</term><note>A gnomon is the vertical rod or pillar of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note>, it is clear that for any given altitude of the Sun, the length of the shadow can be perceived, and vice versa. 

->[Diagram]<-

Just as if there were a gnomon AB, which casts a shadow BC, and since the pointer itself stands perpendicular to the plane of the horizon, it is necessary that it always forms a right angle ABC, by the definition of lines perpendicular to a plane. Therefore, if AC is connected, we will have a right-angled triangle ABC, and for a given altitude of the Sun, we will also have the angle ACB. And by the first rule of triangles, the ratio of the gnomon AB to its shadow BC will be given, along with the length of BC itself. Conversely, when AB and BC are given, the angle ACB will also be established by the third rule of plane geometry, along with the elevation of the Sun producing that shadow at the time. In this way, the ancients, in their description of those segments of the terrestrial globe, assigned the lengths of noon shadows for each segment, both at the equinoxes and at each of the <term>solstices</term> <note>original: "trope", from the Greek for "turning points"</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a right-angled triangle representing a gnomon and its shadow. The vertical gnomon is labeled 'A' at the top and 'B' at the base. A horizontal line extends from 'B' representing the shadow on the ground. A hypotenuse line segment connects 'A' to the end of the shadow line (C). This diagram visually supports the text describing the calculation of solar altitude based on shadow length (gnomonics).</image-desc>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Likewise, for any obliquity of the sphere, or inclination of the horizon, we shall simultaneously demonstrate the longest and shortest day, together with the latitude of rising <note>original: "latitudine ortus"; in modern astronomy, this is called "orthive amplitude," the angular distance of the rising sun from the due east point</note>, and the remaining difference of the days. Now, the latitude of rising is the arc of the horizon circle intercepted between the sunrise at the summer solstice and the sunrise at the winter solstice, or the distance of each from the equinoctial rising. Therefore, let the meridian circle be ABCD, and in the eastern hemisphere

->[A geometrical diagram showing a celestial sphere. It consists of a circle with a vertical diameter AC and a horizontal diameter BD. An arc BED represents the horizon, and another arc AEC represents the equinoctial circle (celestial equator). A point F (the North Pole) is located at the top right. A point G is marked on an internal arc (the ecliptic/zodiac), and a point H is marked on the horizon arc BED. Lines connect F to G and F to H, forming spherical triangles for astronomical computation.]<-

the semicircle of the horizon is BED, and the equinoctial circle is AEC, of which the North pole is F. Taking the rising of the Sun at the summer solstice at point G, let the arc FGH of a <term>great circle</term><note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, like the equator or meridians.</note> be described. Since, therefore, the movement of the terrestrial sphere is performed around the pole F of the equinoctial circle, it is necessary that the points G and H coincide on the meridian ABCD, because parallel circles are around the same poles, through which any great circles cut off similar arcs from them. For this reason, the same time that passes from the rising of point G itself until noon also measures the arc AEH, and the remaining subterranean part of the semicircle CH, from midnight to sunrise. Now, ABC is a semicircle, and AB and BC are quadrants of circles, since they are measured from the pole of ABCD itself: therefore, EH will be half the difference between the longest day and the equinoctial day, and BG will be the latitude between the equinoctial and solstitial rising. Since, therefore, in the triangle BHG, the angle GEH of the obliquity of the sphere <note>the geographic latitude</note> stands next to the arc AB, and the angle GHE is a right angle, with the side GH being the distance of the summer tropic from the equinoctial; then the remaining sides are given through the fourth theorem of spherical triangles <note>referring to the rules of spherical trigonometry used to solve for unknown sides and angles</note>: EH is the half-difference of the equinoctial and longest day, and GB is the latitude of rising. Therefore, if along with the side GH, the side EH (the difference of the longest and equinoctial day) or BG were given, then the angle B of the inclination of the sphere—and likewise the elevation of the pole above the horizon—is also given. Furthermore, even if not the solstice but any other point G in the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signifero"; the circle of the ecliptic containing the twelve signs</note> is taken, both arcs BG and EH will nonetheless be revealed. Because by the table of declinations <note>original: "canonem declinationum"</note> set out above, the arc of declination GH which concerns that part of the zodiac becomes known, and the rest are made clear by the same method of demonstration. From which it also follows, that the parts of the zodiac which are equally distant from the solstice cut off the same arcs of the horizon...

### ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK II.

...distances from the equinoctial rising, and toward those same parts, and they make the lengths of days and nights mutually equal. This is because the same parallel circle contains both degrees of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; the "sign-bearer," referring to the ecliptic circle where the signs of the zodiac are located</note>, since their declination <note>the angular distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> is equal and toward the same direction. However, when equal arcs are taken on either side of the equinoctial intersection <note>the equinox</note>, the latitudes of rising <note>the distance along the horizon from the true east point to where the sun rises</note> happen to be equal again, but in opposite directions; the lengths of the days and nights are likewise swapped. This occurs because they describe equal arcs of the parallels on both sides, just as the signs themselves have an equal distance from the equinox and equal declinations from the equinoctial circle. 

For let the circumferences of the parallels be described in the same figure, and let them be GM and KN, which cut the horizon <note>original: "finientem," the boundary or limit</note> BED at the points G and K; let there also be applied from the Southern pole L a quadrant of a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on a sphere's surface whose plane passes through the center, dividing the sphere into two equal halves</note> LKO. 

->[A circular geometric diagram of a sphere. An outer circle is labeled with points B (left), D (right), and L (bottom). Arcs and lines within the circle are labeled with points A, M, F along the top arc, and internal points E (center), K, O, G, H, and N. Various lines connect these points to demonstrate geometric proofs regarding astronomical declinations.]<-

Since, therefore, the declination HG is equal to the declination KO, there will be two triangles, DFG and BLK, in which two sides are equal to each other: FG is equal to LK, and FD (the elevation of the pole <note>this corresponds to the observer's geographic latitude</note>) is equal to LB, and the angles around BD are right angles. Therefore, the third side DG is equal to the third side BK, from which the remaining arcs GE and EK—the latitudes of rising—are also left equal. 

Wherefore, since here also the two sides EG and GH are equal to the two sides EK and KO, and the angles at the vertex E are equal, the remaining sides EH and EO are equal for that reason. When these equal parts are added together, the whole circumference OBC is found to be equal to the whole circumference ABH. But because the great circles passing through the poles cut off similar arcs of parallel circles, the arcs GM and KN will themselves be similar and equal to each other. Which was to be demonstrated. 

But all these things can also be demonstrated in another way. Let there be described likewise a meridian circle ABCD, whose center is E. Let the diameter of the equinoctial and the common intersection of those circles be AEC; let the diameter of the horizon and the meridian line be BED; let the axis of the sphere be LEM; let the visible pole be L and the hidden pole be M. 

Taking the distance of the summer solstice, or let AF be any other declination, to which the diameter of the parallel FG is drawn, also in the common section with the meridian, which will cut the axis at K and the meridian line at N. Since...

A vertical axis is labeled L at the top and M at the bottom. Lines and arcs intersect at the center E and other points labeled F, K, G, and N.]<-

<meta>This page continues the geometric proof from the previous page, shifting from the general symmetry of days to the specific mathematical calculation of day length using chords and ratios. It transitions from a conceptual explanation to a formal proof citing Euclid and Posidonius.</meta>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

Since, therefore, they are parallel—according to the definition of Posidonius <note>Posidonius of Rhodes (c. 135–51 BCE) was a Stoic philosopher and astronomer who defined parallel lines as those whose perpendicular distances remain constant</note>—which neither incline toward nor away from each other, but maintain equal perpendicular lines between them everywhere, the straight line **KE** will be equal to half the chord subtending double the arc **AF**. Similarly, **KN** will be half the chord subtending the arc of the parallel circle whose radius is **FK**; it is through this difference that the equinoctial day <note>The day when the sun is on the equator, making day and night equal</note> differs from a day of a different length. This is because all the semicircles in which these common sections exist—that is, those for which they are diameters, such as **BED** of the oblique horizon, **LEM** of the right horizon, **AEC** of the equinoctial, and **FKG** of the parallel—are perpendicular to the plane of the circle **ABCD**.

->[A circular geometric diagram illustrating astronomical projections. It features a circle with a main vertical diameter AC and a horizontal diameter BD intersecting at the center K. Points E and N are marked on the horizontal diameter on either side of the center. Point F is on the upper-left circumference with a vertical line dropped to E, and point L is on the upper-right circumference with a vertical line dropped to N. Two additional diameters or chords, FKG and LKM, cross through the center K. This figure is used to geometrically demonstrate the calculations for the duration of daylight based on the declination of a celestial body and the latitude of the observer.]<-

And the sections they make among themselves, according to the 19th proposition of the eleventh book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>Euclid's *Elements* was the standard geometry textbook of the time; Book XI deals with three-dimensional geometry</note>, are perpendicular to that same plane at points **E**, **K**, and **N**. Furthermore, by the 6th proposition of the same book, these lines are parallel. Moreover, **K** is the center of the parallel circle, and **L** is the center of the sphere. For this reason, **EN** is also half of the chord subtending double the arc of the horizon, by which the rising of the parallel differs from the equinoctial rising. 

Therefore, since the declination **AF** is given, along with the remainder of the quadrant **FL**, the halves of the chords of the doubles—**KE** for **AF**, and **FK** for **FL**—will be established in terms of the units in which the radius **AE** is 100,000 <note>Copernicus used a standard radius of 100,000 for his trigonometric tables to allow for high precision without using decimals</note>. In the right-angled triangle **EKN**, the angle **KEN** is given by the polar elevation **DL** <note>The elevation of the celestial pole above the horizon, which is equal to the observer's latitude</note>, and the remaining angle **KNE** is equal to angle **AEB**, because in an oblique sphere <note>A view of the sky from any latitude other than the equator or the poles</note>, the parallels are inclined to the horizon at the same angle. Thus, the sides are given in the same units in which the radius of the sphere is 100,000. 

Accordingly, for whatever units the radius of the parallel **FK** is 100,000, it will also provide the length of **KN** itself, which is half the chord subtending the entire difference between the equinoctial day and the day on the parallel, in the units where the parallel circle is 360 degrees. From these things it is clear that the ratio of **FK** to **KN** consists of two ratios: namely, the chord of double **FL** to the chord of double **AF** (that is, **FK** to **KE**), and the chord of double **AB** to the chord of double **DL** (which is as **EK** to **KN**); for **EK** is taken as the middle term between **FK** and **KN**. Similarly, the ratio of **BE** to **EN** is composed of **BE** to **EK** and **KE** to **EN**. 

In this way, I believe, not only the inequality of days and nights, but also the segments of the parallels described by the <term>diurnal motion</term> <note>The apparent daily rotation of the stars and planets around the Earth</note> of the Moon and the stars (provided their declination is known), can be distinguished between those that are above the earth and those below; through these, their rising and setting can be easily understood.

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof to calculate the variation in day length and the rising/setting points of stars based on their declination and the observer's latitude. By using ratios and chords, he establishes a mathematical method to determine how much of a celestial body's daily path is visible above the horizon.</summary>

<keywords>geometry, declination, day length, Euclid, Posidonius, celestial sphere, diurnal motion, chords, ratio, astronomy</keywords>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

## On hours and the parts of day and night. Chapter VIII.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'E' at the start of the first paragraph, featuring foliage and vine motifs.</note>

From these things, therefore, it is clear that if we take the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>The "difference of days" or "ascensional difference" (differentia dierum) is the amount by which a day deviates from the standard 12-hour equinoctial day due to the observer's latitude and the Sun's position.</note> for a given <term>pole elevation</term><note>The "pole elevation" (elevatio poli) is the observer's geographic latitude.</note> from the table, using the Sun’s current declination, and add it to a quadrant of a circle (90°) for a Northern declination, or subtract it for a Southern declination, and then double the result, we will have the total length of that day. The remaining portion of the circle will be the space of the night. If we divide either of these by 15 degrees (the amount the sky rotates in one equal hour), the result will show how many <term>equal hours</term> that day or night contains. 

Furthermore, if we take a twelfth part of the total day or night, we will have the duration of a <term>temporal hour</term><note>Also known as "seasonal" or "unequal" hours. In this system, both the day and night are always divided into 12 hours regardless of the season, meaning a "day hour" in summer is much longer than one in winter.</note>. These hours take their names from the specific day of which they are a twelfth part; hence we find terms used by the ancients such as "solstitial," "equinoctial," and "brumal" <note>original: "Brumales," referring to the winter solstice.</note> hours. In earliest times, no other hours were in use but these—twelve from sunrise to sunset—while they divided the night into four <term>watches</term> or "guards." This system of hours lasted for a long time by the silent consent of all nations. It was for this reason that <term>clepsydrae</term> <note>original: "clepsydræ." Water clocks that measured time by the flow of water.</note> were invented, which, by the subtraction or addition of dripping water, adjusted the hours to the differing lengths of the days, so that the division of time would not be hidden even when the sky was cloudy. 

Later, however, once <term>equal hours</term> <note>original: "horæ pariles." Modern 60-minute hours where day and night together always total 24 hours.</note> common to both day and night were generally accepted—as they are easier to observe—those older temporal hours became so obsolete that if you were to ask anyone from the common people what the first, third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour of the day is, they would have no answer, or at least one that is entirely irrelevant. Now, even regarding the number of these equal hours, some count from noon, others from sunset, others from midnight, and some from sunrise, according to the established custom of each city.

## On the oblique ascension of the parts of the zodiac, and how for any rising degree, the degree at the midheaven is determined. Chapter IX.

He notes that different regions still use different starting points for the 24-hour cycle.</summary>

<keywords>day length, temporal hours, equal hours, clepsydra, water clocks, watches, solar declination, ascensional difference, midheaven</keywords>

<meta>This page continues from Chapter VIII, moving into Chapter IX. Having established the length of days and nights based on the sun's position, Copernicus now transitions to the concept of oblique ascensions—the timing of how the signs of the zodiac rise relative to the horizon at different latitudes.</meta>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK II

With the sizes and differences of days and nights thus explained, the explanation of **oblique ascensions** follows in the appropriate order. By these I mean the times in which the <term>dodecatemoria</term><note>original: "dodecatemoria"; From the Greek for "twelfth-parts," these are the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac we know as the "signs."</note>—that is, the twelve parts of the zodiac—or any other arcs of it, rise. For there are no other differences between **right and oblique ascensions** than those between the equinoctial day and the unequal days which we have already explained. Furthermore, these <term>dodecatemoria</term> were named after the constellations of the fixed stars, starting from the vernal equinox: **Aries**, **Taurus**, **Gemini**, **Cancer**, and the rest as they follow in order. 

Therefore, for the sake of greater clarity, let us recall the meridian circle **ABCD**, with the equinoctial semicircle **AEC**, and the horizon **BED**, which intersect at point **E**. Let the equinox be assumed at point **H**, through which the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signifer"; literally the "sign-bearer," another name for the ecliptic circle where the zodiac signs reside.</note> circle **FHI** cuts the horizon at **L**. Through this intersection, let a quadrant of a great circle **KLM** descend from the pole of the equinoctial **K**.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram representing the celestial sphere. A large outer circle is labeled with points A (zenith), B (left), C (nadir), and D (right). A vertical line AC and a horizontal line BD intersect at center E. An interior arc labeled F, H, L, I curves through the sphere, representing the ecliptic (signifer). Point H is on the vertical line AC. Point L is the intersection of this arc with the horizontal line BD (the horizon). Another arc KLM originates from point K on the upper right edge and passes through L to point M on the lower right.</image-desc>

It is indeed apparent that while the arc of the zodiac **HL** rises, it does so in the same time as the arc **HE** of the equinoctial. However, in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The "right sphere" refers to the celestial coordinates as seen from the Earth's equator, where the signs rise vertically.</note>, it would rise with **HEM**. The difference between these is **EM**, which we previously demonstrated to be half the difference between the equinoctial and unequal day. But what was added there in Northern <term>declination</term><note>Declination is the distance a celestial object sits north or south of the celestial equator.</note> is subtracted here, and conversely is added in Southern declination to the right ascension, so that the oblique ascension may be produced. Consequently, for as long as a whole sign or any other arc of the zodiac emerges, it will become manifest through the calculated ascensions from the beginning to the end. 

From this it follows that when any given degree of the zodiac is provided, taken from the equinox, the degree which <term>mediates the heavens</term><note>Also called the Midheaven or "Medium Coeli," this is the point of the zodiac that is currently crossing the observer's local meridian (the highest point in the sky).</note> is also given. For when point **L** is given—the point of the zodiac that is rising—along with its declination according to **HL** (the distance from the equinox), and the right ascension **HEM**, then the entire semi-diurnal arc **AHEM** is known. The remaining arc **AH** is therefore given, which is the right ascension of **FH**. This is also found through the table, since the angle of the intersection **AHF** is given along with the side **AH**, and the angle at **FAH** is a right angle. Thus, the entire arc of the zodiac **FHL** between the rising and the midheaven degree is given. Conversely, if the degree that mediates the heaven was given first—for example, the arc **FH**—we would also know the degree that **rises**...

k iij
<meta>catchword: rises (original: oritur)</meta>

<summary>Copernicus begins Chapter IX by defining oblique ascensions and explaining how to calculate the rising and culminating points of the zodiac signs using the difference between the equinoctial and unequal days.</summary>
<keywords>oblique ascension, dodecatemoria, zodiac, right sphere, declination, midheaven, equinox, meridian</keywords>

--- Page 94 ---
<meta>This page concludes Chapter IX, which calculates the lengths of arcs of the zodiac rising above the horizon, and begins Chapter X, focusing on the changing angles formed between the zodiac and the horizon throughout the day.</meta>

...rises: for the declination **AF** will be known, and on account of the angle of the obliquity of the sphere, **AFB** and **FB** are the remainder. In the triangle **BFL**, however, the angle **BFL** is given from the preceding demonstrations, and **FBL** is a right angle with side **FB**: therefore, the sought side **FHL** is given, or it may be found otherwise as shown below.

### On the angle of the intersection of the zodiac with the horizon. Chapter X.

Furthermore, the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signifer"; the "sign-bearer," or the ecliptic circle representing the sun's apparent annual path.</note> circle, because it sits at an angle to the axis of the sphere, creates various angles with the horizon. We have already mentioned, in the section on the differences of shadows, that it rises to the vertical twice for those who live between the tropics. But for our purposes, I think it is enough to have demonstrated only those angles which serve the <term>Heteroscian</term><note>original: "Heteroscĳs"; from the Greek meaning "having different shadows." This refers to people living in temperate zones where the noon shadow always points in one direction—either north or south—unlike those in the tropics.</note> inhabitants—that is, ourselves—from which the universal principle of these angles will be easily understood. 

It is, I think, clear enough that in an "oblique sphere" <note>a latitude where the celestial pole is at an angle to the horizon, neither at the equator nor the poles</note>, when the equinox or the beginning of <term>Aries</term><note>the Ram</note> is rising, the zodiac circle is more inclined and leans toward the horizon by as much as the maximum southern declination (found at the beginning of <term>Capricorn</term><note>the Goat</note>) adds, while [Capricorn] occupies the midheaven. Conversely, the zodiac is more elevated and creates a greater eastern angle when the beginning of <term>Libra</term><note>the Scales</note> emerges and the beginning of <term>Cancer</term><note>the Crab</note> occupies the midheaven. 

This is because these three circles—the <term>equinoctial</term><note>the celestial equator</note>, the zodiac, and the horizon—meet at the same common intersection at the poles of the meridian circle. The arcs intercepted by these circles reveal the size of that eastern angle. However, so that the method of measurement may be open for all other parts of the zodiac: Let there be again the meridian circle **ABCD**, the half of the horizon **BED**, and the half of the zodiac **AEC**. 

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram representing the celestial sphere. An outer circle is marked with points A at the top (zenith), B on the left, C at the bottom (nadir), and D on the right. A horizontal arc labeled BED represents the horizon, and a diagonal arc AEC represents the ecliptic (zodiac). These arcs intersect at point E, the rising point. Points F, G, and H are marked along the upper-left quadrant, representing various points of declination.</image-desc>

Whichever degree of the zodiac rises at point **E**, our goal is to find how great the angle **AEB** is, based on the standard where four right angles equal 360 degrees. Therefore, when the rising point **E** is given, the point in the midheaven is also given from the preceding sections, along with the arc **AE** and the meridian altitude **AB**. And because the angle **ABE** is a right angle, the ratio of the chord of twice the arc **AE** to the chord of twice the arc **AB** is given, just as the ratio of the diameter of the sphere to the chord of twice the angle that measures **AEB**.

<meta>catchword is given</meta>

<summary>Copernicus concludes his calculations on zodiacal arcs and begins Chapter X, explaining how the angle between the ecliptic (the sun's path) and the horizon changes based on which zodiac sign is rising.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the geometric demonstration from Chapter X regarding the angles formed by the intersection of the zodiac (the ecliptic) and the horizon. It concludes the theoretical explanation and introduces the sets of astronomical tables that follow in the manuscript.</meta>

-> ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK II. <-

Therefore, the angle **AEB** itself is also given. But if the degree of the <term>midheaven</term><note>the point where the ecliptic crosses the local meridian</note>—which we will call **A**—is given instead of the degree of the rising point, that angle of the rising point will nonetheless be measured. For by making **E** the pole, let a quadrant of a great circle **FGH** be described, and let the quadrants **EAG** and **EBH** be completed. Since, therefore, the meridian altitude **AB** is given, and the remainder of the quadrant **AF**, the angle **FAG** is also known from the preceding demonstrations, and **FGA** is a right angle. Therefore, the arc **FG** is given, as is the remaining arc **GH**, which measures the sought rising angle. 

Accordingly, it is also clear here how the degree that is rising is given in relation to the degree at the midheaven. This is because the chord of double **GH** is to the chord of double **AB** as the diameter is to the chord that subtends double **AE**, as is the case in <term>spherical triangles</term><note>calculations involving triangles drawn on the surface of a sphere, where sides are arcs of circles</note>. Regarding these matters, we have also appended three examples of tables. 

The first will be for <term>ascensions</term><note>the rising of celestial points</note> in a <term>right sphere</term><note>an "upright" perspective where the celestial equator is vertical to the horizon, as seen from the Earth's equator</note>, beginning from <term>Aries</term><note>the sign of the Ram; the starting point of the zodiac</note> and increasing by six-degree increments of the <term>zodiac</term>. 

The second table is for ascensions in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>the perspective from various latitudes where the pole is tilted relative to the horizon</note>, likewise by six-degree increments, from the parallel where the pole is elevated 39 degrees up to the one that is elevated 57 degrees, with intermediate steps of three degrees. 

The remaining table of horizontal angles is also arranged by six degrees across the same seven segments. All of these are calculated according to the minimum <term>obliquity of the zodiac</term><note>original: "signiferi obliquitatem"; the tilt of the Earth's axis, or the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note> of 23 degrees and 28 minutes, which is roughly accurate for our current age.

## On the use of these tables. Chapter 11.

The use of the tables is now clear from what has been demonstrated. For if we take the known degree of the Sun and find its right ascension <term>right ascension: the distance of a point measured eastward along the celestial equator</term>, and add to it fifteen-degree increments <note>original: "quindena tempora"; since the sky rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, 15 degrees equals one hour</note> for any given equal hour—discarding the 360 parts of a full circle if the sum exceeds that—the remainder of the right ascension will show the degree of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi", the 'sign-bearer' or ecliptic</note> that is at the Midheaven <term>Midheaven: the point where the ecliptic crosses the local meridian</term> at the proposed hour from noon. Similarly, if you do the same regarding the oblique ascension <term>oblique ascension: the position on the celestial equator that rises with a star or point on the ecliptic at a specific latitude</term> of your region, you will have the degree of the zodiac rising at the hour assumed from sunrise.

In the case of any stars which are outside the circle of the signs <note>the ecliptic</note>, whose right ascension has been established as we taught above, these tables give the degrees of the zodiac which reach Midheaven with them from the beginning of Aries through that same right ascension. Furthermore, through their oblique ascension, the tables show which degree of the zodiac rises with them, according as the ascensions and parts of the zodiac present themselves in the corresponding sections of the tables. You shall operate in a similar way, but always through the opposite location, regarding the setting of the stars. 

Furthermore, if a quadrant of a circle <note>90 degrees</note> is added to the right ascension that is at Midheaven, the resulting sum is the oblique ascension of the rising point. Therefore, through the degree of the Midheaven, the degree that is rising is also given, and vice versa. There follows a table of the angles of the zodiac with the horizon, which are taken according to the rising degree of the zodiac; by these, it is also understood how much the ninetieth degree <term>nonagesimal: the point on the ecliptic exactly 90 degrees from the horizon, representing its highest point</term> of the zodiac is elevated from the horizon, which is a most necessary thing to know in solar eclipses.

## On the angles and arcs formed by circles passing through the poles of the horizon to the zodiac circle. Chapter 12.

It follows that we should set forth the reasoning for the angles and arcs created by the intersections of the zodiac with those circles that pass through the vertex <note>the zenith</note> of the horizon, in which the altitude above the horizon is found. Moreover, regarding the meridian altitude of the Sun, or of any degree of the zodiac at Midheaven, and the angle of intersection with the meridian, this has been explained above, since it also...

### On the rising and setting of the stars. Chapter 14.

The rising and setting of the stars also seem to pertain to the daily revolution; not only those simple risings and settings of which we just spoke, but also the ways in which they become "morning" and "evening" events. Although these happen due to the concurrence of the annual revolution <note>the Earth's orbit around the sun</note>, they will nevertheless be discussed more aptly in this place. The ancient mathematicians separate the *true* risings and settings from the *apparent* ones. A true morning rising <note>also known as a heliacal rising</note> is when the star emerges at the same time as the Sun. A morning setting, however, is when the star sets while the Sun is rising; during the whole intervening time, the star was called "morning." But an evening rising is when the star emerges just as the Sun is setting. An evening setting occurs when the star sets together with the setting Sun; during that intervening time it is also called "evening," as much as...

<sig>l iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: inter</meta>

<summary>Copernicus concludes his geometric proofs for calculating the position of the ecliptic and its angles, then introduces the definitions of true morning and evening risings and settings of stars.</summary>
<keywords>meridian, horizon, ecliptic, spherical geometry, Ptolemy, heliacal rising, morning rising, evening setting, zodiac</keywords>

--- Page 102 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 14 of Book II, specifically focusing on the definitions of astronomical risings and settings of stars and planets relative to the Sun's position. # NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

is arranged beforehand during the day, and that which followed at night. The **morning rising** of a star <note>original: "matutinus sideris ortus"</note> is when, at daybreak and before the rising of the Sun, the star first reveals itself by emerging and begins to appear. The **morning setting** <note>original: "occasus matutinus"</note>, however, is that where the star is seen to set for the last time just as the Sun is about to rise. The **evening rising** <note>original: "vespertinus ortus"</note> occurs when the star first appears to rise at twilight. Finally, the **evening setting** <note>original: "occasus vespertinus"</note> is when the star ceases to appear any longer after the setting of the Sun, being hidden from then on by the approach of the Sun, until they reveal themselves again in their previous order at the morning rising. 

These rules apply to the fixed stars <term>fixed stars: the distant stars that appear to stay in the same position relative to each other, as opposed to the "wandering" planets</term>, and likewise to the "freely moving" planets **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**. However, **Venus** and **Mercury** produce their risings and settings differently; for they are not overtaken by the approach of the Sun like the others, nor are they revealed by its departure. Instead, by moving ahead, they mingle with and snatch themselves away from the Sun's brilliance. While the outer planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, when making an evening rising or a morning setting, are not hidden at all but remain visible throughout the night with their own light, these inner planets <note>Venus and Mercury</note> remain hidden without distinction from setting until rising, and cannot be seen anywhere. 

There is also another difference: in the outer planets, the "true" morning risings and settings occur before the "apparent" ones, and the evening ones occur after, according to whether they precede the Sun's rising there or follow its setting here. In the inferior planets <note>Venus and Mercury</note>, however, the apparent morning and evening risings occur after the true ones, while the settings occur earlier. The method by which these are determined can be understood from what was said above, where we explained the oblique ascension of any star whose position is known, and with which degree of the **Zodiac** <term>signifer: literally the "sign-bearer," the belt of the heavens through which the sun and planets move</term> it rises or sets. If the Sun appears in that degree or the one opposite it at that time, the star will perform its true morning or evening rising or setting. 

The apparent events differ from these according to the brightness and magnitude of each star: those which possess greater light have shorter periods of being hidden by the solar rays than those which are dimmer. The limits of this hiding and appearing are measured by the arcs beneath the horizon <note>original: "subterraneis circumferentijs"</note> on circles passing through the poles of the horizon, captured between the horizon itself and the Sun. These limits are roughly:
*   **12 degrees** for the primary fixed stars
*   **11 degrees** for **Saturn**
*   **10 degrees** for **Jupiter**
*   **11.5 degrees** for **Mars**
*   **5 degrees** for **Venus**
*   **10 degrees** for **Mercury**

In total, however, where the remainder of the daylight yields to the night—which comprises twilight <term>crepusculum: evening twilight</term> or dawn <term>diluculum: morning twilight</term>—there are **18 degrees** of the aforementioned circle. Once the Sun has moved down by these degrees, even the smaller stars begin to appear. Indeed, at this distance...

...[Some astronomers] take a parallel line below the horizon, and when the Sun reaches it, they say it begins to dawn or that the night is complete. Therefore, once we have determined with which degree of the **Zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi," literally "the sign-bearer"</note> a star rises or sets, and we know the angle of the intersection of that same Zodiac with the horizon in that region; if we then also find as many degrees of the Zodiac between the rising degree and the Sun as are sufficient and correspond to the Sun’s depth below the horizon—according to the prescribed limits for the star in question—we shall announce that its first emergence <note>its heliacal rising</note> or its hiding <note>its heliacal setting</note> is taking place. Furthermore, what we explained regarding the altitude of the Sun above the earth in the preceding demonstration applies in all respects to its descent below the earth; for they differ in nothing but position. In the same way, those things which set in the visible **hemisphere** rise in the hidden one, and everything occurs in turn and is easy to understand. Therefore, let what has been said about the rising and setting of stars, and thus about the **daily revolution of the terrestrial globe**, suffice.

### Chapter XIV. On seeking the positions of the stars, and the canonical description of the fixed stars.

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'P' at the start of the paragraph, featuring floral motifs and a figure within the square block.</image-desc>

After our explanation of the daily revolution of the globe of the Earth and its consequences, the demonstrations of the annual circuit should now follow. But since some of the ancient mathematicians judged that the phenomena of the **fixed stars** <note>original: "stellarum non errantium," literally "non-wandering stars"</note> should come first, as being the very beginnings of this art, we have decided to follow their opinion. We do so because among our principles and **hypotheses** we have assumed that the sphere of the fixed stars is entirely immobile, and it is against this sphere that the wanderings of all the moving stars <note>the planets</note> are equally compared.

But let no one wonder why we have adopted this order, given that **Ptolemy** in his *Great Composition* <term>Great Composition: Also known by its Arabic title, the *Almagest*, the most influential astronomical manual of the Middle Ages</term> thought that an explanation of the fixed stars could not be provided unless knowledge of the positions of the Sun and Moon had first been established. For that reason, he judged that matters concerning the fixed stars should be deferred until then. If you understand this as referring to the numbers by which the apparent motion of the Moon and Sun is calculated, that opinion will perhaps stand. For **Menelaus the Geometer** also determined most of the stars and their positions through numbers by means of lunar **conjunctions**...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...[planetary movements]. But we shall achieve this much better if, with the support of instruments, we determine the position of any star by means of the carefully examined locations of the Sun and Moon, as we shall soon teach. We are also warned by the failed attempts of those who thought the magnitude of the **solar year** should be defined simply by the equinoxes or solstices, or even by the fixed stars; in this matter, they have never been able to agree among themselves down to our time, so much so that in no part of the science has the discord been greater. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is here revising.</note> had noticed this; when he had calculated the solar year in his own time—not without suspicion that an error might emerge over time—he warned posterity to search for further certainty in this matter thereafter. Therefore, it seemed worthwhile to us to show how the positions of the Sun and Moon are captured by the skill of instruments—namely, how far they are distant from the **vernal equinox** <note>The point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator in spring, used as the starting point for celestial longitude.</note> or other cardinal points of the world—which will then provide us with the means for investigating other stars. By these means, we may also set before our eyes the sphere of the fixed stars woven into constellations, and display its image.

By which instruments the distance of the tropics, the obliquity of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi," literally "the sign-bearer"</note>, and the inclination of the sphere—or the altitude of the equinoctial pole—might be captured, has been set forth above. In the same way, we can take any other meridian altitude of the Sun. This altitude, according to its difference from the inclination of the sphere, will show us how much the Sun declines from the equinoctial circle; through this declination, its position measured from the equinox or solstice will then become even more manifest at noon itself. Moreover, the Sun appears to traverse nearly one degree in the space of 24 hours; thus, 2 1/2 **minutes of arc** <note>original: "scrupula ii. s." where 'scrupula' are minutes and 's' is 'semis' or half</note> result for each hourly portion. From this, its position will be easily estimated for any other appointed hour.

But for observing the positions of the Moon and the stars, another instrument is constructed, which Ptolemy calls an **Astrolabe** <note>Copernicus is describing the 'armillary astrolabe' or armillary sphere, a complex three-dimensional model of the sky, rather than the flat 'planispheric' astrolabe used for navigation.</note>. For two rings are fashioned, or rather the quadrilateral rims of rings, so that they may receive the concave and convex surfaces at right angles with flat sides or "jaws." They should be equal in all respects and similar, and suitable in size—lest, of course, by excessive size they become less manageable, though a larger size allows for finer divisions of the parts. Their width and thickness, however...

...should be at least a thirtieth part of the diameter. They shall then be joined and connected to each other at right angles, with their hollow and convex parts fitting together as if in the roundness of a single globe. Let one of them take the place of the **zodiac** <note>original: "circulus signorum," literally the "circle of signs."</note> and the other take the place of the circle that passes through both poles—that is, I mean, through the poles of the **equator** <note>original: "æquinoctialis."</note> and the zodiac. Therefore, that zodiac circle is to be divided on its sides into 360 equal parts, as is customary, which may be further subdivided according to the capacity of the instrument. On the other circle as well, measuring out quadrants from the zodiac, let the poles of the zodiac itself be assigned; from these, taking a distance according to the measure of the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The angle of the Earth's axial tilt, which determines the path of the Sun through the seasons.</note>, let the poles of the equatorial circle also be marked.

With these things thus prepared, two other rings should be made, crafted to move on those same poles of the zodiac: an outer one and an inner one. These should have thicknesses equal to the space between two planes, and widths of their rims <note>original: "maxillarum," literally "jaws."</note> similar to the others, so arranged that the inner surface of the larger ring touches the outer surface of the zodiac, and the outer surface of the smaller ring touches the inner surface of the zodiac everywhere. Yet, their rotation should not be hindered; rather, they should allow the zodiac itself and its meridian to pass through each other easily and freely. These rings, therefore, we shall skillfully perforate at those poles of the zodiac along the diameter, and we shall insert **axles** <note>original: "axonia."</note> by which they may be joined and rotated. The inner ring is also to be divided into 360 equal parts, so that in each quadrant ninety degrees extend toward the poles.

Furthermore, within its cavity, yet another ring—a fifth one—is to be placed, rotatable within the same plane. To its rims are fixed **sights** <note>original: "systematia... diaugia siue specilla," referring to viewing holes or apertures for sighting stars.</note> having passages and viewing holes positioned diametrically, through which the light of a star can enter and exit, as is usual in a **diopter** <note>A classic surveying instrument used for measuring angles or aligning sightings.</note>, along the very diameter of the ring. To this ring, certain stops or markers are also fitted on both sides to serve as indices for the numbers, for the sake of observing the latitudes on the containing ring.

Finally, a sixth ring must be added to hold and support the entire **Astrolabe** <note>While we usually think of a flat disc, Copernicus here describes a "spherical astrolabe" or armillary sphere, a 3D model of the celestial sky.</note>. It is suspended from the fixed points of the equatorial poles and placed upon a small pillar, supported and erected according to the plane of the horizon. With the poles adjusted to the inclination of the **sphere** <note>This refers to the local latitude of the observer.</note>, it should hold a position similar to the natural meridian and should not wobble from it in the least. 

With the instrument thus prepared, when we wish to take the position of any star—in the evening or when the Sun is about to set, and at a time when we also have the **Moon** in view—we shall align the outer ring to the degree of the zodiac in which...

...once we have determined the Sun's position through the methods previously described, we turn the intersection of the rings toward the Sun itself, until both the **zodiac** ring <note>original: "zodiacus," the ring representing the Sun's annual path.</note> and the outer ring—the one passing through the poles—cast a shadow upon each other equally. Then we also turn the inner ring toward the Moon; with the eye placed at its plane, where we see the Moon opposite us as if it were bisected by that same plane, we shall mark the place on the instrument’s **zodiac** <note>original: "signifero," the 'sign-bearer' or zodiac ring.</note>. For that will then be the position of the Moon in observed longitude. Indeed, without the Moon, there was no way to determine the positions of the stars, since she alone of all celestial bodies is a participant in both day and night.

Then, when night falls and the star whose position we seek can finally be seen, we align the outer ring with the Moon’s recorded position. Using the Moon, we calibrate the position of the **astrolabe** <note>Here referring to the armillary sphere described on the previous page, a skeleton globe of rings.</note> just as we did with the Sun. Then we also turn the inner circle toward the star until it seems to touch the surface of the ring, and is seen through the sights <note>original: "specilla," the viewing apertures or pinholes on the instrument.</note> located on the small inner ring. In this way, we will have discovered both the longitude and the latitude of the star. While these things are being done, the degree of the zodiac that is at **midheaven** <note>original: "caelum mediat," the point where the zodiac intersects the local meridian.</note> will be visible to the eyes, and therefore it will be clearly established at what hour the observation was made.

Take the example of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer whose work Copernicus is here updating.</note>: In the second year of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, on the ninth day of Pharmuthi (the eighth Egyptian month), in Alexandria, around sunset, he wished to observe the position of the star in the breast of Leo called **Basiliskus** or **Regulus** <note>original: "basiliscus sive regulus," the brightest star in the constellation Leo, often called the 'Little King'.</note>. Having prepared the astrolabe relative to the setting Sun, five equinoctial hours having passed since noon, while the Sun was found at 3 degrees and a half-ounce <note>original: "semuncia," 1/24th of a degree or 2.5 minutes of arc.</note> of **Pisces**, he found the Moon followed the Sun by 92 and 1/8 degrees using the inner circle. Because of this, the position of the Moon was seen to be at 5 degrees and a sixth <note>original: "sextante," 1/6th of a degree or 10 minutes of arc.</note> of **Gemini**. 

And after half an hour, when the sixth hour from noon was completed and the star had already begun to appear (with the fourth degree of Gemini at midheaven), he turned the outer ring of the instrument to the already determined position of the Moon. Moving the inner ring, he recorded the distance of the star from the Moon, following the order of the signs, as 57 and 1/10 degrees. Therefore, since the Moon was found at 92 and 1/8 degrees from the setting Sun, as was said, this placed the Moon at 5 degrees and a sixth of Gemini. But it was appropriate to account for the fact that during that half-hour interval, the Moon had moved a quarter of a degree (since the hourly portion of lunar motion covers about half a degree, more or less); however, due to the lunar **parallax** <note>original: "commutationem," the displacement in the apparent position of a celestial body when viewed from different points.</note>, which was then subtractive, the adjustment needed to be slightly less than a quarter...

...which he defined as approximately one-twelfth of a degree; whereby the Moon was in 5 degrees and one-third of Gemini. But when we treat the **lunar parallaxes** <note>original: "commutatiõibus," the apparent shift in the Moon's position when viewed from different points on Earth.</note>, it will be shown that the difference was not so great; it is clear enough that the observed place of the Moon exceeded five degrees of Gemini by more than one-third, and barely less than two-fifths. To these were added 57 degrees and one-tenth of a part, bringing the star’s position to nearly 2 and a half <note>original: "II. s."</note> degrees of Leo, at a distance of about 32 and a half degrees from the Sun’s summer solstice, with a Northern latitude of one-sixth of a degree. This was the position of **Regulus** <note>original: "Basilisci," meaning 'The Little King,' the brightest star in the constellation Leo.</note>, through which the path to the positions of the other fixed stars was opened.

This observation of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer.</note> was made in the year of Christ according to the Roman reckoning 139, on the 24th day of February, in the first year of the 229th **Olympiad** <note>A four-year period used in ancient Greek dating.</note>. Thus that most eminent of mathematicians noted how much of a place each of the stars occupied relative to the **vernal equinox** <note>The point where the sun crosses the celestial equator in spring, used as a zero-point for coordinates.</note> at that time, and he set out the constellations of the heavenly figures.

In this, he has assisted our study in no small way and relieved us of a sufficiently arduous labor. Since we have decided that the positions of the stars should not be referred to the equinoxes—which change over time <note>Copernicus is referring to the precession of the equinoxes, the slow "wobble" of Earth's axis.</note>—but rather that the equinoxes should be referred to the sphere of the fixed stars, we can easily derive a description of the stars from an immutable principle. We have chosen to take this from **Aries**, as the first sign, and from its first star, which is in its head. In this way, the appearance of those things which shine from a permanent seat—as if fixed and coherent—will always remain the same and absolute.

Moreover, through the wonderful care and skill of the ancients, the stars were organized into 48 forms, except for those which were always hidden from view by the circle of the **fourth climate** <note>A geographical latitude zone; here referring to the stars too far south to be seen from the latitude of Rhodes or Alexandria.</note> through Rhodes. Thus those "unformed" stars remained unknown to them. Indeed, according to the opinion of **Theon the Younger** in his commentary on **Aratus**, the stars were formed into images for no other reason than that such a great multitude of them might be distinguished into parts and designated individually by specific names. This is an ancient practice; it is established that certain stars were already named in the Book of **Job**, such as the **Pleiades**, the **Hyades**, **Arcturus**, and **Orion**, and we read of them by name in **Hesiod** and **Homer** as well.

In our description of these stars according to longitude, we shall not use **twelfth-parts** <note>original: "dodecatemorijs," the twelve 30-degree signs of the zodiac (Aries, Taurus, etc.).</note> which are derived from the equinoxes and solstices, but rather a simple and continuous number of degrees. In other matters, we shall follow Ptolemy, with a few exceptions where we have found the data to be either distorted or otherwise different. However, we shall show how far their distance from those cardinal points <note>The equinoxes and solstices.</note> extends in the following book.

-> NICOLAUS COPERNICUS’S REVOLUTIONS: BOOK THREE <-

# On the Precession of the Equinoxes and Solstices. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring floral acanthus motifs and two human figures (putti) amidst the foliage.</image-desc>

Having described the appearance of the fixed stars, we must now pass on to those matters concerning the annual revolution. For this reason, we shall first treat the shift of the equinoxes, because of which the fixed stars themselves are also believed to move. We find that the ancient mathematicians did not distinguish the "turning" or natural year <note>original: "annum uertentem siue naturalem"</note>—which is measured from an equinox or solstice—from the year that is measured by one of the fixed stars. This is why they thought the Olympic years, which they began at the rising of the Dog Star <note>original: "Caniculæ"; referring to Sirius, the brightest star in the sky</note>, were the same as those measured from the solstice, for the difference between the two had not yet been recognized.

However, Hipparchus of Rhodes, a man of wonderful sagacity, was the first to notice that these two types of years differed. While observing the length of the year more closely, he found it to be longer when compared to the fixed stars than when compared to the equinoxes or solstices. From this, he suspected that there was also some motion in the fixed stars "in consequence" <term>in consequence: a technical term in early astronomy meaning moving forward in the order of the zodiac signs, i.e., from West to East</term>, but one so slow as to not be immediately perceptible. But now, with the passage of time, it has become very evident; we now see a far different rising and setting of the signs and stars than what was recorded by the ancients. 

Furthermore, the twelve divisions <term>dodecatemoria: the twelve 30-degree segments of the zodiac (Aries, Taurus, etc.)</term> of the circle of the signs have receded by a significant distance from the signs of the fixed stars, though originally they agreed in both name and position. Moreover, this motion is found to be unequal. Those wishing to explain the cause of this variation have offered different opinions. Some claimed it was a kind of "libration" <term>libration: a slow, oscillating or swinging motion, also known in this period as "trepidation"</term> of the hanging world—similar to the motion we find in the planets regarding their latitudes—and they judged that after it had proceeded a certain distance from its limits, it would eventually return. They estimated that this wandering to either side of the midpoint was no greater than eight degrees. But this opinion is now outdated and can no longer stand, especially because...

<sig>q iii</sig>
<meta>catchword: now</meta>

<summary>Copernicus introduces the phenomenon of the precession of the equinoxes, crediting Hipparchus with its discovery and noting how the zodiac signs have shifted away from their namesake constellations over centuries. He begins to critique previous theories, such as "trepidation," which suggested the stars merely swing back and forth rather than moving in a continuous cycle.</summary>

<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, Hipparchus, sidereal year, tropical year, zodiac signs, libration, trepidation, Sirius, Olympic years</keywords>

--- Page 142 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening chapter of Book III, where Copernicus discusses the historical observations of the precession of the equinoxes. He is transitioning from describing the theories of his predecessors (who added more celestial spheres to explain the movement) to his own revolutionary explanation: the wobbling of the Earth’s axis.</meta>

-> NICOLAUS COPERNICUS <-

it is now clear enough that the head of the constellation Aries <note>original: "caput Arietis stellati"; the starting point of the zodiac</note> is more than twenty-four degrees <note>original: "ter octo gradibus," literally "three times eight degrees"</note> distant from the vernal equinox, and other stars are similarly shifted, while in all these centuries no trace of a return movement has been perceived. Others have indeed thought that the sphere of the fixed stars moves forward, but in unequal steps, though they defined no certain rule for this. In addition, another wonder of nature occurred: the tilt of the zodiac <term>zodiac: original "signiferi," the "sign-bearer" or the path of the sun through the constellations</term> does not appear as great to us as it did to Ptolemy, as we have already said. Because of these things, some scholars invented a ninth sphere, others a tenth, through which they thought these effects were produced; yet they could not deliver what they promised. Now even an eleventh sphere had begun to emerge into the light, but we will easily refute this number of celestial circles as superfluous by means of the motion of the Earth.

For as we have already partially explained in the first book, two revolutions—namely, the annual declination <note>the tilt of the Earth's axis</note> and the movement of the Earth's center—are not exactly equal. Specifically, the completion of the declination slightly anticipates the period of the center. From this it must follow that the equinoxes and solstices <note>original: "conuersiones"</note> appear to move forward, not because the sphere of fixed stars is carried "in consequence" <term>in consequence: moving eastward, in the order of the zodiac signs</term>, but rather because the equinoctial circle <note>the celestial equator</note> moves "in precedence" <term>in precedence: moving westward, against the order of the zodiac signs</term>, being tilted relative to the plane of the zodiac according to the deflection of the axis of the terrestrial globe. 

Indeed, it would be more appropriate to say that the equinoctial circle is tilted relative to the zodiac, rather than the zodiac to the equinoctial, when comparing the smaller to the larger. For the zodiac is much larger—as it is described by the distance between the Sun and the Earth in its annual circuit—than the equinoctial circle, which is traced by the daily motion around the Earth's axis, as has been said. In this manner, those equinoctial points, along with the entire tilt of the zodiac, are seen to advance with the passage of time, while the stars are left behind. 

However, the measure and the reason for the variation of this motion remained hidden to those who came before us because the length of its total revolution is still unknown. This is due to its unexpected slowness; in all the centuries since it first became known to mortals, it has barely completed a fifteenth part of a circle. Nevertheless, as far as we are able, we will make these matters more certain through what we have received from historical observations up to our own memory.

<meta>catchword: History</meta>

<summary>Copernicus argues that the apparent movement of the stars is actually caused by a mismatch between the Earth's daily and annual rotations. He rejects the complicated "extra spheres" added by previous astronomers in favor of a simpler model based on the Earth's shifting axis.</summary>
<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, celestial spheres, Earth's axis, tilt of the zodiac, vernal equinox, Ptolemy, Aries</keywords>

Here, he begins to cite specific astronomical data from antiquity to the Middle Ages to prove that this shifting (precession) happens at an uneven rate.</meta>

-> ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK III. <-

### History of observations proving the unequal precession of the equinoxes and solstices. Chapter 2.

<note>original: "Cap. 11"; likely a transcription of "II" for Chapter 2.</note>

In the first period of 76 years according to Callippus <note>a Greek astronomer who refined the calendar cycle</note>, in its 36th year—which was the 30th year after the death of Alexander the Great—Timochares of Alexandria, who was the first to take care in recording the positions of the fixed stars, reported that **Spica**, which the constellation **Virgo** holds, was 82 1/3 degrees <note>original: "LXXXII. & triente," meaning eighty-two and one-third</note> distant from the summer solstice point, with a southern latitude of two degrees. He also recorded that the star which is most Northerly of the three in the forehead of **Scorpio**, and the first in the order of that constellation’s formation, had a latitude of 1 1/3 degrees, and a longitude of 32 degrees from the autumnal equinox. And again, in the 48th year of that same period, he found **Spica** in Virgo at a longitude of 82 1/2 degrees <note>original: "LXXXII. S." where S stands for semis, or one-half</note> from the summer solstice, while the latitude remained the same.

**Hipparchus**, however, in the 50th year of the third Callippic period (which was the 196th year since Alexander), found the star in the chest of **Leo** called **Regulus** <note>the "Little King" star</note> following the summer solstice by 29 5/6 degrees <note>original: "XXIX. S. & triente," literally twenty-nine, a half, and a third</note>. Later, the Roman geometer **Menelaus**, in the first year of the Emperor Trajan (which was 99 years from the birth of Christ and 422 years from the death of Alexander), reported **Spica** in Virgo to be 86 1/4 degrees distant in longitude from the solstice. He reported the star in the forehead of **Scorpio** to be 35 11/12 degrees <note>original: "XXXVI. minus uncia," thirty-six minus one-twelfth</note> from the autumnal equinox.

Following these, **Ptolemy**—in the second year of Antoninus Pius, as has been said, which was the 462nd year from the death of Alexander—learned that **Regulus** in Leo held 32 1/2 degrees from the solstice, **Spica** held 86 1/2 degrees, and the aforementioned star in the forehead of **Scorpio** held 36 1/3 degrees of longitude from the autumnal equinox, with the latitude having changed not at all, just as was expressed above in the Canonical exposition <note>referring to the star catalogs in his own or Ptolemy's work</note>. We have reviewed these measurements exactly as they were reported by those men.

After a long time, however—specifically in the 1202nd year after the death of Alexander—the observation of **Muhammad al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometi Aracensis," an influential Arab astronomer (c. 858–929 AD) whose work was vital to Copernicus</note> followed, in which we may place the greatest trust. In that year, **Regulus** (also called **Basiliscus**) in Leo was at 44 degrees and 5 minutes from the solstice, and the star in the forehead of **Scorpio** was at 47 degrees and 50 minutes <note>from the autumnal equinox</note>.

<summary>Copernicus compiles a timeline of star positions from ancient Greek, Roman, and medieval Arab astronomers to show how the distance between stars and the equinox points has changed inconsistently over 1,500 years.</summary>
<keywords>Timochares, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, al-Battani, Spica, Regulus, precession of equinoxes, astronomical history, Callippic period</keywords>

--- Page 144 ---
<meta>This page continues the list of historical observations of the star Spica, moving from the records of antiquity to Copernicus’s own era. It sets up a geometric proof to calculate the star's current position.</meta>

...were seen to have arrived from the autumnal equinox. In all of these observations, the latitude of each star always remained the same, so that there is no longer any doubt on this point. For this reason, in the Year of Christ **1525**—the first year after the second leap year, which is the **1849th** Egyptian year from the death of Alexander <note>Copernicus frequently uses "Egyptian years" of exactly 365 days, a standard in ancient astronomy, measuring from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE.</note>—we ourselves observed the often-mentioned star **Spica** in Frombork <note>original: "Frueburgio"; the town in Prussia where Copernicus lived and worked.</note> in Prussia. Its maximum altitude on the meridian circle was seen to be very close to **27** degrees. We have found the latitude of Frombork to be **54** degrees and **19.5** minutes <note>original: "XIX. s." where s. stands for 'semis' or one-half.</note>. Therefore, its declination <note>the angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> from the equator is established as **8** degrees and **40** minutes. From this, its position was revealed as follows.

We have described the meridian circle **ABCD** passing through the poles of both the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally 'the sign-bearer.'</note> and the equator. Let the common sections and diameters be **AC** for the equator and **BD** for the zodiac. Let the North pole be **F** and the axis be **FEG**. Let **B** be the beginning of Capricorn and **D** the beginning of Cancer.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram. A large circle is labeled with points A (right), C (left), B (bottom right quadrant), and D (top left quadrant). The vertical axis is F (top) to G (bottom). The horizontal diameter is AC, representing the equinoctial line. A diagonal diameter BD represents the zodiac axis. A chord HL is drawn parallel to BD, intersecting the vertical axis at I and the equinoctial line at K. Another horizontal line MN is drawn parallel to AC, intersecting HL at point O. A vertical line OP is dropped from O to the line AC.</image-desc>

Now, let the arc **BH** be assumed equal to the star’s southern latitude of two degrees. From point **H**, let a line **HL** be drawn parallel to **BD**, which cuts the axis of the zodiac at **I** and the equator at **K**. Let the arc **MA** also be taken according to the southern declination of the star, being **8** degrees and **40** minutes. From point **M**, let **MN** be drawn parallel to **AC**. This will intersect the parallel of the zodiac **HL**; let it intersect at point **O**. The straight line **OP**, dropped at right angles, will be equal to half the chord of twice the declination **AM** <note>This is a standard geometric method in Renaissance astronomy to calculate sines and coordinates using chords of arcs.</note>.

But indeed, the circles of which **FG, HL, and MN** are diameters are perpendicular to the plane **ABCD**. Their common sections through the **19th** proposition of the eleventh book of Euclid’s *Elements* <note>Copernicus relies heavily on Euclidean geometry to prove that these three-dimensional celestial circles intersect at right angles in his two-dimensional diagram.</note> are at right angles to the same plane at points **O** and **I**; by the sixth proposition of the same book, they are parallel to each other. And since **I** is the center of the circle whose diameter is **HL**, then **OI** will be equal to half the chord of twice the arc in the circle of diameter **HL**—an arc similar to the one by which the star is distant from the beginning of Libra, according to the longitude we are seeking.

It is found in this way: for the angles **OKP** and **AEB** are equal (the exterior to the interior and opposite), and **OPK** is a right angle. Therefore, the ratio of **OP** to **OK** is the same as the ratio of half the chord of twice **AB** to **BE**...

<meta>catchword: to BE</meta>

<summary>Copernicus records his own 1525 observation of the star Spica in Frombork to determine its modern declination. He then begins a geometric demonstration using Euclidean principles to calculate the star's longitude based on these observations.</summary>
<keywords>Spica, Frombork, declination, latitude, Euclid, meridian circle, zodiac, geometry, 1525 observation</keywords>
