<meta>This page continues the geometric calculations following the diagram on page 64. Copernicus is determining the longitude of the star Spica to demonstrate that the rate of the precession of the equinoxes is not constant throughout history.</meta>

# REVOLUTIONS BOOK III.

to **BE**; and the half-chord of the doubled arc **AH** to **HK** <note>In the trigonometry of Copernicus’s era, the "half-chord of the double arc" corresponds to the modern sine function.</note>; for they encompass triangles similar to **OPK**. But **AB** is **23** degrees **28** minutes and a half <note>original: "scrup. XXVIII. s."; 's.' stands for 'semis,' meaning one half.</note>, and its half-chord of the double arc is 39,832 parts, where **BE** is 100,000. And the arc **ABH** is **25** degrees **28** minutes and a half, of which the half-chord of the double arc is 43,010 parts. Moreover, **MA** is the half-chord of the double declination, being 15,069 parts. From these it follows that the whole line **HK** is 107,978 parts, and **OK** is 37,831 parts, and the remaining line **HO** is 70,147 parts. But double **HOI** subtends a segment of the circle **HGL** of **176** degrees; therefore **HOI** itself will be 99,939 parts, where **BE** was 100,000. Consequently, the remaining part **OI** is 29,892 parts. Insofar as **HOI** is the radius <note>original: "dimidia diametri"; half of the diameter.</note> of 100,000 parts, **OI** will be 29,810 parts, to which corresponds an arc of approximately **17** degrees **21** minutes. This was the distance of **Spica** in Virgo from the beginning of **Libra**, and this was the location of the star itself.

Also ten years earlier, namely in the year **1515**, we found it [the star] to have a declination of **8** degrees **36** minutes, and its position at **17** degrees **14** minutes of **Libra**. However, **Ptolemy** reported that this star's declination was only half of one degree; its position would therefore have been at **26** degrees **40** minutes of **Virgo**. This seems more likely to be true when compared with preceding observations.

From this it seems clear enough that for almost the entire time from **Timocharis** to **Ptolemy**, over **432** years, the equinoxes and solstices <note>original: "conuersiones"; literally 'turnings,' a standard term for solstices.</note> were changed by precessing, for the most part, at a rate of one degree every hundred years. A constant ratio was always maintained between the time and the length of their passage, which in total was **4** degrees and one-third. For even regarding the summer solstice <note>original: "aestivam tropen."</note> relative to **Regulus** <note>original: "Basiliscum Leonis"; literally 'The Little King of the Lion.'</note>, from **Hipparchus** to **Ptolemy** in **276** years, the stars moved **2** degrees and two-thirds; thus here too, by comparison of the time, they are found to have anticipated [precessed] by one degree in a hundred years.

Furthermore, regarding the stars in the "forehead of the Scorpion" <note>the star Beta Scorpii.</note> recorded by **Albategnius** <note>The Latinized name of the Arab astronomer al-Battani (c. 858–929 CE).</note> compared to those of **Menelaus**, in the intervening **682** years, since **11** degrees **55** minutes passed, in no way should one degree be attributed to a hundred years, but rather to **66** years. From **Ptolemy**'s time [to al-Battani's], however, in **741** years, one degree would be attributed to only **65** years. Finally, if the remaining interval of **645** years [from al-Battani to our time] is compared to the difference of **9** degrees **11** minutes in our own observation, one degree will be found to take **71** years. From these facts it is evident that the precession was slower...

The other motion increases and decreases the precessions of the solstices and equinoxes by a movement made crosswise from side to side. We call these motions **librations** <term>librations</term> <note>From the Latin "libra" (scale/balance); an oscillation like the swinging of a pendulum.</note>, because, like swinging weights, they follow the same path between two limits, moving fastest in the middle and slowest at the ends. Variations of this kind occur frequently regarding the latitudes of the planets, as we shall see in the proper place. These motions also differ in their cycles, because the inequality of the equinoxes completes two revolutions for every one revolution of the obliquity. 

Just as in every case of apparent unequal motion, a "mean" or average state must be understood so that the rate of the inequality can be measured. Thus, it was necessary to conceive of "mean" poles and a "mean" equinoctial circle, as well as mean equinoctial intersections and points of the solstices. The actual poles and the equinoctial circle of the Earth deflect from these mean points to and fro, yet within fixed limits, making those uniform motions appear diverse. Thus, these two librations occurring together cause the poles of the Earth, over time, to describe lines similar to a **twisted crown** <note>original: "corollæ intortæ"; this refers to the looped or figure-eight path traced by the Earth's axis due to the combined oscillations.</note>.

However, since it is not easy to explain these things adequately with words alone—and I fear they will be even harder to understand by hearing unless they are also seen with the eyes—let us describe a diagram. On the sphere, let us draw the circle of the zodiac signs, **ABCD**. Let its North pole be **E**. Let the beginning of Capricorn be **A**, Cancer **C**, Aries **B**, and Libra **D**. Through the signs **A** and **C** and the pole **E**, let the circle **AEC** be drawn. Let the maximum distance between the poles of the zodiac and the equinoctial be **EF**, the minimum **EG**, and let the mean pole be at the midpoint **I**. Around this mean pole, let the equinoctial circle **BHD** be described, which shall be called the "mean" equinoctial, and **B** and **D** shall be the "mean" equinoxes. 

All these points are carried around pole **E** in a constant motion toward the preceding signs <note>original: "in præcedentia"; this means a westward motion, moving against the natural order of the zodiac signs (Aries to Pisces rather than Aries to Taurus).</note>, that is, against the order of the signs in the sphere of the fixed stars, with a slow motion, as has been stated. Now, let us imagine two reciprocating motions of the terrestrial poles, like swinging pendulums. One motion occurs between the limits **F** and **G**, which shall be called the "anomaly of the declination"—that is, the inequality of the tilt. The other motion is transverse, from the preceding signs toward the following, and back again, which we shall call the "anomaly of the equinoxes," moving twice as fast as the first. In this position, the movement of the equinoxes and solstices will once again appear to be at its slowest, almost exactly as it was at **f**. However, the motion of the obliquity—from the maximum tilt to the minimum—has only completed half of its circuit.

### How a Reciprocal or Oscillating Motion is Composed of Circular Motions. Chapter IV.

We will now demonstrate how this motion agrees with what we observe. In the meantime, however, someone might ask how the regularity of these oscillations <term>librations</term> <note>A "libration" is a slow rocking or swaying motion, like a balance scale (libra) tipping back and forth.</note> can be understood, since we stated at the very beginning that celestial motion is uniform, or composed of uniform and circular motions.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing three circles. A large outer circle is labeled A at the top and B at the bottom, with a vertical diameter line A-B. In this case, two motions appear as one between the two limits, where a pause must necessarily occur. We will admit that these motions are doubled, yet we can demonstrate that they are made of uniform motions in the following way. Let there be a straight line **A B**, divided into four parts at points **C**, **D**, and **E**. Around the center **D**, let concentric circles <term>concentric</term> <note>Circles that share the exact same center point, like ripples in a pond.</note> **A D B** and **C D E** be described in the same plane. On the circumference of the inner circle, let any point **F** be chosen. With **F** as the center and **F D** as the radius, let a smaller circle **G H D** be described, which intersects the straight line **A B** at point **H**, and let the diameter **D F G** be drawn. 

It must be shown that when the twin motions of circles **G H D** and **C F E** occur together, the moving point **H** travels back and forth along the same straight line **A B** in a reciprocating motion. This will happen if we understand that point **H** moves in the opposite direction to point **F**, and at twice the speed. For the same angle **C D F** at the center of circle **C F E** (which also stands on the circumference of circle **G H D**) contains both arcs of these equal circles; thus the arc **G H** is double the arc **F C**. Let us assume that at some moment, when the straight lines **A C D** and **D F G** were joined together, the moving point **H** was at **G** (coinciding with **A**) and **F** was at **C**. But now the center **F** has moved toward the right along arc **F C**, and **H** itself has moved along the circumference **G H** toward the left, a distance twice as great as **F C**...

**Colure of Cancer** <note>A "colure" is one of two great circles on the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles. The Colure of Cancer passes through the summer and winter solstices.</note>. Let the pole of the equator be $f$, through which the great circle $f e t$ is described; this will therefore be the colure of the mean or equal equinoxes. For the sake of a clearer demonstration, let us now separate the **libration** <note>A slow, rhythmic oscillation, like the swinging of a balance scale.</note> of the equinoxes from the obliquity of the zodiac. But if we describe the circle $a g c$ with $k$ as the pole, and it is understood that during the time the libration $f g$ occurs, the true pole did not remain at point $g$ but was moved by the impulse of another libration toward the obliquity of the zodiac along the arc $g o$. Therefore, while the zodiac $b e d$ remains fixed, the true apparent equator will be changed according to the transposition of the pole to $o$. Similarly, the motion of this intersection $l$ (the apparent equinox) will be swifter around the center $e$ and slowest at the extremes, almost proportional to the libration of the poles already demonstrated. This was a point well worth noting.

### On the uniform motions of the precession of the equinoxes and the inclination of the zodiac. Chapter VI.

**Every apparent variation in circular motion occurs within four boundaries:** there is a point where it appears slow, a point where it is fast (as if at the extremes), and points where it is of average speed (as if in the middle). This is because the motion passes from the end of its slowing down and the beginning of its speeding up toward the average speed; from the average speed, it grows into its maximum velocity; then, from the fast stage, it tends back toward the average; finally, what remains of the cycle returns from that equality to the prior slowness. These stages allow us to understand in which part of the circle the location of the **variation** <note>original: "diversitatis sive anomaliæ." In astronomy, "anomaly" refers to the angle used to calculate the irregular part of a planet's or point's motion.</note> or **anomaly** was at any given time, and by what signs the completion of that anomaly is perceived. 

Imagine a circle divided into four parts: let **A** be the place of greatest slowness, **B** the increasing average speed, **C** the end of the increase and beginning of the decrease (maximum speed), and **D** the decreasing average speed. 

Since, as stated previously, the apparent motion of the precession of the equinoxes was found to be slower between the time of **Timocharis** <note>An Alexandrian astronomer (c. 320–260 BCE) whose observations were used by later astronomers to discover precession.</note> and **Ptolemy** than in other periods—and because it appeared equal and uniform for a while, as shown by the observations of **Aristyillus**, **Hipparchus**, **Agrippa**, and **Menelaus** in the intervening years—it argues that the apparent motion of the equinoxes was at its absolute slowest. It was in the middle of that period, at the beginning of its increase, when the ceasing of the deceleration joined with the beginning of the acceleration. Through this mutual compensation, the motion appeared uniform for a time. Therefore, the observation of Timocharis must be placed in the last part of the circle in the quadrant **DA**, while Ptolemy’s observation falls into the first quadrant, **AB**. 

Again, because in the second interval from Ptolemy to **Muhammad of Ar Raqqah** <note>original: "Machometũ Aratenſem," referring to the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani (Albategnius), whose precise observations corrected many of Ptolemy's figures.</note> a faster motion is found than in the third interval, it declares that the maximum velocity—that is, point **C**—was passed during that second time interval. The anomaly has now reached the third quadrant of the circle, **CD**. In the interval leading up to our own time, the cycle of the anomaly is almost complete, returning toward the starting point of Timocharis. 

For if we distribute the total circuit of 360 degrees over the 1,819 years from Timocharis to us, we will have (in proportion to the years) a circumference of 85 degrees and 30 minutes for the first 432 years. For the next 743 years, the circumference is 146 degrees and 51 minutes. In the remaining 645 years, the remaining circumference is 127 degrees and 39 minutes. By this obvious and simple **conjecture** <note>The text ends mid-sentence on the word "conjectura."</note>

<summary>Copernicus analyzes historical astronomical data to map the "anomaly" (irregularity) of the equinoxes onto a four-part circular model, concluding that the Earth is nearing the end of a long-term cycle that began in antiquity.</summary>
<keywords>precession of the equinoxes, anomaly, Timocharis, Ptolemy, Al-Battani, celestial mechanics, historical observations</keywords>

# NICOLAI COPERNICI

...we accepted by conjecture, but reconsidering with a more exact calculation to see how closely they agreed with the observations, we found that the **motion of the anomaly** <note>The "anomaly" refers to the specific cycle of irregularity in the Earth's wobbling motion.</note> in **1,819 Egyptian years** <note>An Egyptian year consists of exactly 365 days, without leap years, commonly used by ancient astronomers for ease of calculation.</note> had already exceeded its complete revolution by **21 degrees and 24 minutes**. We found the time of the full period to be only **1,717 Egyptian years**. By this ratio, the first segment of the circle is shown to contain **90 degrees and 35 minutes**; the second, **155 degrees and 34 minutes**; and the third, over the remaining **543 years**, will contain the remaining parts of the circle, **113 degrees and 51 minutes**.

With these values established, the **mean motion** <note>The "mean motion" is the idealized, perfectly uniform speed of an astronomical body, averaged over time to smooth out temporary fluctuations.</note> of the **precession of the equinoxes** also became clear: it is **23 degrees and 57 minutes** over those same **1,717 years**, during which the entire variation is restored to its original state. This is because in the **1,819 years** we had an apparent motion of nearly **25 degrees and 1 minute**. However, since the time of **Timocharis** <note>An Alexandrian astronomer (3rd century BCE) whose star catalogs were the earliest available to Copernicus.</note> across the **102 years** that separate the **1,717-year** period from the **1,819-year** period, the apparent motion ought to have been about **1 degree and 4 minutes**. This is likely because the motion was somewhat larger then, as it would have exceeded one degree per century; it was still decreasing at that time and had not yet reached the end of its deceleration. 

Therefore, if we subtract one and one-fifteenth degrees from the **25 degrees and 1 minute**, there will remain what we stated for the **1,717 Egyptian years**: a mean and equal motion, adjusted to the varying and apparent motion, which is then equalized at **23 degrees and 57 minutes**. From this, a complete and uniform revolution of the precession of the equinoxes arises in **25,816 years**. During this time, there are approximately **15 cycles and 1/28th** of the anomaly. 

The motion of the **obliquity** <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic" is the angle of the Earth's tilt, which Copernicus correctly identifies as changing over time.</note> also accommodates itself to this ratio; we previously said its return was twice as slow as the precession of the equinoxes. For **Ptolemy** reported the obliquity as **23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds**. He indicates that 400 years before his time, **Aristarchus of Samos** <note>The ancient Greek astronomer who first proposed a sun-centered system; Copernicus cites him here specifically for his measurements of the Earth's tilt.</note> found it had changed very little, which suggests that the tilt was then established near its maximum limit—at a time, evidently, when the precession of the equinoxes was at its slowest motion. But now, while that same restoration of slowness is being approached, the inclination of the axis does not pass into its maximum, but into its minimum. In the intervening time, **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometus Aratensis." A 9th-century Arab astronomer whose precise observations were crucial for medieval and Renaissance science.</note> found it to be **23 degrees and 35 minutes**, as was said. **Al-Zarqali** <note>original: "Arzachel Hispanus." An 11th-century Arab astronomer from Al-Andalus (Spain).</note>, 190 years after him, found it to be **23 degrees and 34 minutes**. Likewise, 230 years after that, **Profacius the Jew** <note>original: "Prophatius Iudaeus." Also known as Jacob ben Machir ibn Tibbon, a 13th-century astronomer and translator in Montpellier.</note> found it nearly two minutes smaller. Finally, concerning our own times, we have found through frequent observation over the last 30 years that it is nearly **23 degrees, 28 minutes, and two-fifths** of a minute. From these values, **Georg von Peuerbach** <note>original: "Georgius Purbachius." A 15th-century European astronomer who helped revive Ptolemaic astronomy.</note> and **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>original: "Ioannes de Monteregio." One of the most influential mathematicians and astronomers of the 15th century, who died before finishing his work.</note>, who...

-># BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

...they differ little from those who preceded us most recently. Here again, it is very clearly evident that the change in **obliquity** <note>The "obliquity of the ecliptic" is the angle of the Earth's tilt relative to its orbit. Copernicus believed this tilt changed slightly over long cycles.</note> from the time of **Ptolemy** over a span of 900 years was greater than in any other interval of time. Therefore, since we now have the circuit of the **anomaly of precession** <note>The cycle of the irregularity in the shifting of the equinoxes.</note> as 1,717 years, we will also have half the period of the obliquity in that same time, and its full restoration in 3,434 years.

Consequently, if we divide 360 degrees by that same number of 3,434 years, or 180 degrees by 1,717, the annual motion of the simple anomaly will come out to be 6 minutes, 17 seconds, 24 thirds, and 9 fourths. <note>Copernicus uses sexagesimal fractions: a "minute" is 1/60, a "second" is 1/3600, a "third" is 1/216,000, and so on.</note> These values, distributed again over 365 days, yield a daily motion of 1 second, 2 thirds, and 2 fourths.

Similarly, when the **mean motion** of the precession of the equinoxes is distributed over 1,717 years—during which it was 23 degrees and 57 minutes—the annual motion will come out to 50 seconds, 12 thirds, and 5 fourths; and from this, the daily motion over 365 days is 8 thirds and 15 fourths.

To make these motions clearer and readily available when needed, we will set out **Tables** or **Canons** of them by the continuous and uniform addition of the annual motion. We will always carry over any values exceeding 60 into the preceding minutes or degrees, and we have compiled these up to the order of 60 years for the sake of convenience. This is because in groups of sixty years, the same pattern of numbers presents itself, with only the denominations of the parts and minutes transposed—so that what were previously seconds become minutes, and so forth. By using these brief tables as a shortcut, it will be possible to calculate and collect the uniform motions for any given years within a 3,600-year range by a simple double entry. The same applies to the number of days.

In the calculation of celestial motions, we will use **Egyptian years** everywhere. Among all civil calendars, these alone are found to be uniform. For it is necessary that a measure agrees with the thing measured; this is not the case with the years of the Romans, Greeks, or Persians, which are intercalated <note>Intercalation refers to adding leap days or months to a calendar to keep it in sync with the seasons.</note> not in one single way, but according to the custom of each nation. The Egyptian year, however, presents no ambiguity: it consists of a fixed number of 365 days. These comprise twelve equal months, which they call by their own names in order: **Thoth, Phaophi, Athyr, Chiach, Tybi, Mechyr, Phamenoth, Pharmuthi, Pachon, Pauni, Epiphi, Mesori**. These equally contain six groups of sixty days, plus five remaining days, which they call **intercalary**. For this reason, Egyptian years are the most suitable for calculating uniform motions, as any other years can be easily reduced to them by resolving the time into days.

# REVOLUTIONS BOOK III.

### Motion of the anomaly of the equinoxes in days and sixty-day periods. <note>The "anomaly" refers to the irregularity or "trepidation" that 16th-century astronomers believed occurred in the precession of the equinoxes. ### Chapter 7. What is the greatest difference between the uniform and apparent precession of the equinoxes?

Now that the mean motions <note>original: "mediis motibus"; the theoretical average movement of the stars over time.</note> have been set forth, we must now investigate how great the maximum difference is between the uniform and the apparent motion of the equinoxes, or the diameter of the small circle through which the motion of the anomaly revolves. For once this is known, it will be easy to distinguish any other differences in these motions. As has been recounted above, there were 432 years between the first observation of **Timocharis** <note>An Alexandrian astronomer (c. 320–260 BCE) whose star coordinates were used by later astronomers to discover the shifting of the stars.</note> and that of **Ptolemy** in the second year of **Antoninus** <note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius; the observation occurred around 139 CE.</note>. In that time, the mean motion was 6 degrees, while the apparent motion was 4 degrees and 20 minutes; the difference between these is 1 degree and 40 minutes. The motion of the double anomaly was also 90 degrees and 35 minutes. It also appeared that near the middle of this time, the apparent motion reached the point of greatest slowness; at that point, it is necessary for the apparent motion to agree with the mean motion, and for the true and mean equinoxes to have been at the same intersection of the circles. Therefore, by dividing the motion and the time into two parts,

[An image of a geometrical diagram is here. It depicts the zodiacal arc ABC and the mean equinoctial line DBE. A vertical line BF drops from the center, and points I and K on the arc are connected to the vertical via lines IG and HK, illustrating the mathematical relationship between the mean and apparent positions of the equinoxes.]

there will be, on both sides, differences between the varying and uniform motion of ten-twelfths <note>original: "dextantes"; a Roman fraction meaning 10/12ths of a unit. Here, 10/12ths of a degree equals 50 minutes.</note> of one degree, which the circumferences of the circle of anomaly comprise on either side across 45 degrees and 17.5 minutes. 

With these values thus established, let **ABC** be the circumference of the zodiac, and **DBE** the mean equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note> line, and let **B** be the mean intersection of the apparent equinoxes (either of Aries or Libra), and let **BF** descend through the poles of **DBE**. Now, let equal circumferences **BI** and **BK** be taken on both sides of **ABC** by ten-twelfths of a degree, so that the whole distance **IBK** is 1 degree and 40 minutes. Let there also be introduced two circumferences of the apparent equinoctial circles, **IG** and **HK**, at right angles to **FB**. I say "at right angles," although

...however, their poles $I, G$ and $H, K$ <note>Referring to the points in the geometric diagram established in the previous section.</note> often lie outside the circle $BF$ because the motion of declination <note>The "motion of declination" refers to the north-south "wobble" or change in the tilt of the Earth's axis (obliquity).</note> is mixed in, as was seen in the hypothesis. But because of the very small distance—which at its maximum does not exceed the 1/450th part of a right angle—we use them as if they were right angles to the senses, for no perceptible error will appear because of it.

Therefore, in triangle $IBG$, the angle $IBG$ is given as 66 degrees and 20 minutes, since the remaining angle from the right angle $DBA$ was 23 degrees and 40 minutes (the angle of the mean obliquity of the zodiac <note>original: "obliquitatis signiferi"; the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit, which Copernicus calculates here at roughly 23.6 degrees.</note>), and $BGI$ is a right angle; also, the angle at $BIG$ is almost equal to $IBD$. Since the side $IB$ is 50 minutes, the circumference $BG$—the distance between the mean and apparent poles—is therefore given as 20 minutes. Similarly, in triangle $BHK$, the two angles $BHK$ and $HBK$ are equal to the two angles $IBG$ and $IGB$; and as side $BK$ is equal to side $BI$, then $BH$ will also be equal to $BG$, namely 20 minutes.

But since all these calculations involve the smallest of quantities—seeing as they do not even reach one and a half degrees of the zodiac <note>original: "zodiaci sesquigradum"</note>—in which straight lines subtending those arcs are almost exactly equal to the arcs themselves, and a difference is scarcely found even in the "thirds" <note>A "third" is a further subdivision of time or measurement: a degree is divided into 60 minutes, a minute into 60 seconds, and a second into 60 thirds.</note>, we commit no error if we use straight lines instead of circular arcs.

Let $ABC$ be the portion of the zodiacal circle <note>original: "circuli signorum"</note> in which $B$ is the mean equinox. With $B$ taken as the pole,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a large arc or circle segment labeled A, B, and C along the bottom/outer curve. An inner semi-circular arc is labeled A, D, C. A vertical line connects point B to point D. A point E is marked on the arc AD, and a vertical line segment drops from E to point F on the horizontal line between A and B.</image-desc>

describe the semicircle $ADC$, which cuts the zodiac at points $A$ and $C$. Let $DB$ also be drawn from the pole of the zodiac, which will also bisect the described semicircle at point $D$. Under $D$, the point of maximum slowness and the beginning of the increase [in motion] is understood to be. In the quadrant $AD$, let arc $DE$ be taken as 45 degrees and 17.5 minutes. Through point $E$, let $EF$ descend from the pole of the zodiac, and let $BF$ be 50 minutes. Our task is to find the total distance $BFA$ from these values.

It is clear, therefore, that twice $BF$ subtends twice the segment $DE$. Just as $BF$ is 7107 parts to $AFB$'s 10,000, so are the 50 minutes of $BF$ to $AFB$'s 70. Thus, $AB$ is given as 1 degree and 10 minutes. This is the maximum difference between the mean and apparent motions of the equinoxes which we were seeking, from which follows the maximum deflection of the poles of 28 minutes.

## On the individual differences of these motions, and
## their tabulated explanation. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>Historiated decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text. Inside the square frame of the letter is a woodcut illustration showing a landscape with buildings, trees, and hills under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

Since, therefore, the arc $AB$ is given as 70 minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum LXX"; minutes of arc (1/60th of a degree). Copernicus is treating this very small curve as a straight line for the sake of calculation.</note>, which as a circumference seems to differ not at all from a straight line subtended according to its length, it will not be difficult to display any other individual differences between the mean and apparent motions. These the Greeks call *Prosthaphæreses* <note>original: "Prosthaphærefes"; from Greek, meaning "additions and subtractions." These are the mathematical corrections applied to an average or "mean" position to find the true "apparent" position of a celestial body.</note>, and the more recent astronomers call *equations*, by whose subtraction or addition the observations are reconciled. We shall use the Greek term instead, as being more appropriate.

If, therefore, the arc $ED$ is three degrees, following the ratio of $AB$ to the subtended line $BF$, we will have the *prosthaphæresis* $BF$ as 4 minutes. If it were six degrees, it would be 7 minutes; for nine degrees, eleven; and so on for the rest.

Regarding the change in obliquity <note>term: obliquity: the angle of the Earth's axial tilt, which Copernicus argues oscillates slightly over long periods of time.</note>, we think we should proceed in a similar way, where 24 minutes have been found between the maximum and minimum values, as we said. These are completed under a semicircle of "simple anomaly" <note>An "anomaly" is the position within a cycle; here, it refers to the 1,717-year cycle of the axial wobble.</note> in 1,717 years. The middle consistency <note>The midpoint of the cycle where the movement is most stable.</note> under a quadrant of the circle will be 12 minutes, where the pole of this small circle of anomaly will be at an obliquity of 24 degrees and 40 minutes <note>original: "partium XXIIII. scrup. XL." Note: most editions of Copernicus record this as 23° 40', suggesting a possible variant or error in this specific transcription's source.</note>. 

And in this manner, as we have said, we shall extract the remaining parts of the difference, nearly proportional to those mentioned above, as contained in the table placed below. Although the apparent motions can be composed in various ways through these demonstrations, that method nevertheless pleased us more by which each individual *prosthaphæresis* is taken separately, so that the calculation of these motions might be easier to understand and more closely match the explanations of the things demonstrated.

We have, therefore, compiled a table of 60 rows, increasing by sets of three degrees <note>original: "triadas partiū"; increments of three degrees.</note> of the circle. For in this way, it will neither occupy an oversized space, nor seem to have an overly cramped brevity; and we shall do the same in other similar cases. This table will now have four columns, of which the first two contain the degrees of each semicircle, which we call the *common number*, because through a simple number the obliquity of the signs of the circle <note>The Ecliptic or Zodiac.</note> is taken, and when doubled it will serve the *prosthaphæresis* of the equinoxes, the beginning of which is taken from the start of the increase...

### REVOLUTIONS BOOK III.

In the third place, the corrections <note>original: "prosthaphæreses"</note> of the equinoxes will be arranged, to be added to or subtracted from the mean motion for each three-degree interval. We measure this mean motion from the first star in the head of Aries <note>Traditionally the starting point of the zodiac; Copernicus uses the stars themselves as a fixed reference frame.</note> toward the vernal equinox. The corrections are subtractive when the anomaly <note>term: anomaly: the specific angle or position within a cycle used to look up a correction in a table.</note> is in the first semicircle (the first column), and additive in the second column and the following semicircle.

Finally, in the last place, are the minutes called the "proportional differences of obliquity," which increase to a total of sixty <note>original: "summam sexagenariam"</note>. Since we set the value of 60 to represent the maximum and minimum excess of 24 minutes of obliquity <note>Copernicus is using a scale where 60 represents the full range of change (24 arc-minutes), allowing for easy fractional calculations.</note>, we arrange the parts for the remaining excesses according to that same ratio. Therefore, at the beginning and end of the anomaly, we place 60. But where the excess reaches 22 minutes—as in an anomaly of 33 degrees—we place 55 in its stead. Likewise, for 20 minutes we place 50, as in an anomaly of 28 degrees; and so on for the rest, as is clear in the table provided below.

<header>BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.</header>

## On the examination and correction of what has been set
## forth concerning the precession of the equinoxes. Chapter IX.

But since we have assumed by conjecture that the beginning of the increase in the differing motion occurred in the middle time—from the 36th year of the first Calippic period <note>A 76-year Greek calendar cycle used for astronomical dating; the 36th year corresponds to roughly 295 BCE</note> to the second year of Antoninus <note>The Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius; his second year corresponds to 139 CE</note>—it is from this beginning that we start the motion of the anomaly <term>anomaly|the irregular or "wobbling" part of the celestial motion</term>. Whether we have done this correctly, and whether it agrees with the observations, we must still put to the test. Let us reconsider those three observations of the stars made by Timocharis, Ptolemy, and al-Battani <note>Original: "Machometis Aratei," referring to the 9th-century astronomer al-Battani</note>. It is clear that in the first interval there were 432 Egyptian years <note>A year of exactly 365 days, used by ancient astronomers for ease of calculation</note>. In the second interval, there were 742 years. The mean <term>mean motion|the theoretical constant, average speed of a celestial body</term> motion in the first space of time was 6 degrees, and the differing motion was 4 degrees and 20 minutes <term>minutes|literally "scrupula" or "scruples," meaning 1/60th of a degree</term>. The motion of the double anomaly <note>Copernicus uses a "double" anomaly in his geometry to represent the back-and-forth movement</note> was 90 degrees and 35 minutes, subtracting 1 degree and 40 minutes from the mean motion. In the second interval, the mean motion was 10 degrees and 21 minutes. The differing motion was 11 and a half degrees. The motion of the double anomaly was 155 degrees and 34 minutes, adding 1 degree and 9 minutes to the mean motion. Now, let the circumference of the zodiac be A B C as before, and let B be the mean vernal equinox. With a pole established, let a small circle A D C E be described with a radius <note>Original: "circumferentia A B," likely referring here to the distance from the center B</note> of 1 degree and 10 minutes. Let the mean motion of B itself be understood to move toward A, that is, in precedence <note>westward, in the direction of the precession of the equinoxes</note>. Let A be the western limit, where the differing equinox precedes the most, and C the eastern limit, where the differing equinox follows the most.

<image-desc>A circular geometrical diagram centered at point B. A horizontal diameter line passes through B, with point A marked on the left edge of the circumference. Points F and G are marked on the upper arc of the circle. Arcs are drawn connecting point F to N, point G to M, and a point P on the lower right circumference to point O.</image-desc>

From the pole of the zodiac through point B, let the line D B E descend, which will cut the small circle A D C E into four equal parts along with the circle of signs <note>the ecliptic or zodiac path</note>, because they intersect each other at right angles through the poles. When the motion in the semicircle A D C is toward the following signs, and the remaining semicircle C E A is toward the preceding signs, the midpoint of the slowness of the apparent equinox will be at D because its motion resists the forward progress of point B. At E, however, there will be the greatest velocity, as the motions both advance in the same direction. Let there also be taken before and after D the arcs F D and D G, each being 45 degrees and 17 and a half minutes. Let F be the first limit of the anomaly, which belongs to Timocharis; G the second, which is Ptolemy's; and the third, P, which is al-Battani's. was 200 degrees and 51 and a half minutes <note>Original: "S." for "semis," meaning one half</note>, and **EP** is the excess over the semicircle of 20 degrees and 51 and a half minutes. Therefore, according to the **Table of Chords** <term>Table of Chords|A precursor to the modern sine table used to calculate the lengths of lines within a circle</term>, **BO** will be as a straight line of 356 parts where **AB** is 1000. But where **AB** is 70 minutes, **BO** will be nearly 24 minutes, and **BM** was established at 50 minutes. Therefore, the whole **MBO** is 74 minutes, and the remaining **NO** is 26 minutes. But in the previous setup, **MBO** was 1 degree and 9 minutes <note>69 minutes</note>, and the remaining **NO** was 31 minutes. Here, 5 minutes are missing, while there they were in excess. Therefore, the circle **ADCE** must be rotated until a compensation for both parts is made.

This will be achieved if we take the circumference **DG** to be 43 and a half degrees, so that in the remainder **DF** there are 48 degrees and 5 minutes. By this, the error on both sides will appear to be satisfied, as well as for all the other points. Since taking the beginning from the highest limit of slowness **D**, the motion of the anomaly in the first term will be the entire circumference **DGCEPAF**, which is 311 degrees and 55 minutes. In the second term, **DG** is 43 and a half degrees. In the third term, **DGCEP** is 198 degrees and 4 minutes. And for those in which **AB** was 70 minutes: in the first term, **BN** will be an additive **prosthaphaeresis** <term>prosthaphaeresis|The difference or "correction" needed to convert mean (average) motion into true, observed motion</term> of 52 minutes according to the previously held demonstrations. In the second term, **MB** will be 47 and a half minutes, which is subtractive. And in the third term, **BO** is again additive, being nearly 21 minutes.

Therefore, the whole **MN** in the first interval collects 1 degree and 40 minutes, and the whole **MBO** in the second interval collects 1 degree and 9 minutes; these agree sufficiently and exactly with the observations. By these calculations, it is also clear that the simple anomaly in the first term is 155 degrees and 57 and a half minutes; in the second, 21 degrees and 15 minutes; and in the third, 99 degrees and 2 minutes. This was what was to be declared.

## Chapter 10. What the Greatest Difference is Between the Intersections of the Equator and the Zodiac.

In a similar way, we shall prove that the explanations given regarding the change of the <term>obliquity|The tilt of the Earth's axis, which causes the seasons</term> of the zodiac and the <term>equinoctial|The celestial equator</term> are correct. For we held that in the second year of Antoninus <note>Ptolemy recorded these observations around 139 CE during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius</note>, according to Ptolemy, the examined <term>simple anomaly|A measure of where an object is in its cycle of variation</term> was 21 degrees and a quarter, under which the maximum obliquity was found to be 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds. From that time to our own observation, there are approximately 1,387 years, in which the position of the simple anomaly is calculated as 145 degrees and 24 minutes; and at this time, the obliquity is found to be 23 degrees, 28 minutes, and nearly two-fifths of one minute.

Based on these figures, let arc **abc** be repeated as the circumference of the zodiac, or a straight line in its place because of its smallness, and upon it place the semicircle of the simple anomaly with pole **b**, as before. Let **a** be the maximum limit of <term>declination|The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator</term>, and **c** the minimum, the difference of which we are investigating.

<image-desc>Geometric diagram of a semicircle. The horizontal diameter is labeled with points A, G, B, K, C from left to right. Above the diameter is a semicircular arc with points E, D, and F. Vertical lines drop from E to G and from F to K. Point D is the apex of the arc, positioned vertically above point B.</image-desc>

Therefore, let arc **ae** of the small circle be taken as 21 degrees and 15 minutes, and the remainder of the quadrant **ed** will be 68 degrees and 45 minutes. However, the entire arc **edf**, according to the calculation, is 145 degrees and 24 minutes; and the remainder **df** is 76 degrees and 29 minutes. Let the perpendiculars **eg** and **fk** be dropped to the diameter **abc**. 

Now, **gk** will be the arc of the great circle known from the difference of the obliquities from Ptolemy's time to our own, which is 22 <term>first minutes|Standard minutes of arc (1/60th of a degree)</term> and 56 seconds. But the line **gb**, being similar to a straight line, is half of the chord subtending double the arc **ed**, or equal to it at 932 parts where **ac**, acting as the diameter, is 2,000 parts. Where **kb** would also be half of the chord subtending double the arc **df**, it is 973 parts. Thus, the total distance **gk** is given as 1,905 parts where **ac** is 2,000. 

But where **gk** was 22 minutes and 56 seconds, **ac** will be approximately 24 minutes—the difference between the maximum and minimum obliquity which we were seeking. By this, it is established that the maximum obliquity between the time of Timocharis and Ptolemy was a full 23 degrees and 52 minutes, and that it now approaches a minimum of 23 degrees and 28 minutes.

### Chapter 11. On establishing the positions of the uniform motions of the equinoxes and the anomaly.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut historiated initial 'H' featuring two figures in a classical architectural setting with pillars.</image-desc>

Having settled all these matters, it remains for us to establish the positions of the motions of the vernal equinox itself. These are called "roots" by some <note>original: "radices"; in astronomy, these are the "epochs" or reference points from which future positions are calculated</note>, and from them, calculations are derived for any proposed time. <term>Ptolemy|A 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work was the standard for over a millennium</term> established the primary reference point for this as the beginning of the reign of <term>Nabonassar|A King of Babylon (reigned 747–734 BCE) whose reign was used as the starting point for astronomical eras</term> of the Chaldeans, which among historians coincides with Shalmaneser, King of the Chaldeans. 

But we, following more well-known times, thought it sufficient to begin from the first Olympiad, which is found to have preceded the Nabonassarean era by 28 years. This era takes its start from the summer solstice, at which time the Dog Star <note>original: "Canicula"; the star Sirius, whose rising marked the hottest part of summer</note> rose for the Greeks and the Olympic Games <note>original: "Agon Olympicus"</note> were celebrated, as Censorinus and other approved authors have recorded. 

Hence, according to a more exact calculation of time, which is necessary for calculating celestial motions, from the first Olympiad at noon on the first day of the Greek month <term>Hekatombaion|The first month of the Attic calendar, falling in mid-summer</term> to Nabonassar and noon on the first day of the Egyptian month <term>Thoth|The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</term>, there are 27 years and 247 days. From here to the death of <term>Alexander|Alexander the Great</term> there are 424 Egyptian years. From the death of Alexander to the beginning of the years of Julius Caesar, there are 278 Egyptian years and 118.5 days, calculated at midnight before the <term>Kalends|The first day of the month in the Roman calendar</term> of January, from which point Julius Caesar made the beginning of the year he established. 

He [Caesar], as <term>Pontifex Maximus|The high priest of the Roman state religion, responsible for the calendar</term> in his third consulship, with Marcus Aemilius Lepidus as his colleague, instituted this year. From this year thus ordered by Julius Caesar, the rest thereafter were called "Julian." From the fourth consulship of Caesar to Octavian Augustus, there were 18 years for the Romans, starting likewise from the Kalends of January—although it was 16 days before the Kalends of February <note>January 16th, 27 BCE</note> that the Emperor Augustus, son of the divine Julius Caesar, was so named by the Senate and the rest of the citizens upon the motion of Munatius Plancus, in his own seventh consulship and that of Marcus Vipsanius [Agrippa]. But the Egyptians, because they had come under the power of the Romans two years earlier, after the death of Antony...

...and the fall of Cleopatra <note>The death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE marked the end of the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the beginning of Roman Egypt</note>, there are 15 years and 246½ days, at noon of the first day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, which for the Romans was the third day before the Kalends of September [August 30]. Therefore, from Augustus to the years of Christ—beginning similarly from January—there are 27 years according to the Romans, but according to the Egyptians, there are 29 of their years and 130½ days. From here to the second year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; his second year was 138–139 CE</note>, in which <term>Claudius Ptolemy|A 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work was the standard for over a millennium</term> described the positions of the stars observed by him, there are 138 Roman years and 55 days, which add 44 days for the Egyptians. From the first Olympiad up to this point, 913 years and 101 days are collected.

During this time indeed, the uniform precession of the equinoxes is 12 degrees and 44 first minutes <note>original: "fcrup. prima"; minutes of a degree</note>. Of the simple anomaly <note>The variation in the speed of the precession</note>, it is 95 degrees and 44 minutes. Yet in the second year of Antoninus, as has been reported, the vernal equinox preceded the first of the stars which are in the head of Aries by 6 degrees and 40 minutes. And since the double anomaly was 42½ parts, the difference between the uniform and apparent motion was a subtractive 48 minutes; when this is added back to the apparent motion of 6 degrees and 40 minutes, it yields the mean position of the vernal equinox itself as 7 degrees and 28 minutes.

If we add the 360 degrees of one full circle to these, and subtract 12 degrees and 44 minutes from the sum, we will have the mean position of the vernal equinox at the first Olympiad—which began at noon of the first day of the month of Hekatombaion <note>original: "Ecatombæonos"; a month in the Athenian calendar roughly corresponding to July/August</note> among the Athenians—at 354 degrees and 44 minutes; namely, that it then followed the first star of Aries by 5 degrees and 16 minutes. In a similar way, if 95 degrees and 45 minutes of simple anomaly are taken away from 21 degrees and 15 minutes, there will remain for the same beginning of the Olympiads the position of simple anomaly as 285 degrees and 30 minutes.

And again, by the addition of motions made according to the distance of times—always rejecting 360 degrees whenever they exceed that amount—we will have the positions or **roots** <note>original: "radices"; the fixed reference values used as the starting point for astronomical tables</note> for: 
For **Alexander**, the mean motion is 1 degree, 2 minutes, and the simple anomaly is 332 degrees, 52 minutes. 
For **Caesar**, the mean motion is 4 degrees, 5 minutes, and the simple anomaly is 2 degrees, 2 minutes. 
For **Christ**, the mean position is 5 degrees, 32 minutes, and the anomaly is 6 degrees, 45 minutes. 
And so, we shall take the roots of the motions for any other chosen starting points of time.

### On the calculation of the precession of the vernal equinox and the obliquity. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or astronomer in academic robes standing behind a stone balustrade and gesturing, framed within a circular border and floral ornaments.</image-desc>

Whenever, therefore, we wish to determine the position of the vernal equinox, if the years from our chosen starting point to the given time are unequal—such as the Roman years we commonly use—we must convert them into equal years, or Egyptian years <note>The ancient Egyptian calendar used a constant year of 365 days with no leap years, making it the standard for astronomers like Copernicus and Ptolemy because it simplified long-term calculations.</note>. For we use no other years in the calculation of uniform motions than the Egyptian ones, for the reason we have already stated. As for the number of years itself, whenever it exceeds sixty, we shall distribute it into groups of sixty <note>original: "sexagenas"; Copernicus uses a sexagesimal or base-60 system for his tables, similar to how we track time in minutes and seconds.</note>. When we enter the tables of motions with these groups of sixty, we will at first pass over the first value that occurs in the motions as if it were a placeholder; then, beginning from the second place (the degrees), we shall take the groups of sixty, if there are any, along with the remaining degrees and <term>minutes|original: "scrupulis"; small fractional parts of a degree, literally 'scruples'</term> that follow. Next, with the remaining years, we enter the table a second time, and from the first place exactly as they lie, we take the groups of sixty, degrees, and minutes we find. We shall do the same for days and for groups of sixty days, when we wish to add the uniform motions to them using the tables of days and minutes. However, in this particular case, the minutes of the days might rightly be ignored—or even the days themselves—on account of the slowness of these motions, since in the daily movement we are dealing only with thirds or fourths of a minute <note>The precession of the equinoxes is so slow (about 1 degree every 72 years) that its daily movement is almost imperceptible.</note>.

Therefore, when we have gathered all these together with their root <note>The 'root' is the fixed starting position for a specific era, like the birth of Christ or the first Olympiad.</note>, adding each part to its own kind, and rejecting groups of 360 degrees if they exceed that amount, we will have the mean position of the vernal equinox for the proposed time. This value tells us how far the equinox precedes the first star of Aries, or how far that star follows the equinox. In the same way, we shall also find the anomaly <note>The 'anomaly' refers to the irregularity or variation in the speed of the precession.</note>. With the simple anomaly, we will find the proportional minutes in the last column of the table of differences, which we shall set aside. Then, with the double anomaly, we will find the <term>prosthaphaeresis|The geometric correction added to or subtracted from a mean (average) position to find the 'true' or apparent position.</term> in the third column of that same table—that is, the degrees and minutes by which the true motion differs from the mean. If the double anomaly is less than a semicircle <note>180 degrees</note>, we shall subtract this prosthaphaeresis from the mean motion. But if it exceeds a semicircle (being more than 180 degrees), we shall add...

[...add the correction] to the mean motion; the sum or remainder produced will contain the true and apparent precession of the vernal equinox. This value represents how far the first star of Aries has moved away from the vernal equinox at that moment. If you seek the location of any other star, simply add the numerical position assigned to it in the star catalog.

Because practical work is usually made clearer by examples, let us set ourselves the task of finding, for the 16th day before the Calends of May <note>April 16</note> in the year of Christ 1525, the true position of the vernal equinox, the obliquity of the zodiac <note>The angle between the Earth's equator and the path of the Sun</note>, and the distance of the star Spica <note>The brightest star in the constellation Virgo</note> from that same equinox.

It is evident that in 1,524 Roman years and 106 days from the beginning of the Christian era to this time, 381 leap days have been intercalated. These, when converted into "equal" years <note>Egyptian years of exactly 365 days</note>, result in 1,525 years and 122 days. In the base-60 system used for our tables, this is expressed as 25 groups of sixty years plus 25 individual years. The 122 days are expressed as two groups of sixty days plus two days. 

Now, in the table of mean motion, 25 groups of sixty years correspond to 20 degrees, 55 <term>minutes|original: "scrupula prima"</term>, and 2 <term>seconds|original: "scrupula secunda"</term>. For the remaining 25 years, the value is 20 minutes and 55 seconds. For the two groups of sixty days, it is 16 seconds; the remaining two days provide values in the "thirds" <note>Very small fractions of a degree</note>. When all these are added to the root—which was 5 degrees and 32 minutes—the total is 26 degrees and 48 minutes, which is the mean precession of the vernal equinox.

Similarly, for the "simple anomaly" <note>The variable that tracks the slow wobble/oscillation of the Earth's axis</note>, 25 groups of sixty years provide two full circles of degrees plus 37 degrees, 15 minutes, and 3 seconds. For the 25 years, we find 2 degrees, 37 minutes, and 15 seconds. For the two groups of sixty days, we find 2 minutes and 4 seconds, and for the final two days, 2 seconds. When these are combined with the root of 6 degrees and 45 minutes, the result is 2 groups of sixty degrees plus 46 degrees and 40 minutes for the simple anomaly. 

By using this value in the final column of the table of differences, I will save the "proportional minutes" found there for the purpose of calculating the obliquity; in this case, only one minute is found. Next, with the "double anomaly" <note>A mathematical variable used to calculate the specific correction or 'prosthaphaeresis'</note>, which amounts to 5 groups of sixty plus 34 degrees and 20 minutes, I find a <term>prosthaphaeresis|original: "prosthaphæresin"; a geometric correction added or subtracted to turn 'mean' motion into 'true' motion</term> of 32 minutes. This is an additive value because the anomaly is greater than a semicircle. When this is added to the mean motion, the true and apparent precession of the vernal equinox comes to 27 degrees and 21 minutes. 

Finally, if I add to this the 170 degrees by which Spica is distant from the first star of Aries, I shall have its position relative to the vernal equinox: 197 degrees and 21 minutes, which is the 17th degree...

Now, the relationship between the **obliquity of the zodiac** <note>The angle of the Earth's tilt relative to its orbit</note> and the **declinations** <note>The distance of a celestial object north or south of the celestial equator</note> is such that when the "minutes of proportion" reach 60, the increases are added to the Table of Declinations. These differences between the maximum and minimum obliquity are added in their entirety to the parts of the declinations. However, in this specific case, one unit of those minutes adds only 24 seconds to the obliquity. Therefore, the declinations of the parts of the <term>signifer|original: "signiferi"; the zodiac</term> placed in the Table remain as they are for this time, because we are now approaching the minimum obliquity, which would otherwise change more noticeably.

For example, if the simple anomaly <note>A mathematical value used to track the Earth's wobbling motion</note> were 99 degrees—as it was in the year 880 of the Egyptian calendar after the birth of Christ—it would yield 25 minutes of proportion. Just as 60 minutes relates to the 24-second difference between maximum and minimum obliquity, 25 relates to 10. When these 10 seconds are added to 23 degrees and 28 minutes, the resulting obliquity for that time is 23 degrees and 38 minutes. 

If I then wished to know the declination of any part of the zodiac—for instance, the 3rd degree of Taurus, which is 33 degrees from the equinox—I find in the Table 12 degrees and 32 minutes, with a proportional increase of 12 minutes. Just as 60 is to 25, so 12 is to 5. When these 5 are added to the degrees of declination, they make 12 degrees and 37 minutes for the 33rd degree of the zodiac. We can use the same method for the angles where the zodiac and the equator intersect, as well as for **right ascensions**, unless one prefers to use the logic of spherical triangles—except that one must always add to the former and subtract from the latter so that all results are more accurately adjusted for the specific time.

->### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

...the temporal year must be distinguished from the sidereal year. Indeed, we call that the **natural** or **temporal year** which regulates the four annual seasons for us. But the **sidereal year** is that which returns to one of the fixed stars. However, that the natural year—which they also call the *turning year* <note>original: "annum vertentem"</note>—is unequal, is shown by the many observations of the ancients. 

For Calippus, Aristarchus of Samos, and Archimedes of Syracuse defined the year as containing 365 days plus a full quarter of a day <note>365.25 days</note>, taking the start of the year from the summer solstice <term>solstice|original: "conuersione"</term> in the Athenian manner. But **Claudius Ptolemy**, noticing that the apprehension of the solstices is difficult and precise <note>original: "scrupulosam"; literally "stony" or "troublesome," implying technical difficulty</note>, did not sufficiently trust their observations. He deferred instead to **Hipparchus**, who left behind records not only of solar solstices but also of **equinoxes** observed at Rhodes, and who reported that the year was slightly less than a quarter of a day. 

Ptolemy later determined this deficiency to be 1/300th part of a day, in the following manner. He took the autumnal equinox observed very accurately by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the 177th year after the death of **Alexander the Great**, on the third intercalary day <note>The Egyptian calendar used 12 months of 30 days plus 5 extra "intercalary" days</note> according to the Egyptians, at midnight, which was followed by the fourth intercalary day. 

Next, Ptolemy records the same equinox observed by himself at Alexandria in the third year of **Antoninus**, which was the 463rd year from the death of Alexander, on the ninth day of the Egyptian month of Athyr, approximately one hour after sunrise. Between this observation and that of Hipparchus, there were therefore 285 Egyptian years, 70 days, 7 hours, and one-fifth of an hour <note>7 hours and 12 minutes</note>. If the "turning year" had been exactly 365 days and a quarter, there should have been 71 days and six hours. Therefore, in those 285 years, there was a deficiency of one day minus 1/20th part of a day. From this, it follows that a whole day is lost every 300 years. 

He also draws a similar conclusion from the **vernal equinox**. For he remembers that it was noted by Hipparchus in the 178th year of Alexander, on the 27th day of Mechir (the sixth Egyptian month) at sunrise. Ptolemy himself, in the 463rd year of Alexander, found it on the seventh day of the month Pachon (the ninth month according to the Egyptians) one hour and a little more after noon. Likewise, in those 285 years, one day was missing, minus 1/20th of a day. Aided by these signs, Ptolemy defined the turning year as being 365 days, 14 <term>minutes|original: "scrupula prima"</term>, and 48 <term>seconds|original: "scrupula secunda"</term> <note>These are sexagesimal fractions of a day, not units of time like our modern minutes/seconds</note>. After these, **Al-Battani** <note>original: "Machometus"; the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani</note> in Raqqa, Syria...

<meta>This page continues the technical comparison of historical observations of the equinoxes, specifically contrasting the findings of Claudius Ptolemy, the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani (referred to here as Mahomet of Raqqa), and Copernicus's own measurements in the 16th century.</meta>

# NICHOLAS COPERNICUS

With no less skill, in the year 1206 after the death of Alexander <note>approximately 882 AD</note>, Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometi Aratensis"; Al-Battani was a famous Arab astronomer who observed from Raqqa (Aracta)</note> observed the autumnal equinox. He found that it occurred following the night of the seventh day of the month of Pachon <note>original: "Pachon"; an Egyptian month</note> at approximately seven and two-fifths hours—that is, four and three-fifths hours before the dawn of the eighth day. 

He then compared this observation of his with the one made by Ptolemy in the third year of Antoninus, which took place one hour after sunrise at Alexandria. Since Alexandria is ten degrees to the west of Raqqa, he adjusted the time to his own meridian at Raqqa, which should have been one hour and two-thirds after sunrise. Therefore, in the interval of 743 equal years, there were 178 extra days, 17 hours, and three-fifths of an hour—whereas the total of the quarter-days <note>the extra 0.25 day in a 365.25 day year</note> should have amounted to 185 days and three-quarters <note>original: "dodrantem"</note>. 

Because there was a deficiency of seven days and two-fifths of an hour, it appeared that one one-hundred-and-sixth part of a quarter-day was missing. He then took that deficiency of seven days and two-fifths of an hour and divided it by the number of years (743). This resulted in 14 <term>minutes|original: "scrupuli horarij"</term> and 36 <term>seconds|original: "secunda"</term> <note>These are sexagesimal fractions of an hour</note>, which he subtracted from the quarter-day. He thus announced that the **natural year** contains 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes, and 24 seconds.

We also observed the autumnal equinox at Frombork <note>original: "Fruëburgo"; Copernicus's base in Poland</note> in the year of Christ 1515, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 14</note>. This was 1,840 Egyptian years after the death of Alexander, on the sixth day of the month of Phaophi <note>original: "Phaophi"; another Egyptian month</note>, half an hour after sunrise. But because Raqqa is more to the east than this region of ours by about twenty-five degrees—which accounts for one hour and two-thirds—the mean time between our observation and that of Al-Battani of Raqqa was 633 Egyptian years, 153 days, and six and three-quarters hours, instead of 158 days and 6 hours. 

Furthermore, from that Alexandrian observation by Ptolemy to the time and place of our own observation, there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and half an hour (for we differ from Alexandria by approximately one hour). Thus, from the time of Al-Battani to us, nearly five days (less one hour and a quarter) would have fallen away in 633 years—or one day every 128 years. From Ptolemy’s time, however, in 1,376 years, nearly 12 days have fallen away—or one day every 115 years. Thus, in both cases, the year is again shown to be unequal.

<summary>Copernicus compares his 1515 observation of the autumnal equinox with those of Ptolemy and Al-Battani, demonstrating that the length of the solar year is not constant but varies over long periods of time.</summary>
<keywords>equinox, solar year, Al-Battani, Ptolemy, Frombork, Raqqa, Alexandria, calendar calculation, astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 175 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's technical comparison of equinox observations across history, transitioning from the 9th-century observations of Al-Battani to Copernicus's own 16th-century measurements and his argument for using the "sidereal year" (measured against the stars) rather than the "tropical year" (measured against the seasons).</meta>

->### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS<-

We also accepted the vernal equinox, which took place in the year 1516 after the birth of Christ, four hours and one-third <note>one-third of an hour is 20 minutes</note> after midnight on the eleventh day of March <note>original: "quintum ante Idus Martij"; five days before the Ides of March, counted inclusively</note>. From that vernal equinox observed by Ptolemy (after comparing the meridian of Alexandria to our own), there are 1,376 Egyptian years, 332 days, and 16 hours and one-third. Here it also becomes apparent that the distances between the vernal and autumnal equinoxes are unequal. It matters greatly, therefore, that the **Solar year** calculated in this way be consistent.

For in the autumnal equinoxes between Ptolemy and us—as has been shown—according to a uniform distribution of years, one one-hundred-and-fifteenth part of a quarter-day was missing. This does not agree with the equinox of Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometano Aratensi"; the 9th-century astronomer Al-Battani from Raqqa</note> by half a day. Nor does the interval from Al-Battani to us (where one one-hundred-and-twenty-eighth part of a day should have been missing from the quarter-day) harmonize with Ptolemy; rather, the calculated number precedes his observed equinox by more than a full day, and precedes Hipparchus's by more than two days. Similarly, Al-Battani's calculation, when taken from Ptolemy, exceeds the Hipparchian equinox by two days.

Therefore, the uniformity of the solar year is more correctly taken from the sphere of the fixed stars <note>meaning the "sidereal year," measured by the earth's position relative to distant stars</note>. This was first discovered by Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebites Choræ filius"; a 9th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, who found its length to be 365 days, 15 <term>minutes|original: "scrupulorum primorum"</term>, and 23 <term>seconds|original: "secundorum"</term>—which are 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 12 seconds. He likely reached this conclusion based on the argument that in the slower approach of the equinoxes and solstices, the year appeared longer than in the faster approach, and this occurred in a certain proportion.

This could not happen unless there was uniformity in comparison to the sphere of the fixed stars. For this reason, Ptolemy is not to be followed in this part; he considered it absurd and irrelevant to measure the annual uniformity of the Sun against any return to the fixed stars, claiming it was no more fitting than if someone were to do this by referencing Jupiter or Saturn. Therefore, the reason is at hand why, before Ptolemy, the "temporal year" <note>the tropical year, measured from equinox to equinox</note> was longer, and why after him it became shorter by a varying difference. But even regarding the <term>sidereal year|original: "asteroterida sive sidereum"</term>, an error can occur, though it is small and far less than the one we have already explained. This is because the same apparent motion of the center of the earth around the Sun is also unequal due to another twofold diversity.

<meta>catchword: Of which (Quarum)</meta>

<summary>Copernicus argues that the length of the year is inconsistent when measured by equinoxes (the tropical year) and proposes instead the sidereal year, measured against fixed stars, as the true standard of uniformity.</summary>
<keywords>vernal equinox, solar year, sidereal year, Thabit ibn Qurra, Al-Battani, Ptolemy, astronomical measurement, year length</keywords>

--- Page 176 ---
<meta>This page continues Copernicus's argument that the solar year—the time it takes for the Earth to complete one circuit around the Sun—is not as constant as it appears, leading him to identify four distinct causes for these perceived irregularities.</meta>

# BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Of these variations, the first and simple one has a yearly completion; the other, which alters the first by changing it, is perceived only over a long stretch of time. Consequently, the principle of the year's uniform length is neither simple nor easily understood. For if anyone simply wishes to determine the year's length relative to the known position of a specific star (which can be done using an astrolabe <note>An ancient instrument used to measure the altitudes of celestial bodies</note> by using the Moon as a bridge, just as we explained regarding the "Little King" in Leo <note>original: "Basiliscum Leonis"; the star we now call Regulus</note>), he will not entirely avoid error, unless at that time the Sun—because of the Earth's motion—either requires no **prosthaphaeresis** <term>prosthaphaeresis: a technical term for the geometric correction added or subtracted to the "mean" or average position of a planet to find its "true" or apparent position</term>, or unless it happens to have a similar and equal correction at both the start and end of the observation.

Unless this occurs, and there is some difference in their inequality, an equal circuit will certainly not seem to have happened in equal amounts of time. But if the total discrepancy is subtracted at both ends, or applied according to a specific ratio, the calculation will be perfect. Furthermore, the understanding of this very discrepancy requires a prior knowledge of the "mean motion" <note>The average speed of a celestial body, assuming its orbit is a perfect circle</note>, which is exactly what we are seeking to find.

Nevertheless, so that we may finally reach a resolution of this knotty problem, we have found four causes in total for the unequal appearance of the Sun. The first is the inequality of the "precession of the equinoxes" <note>The slow wobbling of Earth's axis that changes the timing of the seasons</note>, which we have already explained. The second is that by which the Sun seems to traverse unequal sections of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the belt of constellations</note>, which occurs roughly every year. The third, which also varies this second cause, we shall call the "second diversity." The fourth remains: it changes the highest and lowest **apsides** <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a celestial body is either closest to or farthest from the center of its motion</term> of the Earth's center, as will be seen below.

Of all these, only the second was known to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus was refining</note>. By itself, that second cause could not have produced the annual inequality, but being entwined with the others, it does so more significantly. Indeed, to demonstrate the difference between the uniform and apparent motion of the Sun, an extremely exact calculation of the year does not seem necessary; it is sufficient if, for the purpose of demonstration, we take the length of the year as 365 days and a quarter, during which the first cycle of diversity is completed. This is because a value that differs so little from the whole circle vanishes entirely when taken in a smaller magnitude. But for the sake of good order and ease of instruction, we set forth here the uniform motions of the Earth's center in its annual revolution, which we shall then establish alongside the differences between uniform and apparent motion through the necessary demonstrations.

<meta>catchword: Concerning the uni- (original: "De æqua-")</meta>

<summary>Copernicus identifies four distinct astronomical causes for why the Sun's motion appears irregular and argues that the Earth's motion must be understood through both average (mean) and corrected calculations.</summary>
<keywords>solar year, prosthaphaeresis, Regulus, zodiac, precession of the equinoxes, apsides, Ptolemy, mean motion</keywords>

### On the Uniform and Mean Motions of the Revolutions of the Center of the Earth. Chapter XIV.

We have found the magnitude of the year and its uniformity to be only one second and ten thirds <note>In the sexagesimal (base-60) system used by astronomers, "scrupula" or "scruples" refer to minutes (1/60), seconds (1/3,600), and thirds (1/216,000) of a degree or hour</note> greater than what Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebith Benchoræ"; a 9th-century Sabian astronomer and mathematician who worked in Baghdad</note> reported. Thus, the year consists of 365 days, 15 minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds. This is equal to 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 40 seconds. Its precise uniformity is evident when measured against the sphere of the fixed stars. Therefore, when we multiply the 360 degrees of a single circle by 365 days and divide the sum by 365 days, 15 minutes, 24 seconds, and 10 thirds, we obtain the motion for one Egyptian year <note>An "Egyptian year" was a standard calendar year of exactly 365 days, used by astronomers because of its constant length</note> in units of sixty degrees: 5 units of sixty, 59 degrees, 44 minutes, 49 seconds, 7 thirds, and 4 fourths. The motion for sixty similar years, after discarding the completed circles, is 5 units of sixty, 44 degrees, 49 minutes, 7 seconds, and 4 thirds. Again, if we divide the annual motion by 365 days, we get a daily motion of 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 11 thirds, and 22 fourths.

If we add to these values the mean and uniform precession of the equinoxes, we will also compose the uniform motion for the "temporary" or seasonal years. The annual motion would then be 5 units of sixty, 59 degrees, 45 minutes, 39 seconds, 19 thirds, and 9 fourths; the daily motion would be 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 19 thirds, and 37 fourths. For this reason, we can call that first motion of the Sun—to use a common term—the "simple" uniform motion, while this second one is the "composite" uniform motion. We will set these out in tables, just as we did for the precession of the equinoxes. To these, the motion of the Sun's uniform **anomaly** <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point from the Earth (apogee), used to calculate its irregular speed</term> is added, which we will discuss later.

<summary>Copernicus calculates the precise length of the sidereal year and provides the mathematical breakdown for the Earth's daily and annual "mean motion" in relation to both the fixed stars and the equinoxes.</summary>
<keywords>Thabit ibn Qurra, Egyptian year, mean motion, sidereal year, tropical year, sexagesimal calculation, solar anomaly</keywords>

# Theorems for Demonstrating the Inequality of the Apparent Solar Motion.
## Chapter 15.

To better grasp the apparent **inequality** <note>In astronomy, "inequality" refers to the variation in a celestial body’s speed or position compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> of the Sun, we will demonstrate even more clearly that, with the Sun holding the center of the universe—around which the Earth revolves as if about a center—if the distance between the Sun and the Earth is such that it cannot be compared to the immensity of the sphere of the **fixed stars**, the Sun will appear to move uniformly toward any chosen sign or star of that same sphere.

For let **AB** be the greatest circle in the world in the plane of the <term>zodiac<note>original: *signiferi*, the "sign-bearer," referring to the belt of the heavens containing the twelve signs of the zodiac.</note></term>; let its center be **C**, where the Sun resides. According to the distance between the Sun and the Earth, **CD**, in comparison to which the height of the universe is immense, let the circle **DE** be described in the same plane of the zodiac, in which the annual revolution of the center of the Earth is placed. I say that toward any chosen sign or star in the circle **AB**, the Sun will appear to move uniformly.

Let the chosen point be **A**, toward which the sight of the Sun from the Earth (which is at **D**) is extended along the line **ACD**. Now let the Earth move in any way through the circumference **DE**, and from the point **E** (the Earth's new position), let lines **AE** and **BE** be drawn. The Sun will now be seen from **E** at sign **B**. Since **AC** is immense compared to **CD** (or its equal, **CE**), **AE** will also be immense compared to the same **CE**.

For let any point **F** be taken on **AC**, and let **EF** be connected. Since two straight lines fall from the ends of the base **CE** outside the triangle **EFC**, at point **A**—by the converse of the <note>Copernicus refers to Proposition 21 of Book 1 of Euclid’s *Elements*, which deals with lines drawn to a point within a triangle being shorter than the sides but containing a greater angle. Here he uses it to show the vanishingly small nature of the angle.</note> 21st proposition of the first book of Euclid’s *Elements*—the angle **FAE** will be smaller than the angle **EFC**. Therefore, the straight lines extended into immensity will eventually enclose the acute angle **CAB** to such a degree that it can no longer be discerned. This is the amount by which angle **BCA** is greater than angle **AEC**. Because of such a slight difference, they appear equal, and the lines **AC** and **AE** appear parallel; thus the Sun [appears to move uniformly] toward any sign of the sphere.

<summary>Copernicus provides a geometric proof to explain why the Earth's movement around the Sun does not cause a visible shift (parallax) in the Sun's position relative to the stars, citing the vast distance of the stellar sphere.</summary>
<keywords>solar inequality, heliocentrism, stellar parallax, Euclid, zodiac, fixed stars, geometric proof</keywords>
