<meta>This page continues the geometric proof of why the Sun appears to move at different speeds (inequality) from the perspective of the Earth. Copernicus is explaining that this phenomenon can be modeled mathematically in two ways: using an eccentric circle or using an epicycle on a concentric circle. He demonstrates that these models are geometrically equivalent to the older Earth-centered models of Ptolemy, even though he places the Sun at the center.</meta>

ON THE REVOLUTIONS. BOOK III.

...of the stars to move uniformly, which was to be demonstrated. However, its **inequality** <note>In historical astronomy, "inequality" refers to any variation or irregularity in a celestial body's speed or position compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> is demonstrated by the fact that the motion of the center [of the Earth] and its annual revolution is not centered exactly upon the Sun. This can indeed be understood in two ways: either by an **eccentric circle**—that is, one whose center is not the Sun's—or by an **epicycle** on a **concentric circle** <note>original: *homocentro*. A circle that shares the same center as the universe.</note>.

Now, the proof by the eccentric is explained in this way: Let there be an eccentric circle **ABCD** in the plane of the <term>zodiac<note>original: *signiferi orbis*, the "sign-bearer," referring to the belt of the heavens containing the twelve signs of the zodiac.</note></term>, whose center **E** is located at a significant distance from the center of the Sun or the world, which is **F**. Let its diameter pass through both centers along the line **AEFD**. Let the <term>apogee<note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion.</note></term> be at **A**, which is called the **highest apsis** <note>original: *summa absis*</note> by the Latins—the location furthest from the center of the world. Let **D** be the <term>perigee<note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion.</note></term>, which is the nearest point and the **lowest apsis** <note>original: *infima absis*</note>. 

Therefore, since the Earth is carried uniformly in its orbit **ABCD** around center **E**, as has already been stated, its motion will appear different when viewed from point **F**. For if equal arcs **AB** and **CD** are taken, and straight lines **BE**, **CE**, **BF**, and **CF** are drawn, the angles **AEB** and **CED** will be equal, because they subtend equal arcs around center **E**. However, the angle **CFD**, as it is seen, is greater than angle **CED** (the exterior angle being greater than the interior); therefore, it is also greater than angle **AEB**, which is equal to **CED**. But since the exterior angle **AEB** is also greater than the interior angle **AFB**, the angle **CFD** is all the more greater than **AFB**. Yet both motions were produced in equal time because of the equal arcs **AB** and **CD**. Therefore, the motion will appear uniform around center **E**, but unequal around center **F**. 

The same may be seen even more simply: arc **AB** is further from point **F** than arc **CD**. For according to the seventh proposition of the third book of <term>Euclid’s Elements<note>Euclid's *Elements* was the foundational geometry textbook of the era. Copernicus cites it to prove that lines from an offset center (F) to the circumference vary in length.</note></term>, the lines **AF** and **BF** are longer than **CF** and **DF**; and, as is demonstrated in optics, equal magnitudes that are closer appear larger than those further away. 

Thus, what is proposed concerning the eccentric is clear. Furthermore, the demonstration is exactly the same whether the Earth were at rest at **F** while the Sun moved in the revolving circle **ABC**—as in the work of **Ptolemy** and others—or the reverse. 

The same thing will also be explained by an **epicycle** <note>A smaller circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger circle.</note> on a concentric circle. For let **BCD** be a concentric circle whose center is the center of the world **E**, where the Sun is also located. In the same plane, let **A** be the center of the epicycle **FG**, and let a straight line **CEAF** be drawn through both centers. Let the apogee of the epicycle be **F** and the perigee be **I**. It is therefore clear from the uniformity...

BY NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

...is at **A**, while the inequality <note>In historical astronomy, "inequality" refers to any variation or irregularity in a celestial body's speed or position compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> of its appearance occurs on the epicycle **FG**. For if **A** moves toward **B** (that is, in the direction of the signs <note>original: *in consequentia*; moving forward through the zodiac from Aries to Taurus, etc.</note>), while the center of the Earth moves from the **apogee** <note>The point furthest from the center.</note> **F** in the opposite direction <note>original: *in praecedentia*; moving backward against the order of the signs.</note>, it will appear that **B** moves faster at the **perigee** <note>The point closest to the center.</note>, which is **I**, because both motions (of **A** and **I**) are in the same direction. However, at the **apogee**, which is **F**, **B** will seem to move more slowly, because it is moved only by the difference between two opposing motions. Furthermore, when the Earth is positioned at **G**, it will lead the uniform motion, while at **K** it will follow behind; in both cases, the difference is measured by the arcs **AG** and **AK**, which causes the Sun to appear to move in different ways.

Whatever is achieved through an **epicycle** can happen in the same way through an **eccentric circle**, which the star describes as it travels on the epicycle. This eccentric is equal to the **concentric circle** <note>original: *homocentrus*; a circle sharing the same center as the universe.</note> and in the same plane. The center of this eccentric is distant from the center of the concentric by the length of the epicycle’s radius. This also occurs in three ways. First, if the epicycle on the concentric and the star on the epicycle complete equal revolutions, but in opposite directions, the star’s motion will trace a fixed eccentric, whose **apogee** and **perigee** <note>The highest and lowest points of the orbit.</note> maintain fixed positions. For example, let **ABC** be the concentric circle, with **D** as the center of the world and **ADC** as the diameter. Let us suppose that when the epicycle was at **A**, the star was at the epicycle's apogee, which is at **G**, and the radii formed the straight line **DAG**. Now, let an arc **AB** be taken on the concentric. With **B** as the center and a distance equal to **AG**, let the epicycle **EF** be described. Let lines **DB** and **EB** be extended in a straight line. Let the arc **EF** be taken in the opposite direction and similar to **AB**. Let the star (or the Earth) be at **F**, and let **BF** be joined. On the line **AD**, let a segment **DK** be taken equal to **BF**. Since, therefore, the angles **EBF** and **BDA** are equal, **BF** and **DK** are parallel and equal. According to the 33rd proposition of the first book of **Euclid** <note>Copernicus refers to Euclid's *Elements*, a foundational text of geometry. Proposition 33 states that lines which join the ends of equal and parallel lines are themselves equal and parallel.</note>, if equal and parallel straight lines are joined by straight lines, those lines are also parallel and equal. And since **DK** and **AG** are set...

...are set as equal, and the common line <term>AK</term> is added, then the angle <term>GAK</term> will be equal to <term>AKD</term>: and therefore it is also equal to <term>KF</term>. Therefore, with <term>K</term> as the center and the distance <term>KAG</term>, the circle described will pass through <term>F</term>. described by the combined motion of the star on an eccentric circle, whose <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> has meanwhile migrated from the point <term>G</term> in a preceding direction through the circumference <term>GN</term>. Conversely, if the motion of the star in the epicycle were slower, then the center of the eccentric will move in a following direction, precisely where the center of the epicycle is carried; for example, if the angle <term>EBF</term> were smaller than <term>BDA</term>, and an angle equal to it is constructed as <term>BDM</term>, it is clear that what we have said occurs. From all this, it is evident that the same <term>inequality</term> <note>A variation in the observed speed or position of a planet compared to perfectly uniform motion.</note> of appearance is always produced, whether by an epicycle on a homocentric circle, or by an eccentric circle equal to the homocentric one; they do not differ from each other at all, provided that the distance between the centers is equal to the radius of the epicycle.

...accommodated the <term>eccentrepicycle</term> <note>original: *eccentrepicyclos*; a model combining an eccentric circle and an epicycle.</note> to the wandering stars. From these [models] it is also easily demonstrated that the greatest difference between uniform and apparent motion <note>Uniform motion refers to the idealized constant speed of a planet, while apparent motion is how it actually looks to an observer on Earth. The difference between these is known as the "equation of center."</note> is seen when the star appears midway between the highest and lowest <term>apsis</term> <note>The points in an orbit where the celestial body is furthest (apogee) or closest (perigee) to the center of motion.</note>, according to the eccentric model—or in the case of the epicycle model, at its point of contact, as in Ptolemy. In the eccentric model, it is shown this way: Let the circle be *ABCD* with center *E*, and the diameter *AEC* passing through *F*, where the Sun is located outside the center. Let the line *BFD* be drawn at right angles through *F*, and connect *BE* and *ED*. Let *A* be the <term>apogee</term> <note>original: *apogeum*; the point in an orbit most distant from the center.</note> and *C* the <term>perigee</term> <note>original: *perigeum*; the point in an orbit closest to the center.</note>; from these, *B* and *D* represent the positions of mean appearance. It is manifest that the exterior angle *AEB* comprises the uniform motion, while the interior angle *EFB* comprises the apparent motion, and their difference is the angle *EBF*. I assert that no angle greater than those at *B* or *D* can be constructed over the line *EF* along the orbital path. For if points *G* and *H* are taken before and after *B*, and *GD*, *GE*, *GF* are connected, as well as *HE*, *HF*, *HD*: Since *FG*, being closer to the center, is longer than *DF*, angle *GDF* will be greater than *DGF*. But the angles *EDG* and *EGD* are equal, as they descend to the base of the equal sides *EG* and *ED*. Therefore, angle *EDB* (which is equal to *EBF*) is greater than angle *EGF*. Similarly, *DF* is longer than *FH*, and angle *FHD* is greater than *FDH*; but since the whole *EHD* is equal to the whole *EDH* (because *EH* and *ED* are equal), the remaining angle *EDF* (equal to *EBF*) is also greater than the remaining angle *EHF*. Thus, nowhere except at points *B* and *D* can a larger angle be formed above line *EF*. Therefore, the greatest difference between uniform and apparent motion occurs at the midpoint between apogee and perigee.

From which, if *IC* and *DK* are subtracted (being equal to *AG* and *HB*), there remains *CD* at 86 degrees 51 minutes <note>original: *scrupula*; used here as minutes of a degree.</note>, and the remainder of the arc *CDA* is *DA* at 88 degrees 49 minutes. But to the 86 degrees and 51 minutes correspond 88 days and an eighth part of a day; and to the 88 degrees and 49 minutes correspond 90 days and an eighth part of a day (which is 3 hours). In these times, under the equal motion of the earth, the Sun was seen to pass from the Autumnal equinox to the Winter solstice <note>original: *Bruma*; the winter solstice.</note>, and in the remainder of the year to return from the Winter solstice to the Vernal equinox. *Ptolemy* <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity.</note> testifies that he found these things to be exactly as they had been reported before him by *Hipparchus*. For this reason, he believed that for all time to come, the <term>highest absis</term> <note>The apogee, or the point in the orbit farthest from the center. Original: *summam absidem*.</note> would remain at 24 and a half degrees before the summer solstice, and the <term>eccentricity</term> <note>The distance the center of the orbit is offset from the Sun. Original: *eccentroteta*.</note> would remain, as was said, at a twenty-fourth part of the radius.

Both of these are now found to have changed, with a manifest difference. *al-Battani* <note>original: *Machometus Aratensis*; a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> noted that from the Vernal equinox to the Summer solstice there were 94 days and 35 minutes; and to the Autumnal equinox 182 days and 37 minutes. From these, according to the rule of *Ptolemy*, he derived an eccentricity of no more than 347 parts (where the radius is 10,000). *al-Zarqali* <note>original: *Arzachel Hispanus*; an 11th-century Muslim astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note> the Spaniard agrees with him in the ratio of the eccentricity, but reported the apogee to be 12 degrees and 10 minutes before the solstice, whereas it seemed to *al-Battani* to be 7 degrees and 43 minutes before that same solstice. By these clear signs it was understood that yet another difference remains in the motion of the center of the earth, which is also proved by the observations of our own age.

For in the ten and more years in which we have applied our mind to investigating these matters, and especially in the year of Christ 1515, we found that from the Vernal equinox to the Autumnal, 186 days and 5 and a half minutes are completed. And so that we might be less deceived in capturing the solstices (which some suspect happened at times to our predecessors), we adopted certain other positions of the Sun for this business, which were not at all difficult to observe even outside of the equinoxes—such as the midpoints of the signs of **Taurus**, **Leo**, **Scorpio**, and **Aquarius**. We found, therefore, from the Autumnal equinox to the middle of **Scorpio**, 45 days and 16 minutes; and to the Vernal equinox, 178 days and 53 and a half minutes. Now, the equal motion in the first interval is 44 degrees and 37 minutes. In the second, 176 degrees...

Because of this, the half-excess over FD—which is FK—is 2,000 of those same parts. ### Demonstration of the first and annual Solar inequality, with its particular differences. Chapter 17.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a celestial orbit. A vertical diameter is labeled AC, with A at the top (apogeum, or point furthest from the center) and C at the bottom (perigeum, or point closest to the center). The geometric center is marked E. A point D, representing the Sun, is located on the vertical diameter slightly below the center E. A radius is drawn from center E to a point B on the upper left of the circumference. Since, therefore, several differences in the Solar <term>inequality</term> <note>The "inequality" refers to the observed variation in the Sun's speed and position compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> are found, we believe that the one which is annual, and better known than the others, should be derived first. For this purpose, let circle ABC be repeated with center E and diameter AEC. Let **A** be the apogee, **C** the perigee, and the Sun be located at **D**. 

It has already been demonstrated that the greatest difference between the <term>mean motion</term> <note>The theoretical uniform speed of the Sun.</note> and the <term>apparent motion</term> <note>The speed of the Sun as actually observed from Earth.</note> occurs at the midpoint between both <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to (perigee) or farthest from (apogee) the center of motion.</note> according to appearance. For that reason, let a perpendicular line **BD** be raised from the diameter AEC, cutting the circumference at point **B**, and let **BE** be joined. 

Since, therefore, in the right-angled triangle **BDE**, two sides are given—namely **BE**, which is the radius from the center of the circle to the circumference, and **DE**, the distance of the Sun from the center <note>This distance DE represents the eccentricity of the orbit.</note>—the angle **DBE** will be given. This is the angle by which the mean motion angle **BEA** differs from the right angle **EDB** of the apparent motion. 

Insofar as the distance **DE** is made larger or smaller, the entire shape of the triangle is changed accordingly. Thus, before Ptolemy’s time, the angle **B** was 2 degrees and 23 minutes <note>original: *scrupula*. Early astronomers divided degrees into "scruples," which we now call minutes.</note>. Under Al-Battani <note>original: *Machometo Aratensi*, a 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> and Arzachel <note>original: *Arzachele*, an 11th-century Andalusian astronomer.</note>, it was 1 degree and 59 minutes. Now, however, it is 1 degree and 51 minutes. 

Furthermore, Ptolemy held the arc **AB** (which the angle **AEB** subtends) to be 92 degrees and 23 minutes, and **BC** to be 87 degrees and 37 minutes. Al-Battani found **AB** to be 91 degrees and 59 minutes, and **BC** to be 88 degrees and 1 minute. Now, we find **AB** is 91 degrees and 51 minutes, and **BC** is 88 degrees and 9 minutes.

## On the examination of the uniform motion in longitude. Chapter 18.

These things have been explained concerning the annual inequality of the Sun. However, this is not by a simple difference, as it once appeared, but by one that is mixed with another variation revealed by the passage of long periods of time. We shall distinguish these from each other hereafter. Meanwhile, the mean and uniform motion of the center of the Earth will be established with more certain numbers the more it is separated from these variations of inequality and the longer the interval of time between observations. That shall be established in this manner.

We have taken that Autumnal <term>equinox</term> <note>The moment in the year when day and night are of equal length, marking the start of autumn.</note> which was observed by Hipparchus at Alexandria in the 32nd year of the third <term>Callippic period</term> <note>A 76-year cycle used by ancient Greek astronomers to synchronize the solar year and lunar months.</note>. Therefore, according to the calculation handed down above, the place of the Autumnal equinox under the sphere of the fixed stars was 176 parts and 10 minutes from the head of Aries <note>The "parts" refer to degrees; "minutes" are 60ths of a degree. In this observation, the position of the Autumnal equinox, according to the calculation and the observations, was 152 degrees 45 minutes in the sphere of the fixed stars. It was at a distance from the highest <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center of motion; the apogee.</note> of 83 degrees 20 minutes, according to the preceding demonstration. Let the angle BEA now be set at 83 degrees 20 minutes (where 180 degrees make two right angles). The two sides of the triangle are given: BD is 10,000 parts and DE is 323 parts. By the fourth demonstration of <term>plane triangles</term> <note>Geometry involving triangles on a flat surface, as opposed to spherical geometry.</note>, the angle DBE will be approximately 1 degree 50 minutes. For if a circle circumscribes triangle BDE, the angle BDE on the circumference will be 166 degrees 40 minutes (where 360 degrees make two right angles), and the <term>chord</term> <note>original: subtensa; a straight line segment connecting two points on a curve.</note> BD will be 19,864 parts, where the diameter is 20,000.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle with a vertical diameter line passing through points A (top), D (center), E (below center), and C (bottom). A point B is on the left side of the circle's circumference. Straight lines connect B to A, B to D, and B to E, forming triangles within the circle.</image-desc>

And according to the given ratio of BD to DE, the length of DE itself will be approximately 642 of those same parts. This subtends the angle DBE at the circumference of 3 degrees 40 minutes, but at the center, it is 1 degree 50 minutes. This was the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A mathematical correction used to account for the difference between a planet's average movement and its observed position.</note> and the difference between the uniform and apparent positions. When this is added to angle BED (which was 83 degrees 20 minutes), we have angle BDA and the arc AB as 85 degrees 10 minutes—the uniform distance from the <term>apogee</term>. Thus, the mean position of the Sun in the sphere of the fixed stars is 154 degrees 35 minutes. Therefore, in the interval between both observations, there are 1,662 Egyptian years, 37 days, 18 first minutes, and 45 second minutes <note>Copernicus uses sexagesimal (base-60) fractions of a day: 18/60 and 45/3600.</note>. The mean and uniform motion, beyond the full revolutions (which number 1,660), is 436 degrees and nearly 15 minutes. This is consistent with the number we have set forth in the tables of uniform motions.

He employs geometric proofs involving chords and angles to determine the correction between apparent and uniform solar positions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Copernicus's calculations regarding the Sun's "mean motion"—its steady, average speed. Having previously established the rate of this motion by comparing his own observations with those of the ancient astronomer Hipparchus, he now uses that data to calculate the Sun’s exact position at specific historical turning points, or "epochs." This allows him to create a timeline that connects the astronomy of the ancient Greeks and Egyptians to his own era.</meta>

HEADER: BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

## On the positions and starting points to be established for the uniform motion of the Sun. Chapter 19.

In the time that elapsed from the death of Alexander the Great to the observation of Hipparchus, there are 176 years, 362 days, and 27 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; in this context, Copernicus is referring to fractions of a day (sixtieths), rather than minutes of an hour.</note> and a half. In this period, the mean motion according to the calculation is 312 degrees and 43 minutes. When these degrees are subtracted from the 178 degrees and 20 minutes that were assigned to Hipparchus's observation (after adding the 360 degrees of a full circle), there will remain the position for the beginning of the years of the deceased Alexander the Great. This was at noon on the first day of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar.</note>, the first of the Egyptians, at 225 degrees and 37 minutes. This position is calculated for the <term>meridian</term> <note>An imaginary line of longitude used as a reference point for time and astronomical observations.</note> of Krakow and Frombork <note>original: Fruenburgum; the site of Copernicus’s observatory.</note>, which is the location of our own observations.

From that point to the beginning of the Roman years of Julius Caesar, in 278 years and 118 days and a half, the mean motion is 46 degrees and 27 minutes (after accounting for complete revolutions). When these are added to the numbers for the Alexandrian position, they result in Caesar's position at midnight on the <term>Kalends of January</term> <note>January 1st; the start of the Roman year.</note>, from which the Romans are accustomed to begin their years and days: 272 degrees and 4 minutes.

Then, in 45 years and 12 days—or 323 years and 130 days and a half from Alexander the Great—the position for the birth of Christ arises at 272 degrees and 31 minutes. And since Christ was born in the third year of the 194th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks to measure time, starting from the first Olympic Games.</note> (which total 775 years and 12 days and a half from the beginning of the first Olympiad to the midnight before the Kalends of January), these similarly yield the position for the first Olympiad at 96 degrees and 16 minutes. This was at noon on the first day of the month of Hecatombaeon <note>The first month of the Attic (Athenian) calendar.</note>, the anniversary of which now falls on the Kalends of July according to the Roman years.

In this way, the starting points for the <term>simple Solar motion</term> <note>Movement measured relative to the "fixed" stars, which does not change due to the earth's wobble (precession).</note> are established relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. The <term>composite positions</term> <note>Movement measured relative to the equinoxes, which includes the effect of precession.</note> are also produced by adding the precession of the equinoxes; like the others, these are: for the Olympiads, 90 degrees and 59 minutes; for Alexander, 226 degrees and 38 minutes; for Caesar, 276 degrees and 59 minutes; and for Christ, 278 degrees and 2 minutes. All of these, as we have said, are referred to the Krakow meridian.

NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### On the second and twofold variation that occurs regarding the Sun because of the change of the apsides. Chapter 20.

A greater difficulty now arises regarding the instability of the solar <term>apsis</term> <note>The plural is "apsides." These are the two points in an orbit—the apogee and perigee—where a celestial body is at its maximum and minimum distance from the center.</note>. Ptolemy believed this point was fixed, while others believed it followed the motion of the "eighth sphere" <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; astronomers previously thought the stars and the orbital points of planets moved together at a constant rate.</note>, according to their belief that the fixed stars also moved. Arzachel <note>The Latinized name for Al-Zarqali, an 11th-century Arab astronomer from Al-Andalus.</note> opined that this motion was also unequal, even to the point that it might move backward. He based this conclusion on evidence that when Al-Battani <note>original: "Machometus Aratensis," referring to the 9th-century Arab astronomer Al-Battani.</note> (as has been said) found the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's apparent orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> to be 7 degrees and 43 minutes before the solstice, it had previously progressed nearly 17 degrees over 740 years since Ptolemy's time. Yet, in the 193 years following, it seemed to Al-Battani to have moved backward nearly 4 or 5 degrees.

Because of this, Arzachel thought there was another motion for the center of the annual orbit, traveling along a small circle. This would cause the apogee to deflect forward and backward, and would make the distances from the center of the world to the center of that orbit unequal. This was indeed a clever invention, but it has not been accepted because it does not harmonize with other observations when compared as a whole. For instance, if the sequence of that motion is considered in order: it stood still for some time before Ptolemy; then, in about 640 years, it passed through 17 degrees; next, in 200 years, it returned 4 or 5 degrees; and for the remaining time until our own day, it has progressed forward. No other regression has been perceived in all that time, nor were any "stations" <note>Points where a planet or orbital point appears to stop moving before changing direction.</note> observed, which must necessarily occur between contrary motions. Such things are impossible to understand in a system of uniform and circular motion.

Consequently, many believe that some error crept into the observations of those men. Both were mathematicians of equal zeal and diligence, so it is ambiguous whom we should follow. Indeed, I confess that in no part of astronomy is there a greater difficulty than in determining the Sun's apogee, where we must reason out great conclusions from very tiny and barely perceptible measurements. This is because near the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note> and the apogee, a whole degree of movement changes the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>A mathematical adjustment used to calculate a planet's true position based on its average motion; essentially the "correction" for an elliptical or eccentric orbit.</note> by only about two minutes. However, near the "middle apsides" <note>The points halfway between the furthest and nearest distances.</note>, a difference of just one minute in measurement can cause a shift of 5 or 6 degrees in the position of the apogee. Thus, a modest error can expand into a massive one...

<summary>Copernicus discusses the historical debate over whether the Sun's apogee is fixed or moving, critiquing previous theories by Arab astronomers Al-Battani and Al-Zarqali. He highlights the extreme difficulty of precisely measuring the solar apogee due to how tiny errors in observation lead to massive errors in orbital calculations.</summary>
<keywords>solar apogee, apsis, Ptolemy, Arzachel, Al-Battani, prosthaphaeresis, orbital variation, astronomical observation errors</keywords>

# BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS

However much the Earth describes the circumference FO of its second epicycle, it will no longer describe an <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the center is offset from the central body (the Sun).</note> whose center meets line A, but rather one in the line that is parallel to DO, such as LP. Because of this, the Sun's <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in the Sun's path where it is furthest from the Earth.</note> will be seen to precede line A in the line CP. From this, it is also manifest that the same thing happens through an <term>eccentrepicycle</term> <note>original: "eccentrepicyclum"; a composite model using both an eccentric circle and an epicycle.</note>. For since the Earth's center revolves in the circumference FO under the aforementioned conditions—that is, slightly more than an annual revolution—within a single eccentric previously described by the <term>epicycle</term> D around center L, it will induce another eccentric around center P, and exactly the same things will happen. Since so many modes lead to the same numerical result, I could not easily say which one actually holds place, except that the perpetual harmony of numbers and appearances forces us to believe it is one of them. <note>This is a famous admission by Copernicus that mathematical models are "equivalent" if they predict the same observations, though he seeks the one that matches physical reality.</note>

## How the uniform and varying motion of the solar apogee is explained. Chapter 22.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a scene with a scholar or astronomer seated at a desk, surrounded by books and possibly scientific instruments.</image-desc>

Since, therefore, the time in which the maximum <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: "eccentrotes"; the distance that the center of the Earth's orbit is offset from the Sun.</note> coincided with the beginning of the first and simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>An astronomical term for the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee).</note> was the third year of the 178th Olympiad [158 BCE], and the 260th year after Alexander the Great according to the Egyptian calendar, the true and mean position of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the center.</note> was for that reason at 5 1/2 degrees of Gemini—that is, 65 1/2 degrees from the Spring equinox. Moreover, the true <term>precession</term> <note>The slow, "wobbling" shift of the Earth's axis that causes the equinoxes to move backward through the zodiac over thousands of years.</note> of the equinox—which at that time also coincided with the mean position—was 4 degrees and 38 1/2 scruples. When these are subtracted from the 65 1/2 degrees, there remained 60 degrees and 52 scruples from the "head of Aries" in the sphere of the fixed stars as the position of the apogee. 

Again, in the second year of the 573rd Olympiad, or the year of Christ 1515, the position of the apogee was found at 6 2/3 degrees of Cancer. But since the precession of the Spring equinox according to the calculation was 27 degrees and a quarter (15 minutes), if these are subtracted from 96 degrees and 40 minutes [6 2/3 degrees of Cancer], they leave 69 degrees and 25 scruples. It was shown, however, that while the first anomaly was 165 degrees and 39 scruples, the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> was 2 degrees and 7 scruples, by which the true position preceded the mean. Therefore, the mean position of the solar apogee itself was clearly 71 degrees and 32 scruples. 

Therefore, in the intervening 1,580 Egyptian years, the mean and uniform motion of the apogee was 10 degrees and 41 scruples. When these are divided by the number of those years, we will have an annual portion of 24 <term>seconds</term>, 20 <term>thirds</term>, and 14 <term>fourths</term> <note>original: "secunda, tertia, quarta"; these are further 1/60th subdivisions of a degree, just as a minute is 1/60th of a degree.</note>.

### On the Calculation of the Solar Appearance. Chapter 25.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'E' depicting a scholar or astronomer sitting at a desk with a book, possibly in a study or library setting.</image-desc> From these matters, I believe it is now sufficiently clear how the apparent position of the Sun is calculated for any given time. For at that specific time, one must seek the true position of the Vernal Equinox, or its <term>precession</term> <note>original: antecessio; the slow movement of the equinoxes along the ecliptic</note>, together with its first simple <term>anomaly</term> <note>Anomaly refers to the angular distance of a celestial body from its furthest or nearest point to the center of motion.</note>, as we explained above. Next, find the simple mean motion of the Earth's center (or the motion of the Sun, if you prefer to call it that) and the annual anomaly through the tables of uniform motions; these are to be added to their established starting points. 

Therefore, with the first and simple anomaly, and its number being found in the first or second column of the preceding table—or the value nearest to it—you will find the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A mathematical correction used to find the "true" position from the "mean" position; literally "addition-subtraction."</note> of the annual anomaly corresponding to it in the third column, and you should save the following proportional <term>scruples</term> <note>Small fractions of a degree, usually 1/60th.</note>. Now, add the prosthaphæresis to the annual anomaly if the first anomaly was less than a semicircle (that is, if its number was found in the first column); otherwise, subtract it. What remains or is gathered as a sum will be the adjusted anomaly of the Sun. 

By this adjusted value, you again take the prosthaphæresis of the annual orbit, which occupies the fifth column, along with the following excess. If this excess, when multiplied by the previously saved proportional scruples, produces any result, it should always be added to this prosthaphæresis, and it will become the equalized prosthaphæresis. This value should be subtracted from the mean position of the Sun if the number of the annual anomaly was found in the first column (meaning it is less than a semicircle). However, let it be added if it was larger, or if it occupied the second column of numbers. 

For whatever is left or collected in this way will determine the true position of the Sun, measured from the head of the constellation Aries. If the true precession of the Vernal Equinox is finally added to this, it will immediately show the Sun’s position relative to the equinox itself in the <term>twelve signs</term> <note>original: dodecatemorijs; the twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac</note> and the degrees of the signs of the circle. If you wish to achieve this in another way, take the compound uniform motion instead of the simple motion, and perform the rest as described, except that for the precession of the equinox, you only add or subtract its prosthaphæresis, as the situation requires. Thus stands the explanation of the Sun's appearance through the movement of the Earth, agreeing with both ancient and more recent observations, by which it is even more...

### On the <term>Nychthemeron</term> <note>Greek: νυχθημερῳ; a period of 24 hours comprising both a day and a night.</note>, That is, the Difference of the Natural Day. Chapter 26.

It remains to say something further regarding the Sun about the inequality of the natural day. This is the span of time comprised of 24 equal hours, which we have used until now as the common and certain measure of celestial motions. Some define such a day as the time between two sunrises, such as the Chaldeans and the ancient Jews; others between two sunsets, as the Athenians did; others from midnight to midnight, like the Romans; and others from noon to noon, as the Egyptians did. It is manifest, however, that within this time the proper revolution of the Earth’s globe is completed, along with that which is added in the meantime by the annual progress according to the Sun’s apparent motion. 

That this addition is made unequally is shown, first, by the Sun's own apparent unequal course, and furthermore, because that natural day occurs relative to the poles of the <term>equinoctial circle</term> <note>The celestial equator, which defines the 24-hour rotation.</note>, while the annual motion occurs along the <term>circle of signs</term> <note>The Zodiac or ecliptic.</note>. For these reasons, that apparent time cannot be a common and certain measure of motion, since day does not agree with day, and they are not consistent with each other in every part. Therefore, it was necessary to choose from these a certain mean and equal day, by which one might [measure] without hesitation...

...to measure the equality of motion. Since, therefore, within the circle of a whole year there are 365 revolutions at the poles of the Earth, to which a nearly whole extra revolution is added daily through the apparent progress of the Sun, it follows that the 365th part of that total is what fills out the natural day in an equal manner. Therefore, we must define and distinguish the **equal day** from the **unequal, apparent day**. 

We define an **equal day** as one that contains the entire revolution of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator, the projection of Earth's equator into space.</note> and, in addition, that portion which the Sun is seen to traverse by its equal motion during that time. On the other hand, we define an **unequal and apparent day** as one which comprises the 360 units of one revolution of the equinoctial circle, plus whatever rises on the horizon or meridian along with the Sun's apparent progress. 

The difference between these days, although very small and not immediately noticeable, accumulates into an evident amount after several days. There are two causes for this: first, the inequality of the solar appearance; and second, the unequal ascent of the oblique <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: *signiferi*; literally "the sign-bearer," the path of the Sun through the constellations.</note>. 

The first cause exists because of the Sun’s unequal and apparent motion. It has already become clear that in the semicircle in which the <term>highest apsis</term> <note>original: *summa absis*; the apogee, or the point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> is located, there was a deficit of 4 and 3/4 units <note>original: *dodrante*; a Roman term for three-fourths.</note> of the zodiac according to Ptolemy, while in the other semicircle, where the <term>lowest apsis</term> <note>original: *infima absis*; the perigee, or the point closest to the center.</note> was, there was an excess of the same amount. Therefore, the total excess of one semicircle over the other was 9 and a half units. 

In the second cause, which relates to rising and setting, the greatest difference occurs between the semicircles of each solstice <note>original: *conuersionis*; referring to the "turning" points of the Sun at midsummer and midwinter.</note>; this difference exists between the shortest and longest day and varies greatly, being specific to each region. However, the difference that occurs relative to noon or midnight <note>i.e., the time it takes for the Sun to return to the meridian.</note> is everywhere contained within four boundaries. 

For from the 16th degree of Taurus to the 14th of Leo, 88 degrees [of the zodiac] pass across the meridian in approximately 93 units of time <note>In this context, "units of time" refer to degrees of the celestial equator; 15 units equal one hour.</note>; and from the 14th of Leo to the 16th of Scorpio, 92 degrees pass in 87 units of time. Thus, in the latter case, five units of time are missing, while in the former, five are in excess. In this way, the days collected in the first segment exceed those in the second by ten units of time, which make up two-thirds of an hour. The same happens alternately in the other semicircle under the remaining diametrically opposite boundaries. It has, however, pleased the Mathematicians...

### BOOK III OF THE REVOLUTIONS.

...maticians <note>original: *mathematicis*; referring to astronomers and mathematicians</note> the beginning of the natural day is taken not from sunrise or sunset, but from noon or midnight. For the difference taken from the horizon is more complex, as it extends to several hours, and moreover it is not the same everywhere, but varies in many ways according to the tilt of the sphere <note>The "obliquity of the sphere" refers to the angle of the Earth's axis relative to the observer's latitude.</note>. That which pertains to the meridian, however, is the same everywhere and is simpler. 

Therefore, the total difference, which is established from both of the aforementioned causes—both because of the Sun's unequal apparent progress and because of the unequal transit across the meridian—before the time of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose model Copernicus is refining.</note>, taking the beginning of the decrease from the middle of **Aquarius** and increasing from the beginning of **Scorpio**, used to accumulate 8 units and one-third of a unit of time <note>Copernicus uses "times" (*tempora*) to refer to degrees of the celestial equator; 15 degrees equals one hour.</note>. This has now, from the twentieth degree of **Aquarius** or nearby, by decreasing to the tenth degree of **Scorpio**, and increasing from the tenth of **Scorpio** to the twentieth of **Aquarius**, been contracted into 7 units of time and 48 minutes. 

For these things also change over time because of the instability of the **perigee** <note>The point in the orbit closest to the center.</note> and the **eccentricity** <note>original: *eccentrotetis*; the measure of how much an orbit deviates from a perfect circle.</note>. If finally the maximum difference in the precession of the equinoxes is also added to these, the total difference of the natural days could extend over ten units of time over a certain number of years. In this, a third cause of the inequality of days has remained hidden until now: because the revolution of the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> was found to be equal in relation to the mean and equal equinox, but not in relation to the apparent equinoxes, which, as has been shown, are not entirely equal. 

Therefore, ten units of time doubled make one hour and a third, by which the longer days can sometimes exceed the shorter ones. Regarding the annual progress of the **Sun** and the slower motion of the other stars, these differences could perhaps be ignored without obvious error. But because of the **Moon's** speed, through which an error of half a degree and a third could be committed, they are by no means to be ignored. 

Therefore, the method for coordinating equal time with the varying apparent time, in which all differences agree, is this: For any given time, one must find at both limits of that time—the beginning and the end—the Sun's mean position from the equinox through its equal motion (which we called composite), as well as its true apparent position from the true equinox, and consider how many units of time have passed in **right ascensions**...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

around noon or midnight, or whatever intervals exist between them, from the first true position to the second true position. For if these [temporal parts] are equal to the degrees that lie between both mean positions, then the apparent time taken will be equal to the mean time. But if the temporal parts <note>Copernicus refers here to 'parts of the equator' used to measure time.</note> exceed them, the excess itself should be added to the given time; if, however, they are less, the deficit should be subtracted from the apparent time. By doing this, from the sums or remainders, we will have the time converted into uniformity, by taking four minutes of an hour for each temporal part, or ten seconds of one-sixtieth of a day.

Furthermore, if the mean time is given and you wish to know how much apparent time corresponds to it, the opposite must be done. Now, for the first Olympiad <note>The starting point of the ancient Greek calendar, 776 BCE.</note>, we had the mean position of the Sun relative to the mean Vernal Equinox at noon on the first day of the first month according to the Athenians, called Hecatombaeon <note>original: "Hecatombæonos"; the first month of the Attic calendar.</note>, at 90 degrees and 59 minutes; and from the apparent equinox at 0 degrees and 36 minutes of Cancer. 

However, for the years of Christ <note>The beginning of the Common Era.</note>, the mean motion of the Sun was 8 degrees and 2 minutes of Capricorn. Its true motion was 8 degrees and 48 minutes of the same sign. Therefore, in the right sphere <note>The celestial sphere as viewed from the equator, where the horizon cuts the celestial equator at right angles.</note>, from 0 degrees and 36 minutes of Cancer to 8 degrees and 48 minutes of Capricorn, there ascend 188 temporal parts and 54 minutes, exceeding the distance of the mean positions by 1 temporal part and 54 minutes. These constitute 7 and a half minutes of an hour. And so on for the rest, by which the course of the Moon—which will be discussed in the following book—can be most exactly examined.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS ON THE REVOLUTIONS: BOOK FOUR.

<note>Copernicus begins this book by justifying why the Moon must be studied before the planets: it is our closest neighbor and the primary tool for measuring the positions of other stars.</note>

Since in the preceding book we have explained, to the best of our modest ability, the phenomena appearing because of the Earth's motion around the Sun, and since it is our purpose by the same means to distinguish the motions of all the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" refers to the planets, from the Greek 'planētēs'.</note>, the course of the Moon now interrupts our progress. This is necessary because it is through the Moon—which participates in both day and night—that the positions of any stars are chiefly captured and examined. Furthermore, of all the heavenly bodies, the Moon alone refers its revolutions (however diverse they may be) entirely to the center of the Earth, being most closely related to the Earth. For that reason, as far as its own nature is concerned, the Moon indicates nothing about the Earth's mobility—except perhaps for the daily rotation. Indeed, for this very reason, men formerly believed that the Earth was the center of the universe and the common center of all revolutions. In our explanation of the lunar course, we do not differ from the opinions of the ancients regarding its motion around the Earth. However, we shall bring forward certain points different from those we received from our ancestors, which are more consistent, and by which we shall establish the lunar motion with as much certainty as possible.

## The hypotheses of the lunar circles according to the
## opinion of the ancients. Chapter I.

The lunar course has this characteristic: it does not follow the middle circle of the signs <note>The Ecliptic, or the apparent path of the Sun through the Zodiac.</note>, but follows its own inclined circle, which bisects the former and is in turn bisected by it, crossing over from it into both latitudes <note>North and south of the Sun's path.</note>. These movements behave much like the annual conversions of the Sun, which is not surprising, since what the year is to the Sun, the month is to the Moon. The mean positions of these intersections are called "ecliptic" points, or by others, "nodes." The conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon occurring in these points are called "ecliptic" <note>original: "eclypticæ"; referring to the points where eclipses can occur.</note>...

are called <note>original: "uocantur." Referring to the nodes or "Dragon's points" where the orbits intersect.</note>. For there are no other signs common to both circles except these, in which eclipses of the Sun and Moon can occur. In other locations, the diversion of the Moon ensures that the lights <note>The Sun and Moon were traditionally called the "Two Luminaries."</note> do not obstruct each other at all, but pass by without hindrance. Furthermore, this oblique orbit of the Moon, along with its four cardinal points, is carried uniformly around the center of the earth, moving nearly three minutes of one degree every day, completing its revolution in the nineteenth year <note>This refers to the 18.6-year nodal cycle.</note>. Beneath this orbit and its plane, the Moon is always seen moving in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia," meaning eastward or counter-clockwise in modern terms.</note>, but sometimes at a minimum speed and sometimes at a maximum. For it is as much slower when it is higher as it is faster when it is nearer to the earth. This could be discerned more easily in the Moon than in any other star because of its proximity. They understood, therefore, that this happened by means of an **epicycle** <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term>, since the Moon, running around that circle, would subtract from uniform motion on the upper circumference and add to it on the lower. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that what occurs through an epicycle can also occur through an **eccentric** <term>eccentric: a circular orbit whose center is offset from the Earth</term>. 

But they chose the epicycle because the Moon seemed to admit a double irregularity. For when it was at the highest or lowest summit <note>original: "abside," referring to the apogee or perigee.</note> of the epicycle, no difference from uniform motion appeared. However, near the contact points of the epicycle, the difference was not of one kind, but far greater during the waxing and waning half-moons than when it was full or "thirsty" <note>original: "sitiens," likely a metaphor for the New Moon/conjunction.</note>, and this happens in a certain and orderly succession. For this reason, they judged that the circle in which the small epicycle moves is not concentric with the earth, but is an **eccentric-epicycle** in which the Moon is carried under this law: that in all mean oppositions and conjunctions of the Sun and Moon, the small epicycle is at the apogee of the eccentric, but in the middle quadrants of the circle, it is at the perigee of the same. 

Therefore, they imagined two motions equal to each other but in opposite directions around the center of the earth: namely, that the epicycle moves in the order of the signs, while the center of the eccentric and its summits move against the order of the signs, with the line of the mean position of the Sun always mediating between both. In this manner, the epicycle traverses the eccentric twice a month. To place these things before the eyes: Let the oblique circle of the Moon, concentric with the earth, be <term>abcd</term>, divided into four parts by the diameters <term>aec</term> and <term>bed</term>. Let the center of the earth be <term>e</term>. Let the mean conjunction of the Sun and Moon be on the line <term>ac</term>, and at the same place and time, let there be the apogee of the eccentric, whose center is <term>f</term>, and the center of the epicycle...

The epicycle MN moves simultaneously. Now, let the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> of the eccentric circle move in the direction of the preceding signs <note>Westward, or against the order of the zodiac.</note>, just as much as the epicycle moves in the direction of the following signs <note>Eastward, or with the order of the zodiac.</note>. Both move equally around center E with equal monthly revolutions relative to the mean conjunctions or oppositions of the Sun. Let the line AEC always be the mean position of the Sun between them, and let the Moon move again in the preceding direction from the apogee of the epicycle. For with these arrangements, they believe the appearances <note>The observed positions of the Moon in the sky.</note> agree. For when the epicycle completes a semicircle from the Sun in a six-month period, but completes a full revolution from the apogee of the eccentric, it follows that in the middle of this time—which is around the half-moon—they are positioned opposite one another along the diameter BD. Then the epicycle becomes perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> on the eccentric, as at sign G; where, having been made closer to the Earth, it produces greater differences in inequality. For equal magnitudes viewed at unequal distances appear larger when closer to the eye. Therefore, the differences were smallest when the epicycle was at A, but largest at G. This is because the diameter MN of the epicycle will have its smallest ratio to line AE, but a larger ratio to GE than all others found in other places, since GE itself is the shortest of all, and AE (or its equal DE) is the longest of those lines that can be extended from the center of the earth into the eccentric circle.

### On the defect of these assumptions. Chapter II.

The ancients certainly adopted such a composition of circles as being consistent with lunar appearances. But if we consider the matter itself more diligently, we will find this hypothesis is neither sufficiently fit nor adequate. This we can prove by both reason and the senses. For while they admit that the motion of the center of the epicycle is uniform around the center of the earth, they must also admit it is non-uniform in its own orbit which it describes, the eccentric. For if, for example, the angle AEB is taken as 45 degrees—that is, half a right angle—and equal to AED so that the whole BED becomes a right angle, and the center of the epicycle is taken at G,

And if line GF is connected, it is manifest that angle GFD is greater than angle GEF; for the exterior angle is greater than the interior and opposite angle. For this reason, the circumferences DAB and DG, both described in the same amount of time, are dissimilar. Thus, when DAB is a quadrant <note>A quarter of a circle, or 90 degrees.</note>, DG, which the center of the epicycle has described in the meantime, would be greater than a quadrant of the circle. However, it was evident in the case of the half-moon that both DAB and DG were semicircles; therefore, the motion of the epicycle on its eccentric <term>eccentric: a circular orbit where the center of motion is offset from the center of the Earth</term> which it describes is unequal. 

If this is the case, what shall we respond to the axiom <note>A fundamental principle of ancient astronomy derived from Plato and Aristotle.</note> that the motion of the heavenly bodies is uniform, and only appears unequal to the sight, if the apparent uniform motion of the epicycle is in reality unequal? It would happen that the result is entirely contrary to the established and assumed principle. 

But if you say that it moves uniformly around the center of the Earth, and that this is enough to maintain uniformity, what kind of uniformity will that be in a foreign circle in which its motion does not exist, but rather in its own eccentric? Indeed, we also marvel at this: that they wish the uniformity of the Moon itself within the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term> to be understood not by comparison to the center of the Earth through the line EGM—to which the uniformity ought rightly to be referred, being in agreement with the center of the epicycle itself—but rather to a certain different point. They place the Earth in the middle between that point and the center of the eccentric, and use the line IGH as if it were the pointer of the Moon's uniformity in the epicycle; this demonstrates well enough that this motion is also unequal in reality. 

For the appearances, which partly follow this hypothesis, force us to admit this. Thus, with the Moon also traversing its epicycle unequally, if we now wish to prove the inequality of the appearance from unequal motions, one may notice what kind of argument that will be. For what else shall we do but provide an opportunity to those who disparage this art? 

Furthermore, experience and the senses themselves teach us that the parallaxes <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points, used here to measure distance</term> of the Moon do not agree with those which the ratio of their circles promises. For parallaxes—which they call "commutations"—occur because of the evident size of the Earth in relation to the proximity of the Moon. Since the straight lines which extend from the surface of the Earth and from its center to the Moon do not appear parallel, but...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

Because of the manifest inclination <note>The angle or tilt of the lunar orbit</note> where these circles intersect in the body of the Moon, they must necessarily produce a difference in the Moon's appearance. Thus, it appears in a different location to those viewing it obliquely from the surface of the Earth than to those who might view the Moon from the Earth's center or from their own zenith. Such changes, therefore, vary according to the ratio of the Moon's distance from the Earth. Indeed, by the consensus of all mathematicians, the maximum distance is 64 parts and one-sixth <note>64 1/6 Earth radii</note>, where the distance from the center of the Earth to the surface is one part. However, according to their symmetry <note>The proportions of the Ptolemaic model</note>, the minimum distance ought to have been 33 parts and as many minutes <note>33 parts and 33 minutes</note>. This would mean the Moon would approach us by almost half the distance; consequently, it would follow that the parallaxes <note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from different locations</note> at the minimum and maximum distances would differ from each other by nearly double.

We, however, observe that those parallaxes which occur when the Moon is halved—both waxing and waning—even when it is at the perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to Earth</note> of the epicycle, differ very little or not at all from those which happen during eclipses of the Sun and Moon, as we shall demonstrate sufficiently in the proper place. But the error is most clearly declared by the body of the Moon itself, which by the same logic would happen to appear twice as large or twice as small in its diameter. Just as circles are in a double ratio to their diameters <note>Copernicus refers here to the linear diameter; the area would be fourfold</note>, the Moon would generally appear four times larger in its quadratures <note>The quarter-moon phases</note> when nearest the Earth than when opposite the Sun <note>The Full Moon</note>, if it were to shine fully. But since it shines as a half-moon, it would nonetheless shine with twice the light as it does when it is full in the latter position.

Although the opposite of this is manifest in itself, if anyone is not content with simple sight and wishes to experiment with the Hipparchan dioptra <note>An ancient sighting instrument used for measuring angular diameters</note> or any other instruments by which the Moon's diameter may be captured, he will find that it does not differ except by as much as the epicycle requires without that eccentric circle. For that reason, Menelaus and Timochares <note>Ancient Greek astronomers whose observations Copernicus used to track the precession of the equinoxes</note>, in their investigation of the fixed stars by means of the Moon's position, did not hesitate to always use the same lunar diameter of half a degree, which is the amount the Moon is generally seen to occupy.

### Another Opinion on the Motion of the Moon. Chapter III.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap 'I' featuring a landscape with a seated human figure, possibly a shepherd, amidst trees and rolling hills.</image-desc>
It is indeed apparent, then, that there is no eccentric circle through which the epicycle appears larger and smaller, but rather another arrangement of circles.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Let there be an epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain complex planetary motions.</note> AB, which we shall call the first and larger one; let its center be C. From the center of the Earth, which is D, let the straight line DC be extended to the highest point <note>original: "summam absidem"</note> of the epicycle. At point A, let another small epicycle EF be described, and let all these be in the same plane as the Moon's oblique orbit.

->[Diagram showing the Earth (D) at the base, with a line extending through the center (C) of a large epicycle to a smaller epicycle (EF) at the top.]<-

Now, let center C move in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" — moving eastward through the zodiac</note>, while A moves in the opposite direction <note>original: "in præcedentia" — moving westward</note>. Furthermore, let the Moon move from F, the upper part of the epicycle EF, in the order of the signs. This order is maintained so that whenever the line DC is aligned with the mean position of the Sun, the Moon is always closest to center C—that is, at point E. However, during the quadratures <note>The points where the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun, such as the first and last quarters.</note>, the Moon is at its most distant point, F.

With these arrangements established, I assert that the observed appearances of the Moon agree with this model. For it follows that the Moon circles the small epicycle EF twice a month, during which time center C returns once to the Sun. At the New and Full Moon, it will appear to describe the smallest circle—namely, the one whose radius is CE. In the quadratures, however, it describes the largest circle according to the distance from the center CF. Thus, it will produce smaller differences between the uniform and apparent motion in the former case, and larger differences in the latter, moving along similar but unequal arcs around center C.

Since the center of the epicycle C is always on a circle concentric with the Earth, it will not show such diverse parallaxes <note>The displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</note>, but only those conforming to the epicycle itself. The reason why the lunar body appears somewhat similar to itself will be readily apparent, and all other phenomena observed regarding the lunar course will happen in this way.

We shall subsequently demonstrate these things through this hypothesis of ours, although the same results could be achieved through eccentrics <note>A circular orbit where the Earth is not at the exact center.</note>, just as we did with the Sun, provided the proper proportions are maintained. We shall begin with the uniform motions, as we did above, for without them the non-uniform motion cannot be discerned. But here a significant difficulty exists because of the parallaxes we mentioned. For this reason, the Moon's position is not easily observable through Astrolabes <note>An ancient astronomical instrument used for measuring the altitudes of celestial bodies.</note> or any other instruments. However, the kindness of nature has provided for human desire even in this part, so that its position may be grasped more certainly through its eclipses <note>original: "defectus"</note> than by the use of instruments, and without suspicion of error.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

For since the rest of the universe is pure and full of daylight, it is established that night is nothing other than the shadow of the earth, which extends into a conical shape and ends in a point. Falling into this shadow, the Moon is dimmed, and when positioned in the midst of the darkness, it is understood to have reached the point directly opposite the Sun. However, solar eclipses, which occur by the interposition of the Moon, do not provide a certain proof of the Moon's position. For it happens then that we see a conjunction of the Sun and Moon which, in comparison to the center of the earth, has either already passed or not yet occurred, due to the aforementioned cause of parallax <note>original: "commutationis"; the shift in apparent position of an object when viewed from different points.</note>. Therefore, we do not see the same solar eclipse as equal in magnitude and duration in all lands, nor similar in its phases. But in lunar eclipses, no such impediment occurs, but they are everywhere similar to themselves. Since the earth transmits the axis of that dimming shadow from the Sun through its own center, lunar eclipses are therefore most suitable for apprehending the course of the Moon with the most certain reasoning.

## On the revolutions of the Moon and its particular motions. Chapter IV.

<note>The decorative initial 'E' marks the beginning of the historical survey of lunar cycles.</note>
Among the most ancient of those who took care that this matter be handed down to posterity in numbers, Meton the Athenian is found, who flourished in the thirty-seventh Olympiad. He declared that in 19 solar years, 235 months are completed; hence that great year was called the *nineteen-year cycle* <note>original Greek: "ἐννεαδεκαετηρίς" (enneadekaeteris)</note>, that is, the Metonic nineteen-year period. This number was so pleasing that it was posted in the forums at Athens and other famous cities, and it is even accepted by the common people to the present day, because they believe that through it the beginnings and ends of months are established in a certain order. He also made the solar year of 365 and a quarter days commensurable with the months. From this came that Callippic period of 76 years, in which one day is intercalated nineteen times, and they named it the Callippic year. But the skill of Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) considered the father of trigonometry.</note> discovered that in 304 years a whole day was added, and it is only verified when the solar year is smaller by the 300th part of a day. Thus, by some, this great year was also named after Hipparchus.

was born, in which 760 months were completed. These things have been stated in a simpler and, as they say, "cruder" <note>original: "crassiori... minerua" - a Latin idiom meaning a rough or plain approach without excessive refinement</note> manner. Since the restorations of the anomaly <note>The "anomaly" refers to the irregularity in the moon's speed as it moves along its elliptical-like orbit</note> and the latitude are also sought. For this reason, the same Hipparchus <note>A famous Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who laid the foundations for trigonometry</note> investigated these matters further, namely by comparing the notes which he most diligently observed in lunar eclipses to those which he received from the Chaldeans <note>Babylonian astronomers known for their long-term records of celestial events</note>. He defined the time in which the revolutions of the months and the anomalies would return together to be 345 Egyptian years, 82 days, and one hour; and in that time, 4,267 months and 4,573 cycles of anomaly are completed. Therefore, when the proposed multitude of days—which is 126,007 days and one hour—is distributed by the number of months, one month is found to be equal to 29 days, 31 minutes, 50 seconds, 8 thirds, 9 fourths, and 20 fifths <note>Copernicus is using sexagesimal fractions (base-60) to achieve extreme precision in timekeeping</note>. By this calculation, the motion for any given time also became clear.

For by dividing the 360 degrees of one monthly revolution by the monthly time, the daily course of the Moon away from the Sun came out to be 12 degrees, 11 minutes, 26 seconds, 41 thirds, 20 fourths, and 18 fifths. These, collected 365 times, produce the annual motion beyond twelve revolutions: 129 degrees, 37 minutes, 31 seconds, 28 thirds, and 29 fourths. Furthermore, since 4,267 months to 4,573 cycles of anomaly are composite numbers—inasmuch as the number 17 measures them both—they will be in the smallest numbers as 251 to 269. In this ratio, according to the 15th theorem of the fifth book of Euclid, we will have the lunar course in relation to the motion of the anomaly. Thus, when we have multiplied the motion of the Moon by 269 and divided the product by 251, the annual motion of the anomaly will result (after 13 complete revolutions) as 88 degrees, 43 minutes, 8 seconds, 40 thirds, and 20 fourths; and likewise the daily motion is 13 degrees, 3 minutes, 54 seconds, 56 thirds, and 29 fourths.

However, the revolution of latitude <note>The "latitude" refers to the moon's north-south position relative to the ecliptic (the sun's path)</note> has another calculation. For it does not coincide within the predefined time in which the anomaly is restored; rather, we understand the latitude of the Moon to have returned only then, when a later eclipse of the Moon is in all respects similar and equal to an earlier one—namely, when the obscurations on the same side were equal in both magnitude and duration. This happens when the distances from the highest or lowest apsis <note>The "apsis" is the point in the orbit where the moon is furthest from or closest to the Earth</note> of the Moon are equal; for then it is understood that the Moon has passed through equal shadows in an equal time.

->ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.<-

According to Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who laid the foundations for trigonometry and lunar observation.</note>, such a return occurs in 5,458 months, to which correspond 5,923 revolutions in latitude. By this same reasoning, the particular motions of latitude in years and days were established, just like the others. For when we have multiplied the Moon's motion from the Sun by 5,923 months and divided the total by 5,458, we will have the Moon's motion in latitude. In years, after the full revolutions, this is 168 degrees, 42 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula prima"</note>, 46 seconds, 20 thirds, and 3 fourths. In days, however, it is 13 degrees, 13 minutes, 45 seconds, 39 thirds, and 40 fourths. In this manner, Hipparchus fixed the uniform motions of the Moon, which no one before him approached more closely; nevertheless, succeeding centuries have shown that these figures were not yet absolute in all their numbers.

For Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), whose Almagest was the standard astronomical text before Copernicus.</note> found the same mean motion from the Sun as Hipparchus, but found that the annual motion of <term>anomaly</term> <note>The irregularity or variation in the Moon's speed due to its elliptical-like path.</note> fell short of his by 1 second, 11 thirds, and 39 fourths. The annual motion in latitude, however, exceeded his by 52 thirds and 41 fourths. We ourselves, after the passage of much more time, have found that Hipparchus's mean annual motion also falls short by 1 second, 7 thirds, and 56 fourths; while for the anomaly, only 26 thirds and 55 fourths are lacking. For the motion in latitude, there is an excess of 1 second, 2 thirds, and 42 fourths. Therefore, the uniform motion of the Moon, by which it differs from the Earth's motion, will be annually 129 degrees, 37 minutes, 22 seconds, 36 thirds, and 25 fourths. The anomaly is 88 degrees, 43 minutes, 9 seconds, 7 thirds, and 15 fourths. The latitude is 148 degrees, 42 minutes, 45 seconds, 17 thirds, and 21 fourths.

<header>NICOLAUS COPERNICUS</header>

## Chapter V. Demonstration of the first inequality of the Moon, which occurs at the new and full moons.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'M' with foliate and vine motifs.</image-desc>

We have set forth the uniform motions of the Moon as far as they have been able to become known to us up to the present. Now we must approach the logic of its inequality <note>Copernicus uses "inequality" to describe the variation or anomaly in a planet's speed and position compared to a perfectly uniform circular motion</note>, which we shall demonstrate by means of an epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; a standard tool in pre-modern astronomy to explain retrograde motion and varying speeds</note>. First, we address that inequality which occurs at the conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun <note>The New and Full Moons</note>, concerning which the ancient mathematicians used a wonderful ingenuity by means of triads of lunar eclipses. We shall follow the path thus prepared for us by them, and we will take three eclipses diligently observed by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the most influential astronomer of antiquity</note>, with which we will compare three others noted with no less diligence, so that the uniform motions already set forth may be examined to see if they are correctly established. In their explanation, we shall use the mean motions of the Sun and Moon from the position of the Vernal Equinox as if they were uniform, in imitation of the ancients. This is because the variation which occurs due to the unequal precession of the equinoxes is not perceived in so short a time, even over ten years.

Ptolemy therefore takes the first eclipse as having occurred in the 17th year of the Emperor Hadrian, on the twentieth day of the month of Pauni according to the Egyptians. In the years of Christ, it was the 133rd year, on the sixth day of the month of May, or the day before the Nones. It was a total eclipse, the midpoint of which was three-quarters of an equal hour before midnight at Alexandria; but at Frombork <note>original: "Fruenburgi"</note> or Kraków, it would have been one hour and three-quarters before the midnight followed by the seventh day. The Sun was holding 13 degrees and a quadrant of a degree of Taurus, but according to the mean motion, it was at 12° 21' of Taurus.

He says the second eclipse was in the 19th year of Hadrian, after two days of the month of Chiach, the fourth month of the Egyptians. It was in the year of Christ 134, on the 13th day before the Kalends of November <note>October 20</note>. It was eclipsed from the North by ten-twelfths <note>original: "dextantem"</note> of its diameter. Its midpoint was one equinoctial hour before midnight at Alexandria, but at Kraków, two hours before midnight. The Sun was in the 25th degree and a sixth part of the sign of Libra, but by mean motion at 26° 43' of the same.

The third eclipse was also in the 20th year of Hadrian, after 19 days of Pharmuthi, the eighth month of the Egyptians. In the years of Christ—

After the 135th year <note>original: "CXXXV." referring to the era of Nabonassar</note>, on the 6th of March, the Moon was again eclipsed in the North by half of its diameter. The midpoint of this eclipse was at Alexandria at four equinoctial hours <note>hours of equal length, regardless of the season</note>, but at Krakow it was three hours after midnight, on the morning of the Nones of March <note>March 7th</note>. At that time, the Sun was in 14 degrees and 12 minutes of Pisces, but by its mean motion <note>the theoretical uniform motion of a celestial body</note> it was in 11 degrees and 44 minutes of Pisces.

It is evident that in the middle space of time between the first and second eclipse, the Moon traveled as far as the Sun in its apparent motion—discarding, I say, the full circles—which was 161 degrees and 55 minutes <term>scrupula: minutes of a degree</term>. And from the second to the third, it traveled 137 degrees and 55 minutes. In the first interval, there was one year, 166 days, and 23 and three-quarter hours according to apparent time, but by exact calculation, 23 hours and five-eighths. In the second distance, there was one year, 137 days, and 5 hours simply, but exactly 5 hours.

The equal motion of the Sun and Moon combined in the first interval, discarding full circles, was 169 degrees and 37 minutes, and the motion of the anomaly <note>the position of a planet relative to its furthest point from Earth</note> was 110 degrees and 21 minutes. In the second interval, the equal motion of the Sun and Moon was similarly 137 degrees and 33 minutes. It is clear, therefore, that in the first distance, the 110 degrees and 21 minutes of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term> subtract 7 degrees and 42 minutes from the mean motion of the Moon. In the second, 81 degrees and 36 minutes add 1 degree and 21 minutes.

With these things thus proposed, let the lunar epicycle ABC be described, in which the first eclipse was at A, the second at B, and the remaining one at C; let the passage of the Moon be understood in that same order moving forward. Let the arc AB be 110 degrees and 21 minutes, which subtracts (as we said) 7 degrees and 42 minutes; and let BC be 81 degrees and 36 minutes, which adds 1 degree and 21 minutes. The remainder of the circle, CA, will be 168 degrees and 3 minutes, adding the remaining 6 degrees and 21 minutes.

Since the highest point <note>original: "absis," the apogee</note> of the epicycle is not in the arcs BC and CA (since they are additive and less than a semicircle), it is necessary that it be found in AB. Let us therefore take D as the center of the Earth, around which the epicycle is carried uniformly. From there, let lines be drawn to the points of the eclipses, DA, DB, and DC, and let BC, BE, and CE be connected. Since the arc AB subtends 7 degrees and 42 minutes of the zodiac, the angle ADB will be 7 degrees and 42 minutes, of which 180 are two right angles; but where 360 make two right angles, the angle itself will be 15 degrees and 24 minutes.
