We noted the second eclipse in the year of Christ 1522, in the month of September, after five days had elapsed. This was also a total eclipse. The Sun was in 22 degrees and a fifth of Virgo, but by mean motion in 24 degrees 49 minutes of Virgo.

The third was in the year of Christ 1523, after 25 days of the month of August had passed. It began three hours minus a fifth of an hour after midnight, and the middle time of the eclipse (which was also total) was four and a half hours minus a twelfth of an hour after midnight, as the seventh day before the Calends of September was breaking. The Sun was in 11 degrees 21 minutes of Virgo, with its mean motion at 14 degrees 2 minutes of Virgo. Here also it is manifest that the distance of the true positions of the Sun and Moon from the first eclipse to the second was 339 degrees.

38 minutes. In the second of the following lunar eclipses of our own time, the motion of the Moon from the Sun was 182 degrees, 50 minutes; the motion of the anomaly <note>The "anomaly" refers to the irregularity in a planet's or the moon's motion caused by its elliptical orbit or epicycle.</note> was 74 degrees, 27 minutes. It is evident that in the intervening time, 17,166 months were completed, and in addition, first minutes amounting to nearly four degrees. Of the motion of the anomaly, after rejecting full circles, there remained 9 degrees, 49 minutes. Now, the time that elapsed from the nineteenth year of Hadrian, in the Egyptian month of Choiak, on the second day and two hours before midnight (which the third day of the month followed), until the year of Christ 1522, on the fifth day of September, at one and one-third hours of apparent time—which, when equated <note>Equated time refers to "Local Apparent Time" adjusted to "Mean Time" to account for the Earth's axial tilt and orbital eccentricity.</note>, results in 1,388 Egyptian years, 302 days, 3 hours, and 34 minutes. In this time, after the completion of 17,165 equal revolutions of months, according to Hipparchus and Ptolemy <note>Ancient Greek astronomers whose work formed the basis of medieval science.</note>, there would have been 358 degrees, 38 minutes. But of the anomaly, according to Hipparchus, 9 degrees, 49 minutes; yet according to Ptolemy, 9 degrees, 11 minutes. Therefore, there are lacking from those motions of the Moon 26 first minutes, and of the anomaly 38 first minutes, which are added to our numbers and agree with the figures we have set forth.

## On the Positions of Lunar Longitude and Anomaly. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>A decorative drop-cap 'T' within a square woodcut border, depicting a seated figure against a landscape background.</image-desc>
Just as we did above, the positions for these must also be established at the fixed beginnings of years: the Olympiads, the era of Alexander, Caesar, Christ, and any others that may please anyone. If, therefore, we consider that second of the three ancient eclipses, which occurred in the nineteenth year of Hadrian, on the second day of the Egyptian month of Choiak, one equinoctial hour before midnight at Alexandria—but for us, under the meridian of Krakow, two hours before midnight—we shall find from the beginning of the years of Christ until this moment 133 Egyptian years, 325 days, 22 hours simply, but exactly 21 hours and 37 minutes. In this time, the lunar motion according to our calculation is 332 degrees, 49 minutes. Of the anomaly, 217 degrees, 32 minutes. Which, when from—

When these values have been subtracted from those found in the eclipse—each from its own kind—there remains the mean lunar position from the Sun at 209 degrees, 58 minutes, and the Anomaly <note>The "Anomaly" refers to the Moon's irregular movement along its orbital path.</note> at 207 degrees, 7 minutes, at the beginning of the years of Christ, at midnight before the Kalends of January <note>January 1st.</note>. Again, reaching back from this beginning of Christ, there are 193 Olympiads, 2 years, 194.5 days, which make 775 Egyptian years, 12.5 days; or more precisely, 12 hours and 7.5 minutes. Similarly, from the death of Alexander to the birth of Christ, they calculate 323 Egyptian years, 130.5 days in apparent time, but precisely 12 hours and 14 minutes. And from Caesar to Christ there are 45 Egyptian years, 12 days, in which the calculation of both equal and apparent time agrees. Therefore, when we have subtracted the motions concerning these differences of time from the positions at Christ's birth—subtracting each from each—we shall have, for the noon of the first day of the month Hecatombaeon of the first Olympiad, the equal distance of the Moon from the Sun as 39 degrees, 44 minutes, and the Anomaly as 46 degrees, 20 minutes. For the years of Alexander, at the noon of the first day of the month Thoth, the Moon from the Sun is 310 degrees, 44 minutes, and the Anomaly is 85 degrees, 41 minutes. And for Julius Caesar, at midnight before the Kalends of January, the Moon from the Sun is 350 degrees, 39 minutes, and the Anomaly is 17 degrees, 58 minutes. All these are referred to the meridian of Krakow. Since Frombork <note>original: "Fruëburgum"</note>, where we have mostly made our observations at the mouth of the Vistula <note>original: "Istolæ"</note> river, lies on this same meridian, as the eclipses of the Moon and Sun observed simultaneously in both places teach us; in which meridian Dyrrhachium in Macedonia (which was called Epidamnum in antiquity) is also contained.

### Regarding the second lunar inequality, and the ratio of the first epicycle to the second. Chapter 8.

Thus, therefore, the equal motions of the Moon together with its first inequality have been demonstrated. We must now investigate the ratio of the first epicycle to the second, and both to the distance from the center of the earth. Now, the greatest difference is found, as we said, in the mean quadratures <note>The "quadratures" are the points where the Moon is at a 90-degree angle from the Sun, appearing as a half-moon.</note>, when the Moon is halved, waxing or waning, which reaches seven degrees...

...and rises by two-thirds <note>of a degree</note>, just as the records of the ancients also maintain. For they observed the time in which the half-moon had nearly reached the middle distance of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain complex planetary orbits</term>, and this occurred near the contact of the line proceeding from the center of the Earth, which could easily be perceived through the calculations set forth above. And with the

-> [Diagram of the lunar epicycle as described in the text] <-

Moon itself then being located around the ninetieth degree of the zodiac <note>original: signiferi, the "sign-bearer" or zodiac</note> as measured from the rising or setting, they avoided the error which parallax <term>parallax: the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</term> could introduce into the motion of longitude. For at that time, the circle which passes through the vertex of the horizon <note>the zenith</note> divides the zodiac at right angles, and does not allow for any shift in longitude, but the entire shift falls into latitude. Accordingly, by the skill of the Astrolabe instrument <note>an ancient astronomical "computer" for solving problems relating to time and the position of the Sun and stars</note>, they took the position of the Moon relative to the Sun; having made the comparison, the Moon was found to differ from the mean motion by seven degrees and two-thirds of one <note>7° 40'</note>, as we said, instead of five degrees. 

Now let the epicycle AB be described, its center being C; and from the center of the Earth, which is D, let the straight line DBCA be extended, where the apogee <term>apogee: the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth</term> of the epicycle is A, and the perigee <term>perigee: the point in the orbit closest to the Earth</term> is B. Let the tangent to the epicycle DE be drawn, and connect CE. Therefore, since the maximum prosthaphaeresis <term>prosthaphaeresis: the correction or "addition-subtraction" needed to find the true position of a planet from its mean position</term> is in the tangent, which in this case is 7 degrees and 40 minutes, which is also the angle BDE, and the angle at CED is a right angle, namely at the contact of circle AB. 

Because of this, CE will be 1,334 parts, of which the distance from the center CD is 10,000. But in the position of the full and new Moon, it was much smaller, namely about 861 of those same parts. Let CB be cut back, and let CF be 860 parts; there will be a circle running around the same center F, which the new and full Moon followed. The remainder FE, therefore, will be 474 parts, which will be the diameter of the second epicycle; by dividing this in two at center G, the whole CFG will be 1,097 parts from the center of the circle which the center of the second epicycle described. Thus, the ratio of CG to GE is established as 1,097 to 237, of which parts CD was ten thousand.

# BOOK IV OF THE REVOLUTIONS

## Concerning the remaining variation, by which the Moon is seen to move unequally from the highest apsis of the epicycle. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating lunar epicycles and their mathematical relationships. A large circle has a central vertical diameter with points labeled A at the apex, C at the center, B below it, and D at the base. A smaller circle, an epicycle, is centered at point E on the upper right edge of the larger circle's circumference. A line segment connects center C to E and extends to a point F on the outer edge of the small circle. From C, two tangent lines are drawn to the small circle, touching it at points L and M. An arc with a directional arrow is shown on the small circle between points F and L. Dotted construction lines are visible for alignment.</image-desc>

Through this <term>induction</term><note>original: "epagogen"; a logical method of proving a general rule from specific instances</note> it is also given to be understood how the Moon moves unequally in its first <term>epicycle</term><note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-modern astronomy to explain complex planetary orbits</note>, the greatest variation of which happens when it is curved into horns <note>the crescent phase</note>, or is <term>gibbous</term><note>the phase where more than half but not all of the Moon is illuminated</note>, and exists as a half-full orb. Let that first epicycle be AB, which the center of the second epicycle describes in a uniform manner; let its center be C, the <term>highest apsis</term><note>original: "summa absis"; the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion</note> be A, and the lowest be B. Let a sign E be taken anywhere on the circumference, and let CE be joined. Let the ratio of CE to EF be as 1097 to 237. With E as the center and the distance EF, let a second small epicycle be described, and let the straight lines CL and CM be drawn from C tangent to it on both sides. Let the motion of the small epicycle be from A toward E—that is, upward and <term>in precedence</term><note>moving from East to West, or clockwise in this geometric context</note>—while the Moon moves from F to L, also in precedence. It is clear, therefore, that while the motion AE is uniform, the second epicycle adds the arc EL to that uniformity through the path FL, and subtracts through MF. Since in the triangle CEL the angle at L is a right angle, and EL is 237 parts where CE was 1097, then where CE is 10,000, EL will be 2160. According to the <term>Table</term><note>original: "Canonem"; referring to a mathematical table of chords or sines</note>, this subtends the angle ECL of 12 degrees and 28 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula"; literally 'scruples', used here for the sexagesimal division of a degree</note>, which is equal to angle MEF, since the triangles are similar and equal. And this is the greatest variation by which the Moon deviates from the highest apsis of the first epicycle. This happens when the Moon, by its <term>mean motion</term><note>The theoretical uniform motion of a celestial body, ignoring periodic fluctuations</note>, stands away from the line of the mean motion of the Earth by 38 degrees and 46 minutes, both before and after. Thus it is truly manifest that these greatest <term>prosthaphæreses</term><note>The geometric corrections or "equations" added to or subtracted from the mean motion to find the true position</note> occur at a mean distance between the Sun and Moon of 38 degrees and 46 minutes, and at the same distance on either side of the mean opposition.

## How the apparent motion of the Moon is demonstrated from the given uniform motions. Chapter 10.

Having provided all these preliminaries, we now wish to show how the apparent and uniform motion of the Moon is determined from those proposed uniform motions through a graphic method. We shall take an example from the observations of Hipparchus <note>Hipparchus of Nicaea (c. 190–120 BCE) was a Greek astronomer whose data Copernicus relied upon heavily to bridge ancient and "modern" observations.</note>, so that the theory may be simultaneously proven by experiment. In the 197th year after the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great; this refers to the Era of Alexander used in ancient dating.</note>, on the 17th day of the month of Pauni (which is the tenth Egyptian month), when nine and one-third hours of the day had passed in Rhodes, Hipparchus found by means of an astrolabe <term>astrolabe: an ancient instrument used to measure the altitudes and positions of celestial bodies</term> that the Sun and Moon were 48 degrees and one-tenth of a degree apart, with the Moon following the Sun. Since he judged the position of the Sun to be at 10 and nine-tenths degrees of Cancer, it followed that the Moon occupied 29 degrees of Leo. At that same time, the 29th degree of Scorpio was rising, with the 10th degree of Virgo at mid-heaven in Rhodes (where the North Pole is elevated 36 degrees). By this reasoning, it was established that the Moon—being positioned about 90 degrees from the horizon on the zodiac—admitted no parallax <note>original: "uisus commutationẽ" (change of vision). Parallax is the displacement in apparent position when viewed from different points; here, Copernicus notes it was negligible.</note> in longitude at that time, or at least an imperceptible amount.

Now, because this observation was made three and one-third hours after noon on that 17th day, which in Rhodes corresponds to four equinoctial hours, the time in Krakow would have been 3 and one-sixth equinoctial hours, according to the distance by which Rhodes is closer to us than Alexandria by one-sixth of an hour. Therefore, from the death of Alexander, there were 196 years, 286 days, and 3 and one-sixth hours in simple time; but in mean time <note>original: "regulariter". Copernicus distinguishes between apparent solar time and uniform mean time.</note>, it was approximately 3 and one-third hours. In this time, the Sun by its mean motion reached 12 degrees and 3 minutes of Cancer, but in apparent motion reached 10 degrees and 40 minutes of Cancer. From this, it appears that the Moon was truly at 28 degrees and 37 minutes of Leo. Furthermore, the uniform motion of the Moon according to its monthly revolution was at 45 degrees and 5 minutes, and its anomaly <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet or the moon from its furthest point (apogee) in its orbit</term> from the highest apogee was 333 degrees according to our calculation. With this example proposed, let us describe the first epicycle AB, and its center C...

of its <term>c</term> <note>Referring to the center of the epicycle</note>, the diameter <term>ACB</term>, which is extended in a straight line to the center of the Earth, and let it be <term>ABD</term>. Let there also be taken on the epicycle the circumference <term>ABE</term> of <term>333</term> degrees. Let <term>CE</term> be joined and cut at <term>F</term>, so that <term>EF</term> is <term>237</term> parts, where <term>EC</term> is <term>1097</term>. With center <term>E</term> and distance <term>EF</term>, let the smaller epicycle <note>original: "epicycli epicyclium"</note> <term>FG</term> be described. Let the Moon be at point <term>G</term>. Furthermore, let the circumference <term>FG</term> be <term>90</term> degrees and <term>10</term> minutes, by reason of the double equal motion from the Sun, which was <term>45</term> degrees and <term>5</literal> minutes. Let <term>CG</term>, <term>EG</term>, and <term>DG</term> be connected.

Since, therefore, in the triangle <term>CEG</term>, two sides are given—<term>CE</term> of <term>1097</term> parts and <term>EG</term> of <term>237</term> (which is equal to <term>EF</term>)—along with the angle <term>GEC</term> of <term>90</term> degrees and <term>10</term> minutes. Therefore, through the proofs of plane triangles, the remaining side <term>CG</term> is given as <term>1123</term> of the same parts, and the angle <term>ECG</term> as <term>12</term> degrees and <term>11</term> minutes. By these also consist the circumference <term>EI</term> and the additive <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>A term from Greek meaning "addition or subtraction," used to calculate the difference between the mean and true positions of a planet</note> of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its furthest point (apogee)</note>. Let the whole <term>ABEG</term> be <term>345</term> degrees and <term>11</term> minutes, and the remaining angle <term>GCA</term> be <term>14</term> degrees and <term>48</term> minutes, which is the true lunar distance from the highest apogee of the epicycle <term>AB</term>; and the angle <term>BCG</term> is <term>165</term> degrees and <term>11</term> minutes.

For this reason, in triangle <term>GDC</term>, two sides are also given: <term>GC</term> of <term>1123</term> parts (where <term>CD</term> is ten thousand) and the angle <term>GCD</term> of <term>165</term> degrees and <term>11</term> minutes. From these we will also have the angle <term>CDG</term> of one degree and <term>29</term> minutes, and the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> which was added to the mean motion of the Moon, so that the true distance of the Moon from the mean motion of the Sun was <term>46</term> degrees and <term>34</term> minutes, and its apparent position was in <term>28</term> degrees and <term>37</term> minutes of Leo, distant from the true position of the Sun by <term>47</term> degrees and <term>57</term> minutes—falling short of Hipparchus's observation by nine minutes.

But lest anyone should suspect on that account that either his investigation or our calculation has failed (although the difference is slight), we shall nevertheless show that neither he nor we committed an error, but that the matter stands correctly in this way. For if we remember that the lunar circle is oblique, which the Moon itself follows, we will also admit that it produces some diversity in longitude in the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signifero," literally the "sign-bearer"</note>, especially around the middle positions, which are between both the Northern and Southern limits and both the ecliptic sections, in much the same way as between the obliquity of the zodiac...

the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," the "sign-bearer," a common Renaissance term for the zodiacal circle</note> and the equinoctial circle, just as we explained regarding the inequality of the natural day. So also, if we transfer these ratios to the orbit of the Moon (which Ptolemy showed to be inclined to the zodiac), we find that in those positions, it creates a longitudinal difference of seven minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum primorum," literally "first small parts" or minutes of a degree</note> relative to the zodiac, which when doubled makes 14 minutes; and this happens similarly by increasing and decreasing. Since, when the Sun and Moon are separated by a quadrant of a circle, if the northern or southern limit of latitude is midway between them, then the intercepted circumference of the zodiac is 14 minutes greater than a quadrant of the lunar circle. Conversely, in the other quadrants which the ecliptic intersections <note>the nodes</note> bisect, the circles passing through the poles of the zodiac intercept just as much less than a quadrant; and so it is in the present case. Since the Moon was moving near the midpoint between the southern limit and the ascending ecliptic intersection (which the moderns <note>referring to medieval Arabic and Latin astronomers</note> call the **Head of the Dragon** <note>the ascending node</note>), and the Sun had already passed the other descending intersection, which they call the **Tail** <note>the descending node</note>, it is no wonder if that lunar distance of 47 degrees and 57 minutes on its oblique orbit, when compared to the zodiac, increased by at least 7 minutes. This is even without considering that the Sun, sinking toward the setting, may have introduced some subtractive parallax <note>original: "uisus commutationem," change of vision</note>, about which we shall speak more clearly in the explanation of parallaxes. And thus, that distance between the luminaries according to Hipparchus, which he had recorded by instrument as 48 degrees and 6 minutes, agrees with our calculation with wonderful consensus and as if by prior agreement.

### Canonical Exposition of the Prosthaphæreses, or
### Lunar Equations. Chapter XI.

I believe, therefore, that by this example the method of discerning the lunar courses can be understood generally. Since the two sides *eg* and *ce* of the triangle *ceg* always remain the same, but according to the angle *gbc*, which changes continuously, we nevertheless discern the remaining side *gc* along with the angle *ecg*, which is the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>from Greek, meaning "addition or subtraction"; the correction applied to a mean motion to find the true position</note> of the anomaly to be equated. Then also in the triangle *cdg*, when the two sides *dc* and *cg* have been calculated along with the angle *dcg*, the angle *d* around the center of the earth becomes manifest in the same way, representing the difference between the uniform and the true motion. So that these things may be even more ready—

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

To make these matters clearer, we shall set forth the Table of the <term>prosthaphæreses</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreseon"; these are the "additions or subtractions" used to correct mean motion to find the true position of a planet</note>, which will contain six columns. For after the two columns of common circular degrees, in the third place will be the prosthaphæreses which, proceeding from the small <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> according to the doubled motion of the months, vary the uniformity of the first <term>anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet from its point of least or greatest distance</note>. Then, leaving the next place temporarily empty for future numbers, we shall occupy the fifth column. In this, we shall write the prosthaphæreses of the first and larger epicycle which occur at the mean conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon; the greatest of these is 4 degrees and 56 minutes. In the penultimate <note>second to last</note> place are set the numbers by which the prosthaphæreses occurring at the half-moon exceed those first ones; the greatest of these is 2 degrees and 44 minutes. However, so that the remaining excesses might also be rated, the "minutes of proportion" were devised, the ratio of which is as follows. We take those 2 degrees and 44 minutes as 60 <note>representing a full unit in the sexagesimal system used in astronomy</note> in relation to any other excesses occurring at the contact of the epicycle. Just as in that same example, where we had the line CG as 1123 parts (where ED is 10,000), which produces a total prosthaphæresis at the contact of the epicycle of 6 degrees and 29 minutes, exceeding that first one by 1 degree and 33 minutes. Now, as 2 degrees and 44 minutes is to 1 degree and 33 minutes, so is 60 to 34. And thus we have the ratio of the excess occurring in the semicircle of the small epicycle to that which occurs under the given circumference of 90 degrees and 18 minutes. We shall therefore write 34 minutes in the table opposite the 90-degree mark. In this way, for each individual circumference of the same circle marked in the Table <note>original: "Canonem"</note>, we shall find the minutes of proportion to be set forth in the fourth place, which was left vacant. Finally, in the last place, we have added the degrees of latitude, both Northern <note>original: "Boreas"</note> and Southern <note>original: "Austrinas"</note>, which we shall discuss below. For convenience and ease of operation have advised us to arrange them in this order.

## On the calculation of the Moon’s course. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring an architectural scene with a building and a tall tower/steeple, possibly a city view.</image-desc>

The method for calculating the Moon's appearance is now clear from what has been demonstrated, and it is as follows. We shall reduce the proposed time for which we seek the Moon's position to a mean <note>uniform or average</note> time. Through this, we derive the mean motions of longitude, anomaly, and latitude—which we shall soon define—in the same manner we did for the Sun, starting from the birth of Christ or another established epoch, and we shall fix the positions of each for the proposed time. Next, we look up the mean longitude of the Moon, or its doubled distance from the Sun, in the table; we will note the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>original: "prosthaphærefim"; an adjustment or "equation" used to correct mean motion to true motion</note> found in the third column, along with the proportional minutes that follow. If the number we entered with is found in the first section—that is, if it is less than 180 degrees—we add the prosthaphaeresis to the lunar anomaly. If, however, it is greater than 180 degrees or found in the second section, it is subtracted from it. We will then have the corrected anomaly of the Moon and its true distance from the highest apse <note>the point in the orbit furthest from the center</note>. Entering the <term>Table</term> <note>original: "Canonem"; a set of mathematical tables</note> again with this value, we take the corresponding prosthaphaeresis in the fifth column, and the excess following in the sixth column, which the second <term>epicycle</term> <note>original: "epicyclus"; a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> adds over the first. A proportional part of this excess, taken according to the ratio of the discovered minutes to sixty, is always added to this prosthaphaeresis. The resulting sum is subtracted from the mean motion of longitude and latitude, provided the corrected anomaly is less than 180 degrees (or a semicircle), and added if the anomaly is greater. In this way, we will have the true distance of the Moon from the mean position of the Sun, as well as the corrected motion of latitude. Consequently, the true position of the Moon will not be unknown, whether measured from the first star of Aries by the simple motion of the Sun, or from the Vernal Equinox in the composite motion, or by adding its precession. Finally, through the corrected motion of latitude, we will find in the seventh and last column of the <term>Table</term> the degrees of latitude by which the Moon is distant from the center of the circle of the signs <note>the ecliptic</note>. This latitude will be Northern when the motion of latitude is in the first part of the table...

<meta>catchword: ...found in the table</meta>

And for that reason, the Moon will be descending from the North until it reaches 180 degrees, and from there climbing from the Southern limit until it has completed the remaining parts of the circle. Thus, the apparent lunar course has, in a sense, as many complications around the center of the Earth as the center of the Earth has around the Sun. <note>Copernicus is drawing a parallel between the Earth's motion around the Sun and the Moon's motion around the Earth to show the consistency of his heliocentric system.</note>

## How the motion of lunar latitude is examined and demonstrated. Chapter XIII.

Now a reckoning must also be given for the motion of the lunar latitude, which for that reason seems more difficult to discover, because it is hindered by more circumstances. For as we have said before, if two eclipses of the Moon were similar and equal in every respect—that is, with the eclipsed parts in the same Northern or Southern position, and around the same section of the ecliptic <note>term: ecliptic; the apparent path of the Sun, which the Moon crosses at "nodes."</note> whether climbing or descending—and if its distance from the Earth or from the highest apogee <note>term: apogee; the point in the orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> were equal. Since these factors agree, it is understood that the Moon has completed full circles of its latitude in its true motion. For since the shadow of the Earth is conical, and if a right cone is cut by a plane parallel to the base, the section is a smaller circle at a greater distance and a larger circle at a lesser distance from the base, and likewise equal at an equal distance; thus indeed the Moon, at equal distances from the Earth, passes through equal circles of the shadow, and represents equal disks of itself to our sight. It follows that when the Moon stands out by equal parts on the same side, at an equal distance from the center of the shadow, it makes us certain of equal latitudes; from which it must follow that it has returned to its previous place of latitude at equal intervals from the same ecliptic connection. This is especially true if the position also agrees on both sides, for the approach and retreat of the Moon (or the Earth) changes the entire magnitude of the shadow, in

<meta>catchword: the same</meta>

...by a small amount, however, which can scarcely be perceived. Therefore, the greater the interval of time that has mediated between both observations, the more definite a motion of the Moon's latitude we can obtain, as was said regarding the Sun. But since it is rare to find two eclipses matching these conditions, none have certainly come to our attention at present. We have noticed, however, that there is also another way through which this can be achieved. Since, other conditions remaining the same, if the Moon has also eclipsed in different parts <note>i.e., on opposite sides of the ecliptic</note> and around opposite sections <note>the nodes, or points where the Moon's path crosses the Earth's orbit</note>, it will signify then that the Moon in the second eclipse has reached a place diametrically opposite to the first, and besides full circles, has described a semicircle. This will be seen to satisfy the inquiry into this matter. 

We found, therefore, two eclipses related in almost these ways. The first in the seventh year of Ptolemy Philometor <note>King of Egypt, 180–145 BCE</note>, which was the one hundred and fiftieth year of Alexander <note>The era of Alexander the Great</note>, after twenty-seven days had passed, as Claudius <note>Ptolemy</note> says, of the seventh Egyptian month Phamenoth, in the night followed by the twenty-eighth day. The Moon was eclipsed from the beginning of the eighth hour until the end of the tenth hour, in the nocturnal seasonal hours of Alexandria, at most seven <term>digits</term> <note>A digit is 1/12th of the diameter of the celestial body</note> of the lunar diameter from the North, near the descending section <note>the descending node</note>. Therefore, the middle time of the eclipse was two seasonal hours (he says) from midnight, which make two and one-third equinoctial hours, since the Sun was in the sixth degree of Taurus; but at Krakow it would have been one and one-third hours. 

The second we observed under the same meridian of Krakow, in the year of Christ 1509, on the fourth day before the Nones of June <note>June 2nd</note>, with the Sun in the 21st degree of Gemini. Its midpoint was eleven and three-fifths equinoctial hours after noon of that day, in which nearly eight digits of the lunar diameter were eclipsed from the Southern part near the ascending section <note>the ascending node</note>. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Alexander, there are one hundred forty-nine Egyptian years, 206 days, 14 ⅔ hours at Alexandria, but at Krakow 14 and one-third hours according to appearance, but 13 ½ hours when precisely examined. In which time the place of the <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet from its perihelion or aphelion</note> was equal according to our calculation (agreeing almost with Ptolemy) to 163 degrees and 34 minutes, and the <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>The correction added or subtracted to find the true position from the mean position</note> was 1 degree and 24 minutes, by which the true place of the Moon was less than the equal <note>mean</note> place. Regarding the second eclipse from...

From the same established starting point of Alexander <note>The Era of Alexander the Great, 323 BCE</note>, there are one thousand eight hundred thirty-two Egyptian years, 295 days, eleven hours, and 45 minutes in apparent time; in equalized time, however, 11 hours and 55 minutes. From this, the equal motion of the Moon was 182 degrees and 18 minutes. The position of the anomaly <note>The irregularity in the Moon's orbital speed</note> was 159 degrees and 55 minutes, but the equalized position was 161 degrees and 13 minutes. The prosthaphaeresis <note>term: prosthaphaeresis; the geometrical correction added or subtracted to find the true position from the mean position</note> by which the equal motion was less than the apparent motion was one degree and 44 minutes. It is evident, therefore, that in both eclipses the Moon's distance from the Earth was equal, and the Sun was nearly at its apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from Earth</note> in both cases, but there was a difference of one "digit" <note>term: digit; a unit of measurement for the extent of an eclipse, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body</note> in the obscurations. Since the Moon's diameter usually occupies nearly half a degree, as we shall show later, its twelfth part—representing one digit—will be 2 and a half minutes. To these minutes, in the oblique orbit of the Moon around the ecliptic intersections <note>The nodes where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's path</note>, corresponds nearly half a degree. By this amount, the Moon in the second eclipse was further from the ascending node than it was from the descending node in the first eclipse. From this, it is most clear that the true motion of the Moon's latitude, after completed revolutions, was 179 and a half degrees. But the lunar anomaly between the first and second eclipse adds 21 minutes to the equality, by which the prosthaphaereses exceed one another. We shall have, therefore, the equal motion of the Moon's latitude, after whole circles, as 179 degrees and 51 minutes. The time between both obscurations was one thousand six hundred eighty-three years, eighty-eight days, 22 hours, and 35 minutes in apparent time, which agreed with the equal time. In this period, after 22,577 completed equal revolutions, there remain 179 degrees and 51 minutes. These agree with our figures, which we have already set forth.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

All conditions having been preserved, as we have said, according to the Ptolemaic rule <note>Copernicus refers to the methods established by Claudius Ptolemy in the *Almagest*</note>, by which we shall obtain our purpose without error. Therefore, the first eclipse—which we also used in investigating other motions of the Moon—was that which we said was observed by Claudius Ptolemy in the nineteenth year of Hadrian, after two days of the month of Choiak <note>An Egyptian month</note> had passed, one equinoctial hour before midnight at Alexandria, but at Kraków two hours before midnight, which the third day followed. The Moon failed <note>was eclipsed</note> in the very middle of the eclipse by nine-twelfths <note>original: "dextante," meaning 10/12 or 5/6</note> of its diameter, that is, ten digits from the North, while the Sun was in 25° 10' of Libra; and the position of the lunar anomaly <note>The Moon's irregular motion from its mean path</note> was 64° 38', and its subtractive prosthaphaeresis <note>term: prosthaphaeresis - a correction value added or subtracted to find the true position from the mean position</note> was 4° 20' near the descending node <note>original: "sectionem descendentem"</note>.

The second [eclipse] we also observed with great diligence at Rome, in the year of Christ 1500, after the Nones of November, two hours after midnight, which dawned on the eighth day before the Ides of November. But at Kraków, which follows five degrees to the East, it was two hours and a third of an hour after midnight, while the Sun was in 23° 11' of Scorpio, and again ten digits failed from the North. Therefore, from the death of Alexander [the Great], 1,824 Egyptian years, 84 days, 14 hours, and 20 minutes are collected in apparent time, but in equal time 14 hours and 16 minutes. Therefore, the mean motion of the Moon was at 174° 16'. The lunar anomaly was 294° 40', equated to 291° 35'. The additive prosthaphaeresis was 4° 28'.

It is manifest, therefore, that the Moon in both of these eclipses had a distance from its highest apogee <note>The point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> that was nearly equal, and the Sun was in both cases near its middle apogee, and the magnitude of the shadows was equal. These things declare that the Southern latitude of the Moon was equal, and from that, the Moon itself had equal distances from the nodes <note>original: "sectionibus"</note>, but in the former case ascending, and in the latter descending. Therefore, between the middle of both eclipses there are 1,366 Egyptian years, 358 days, 4 hours, and 20 minutes in apparent time; but in equal time 4 hours and 24 minutes. In which time the mean motion of latitude is 159° 55'. Now let the oblique circle of the Moon be that whose diameter is the line AB, the common section with the zodiac; let C be the Northern limit, and D the Southern.

By finding two eclipses with nearly identical physical characteristics, he can precisely measure the time elapsed and the intervening cycles of the Moon.</summary>

## ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a circle representing astronomical orbits. A horizontal diameter is marked with points A (left) and B (right). Point C is at the apex. On the lower right arc of the circumference, points E, L, B, F, and K are marked. Lines connect the center or other points to indicate various arcs used for calculating lunar positions.</image-desc>

<margin>a</margin> The descending intersection of the ecliptic <note>The point where the moon's path crosses the sun's path moving south</note>, <margin>b</margin> the ascending intersection. Let two equal arcs, **AF** and **BE**, be taken toward the southern parts, according as the first eclipse was at <margin>f</margin> sign, and the second at <margin>e</margin>. And again, let <margin>f k</margin> be the <term>prosthaphaeresis</term> <note>From Greek: an adjustment or correction used to find the true position from the mean position</note> to be subtracted in the first eclipse, and <margin>e l</margin> to be added in the second. Therefore, since the arc **KL** consists of 159 degrees and 56 minutes, to which are added **FK**, which was 4 degrees and 20 minutes, and **EL**, 4 degrees and 28 minutes, the total **FKLE** will be 168 degrees and 43 minutes. The remainder of this from a semicircle is 11 degrees and 17 minutes, the half of which is 5 degrees and 39 minutes, equal to both **AF** and **BE**, the true distances of the Moon from the segment **AB**. Because of this, **AFK** is 9 degrees and 59 minutes. From this it is also established that from the northern limit—that is, **CAFK**—the mean position of latitude is 99 degrees and 59 minutes. 

At this position and time of that Ptolemaic observation, there are 457 Egyptian years, 91 days, and 10 hours in apparent time from the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, whose death was a standard chronological epoch</note>, but 9 hours and 54 minutes in equalized time. During this interval, the motion of latitude is 50 degrees and 59 minutes. When these are subtracted from the 99 degrees and 59 minutes, there remain 49 degrees at noon on the first day of the first month, <term>Thoth</term> <note>The first month of the ancient Egyptian calendar</note>, according to the Egyptians, at the beginning of the years of Alexander. 

From here, the positions of the Moon's course in latitude, taken from the northern limit, are given for other epochs according to the differences in time, from which we derive the motion itself. Since from the first <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used in Greek chronology; the first began in 776 BCE</note> to the death of Alexander there are 451 Egyptian years and 247 days, for which 7 minutes of an hour are subtracted for the equalization of time, during which time the course of latitude is 136 degrees and 57 minutes. Again, from the first Olympiad to Caesar <note>Julius Caesar, marking the start of the Julian calendar</note> there are 730 Egyptian years and 12 hours, but ten hourly minutes are added for equalization, during which time the equal motion is 206 degrees and 53 minutes. Then, to the birth of Christ, there are 45 years and 12 days. 

If, therefore, 136 degrees and 57 minutes are subtracted from 49 degrees (with 360 degrees of the circle added to accommodate the calculation), there remain 272 degrees and 3 minutes at noon on the first day of <term>Hecatombaeon</term> <note>The first month of the Attic/Greek year</note> of the first Olympiad. If to these are added again 206 degrees and 53 minutes, the result is 118 degrees and 56 minutes at midnight before the <term>Kalends of January</term> <note>January 1st, the start of the Roman year</note>.

->The construction of the parallactic instrument. Chapter 15.<-

<image-desc>A large square woodcut decorative initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, likely an astronomer or scholar, surrounded by ornate vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>Since, however, the maximum latitude of the Moon—according to the angle of intersection of its orbit and the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"</note>—is five degrees (of which a circle is 360), fortune did not grant us the same opportunity for testing this as it did to Claudius Ptolemy, due to the interference of lunar parallaxes <note>Parallax is the displacement or difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight</note>. For he, at Alexandria, where the North Pole is elevated 30 degrees and 58 minutes, watched how closely the Moon would approach the zenith of the horizon, specifically while it was at the beginning of Cancer and at its northern limit, which could already be predicted by numbers. He then found, by means of a certain instrument which he calls "parallactic," manufactured for detecting the parallaxes of the Moon, its minimum distance from the zenith to be only two and one-eighth degrees. If any parallax occurred at that distance, it necessarily had to be very slight in such a short interval. Therefore, by subtracting two degrees and one-eighth from 30 degrees and 58 minutes, there remain 28 degrees and 51.5 minutes. This exceeds the maximum obliquity of the zodiac <note>The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbit</note>—which was then 23 degrees, 51 minutes, and 20 seconds—by almost five whole degrees. This latitude of the Moon is found to agree with other specific observations up to the present. The parallactic instrument, indeed, consists of three rods <note>original: "regulis"</note>, two of which are equal in length (at least four cubits), and the third somewhat longer. This third rod and one of the former two are joined at their ends; the remaining parts are joined by skillful perforation and pins or pegs fitting into them, so that they are mobile in those joints within the same plane and do not wobble. On the longer rod <note>term: "norma" (the ruler or square used as a base)</note>, a straight line is carved through its entire length starting from the center of its joint. From this line, a segment equal to the exact distance between the joints [of the other rods] is taken. This segment is divided into a thousand equal parts (or more if possible), and the division is extended onto the remainder of the rod according to

along the same sections, until the total reaches 1414 parts <note>This value represents the square root of 2 multiplied by 1000, which is the length of the side of a square inscribed in a circle with a radius of 1000</note>, which subtends the side of a square inscribed in a circle whose radius is one thousand parts. Furthermore, whatever remains of this ruler may be cut off as superfluous. On the other ruler, a line should be drawn from the center of the joint equal to those one thousand parts, or to the distance existing between the centers of the joints. It should have sighting holes <term>specilla: small apertures or lenses used for sighting</term> fixed to its side, as is customary in a sighting tube <term>dioptra: a classical surveying and astronomical instrument</term>, through which the sight passes. These are so arranged that the openings themselves do not deviate at all from the line marked along the length of the ruler, but are equally distant from it. Provision must also be made so that the end of this line, when extended toward the longer ruler, can touch the divided line. In this way, by the function of the rulers, an isosceles triangle is formed, the base of which will be measured in the parts of the divided line. 

Then, a pole, perfectly squared and smoothed, is erected and secured. To this pole, the instrument is attached by certain hinges at the ruler where both joints are located, so that it can be rotated like a door. This must be done in such a way that the straight line passing through the center of the ruler's joints always corresponds to a plumb line and stands toward the zenith <note>original: "verticem horizontis"</note> of the horizon as an axis. Therefore, when one wishes to seek the distance of any star from the zenith of the horizon, once the star itself is held in view through the sighting holes of the ruler, and the ruler with the divided line is applied from below, the observer will understand how many parts subtend the angle existing between the line of sight and the axis of the horizon. Of these parts, the diameter of the circle would be 20,000; and by using the Table <note>The Table of Chords</note>, one will have the sought-after circumference of the great circle between the star and the zenith.

With this instrument, as we have said, Ptolemy discovered the maximum latitude of the Moon to be five degrees. Then he turned to perceive its parallax <term>commutationem: change in apparent position, i.e., parallax</term>, and says that he found it at Alexandria to be one degree and 7 minutes, while the Sun was at 5 degrees and 28 minutes of Libra. The mean distance of the Moon from the Sun was 78 degrees and 13 minutes. The uniform anomaly <note>The position of the moon in its epicycle</note> was 262 degrees and 20 minutes; the motion in latitude was 354 degrees and 40 minutes; and the additive correction <term>prosthaphairesis: the geometric correction used to find the true position from the mean position</term> was 7 degrees and...

And therefore the position of the Moon was 3 <term>degrees</term> <note>Latin: gradus</note> and 9 <term>minutes</term> <note>Latin: scrupula; literally "scruples," used here for minutes of a degree</note> of Capricorn. But it is now evident to those willing to consider it that these things are far different, as we have experienced in many ways. Nevertheless, we shall review two observations which declare again that our hypotheses concerning the Moon are so much more certain as they agree more with appearances and leave no room for doubt. In the year of our Lord 1522, on the fifth day before the Kalends of October <note>September 27</note>, five and two-thirds equal hours after noon, around sunset at Frombork <note>Latin: Fruenburgi; the Polish city where Copernicus lived and worked</note>, we took the center of the Moon in the meridian circle through a <term>parallactic instrument</term> <note>A device used to measure the altitude or parallax of celestial bodies</note>, from which we found its distance from the zenith of the horizon to be 82 degrees and 50 minutes. Therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ until this hour, there were 1,522 Egyptian years, 284 days, 17 hours, and two-thirds of an hour according to apparent time. In equated time, however, it was 17 hours and 24 minutes. Therefore, the apparent position of the Sun according to calculation was in the 13th degree and 29th minute of Libra. The mean motion of the Moon from the Sun was 87 degrees and 6 minutes. The mean <term>anomaly</term> <note>The angular distance of a planet or the moon from its perihelion or apogee</note> was 357 degrees.

## A demonstration of the Moon's distance from the Earth, and the ratio they have in parts where the distance from the Earth's center to its surface is one. Chapter XVII.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing Earth and the Moon. A circle with center C represents the Earth, with points A (on the surface) and B (opposite A). A vertical line extends from the zenith D through A to the center C. To the right, point E represents the Moon. A triangle ACE is formed by the Earth's center, the observer at A, and the Moon at E. A dashed line connects the zenith D to the Moon E, forming an angle DAE at point A.</image-desc>

From these things it will now appear how great the distance of the Moon from the Earth is, without which a certain ratio of the <term>parallaxes</term> <note>original: "commutationum"; Copernicus uses this term for parallax, the apparent shift in an object's position when viewed from different points.</note> cannot be assigned, for they are mutually dependent; and it shall be declared in this manner. Let the great circle of the Earth be AB, and its center C. Around this, let another circle be described, in relation to which the Earth has a significant size, and let it be DE, with D being the pole of the horizon <note>the zenith, or the point directly overhead</note>, and the center of the Moon at E, so that its known distance from the zenith is DE. Therefore, since the angle DAE in the first observation was 82 degrees and 50 <term>minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; literally "scruples," used here for minutes of a degree.</note>, and the angle AEC was 50 minutes (which was the parallax), we have the triangle ACE with given angles, and therefore also with given sides. For on account of the given angle CAE, the side CE will be 99,219 parts, where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle AEC is 100,000; and AC will be 1,454 such parts. These [parts of AC] are contained in CE nearly sixty-eight times, where AC (the radius from the center of the Earth) is one part. And this was the distance of the Moon from the center of the Earth in the first observation.

But in the second observation, the apparent angle DAE was 81 degrees and 55 minutes, while the calculated angle ACE was 80 degrees and 55 minutes, and the remaining angle AEC was 60 minutes. Therefore, the side EC is 99,006 parts and AC is 1,747 parts, where the diameter of the circle circumscribing the triangle is 100,000. Thus, the distance of the Moon CE was 56 parts and 41 minutes, where the radius from the center of the Earth AC is one part.

Now let the larger <term>epicycle</term> <note>a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; used in pre-modern astronomy to explain planetary motions.</note> of the Moon be ABC, whose center is D, and let E be taken as the center of the Earth, from which a straight line EBDA is drawn, so that A is the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in orbit farthest from Earth</note> and B is the <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in orbit closest to Earth</note>. Let the arc ABC be taken as 242 degrees and 10 minutes, according to the calculated uniform <term>anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet or the Moon from its apogee</note> of the Moon. With C as the center, let a second small epicycle FGK be described, whose arc FGK is 194 degrees and 12 minutes (the doubled distance of the Moon from the Sun). Let DK be connected, which subtracts from the anomaly...

## On the diameter of the Moon and of the terrestrial shadow, at the place of the Moon’s passage. Chapter XVIII.

The apparent diameters of the Moon and the shadow also vary according to the Moon's distance from the Earth; therefore, it is pertinent to speak of these matters. And although the diameters of the Sun and Moon are correctly captured through the dioptra <note>A sighting instrument used by ancient astronomers to measure angular distances or diameters.</note> of Hipparchus, it is nevertheless thought that this is achieved much more certainly for the Moon through several partial lunar eclipses. In these, the Moon should be at an equal distance from its highest or lowest apogee <note>original: "abside"; the points in an orbit farthest from or closest to the Earth.</note>, especially if the Sun has also positioned itself in the same way, so that the circle of the shadow which the Moon passes through in both cases is found to be equal—except that the eclipses themselves occur in unequal parts. For it is manifest that the difference between the eclipsed parts and the latitude of the Moon, when compared to one another, shows how much of the circumference around the center of the Earth the diameter of the Moon subtends; once this is perceived, the semi-diameter of the shadow is also soon understood.

This will be made clearer by an example. Suppose that in the middle of a first eclipse, three "digits" <note>term: digits (Latin: "digiti"). A traditional unit for measuring eclipses, where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 parts.</note> or inches of the lunar diameter were eclipsed, with the Moon having a latitude of 47 minutes and 54 seconds. In a second eclipse, ten digits were eclipsed, with a latitude of 29 minutes and 37 seconds. The difference in the obscured parts is seven digits, and the difference in latitude is 18 minutes and 17 seconds. Proportional to these are 12 digits to 31 minutes and 20 seconds, which subtend the diameter of the Moon.

It is clear, therefore, that the center of the Moon in the middle of the first eclipse exceeded the shadow by a quarter of its diameter, in which there are 7 minutes and 50 seconds of latitude. If these are subtracted from the 47 minutes and 54 seconds of the total latitude, there remain 40 minutes and 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Likewise in the second eclipse, in which the shadow occupied a third of the lunar diameter beyond the Moon's latitude of 10 minutes and 27 seconds; when these are added to the 29 minutes and 37 seconds, they likewise produce 40 minutes and 4 seconds for the semi-diameter of the shadow. Thus, indeed, in the opinion of Ptolemy, while the Sun and Moon are joined or opposed at their greatest distance from the Earth, the diameter of the Moon is [31] minutes...

<summary>Copernicus explains how to calculate the apparent diameters of the Moon and the Earth's shadow using data from partial lunar eclipses and the geometry of lunar latitude. He demonstrates the method by comparing two eclipses to derive a consistent semi-diameter for the shadow.</summary>

<keywords>lunar diameter, Earth's shadow, lunar eclipse, Hipparchus, Ptolemy, celestial geometry, digits, latitude, astronomy</keywords>

However, the diameter of the shadow [at the Moon's crossing] he found to be 31 minutes and one-third. He estimated that these values relate to each other in a ratio of 13 to 5, which is a ratio of two and three-fifths.

## How the distances of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the diameter of the shadow at the Moon’s crossing, and the axis of the shadow are demonstrated together. Chapter 19.

<note>The following section begins with a decorative woodcut initial 'Q' showing an astronomer with an armillary sphere.</note>

Since the Sun produces a certain parallax <note>term: parallax (the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points; here used to calculate distance)</note> which, because it is so small, is not easily perceived, these elements are nonetheless interconnected: namely, the distances of the Sun and Moon from the Earth, their diameters, the diameter of the shadow at the Moon's crossing, and the axis of the shadow. Consequently, they reveal one another through analytical demonstrations. First, we shall review the teachings of Ptolemy on these matters and how he demonstrated them, from which we will extract what appears to be most true. He assumes the apparent diameter of the Sun to be 31 minutes and one-third, a value he uses without variation. He also takes the diameter of the Moon at full and new moon to be equal to this when it is at its farthest point from Earth <note>term: apogee (the point in the orbit of the moon or a satellite at which it is furthest from the earth)</note>, which he says occurs at a distance of 64 parts and 10 minutes, where one part is the radius of the Earth. From these values, he demonstrated the rest in this manner:

Let the circle of the Solar globe be $ABC$ around its center $D$, and that of the Earth at its greatest distance from the Sun be $EFG$ around its center $K$. Let the straight lines $AG$ and $CE$ be tangent to both, extending to meet at the point of the shadow's cone at $S$. Through the centers of the Sun and Earth, let the line $DKS$ be drawn. Let $AK$ and $KC$ also be drawn, and connect $AC$ and $GE$; these lines differ very little from the diameters because of the vast distance. On the line $DKS$, let equal segments $LK$ and $KM$ be taken according to the distance the Moon reaches at apogee when full or new, which according to his opinion is 64 parts and 10 minutes, where $EK$ is one part. Let $QMR$ be the diameter of the shadow at that same lunar crossing, and $NOL$ be the diameter of the Moon at right angles to $DK$, and let $LOP$ be extended. The first goal is to find the ratio of $DK$ [the Sun's distance] to $EK$ [the Earth's radius]. Since the angle $NKO$ [the Moon's apparent semi-diameter] is 31 minutes and one-third, of which four right angles are 360 degrees...

360. The half-segment $LKO$ will be 15 <term>minutes</term><note>original: "scrupula" - used here as minutes of arc</note> and two-thirds. Since the angle at $L$ is a right angle, in the triangle $LKO$, the ratio of the sides $KL$ to $LO$ is given because the angles are known. Thus, $LO$ itself is 17 minutes and 33 seconds in length, where $LK$ is 64 parts and 10 minutes (or where $KB$ is one part). According to the ratio of $LO$ to $MR$, which is as 5 to 13, $MR$ will be 45 minutes and 38 seconds of those same parts. 

Now, because $LOP$ and $MR$ are parallel to $KB$ at equal intervals, $LOP$ and $MR$ together will be double $KB$. After subtracting $MR$ and $LO$, there remained $OP$ at 56 minutes and 49 seconds. According to the sixth theorem of Euclid <note>referring to Euclid's Elements, Book VI, regarding proportional sides in similar triangles</note>, the lines $BC$ to $PC$, $KC$ to $OC$, and $KD$ to $LD$ are proportional in the same ratio as $KB$ to $OP$. This ratio is 60 minutes to 58 minutes and 48 seconds. Similarly, $LD$ is given as 56 minutes and 49 seconds, where the whole $DLK$ was one part; therefore, the remaining $KL$ is 3 minutes and 11 seconds. 

Insofar as $KL$ was 64 parts and 10 minutes (of which $FK$ is one), the whole $KD$ will be 1,210 parts. It has also now been shown that $MR$ was 45 minutes and 38 seconds of such parts. From this, the ratio of $KB$ to $MR$ and $KMS$ to $MS$ is established; of the whole $KMS$, $KM$ itself will be 14 minutes and 22 seconds. Separately, where $KM$ was 64 parts and 10 minutes, the whole <term>axis of the shadow</term><note>original: "axis umbrae"</note> $KMS$ will be 268 parts.

This was the finding of Ptolemy. Others after Ptolemy, however, found that these figures did not sufficiently agree with the observed appearances and reported other findings concerning them. They nevertheless admit that the greatest distance of the full and new Moon from the Earth is 64 parts and 10 minutes. They concede that the apparent diameter of the Sun at <term>apogee</term><note>the point in orbit farthest from the Earth</note> is 31 minutes and one-third. They also agree that the diameter of the shadow at the point of the Moon's passage is as 13 to 5, just as Ptolemy himself held. 

However, they deny that the apparent diameter of the Moon at that time is greater than 29 and a half minutes. For that reason, they set the diameter of the shadow at one degree and nearly 16 and three-quarters minutes. From these values, they calculate that the distance of the Sun at apogee from the Earth is 1,146 parts, and the axis of the shadow is 254 parts, where the radius of the Earth is one part.

### On the magnitude of these three bodies, the Sun, Moon, and Earth, and their comparison with one another. Chapter XX.

Furthermore, it is also manifest that KL is contained eighteen times within KD, and the ratio of LO to DC is in that same proportion. Now, eighteen times LO produces nearly 5 parts and 27 minutes, of which KE is one. Or, as SK is to KE (that is, 265 parts to one), so is the total SKD of 1,444 parts to the 5 parts and 27 minutes of DC itself. For these are also proportional; this will be the ratio of the diameters of the Sun and the Earth. Since indeed spheres are in a triplicate ratio <note>The volume of a sphere is proportional to the cube (triplicate) of its diameter</note> of their diameters, when we have cubed five and 27 minutes, the result is 161 and nearly 7/8 parts <note>original: "162 minus one eighth"</note>, by which the Sun is larger than the terrestrial globe. Again, since the semi-diameter <term>radius</term> of the Moon is 17 minutes and 9 seconds, where KE is one part.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

Therefore, the diameter of the Earth is to the diameter of the Moon as seven is to two—that is, in a triple sesquialterate ratio <note>original: "tripla sesquialtera ratione"; a ratio of 3.5 to 1</note>. When this ratio is cubed, it shows that the Earth is forty-three times larger than the Moon, less an eighth part of the Moon. Consequently, the Sun will also be seven thousand times larger than the Moon, less sixty-two.

### On the apparent diameter of the Sun and its parallaxes. Chapter XXI.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'Q' containing a depiction of a seated scholar, likely an astronomer, at a desk with books and scientific instruments.</image-desc>
Since indeed the same magnitudes appear smaller when more remote than when they are nearer, it follows that the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth's shadow vary according to their unequal distances from the Earth, no less than their parallaxes <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions</note>. All these things are easily discerned from the aforementioned for any other elongation. First, this is manifest in the Sun. For we have demonstrated that the Earth's greatest distance from it is 10,323 parts (where the radius of the annual orbital revolution is 10,000), and at the remaining part of the diameter, the closest distance is 9,678 parts. Therefore, in those parts where the radius of the Earth is one, the highest apogee <note>original: "summa absis"; the point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> is 1,179 parts, the lowest will be 1,105 of the same parts, and the mean distance will be 1,142 parts.

Therefore, when we divide 100,000 by 1,179, we obtain 84.8 parts, which in a right-angled triangle <note>original: "orthogonio"</note> subtends the minimum angle of 2 minutes and 55 seconds <note>original: "scrup. primorum II, secundorum LV"; Copernicus uses 'scruples' for minutes of a degree</note> of the maximum parallax which occurs near the horizon. Similarly, by dividing 1,000,000 by 1,105 (the parts of the minimum distance), there result 905 small parts, subtending an angle of 3 minutes and 7 seconds of the maximum parallax at the lowest apogee.

It has been shown, moreover, that the diameter of the Sun is 5 parts and 27 minutes where the diameter of the Earth is one part; and that at the highest apogee it appears as 31 minutes and 48 seconds. For the ratio of 1,179 parts to 5 parts and 27 minutes is proportional to the ratio of 200,000 (the diameter of a circle) to 9,245, which subtends 31 minutes and 48 seconds. It follows that at the minimum distance of 1,105 parts, the diameter is 33 minutes and 4 seconds. The difference between these is therefore 2 minutes and 6 seconds. Between the parallaxes, however...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

Indeed, these are only twelve seconds. Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is here refining.</note> thought both should be disregarded because of their smallness, considering that one or two minutes <note>term: scrupula (scruples). In this context, these are "first small parts" or arcminutes (1/60th of a degree).</note> are not easily perceived by the senses; how much less possible is it for this to happen with seconds. Therefore, if we maintain the maximum parallax of the Sun at three minutes everywhere, we will not seem to have committed any error. We shall take the mean apparent diameters of the Sun through its mean distances; or, as some do, through the apparent hourly motion of the Sun, which they estimate to be to its diameter as 5 is to 66, or as 1 is to 13 and one-fifth. For the hourly motion itself is almost proportional to its distance.

### On the Unequal Apparent Diameter of the Moon and its Parallaxes. Chapter XXII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring floral motifs and a structured background.</image-desc>
A greater diversity appears in both regarding the Moon, as it is the nearest star <note>In the 16th century, "star" (sidus) was a general term for any celestial body, including planets and the Moon.</note>. For since its maximum distance from the Earth is 65 and a half parts <note>These "parts" are units where the Earth's radius equals 1.</note> at the new and full moon, its minimum distance (as demonstrated above) will be 55 parts and 8 minutes. However, the maximum distance of the half-moon <note>term: diuidua (divided). Refers to the Moon at its quadrature phases, such as the first or last quarter.</note> is 68 parts and 21 minutes, and the minimum is 52 parts and 17 minutes. Therefore, at these four limits, we will have the parallaxes <note>term: parallaxes (commutationes). The shift in the Moon's apparent position when viewed from the surface of the Earth versus the center.</note> of the rising or setting Moon when we divide the radius of the circle by the Moon's distances from the Earth. For the most remote half-moon, the parallax is 50 minutes and 18 seconds; for the full and new moon, 51 minutes and 24 seconds. For the nearest full moon, 62 minutes and 21 seconds; and for the nearest half-moon, 65 minutes and 45 seconds. From these, the apparent diameters of the Moon are also evident. For it has been shown that the diameter of the Earth is to the diameter of the Moon as seven is to two; and the ratio of the Earth's radius to the Moon's diameter will be as seven is to four. In this same ratio are the parallaxes to the angles of the Moon's diameters. Since the straight lines which encompass the angles of the greater parallaxes do not differ at all from the apparent diameters during the same passage of the Moon, and the angles themselves are almost proportional to their subtending straight lines, their difference is not perceptible to the senses. By this shortcut, it is manifest that under the first limit of the parallaxes already set forth, the apparent diameter of the Moon

### On the Reason for the Variation in the Earth’s Shadow, Chapter 24

We have already demonstrated that the ratio of the diameter of the [Earth's] shadow to the diameter of the Moon is as 403 to 150. Therefore, at the full and new Moon, when the Sun is at its <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>, the shadow is found at its minimum of 80 scruples and three-fifths; but at its maximum, it is 95 scruples and 44 seconds. The maximum difference is thus 14 scruples and 8 seconds. The Earth's shadow also varies, even during the same passage of the Moon, because of the unequal distance of the Earth from the Sun, in the following manner:

Let us repeat, as in the preceding figure, the straight line through the centers of the Sun and the Earth, **DKS**, and the line of contingency **CES**, with **DC** and **KE** joined. Since, as has been demonstrated, when the distance **DK** was 1,179 parts (of which **KE** is one part) and **KM** was 62 of those same parts, the <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>radius</note> of the shadow **MR** was 46 scruples and 1 second of that same part **KE**, and the angle of appearance **MKR** was 42 scruples and 32 seconds. With **KR** connected, the axis of the shadow **KMS** consists of 265 parts. 

However, when the Earth is nearest to the Sun, so that **DK** is 1,105 parts, we shall estimate the Earth's shadow in the same passage of the Moon in this way: Let **EZ** be drawn [parallel] to **DK**; then **CZ** will be proportional to **ZE**, as **EK** is to **KS**. But **CZ** is 4 parts and 27 scruples, and **ZE** is 1,105 parts. For **ZE** and the remaining **DZ** are equal to **DK** and **KE**, since **KZ** is a <term>parallelogram</term>. Therefore, **KS** will be 248 parts and 19 scruples, of which **KE** is one. Since **KM** was 62 of those same parts, the remaining **MS** will therefore have 186 parts and 19 scruples. And since **SM** is also proportional to **MR**, and **SK** to **KE**, **MR** is given as 45 scruples and 1 second, of which...

### A Canonical Explanation of the Particular Parallaxes of the Sun and Moon in the Circle Passing Through the Poles of the Horizon. Chapter 24.

Now there will also be no doubt about how to determine the individual <term>parallaxes</term> <note>Parallax is the apparent displacement of a celestial object when viewed from different positions, such as from the Earth's surface versus its center.</note> of the Sun and the Moon. For let us represent the terrestrial circle AB passing through the center C and the zenith of the horizon. In the same plane, let there be the circle of the Moon DB and of the Sun FG. Let the line CDE pass through the zenith, and CEG be the line in which the true positions of the Sun and Moon are understood to be, to which positions the lines of sight AG and AE are connected. Therefore, the solar parallax is according to the angle AGC, and the lunar parallax according to AEC. The <term>difference in position</term> <note>original: "commutatio"; here referring to the relative parallax between the two bodies.</note> between the Sun and Moon is the angle GAE, which remains as the difference between the angles AGC and AEC. Now let us take the angle ACG <note>The zenith distance.</note> to which we wish to compare these; let it be, for example, thirty degrees. It is clear from the demonstrations of plane triangles that when we set the line CG at 10,142 parts (of which AC is one), the angle AGC—by which the true altitude of the Sun differs from the visible altitude—will be one and a half minutes. However, when the angle ACG is 60 degrees, AGC will be 2 minutes and 36 seconds. The others will be revealed in a similar manner. But regarding the Moon, this occurs at its four limits. Since if it were at its maximum distance from the Earth, in which CE would be (as we said) 68 parts...

However, we will use groups of six degrees, by which the doubled number is understood, ranging from the zenith of the horizon to a maximum of ninety.

We have indeed organized the Table itself into nine columns. For in the first and second columns will be the common numbers of the circle. In the third, we will place the parallaxes of the Sun. Then the Lunar parallaxes: in the fourth place, the differences. In the fifth, the minimum parallaxes, which occur when the Moon is at its half-phase and at its <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in the orbit farthest from Earth</note>; these are less than those following at the full and new Moon. The sixth column will contain those parallaxes produced by the full or "thirsty" <note>original: "sitiens" - likely referring to the Moon's appearance or a specific phase alignment</note> Moon at its <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in the orbit closest to Earth</note>. The minutes that follow are the differences by which the parallaxes occurring when the Moon is at its half-phase and nearest to us exceed those closer to them. Finally, the remaining two spaces that are left are reserved for the proportional minutes. By these, the parallaxes can be calculated between these four limits. We shall also explain these, starting first with the apogee and those between the prior limits, in this manner. Let there be, I say, a circle...

Let **AB** be the first epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves on the circumference of a larger circle</note> of the Moon, whose center is **c**. Having taken **D** as the center of the Earth, let the straight line **DBCA** be drawn. With the center at **A** (the apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note>), let a second epicycle **EFG** be described. Let the arc **EG** be taken as 60 degrees, and let **AG** and **CG** be connected. 

Since it was demonstrated in the preceding sections that the straight line **CE** consists of 5 parts and 11 minutes <note>original: "scrupula" - here referring to 1/60th of a part</note> (where the Earth's radius is one part), and **DC** is 60 parts and 18 minutes, and **EF** is 2 parts and 51 minutes: therefore, in the triangle **ACG**, the sides **GA** (1 part, 25 minutes) and **AC** (6 parts, 36 minutes) are given, along with the angle **CAG** contained between them. 

Thus, by the proven rules of plane triangles, the third side **CG** will be 6 parts and 7 minutes. Therefore, the total line **DCG** when extended straight—or its equivalent **DCL**—will be 66 parts and 25 minutes. But **DCE** was 65 parts and 30 minutes. There remains, therefore, an excess **EL** of approximately 55 minutes. 

By this given ratio, when **DCE** is 60 parts, **EF** will be 2 parts and 37 minutes, and **EL** will be 46 minutes. Insofar as **EF** is 60 minutes, the excess **EL** will be approximately 18. We shall mark these values in the seventh column of the Table <note>original: "Canon"</note> opposite the 60-degree mark.

<column-break/>

Similarly, we shall demonstrate the values around the perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> **B**, where the second epicycle **MNO** is repeated. With the angle **MBN** at 60 degrees, a triangle **BCN** is formed, with sides and angles given as before. Similarly, the excess **MP** is approximately 55 minutes (where the Earth's radius is one). 

But since **DBM** is 55 parts and 8 minutes, if it is set as 60 parts, then **MBO** will be 3 parts and 7 minutes, and the excess **MP** will be 55 minutes. Just as 3 parts and 8 minutes is to 55 minutes, so 60 is to approximately 18—the same as before, though they differ by a few seconds. 

In this manner, we shall proceed with the rest, with which we shall complete the eighth column of the Table. If we use these values instead of those set forth in the Table of Prosthaphæreses <note>term: Prosthaphæresis - a Greek-derived word meaning "addition and subtraction," used for the geometric corrections needed to find the true position of a planet</note>, we shall commit no error, for they are nearly the same, even regarding the smallest details...
