# ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book 4.

## On the calculation of the parallax of the Sun and Moon. Chapter 25.

We shall also briefly explain the method of calculating the parallaxes <note>The apparent displacement of an object against a distant background due to the observer's perspective</note> of the Sun and Moon by means of the Table <note>original: "Canonem"</note>. Indeed, by doubling the distance from the zenith <note>original: "uertice"; the point directly overhead</note> of the Sun or Moon, we will take the corresponding parallaxes found in the table. For the Sun, this is done simply; for the Moon, however, it is done within its four limits. With the motion of the Moon—or its doubled distance from the Sun—we take the first proportional minutes <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; small units used for scaling ratios</note>, with which we take the proportional parts (relative to 60) of the difference between the first and last limits of both. We always subtract these from the next following parallax, and add the later ones to that which is always in the penultimate limit. We will then have two rectified parallaxes of the Moon at the apogee <note>the point in orbit farthest from Earth</note> and perigee <note>the point in orbit closest to Earth</note>, which the smaller epicycle increases or decreases.

Then, with the lunar anomaly <note>the angular distance of the Moon from its furthest point in its orbit</note>, we will take the last proportional minutes, by which we also take a proportional part from the difference of the parallaxes just found. We always add this to the first examined parallax (that at the apogee), and the sought-after parallax of the Moon for that place and time will result, as in the example:

Let the distance from the zenith be 54 degrees, the mean motion of the Moon 15 degrees, and the adjusted anomaly 100 degrees. From these, I wish to find the lunar parallax through the Table. I double the degrees of distance, making 108. To these in the Table correspond: the excess between the first and second limit, 1 minute 48 seconds; the parallax of the second limit, 42 minutes 50 seconds; the parallax of the third limit, 50 minutes 49 seconds; and the excess of the third and fourth, 2 minutes 46 seconds. I shall note these individually. The doubled motion of the Moon makes 30 degrees; with this, I find the first 5 proportional minutes. With these, I take the proportional part relative to 60, which from the first excess is 9 seconds. I subtract these from the 42 minutes 50 seconds of the parallax; 42 minutes 41 seconds remain. Similarly, from the second excess (which was 2 minutes 46 seconds), the proportional part is 14 seconds, which I add to the 50 minutes 49 seconds of the second parallax; they become 51 minutes 14 seconds. The difference between these parallaxes is 8 minutes 32 seconds. After this, with the degrees of the adjusted anomaly, I take the final proportional minutes, which are 34; and through these, I take the proportional part of the 8 minute 31 second difference, which is 4 minutes 50 seconds.

### How the parallaxes of longitude and latitude are distinguished. Chapter 26.

<note>The diagram illustrates the intersection of the ecliptic and the horizon's vertical circle to show how the Moon's apparent displacement is split into two directions.</note>

The parallax is simply distinguished into longitude and latitude—or that which exists between the Sun and the Moon—by means of the circumferences and angles of the intersecting circles: namely, the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signifer," the "sign-bearer" or the circle of the zodiac signs</note> and the circle passing through the poles of the horizon <note>the vertical circle of altitude</note>. For it is clear that when this vertical circle rests at right angles to the zodiac, it produces no parallax in longitude, but the entire shift passes into latitude, since the circles of latitude and altitude are the same. But when, conversely, it happens that the zodiac stands perpendicular to the horizon and becomes the same as the circle of altitude, then if the Moon lacks latitude <note>i.e., is sitting exactly on the ecliptic line</note>, it admits no parallax other than that of longitude. However, if it is pulled away into latitude, it will not escape some change in longitude. 

For example, let <term>ABC</term> be the zodiac circle standing perpendicular to the horizon, and let <term>A</term> be the pole of the horizon <note>the Zenith</note>. Therefore, the orbit <term>ABC</term> itself will be the same as the circle of altitude for a Moon lacking latitude. If its position is at <term>B</term>, its entire <term>shift</term> <note>original: "commutatio," another term Copernicus uses for parallax</note> <term>BC</term> will be in longitude. But when it also possesses latitude, a circle <term>DBE</term> is described through the poles of the zodiac. Having taken the Moon's latitude as <term>DB</term> or <term>BE</term>, it is clear that the side <term>AD</term> or <term>AE</term> will not be equal to <term>AB</term>, nor will the angle at <term>D</term> or <term>E</term> be a right angle, since <term>DA</term> and <term>AE</term> are not circles passing through the poles of <term>DBE</term>. Thus, the shift will participate in some latitude, and all the more so the closer the Moon is to the <term>vertex</term> <note>the Zenith or highest point</note>. For while the base <term>DE</term> of the triangle <term>ADE</term> remains the same, the shorter sides <term>DA</term> and <term>AE</term> will enclose more acute angles at the base. And the further the Moon is from the vertex, those angles become more like right angles. Now, let the circle of altitude <term>DBE</term> be oblique to the zodiac <term>ABC</term> for a Moon having no latitude, as in an eclipse...

which is at B. Moreover, let the <term>parallax</term><note>The apparent displacement of a celestial body when viewed from different positions.</note> in the <term>circle of altitude</term><note>A vertical circle passing through the zenith and the object.</note> be BE, and let the circumference EF of a circle be drawn through the poles of the same ABC <note>original: "per polos ipsius ABC"</note>. Therefore, since in the triangle BEF, the angle at EBF is given (as shown above), and the angle at F is a right angle, the side BE is also given. Therefore, by the demonstrations of **spherical triangles**, the remaining sides BF and FE are given—the latter being the latitude and the former the longitude—corresponding to the position B. But since BE, EF, and FB differ from straight lines by a small and imperceptible amount due to their shortness, we shall not err if we use the right-angled triangle as if it were **rectilinear**; and for that reason, the calculation will become easy.

It is more difficult in the case of the Moon having latitude. For let the <term>Zodiac</term><note>original: "signifer" - the 'sign-bearer' or ecliptic circle.</note> ABC be repeated, which the oblique circle DB intersects through the poles of the horizon; and let B be the position of the Moon's longitude, with the northern latitude being FB, or the southern being BE. From the vertex of the horizon <note>The zenith.</note>, which is D, let the circles of altitude DEK and DFC descend upon the Moon itself, in which the <term>parallaxes</term><note>original: "commutationes" - a synonym for parallax used by Copernicus.</note> are EK and FG. The true positions of the Moon in longitude and latitude will be at the points E and F, but the visible positions will be at K and G. From these points, let the circumferences KM and LG be drawn at right angles to the Zodiac ABC itself. 

Therefore, when the longitude and latitude of the Moon are established along with the latitude of the region, two sides DB and BE will be known in the triangle DBE, as well as the angle of intersection ABD; and with the right angle, the whole angle DBE is known. For that reason, the remaining side DE will be given along with the angle DEB. Similarly, in triangle DBF, since the two sides DB and BF will have been given with the angle DBF (which is the remainder of the angle ABD subtracted from a right angle), DF will also be given along with the angle DFB. Therefore, for both circumferences DE and DF, the parallax EK and FG is given by the **Table** <note>Referring to the parallax tables provided earlier in the book.</note>, as well as the true distance of the Moon from the vertex, DE or DF. Likewise, the visible distances DEK or DFG are found. 

And in triangle EBN, with the intersection of DE and the Zodiac made at point N, the angle NEB is given and NBE is a right angle; with the base BE, the remaining angle BNE will also be known, along with the remaining sides BN and NE. Similarly, in the whole triangle NKM, from the given angles M and N and the whole side KEN, the base KM will be established. And this is the **visible southern latitude** of the Moon, the excess of which over EB is the parallax of latitude; and the remaining side NBM is given, from which, if NB is subtracted, there remains BM, the **parallax of longitude**. Just as also in the northern triangle BFC, when the side BF has been given with the angle BFC...

And because the sides $BLC$ and $FGC$ are given, along with the remaining angle $C$, and by subtracting $FG$ from $FGC$, the side $GC$ is left as a known side in the triangle $GLC$. With the two angles $LCG$ and $CLG$ being right angles, the remaining sides $GL$ and $LC$ are consequently given. Then, what remains from $BC$ is $BL$, the <term>parallax of longitude</term><note>original: "commutatio longitudinis"; the apparent shift in the Moon's position along the ecliptic due to the observer's perspective.</note>, and $GL$ is the <term>apparent latitude</term><note>The Moon's observed distance from the ecliptic, which differs from its true position due to parallax.</note>, of which the parallax is the excess of the true latitude $BF$. However, as you can see, this calculation involves more labor than benefit, as it expends effort on the smallest details. For it will be sufficient if we use the angle $ABD$ for $DCB$, and $DBF$ for $DEB$, and simply use the arcs $DE$ and $EF$ as before, always taking the mean $DB$ and neglecting the lunar latitude. For no visible error will arise from this, especially in the regions of the Northern track. But in very Southern parts, where $B$ might reach the zenith of the horizon with a maximum latitude of five degrees, and with the Moon being closest to the Earth, the difference is nearly six minutes. In solar eclipses, however, where the latitude of the Moon cannot exceed one and a half degrees, the difference can be only one and three-quarters of a minute. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that in the eastern quadrant of the <term>zodiac</term><note>original: "signiferi"; literally the "sign-bearer," referring to the circle of the zodiac.</note>, the parallax of longitude is always added to the true place of the Moon, and in the other quadrant it is always subtracted, so that we may have the apparent longitude of the Moon. And we find the apparent latitude through the parallax of latitude: for if they are in the same direction, they are joined together; if in different directions, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and what remains is the apparent latitude of that same part toward which the larger declines.

### Confirmation of those things which have been
### explained concerning the parallaxes of the Moon. Chapter 27.

That the parallaxes of the Moon thus explained are in conformity with the appearances, we are able to affirm by many other experiments, such as this one which we had at Bologna on the seventh day before the Ides of March <note>March 9th</note>, after the setting of the Sun, in the year of Christ 1497. For we observed that

The Moon was about to hide the bright star of the Hyades, which the Romans call the Palilicium <note>original: "Palilicium"; now commonly known as Aldebaran</note>. Having waited for this, we saw the star positioned against the dark part of the Lunar body, already hiding between the horns of the Moon at the fifth hour of the night. It was closer to the Southern horn by about one-third of the Moon's width or diameter. Since the star, according to calculation, was at 2 degrees and 52 minutes of Gemini with a Southern latitude of five and one-sixth degrees, it was clear that the center of the Moon, as seen, preceded the star by half a diameter. Therefore, its visible position in longitude was 2 degrees and 36 minutes, and in latitude nearly 5 degrees and 2 minutes. From the beginning of the years of Christ, there were 1,497 Egyptian years, 76 days, and 23 hours at Bologna. At Krakow, however, which is further east by nearly 9 degrees, it was 23 hours and 36 minutes, to which the equation adds 4 minutes <note>Copernicus is adjusting for the difference in longitude and local time between the two cities</note>. For the Sun was at 28 and a half degrees of Pisces. Therefore, the Moon's uniform motion from the Sun was 74 degrees; the adjusted anomaly <term>anomaly: the angular distance of a planet or the moon from its perigee or apogee</term> was 111 degrees and 10 minutes. The true position of the Moon was 3 degrees and 24 minutes of Gemini, with a Southern latitude of 4 degrees and 35 minutes. For the true motion of latitude was 203 degrees and 41 minutes. At that time also, the 26th degree of Scorpio was rising at Bologna, with an angle of 59 and a half degrees; the Moon was 84 degrees from the zenith of the horizon, and the angle of the intersection of the circles of altitude and the zodiac was nearly 29 degrees. The parallax <term>parallax: the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points</term> of the Moon was one degree: 51 minutes in longitude and 30 minutes in latitude. These figures agree very well with the observation, so that no one should doubt that our hypotheses and the things produced from them are correct.

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

## On investigating the true conjunctions and oppositions of the Sun and Moon. Chapter 29.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'C' containing a figure, likely an astronomer, holding a celestial sphere.</image-desc>

When we have obtained, as has been said, the time of the mean <note>The "mean" position refers to a theoretical uniform motion, as if the planets moved in perfect circles at constant speeds.</note> conjunction or opposition of these stars along with their motions, it is necessary to find their true distance—by which they precede or follow one another—in order to find the true moments of these events. For if the Moon is ahead of the Sun in a conjunction or opposition, it is clear that the true event is yet to come; but if the Sun has already passed the true point we seek, the event has passed. These things become manifest from the *prosthaphaeresis* <term>prosthaphaeresis: a Greek-derived term meaning "addition or subtraction," used to describe the correction needed to turn a "mean" position into a "true" observed position</term> of each. Since if there are no corrections, or if they are equal and of the same type—that is, if both are to be added or both subtracted—it is evident that the true conjunctions or oppositions coincide with the mean ones at that same moment. 

If, however, they are unequal, the difference itself indicates their distance, and that the star whose correction is greater (whether additive or subtractive) precedes or follows the other. But when the corrections are in opposite directions <note>i.e., one is additive and the other subtractive</note>, the star whose correction was subtractive will precede by that much more, and the two corrections joined together determine the distance between them. Based on this distance, we shall estimate how many whole hours it would take for the Moon to traverse it, taking two hours for every one degree of distance. For example, if they were at a distance of about 6 degrees, we would assume 12 hours for them. 

Therefore, for this interval of time so established, we will seek the true elongation <note>original: "evectionem," here referring to the lunar separation from the sun</note> of the Moon from the Sun. We will accomplish this easily when we know that the mean motion of the Moon—one degree and one minute—is completed in just under two hours. Indeed, the hourly motion of the anomaly <note>The "anomaly" refers to the Moon's position on its epicycle, which accounts for its varying speed.</note> and its true motion around the New and Full Moon is nearly 50 minutes; these will combine in six hours to an equal motion of 3 degrees and 3 minutes, and a true progression of the anomaly of five parts. With these, we shall consider the difference between the corrections themselves in the Table <note>original: "Canone"</note> of lunar prosthaphaereses. We shall add this to the mean motion if the anomaly is in the lower part of the circle, or subtract it if in the upper part. For whatever is collected or left over is the true motion of the Moon in the assumed hours. If this motion is equal to the previously existing distance, it is sufficient. Otherwise, we shall divide the distance (multiplied by the number of estimated hours) by this motion, or by the accepted true hourly motion.

<summary>Copernicus explains the mathematical methods for calculating the exact timing of solar and lunar conjunctions (New Moons) and oppositions (Full Moons) by correcting mean motions using prosthaphaeresis.</summary>
<keywords>astronomy, Moon, Sun, conjunction, opposition, prosthaphaeresis, anomaly, orbital mechanics, Nicolaus Copernicus</keywords>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

If we divide the simple distance, the result will be the true difference in time, in hours and minutes <note>original: "scrupulis," literally small parts or scruples</note>, between the mean and true conjunction or opposition. We shall add this to the time of the mean conjunction or opposition if the Moon is ahead of the Sun (or ahead of the point diametrically opposite the Sun), or subtract it if it is behind; we will then have the time of the true conjunction or opposition. Although we admit that the Sun's own inequality <note>the variation in the Sun's apparent speed</note> adds or subtracts something, it is rightly disregarded; indeed, in the entire tract, even at the maximum elongation which extends beyond seven degrees, it cannot complete a single minute. This method of calculating the lunations is more certain. For those who rely solely on the hourly motion of the Moon—which they call the "hourly excess"—are sometimes deceived and are frequently forced to repeat their calculations. For the Moon is changeable even from hour to hour and does not remain consistent with itself. Therefore, for the time of the true meeting <note>conjunction</note> or opposition, we shall arrange the true motion of latitude to learn the latitude of the Moon itself, and the true position of the Sun from the Vernal Equinox (that is, the sign), by which the position of the Moon is also understood to be the same or opposite. And since time of this sort is understood as mean and uniform relative to the meridian of Krakow <note>original: "Cracouieñ." Copernicus lived and worked in Poland</note>, we shall reduce it to apparent time by the method delivered above. If we wish to establish these for any other place besides Krakow, we shall consider its longitude; for every degree of longitude we shall take 4 minutes of an hour, and for every minute of longitude 4 seconds of an hour. We shall add these to the Krakow time if the other place is further east, and subtract them if it is further west; the remainder or sum will be the time of the conjunction or opposition of the Sun and Moon.

### How the Ecliptic Conjunctions and Oppositions of the Sun and Moon are Distinguished from Others. Chapter 30.

Whether they are indeed ecliptic <note>causing an eclipse</note> or not is easily discerned in the case of the Moon. Since if its latitude is less than half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and the shadow, the Moon will undergo an eclipse; if greater, it will not. But regarding the Sun, there is more than enough trouble, as the parallax of both <note>the Sun and Moon</note> interferes, by which the visible conjunction usually differs from the true one. Therefore, when we have examined...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

<note>original: "Nicolaus Copernicus"</note>
...we have determined what the change <note>parallax</note> is between the Sun and Moon according to longitude at the time of true conjunction. Similarly, for the space of one hour preceding the true conjunction in the eastern quadrant of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi," the 'sign-bearer' or zodiac</note>, or following it in the western quadrant, we will seek the apparent longitude of the Moon from the Sun, so that we may understand how far the Moon is moved from the Sun in an hour according to its appearance. Therefore, when we have divided that change in longitude by this hourly motion, we will have the difference in time between the true and apparent conjunction <note>original: "coitum," literally a 'coming together' or meeting</note>. When this is subtracted from the time of true conjunction in the eastern part of the zodiac, or added in the western part (for in the former the apparent conjunction precedes the true, and in the latter it follows), the sought-after time of the true conjunction will result. Therefore, at this time, we will calculate the apparent latitude of the Moon from the Sun, or the distance between the centers of the Sun and Moon at the visible conjunction, after deducting the parallax of the Sun. If this latitude is greater than half the diameters of the Sun and Moon, the Sun will not undergo an eclipse; if it is less, it will. And from these things it is manifest that if the Moon at the time of true conjunction does not produce any parallax of longitude, then the apparent and true conjunction will be the same, which happens around the ninetieth degree of the zodiac measured from the east or west.

## How great the eclipse of the Sun and Moon will be. Chapter 31.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'P' depicting a figure, likely a scholar or astronomer, in a long gown standing in a landscape with a tree and a small building or pedestal.</image-desc>
After we have learned that the Sun or Moon will fail <note>original: "defecturam," referring to an eclipse or 'defect' in light</note>, we will also easily know how great their eclipse <note>original: "defectus"</note> will be. In the Sun, indeed, this is done through the apparent latitude which is between the Sun and Moon at the time of the visible conjunction. For if we subtract this from half the diameters of the Sun and Moon, the remainder is that part of the Sun which will fail according to the diameter. When we have multiplied this by 12 and divided the result by the diameter of the Sun, we will have the number of digits <term>digits: a traditional unit for measuring eclipses, where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 parts</term> failing. But if there is no latitude between the Sun and Moon, the whole Sun will fail, or as much of it as the Moon is able to cover. In almost the same way, we proceed in a lunar eclipse, except that instead of the apparent latitude, we use its simple latitude; when this is taken from half the diameters of the Moon and the shadow, the part of the Moon failing remains, provided that the latitude of the Moon...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK IV.

If the latitude of the Moon is not less than half the sum of the diameters <note>original: "dimidio diametrorum"</note> in terms of the Moon's diameter, the Moon will be totally eclipsed. Furthermore, a smaller latitude will also add some duration to the time spent in darkness, which will be greatest when there is no latitude at all—a fact which I believe is perfectly clear to those considering the matter. Therefore, in a partial lunar eclipse, when we multiply the eclipsed part by twelve and divide the product by the diameter of the Moon, we will have the number of "digits" <term>digits: a traditional unit of measure for eclipses, where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 parts</term> eclipsed, just as was said regarding the Sun.

### On foretelling how long an eclipse will last. Chapter XXXII.

It remains to see how long an eclipse will endure. Here it must be noted that we use the arcs that occur between the Sun, the Moon, and the shadow as if they were straight lines; because of their smallness, they seem to differ in no way from a straight line. Therefore, taking the center of the Sun or the shadow at point A, and line BC for the transit of the Moon—where the center of the Moon touching the Sun or shadow is at B at the beginning of the incidence <note>the start of the eclipse</note> and at C at the end of the clearance <note>original: "expurgationis," the end of the eclipse</note>—let AB and AC be connected, and let the perpendicular AD be dropped to BC.

->[Geometric Diagram]<-
<note>The diagram illustrates the geometry of an eclipse path. Point A represents the center of the Earth's shadow or the Sun. Line BC is the Moon's path. AD represents the Moon's latitude at the midpoint of the eclipse.</note>

It is manifest that when the center of the Moon is at D, it will be the middle of the eclipse. For AD is the shortest of the lines descending from A, and BD is equal to DC, since AB and AC are also equal. Both of these lines consist of half the sum of the diameters of the Sun and Moon in a solar eclipse, and of the Moon and shadow in a lunar eclipse; and AD is the true or apparent latitude of the Moon at the middle of the eclipse. Therefore, when we subtract the square of AD from the square of AB, the square of BD remains; thus the length of BD will be given. When we divide this by the true hourly motion of the Moon during its eclipse (or the apparent motion in a solar one), we will have the time of half the duration. But since the Moon often lingers in the midst of darkness—which happens when half the sum of the diameters of the Moon and shadow exceeds the latitude of the Moon by more than its own diameter, as we have said—let us then place E as the center of the Moon at the beginning of the total...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

->of the obscuration, where the Moon touches the surrounding shadow<-
from the inside, and at the other contact point, where it first emerges. By connecting lines AB and AF, it will be demonstrated in the same manner as before that ED and DF are the halves of the duration in darkness <note>original: "morae in tenebris"; referring to the time spent in total eclipse</note>, because AD is the known latitude of the Moon, and AE (or AF), which is the half-diameter of the shadow, is greater than the half-diameter of the Moon. Therefore, ED or DF will be established; when these are divided again by the true hourly motion of the Moon, we will have the time of the half-duration that was sought.

However, it must be noticed here that when the Moon moves in its orbit, it does not cut parts of the longitude of the zodiac <note>original: "circuli signorum"</note> entirely equal to those in its own orbit, by means of the circles that pass through the poles of the zodiac. Yet the difference is very small; in the total distance of 12 degrees from the ecliptic intersection—within which the extreme limits of the eclipses of the Sun and Moon almost always fall—the circumferences of the orbits themselves do not exceed each other by more than two minutes <note>original: "scrupulis"; small units of measurement</note>, which would make up only a fifteenth part of an hour. For that reason, we often use one for the other as if they were the same. Thus, we use the same latitude of the Moon at the boundaries of the eclipse as we do in the middle of the eclipse, although the latitude of the Moon itself is always increasing or decreasing. Consequently, the spaces of the onset <note>original: "incidentiae"</note> and the clearing <note>original: "expurgationis"</note> are not perfectly equal, but the difference is so slight that it would seem a waste of time to investigate them more exactly.

In this way, the times, durations, and magnitudes of eclipses have been explained according to diameters. But since it is the opinion of many that the eclipsed parts ought to be determined not by diameters but by surfaces—for it is not lines but surfaces that fail <note>i.e., the visual area of the disk is what appears to disappear</note>—let ABCD be the circle of the Sun or the shadow, whose center is E, and let the lunar circle be AFCG, whose center is I. Let them intersect each other at points A and C, and let the straight line BEIF be drawn through both centers. Let AE, EC, IA, IC be connected, and let AKC be drawn at right angles to AF. From these, we wish to investigate how great the obscured surface ADCG was, or how many "ounces" <note>term: "unciarum"; Copernicus uses "ounces" to refer to twelfths of the total area, similar to "digits" of a diameter</note> of the whole plane of the solar or lunar disk are missing in part. Since, therefore, from the previous calculations the diameter of each disk (AE and AI) is given, as well as the distance of the centers (or the lunar latitude EI), we have the triangle...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK IV.

The triangle $AEI$ has sides of given lengths, and therefore its angles are also given through the demonstrations provided above; the triangle $HEC$ is similar and equal to it. Therefore, the arcs $ADC$ and $AGC$ will be given in parts where the circumference of the circle is 360 degrees. Furthermore, Archimedes of Syracuse, in his *On the Measurement of the Circle*, <note>Archimedes (c. 287–212 BCE) was a Greek mathematician; Copernicus here cites his famous approximation of Pi.</note> put forward that the ratio of the circumference to the diameter is less than three and one-seventh <note>original: "triplam sesquiseptimam," or 22/7</note>, but greater than three and ten-seventy-firsts <note>original: "triplam superpartientem septuagesimas primas decem," or 223/71</note>. Between these, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Alexandrian astronomer.</note> assumes a mean value of 3 parts, 8 first minutes, and 30 second minutes to 1 <note>This sexagesimal value (3 + 8/60 + 30/3600) equals 3.1416.</note>. By this ratio, the arcs $AGC$ and $ADC$ will also be revealed in the same units as their diameters, such as $AE$ and $AI$. The areas contained under $BA, AD$ and under $IA, AG$ are equal to the sectors $AEC$ and $AIC$ respectively. Moreover, for the isosceles triangles $AEC$ and $AIC$, the common base $AKC$ and the perpendiculars $EK$ and $KI$ are given. Therefore, the product of $AK$ and $KG$ is given, which is the area of triangle $AEC$; similarly, the product of $AK$ and $KI$ gives the area of triangle $ACI$. When both triangles are subtracted from their respective sectors, the segments of the circles $AFC$ and $ACD$ will remain, which together constitute the total area $ADCG$ that was sought. Furthermore, the entire area of the circle—contained by $BE$ and $BAD$ in a solar eclipse, or by $FI$ and $FAG$ in a lunar eclipse—is given. Thus, it will become clear how many "digits" <note><term>unciarum</term>: literally "ounces" or "twelfths," used here as "digits," the standard historical measure for the magnitude of an eclipse.</note> the area $ADCG$ is, representing the portion missing from the whole circle of either the Sun or the Moon.

Let these remarks on the Moon suffice for now, as these matters have been treated more extensively by others; for we are hurrying toward the revolutions of the remaining five planets, which shall be discussed in the following books.

# BY NICOLAUS COPER-
## NICUS, ON THE REVOLUTIONS
### BOOK FIVE.

<image-desc>A large woodcut historiated initial 'H' featuring a seated figure, likely a scholar or astronomer, in a study or architectural setting, surrounded by ornate decorative foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>
HITHERTO we have completed the revolutions of the Earth around the Sun, and of the Moon around the Earth. We now approach the movements of the five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" or *planetae* refer to the five planets known since antiquity: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note>, the order and magnitudes of whose orbits are connected by the mobility of the Earth itself with a wonderful harmony and certain symmetry, as we briefly reviewed in the first book, while we were showing that these orbits have their centers not around the Earth, but rather around the Sun. It remains, therefore, for us to demonstrate all these things individually and more clearly, and to fulfill our promises as far as we are able, especially by employing the apparent observations <note>original: "experimentis," here meaning empirical observations or data.</note> which we have received both from the ancients and from our own times, by which the logic of their movements may be held more certain. Now, these five stars are named in Plato's *Timaeus* according to the appearance of each. Saturn is called *Phaenon*, as if you were to say "shining" or "appearing," for it is hidden least of all the others and emerges more quickly after being concealed by the Sun. Jupiter is called *Phaethon* from its brilliance. Mars is *Pyrois* from its fiery glow. Venus is sometimes *Phosphoros* <note>original: "φωσφόρος"</note>, sometimes *Hesperos* <note>original: "ἕσπερος"</note>, that is, the Light-bringer and the Evening-star, according as it shines in the morning or the evening. Finally, Mercury is called *Stilbon* from its sparkling and vibrating light. These also travel in longitude and latitude with a greater variation than the Moon.

->On their revolutions and mean motions. Chapter I.<-

<image-desc>A smaller woodcut historiated initial 'B' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile wearing a soft cap, set within a circular frame and surrounded by decorative motifs.</image-desc>
Two very different movements in longitude appear in them. One is due to the movement of the Earth which we have mentioned. The other is proper to each planet. It has pleased us, not without reason, to call the first the "motion of commutation" <term>motion of commutation: the apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement around the Sun</term>, since it is this which produces in all of them their stations, progressions, and retrogressions—

<summary>Copernicus introduces the fifth book of his work, shifting focus to the five planets and explaining how their apparent movements are unified by the Earth's motion around the Sun. He provides the classical Greek names for the planets and begins defining the two types of longitudinal motion.</summary>
<keywords>planetary motion, heliocentrism, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, motion of commutation, Plato's Timaeus, astronomy</keywords>

--- Page 283 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary theory from Book V, specifically addressing the apparent retrograde motions of the planets and the calculation of their orbital periods.</meta>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

it appears to happen, not because the planet is actually pulled back—for it always proceeds forward in its own motion—but because it appears so by way of <term>commutation</term><note>Copernicus uses "commutation" to describe the optical effect caused by the Earth's own motion as it overtakes or is overtaken by other planets.</note>, which the motion of the Earth produces according to the difference and size of those orbits. It is clear, therefore, that the true positions of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars only become visible to us when they are <term>at opposition</term><note>original: "ἀκρονύκται" (akronyktos). This refers to a planet being opposite the sun in the sky, rising at sunset.</note>, which happens roughly in the middle of their <term>retrogradations</term><note>original: "repedationum". The apparent backward movement of a planet in the night sky.</note>. For at that time, they coincide with the mean position of the Sun in a straight line, being stripped of that commutation. Furthermore, in the case of Venus and Mercury, the reasoning is different. For they are hidden when they are <term>under the sun's rays</term><note>original: "hypaugi". From the Greek, meaning they are too close to the Sun to be seen.</note>, and they show only the elongations they make from the Sun on either side, so that they are never found without this commutation. Therefore, each planet has its own private revolution of commutation—I mean the motion of the Earth relative to the planet—which they unfold between themselves. For we say that the motion of commutation is nothing other than that in which the uniform motion of the Earth exceeds their motion (as in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) or is exceeded by it (as in Venus and Mercury). Since, however, such periods of commutation are found to be unequal by a manifest difference, the ancients recognized that the motions of those stars were also unequal, and that the circles had <term>apsides</term><note>The highest or lowest points in an orbit.</note> to which their inequality returned; and they thought these had permanent seats in the sphere of the fixed stars. By this argument, the path was opened to learning their mean motions and uniform periods. For when they had a record of the position of any planet according to a certain distance from the Sun and a fixed star, and found after an interval of time that the star itself had reached the same position with a similar distance from the Sun, the planet was seen to have completed its full cycle of inequality and to have returned in all respects to its prior state relative to the Earth. And so, through the time that intervened, they calculated the number of whole and uniform revolutions, and from these, the particular motions of the star. Moreover, Ptolemy reviewed these circuits under a number of solar years, just as he admits he received them from Hipparchus. However, he intends "solar years" to be understood as those taken from the equinox or solstice. But it has already become clear that such years are not entirely uniform; therefore, we shall use those taken from the fixed stars, by which we have also restored the motions of these five stars to a more corrected state, just as in our own time...

<summary>Copernicus explains that the retrograde motion of planets is an optical illusion caused by Earth's movement (commutation) and argues for calculating planetary periods relative to fixed stars rather than equinoxes.</summary>

we have found that something was either lacking or in excess in this manner. For in the case of **Saturn**, the Earth completes fifty-seven revolutions—which we have called the motion of commutation <note>original: "commutationis"; this refers to the apparent motion of a planet caused by the Earth's own movement</note>—in 69 of our solar years, plus one day, approximately 7 first minutes <note>term: "scrupulis primis" — minutes of a degree or hour</note>, and 18 second minutes <note>term: "secundis" — seconds of a degree or hour</note>. In this time, the star <note>Copernicus often uses "star" to refer to a planet</note> completes two circuits by its own motion, with the addition of approximately one degree, 5 minutes, and 50 seconds.

**Jupiter** is overtaken by the Earth 65 times in 71 solar years, minus 5 days, 54 minutes, and 13 seconds; during this time the star revolves six times, lacking 5 degrees, 42 minutes, and 32 seconds.

For **Mars**, the revolutions of commutation are 37 in 79 solar years, two days, 24 minutes, and 45 seconds. In this period, the star completes 42 periods by its own motion and adds 2 degrees, 21 minutes, and 44 seconds.

**Venus** overtakes the motion of the Earth five times in 8 solar years, minus 2 days, 26 minutes, and 44 seconds. Indeed, in this time it circles the Sun 13 times, minus two degrees, 24 minutes, and 29 seconds.

Finally, **Mercury** makes 145 periods of commutation in 46 solar years, with the addition of one day and 25 minutes; in this same time it also overtakes the motion of the Earth, with which it returns around the Sun 191 times, with the addition of 21 minutes and 54 seconds.

Therefore, the individual circuits of commutation for each are:
* For **Saturn**: 378 days, 5 minutes, 32 seconds, 42 thirds.
* For **Jupiter**: 398 days, 54 minutes, 3 seconds, 57 thirds.
* For **Mars**: 779 days, 56 minutes, 13 seconds, 55 thirds.
* For **Venus**: 583 days, 55 minutes, 17 seconds, 50 thirds.
* For **Mercury**: 115 days, 52 minutes, 38 seconds, 54 thirds.

When these are reduced into degrees of a circle and multiplied by 365, and we have divided them by the number of their days and minutes, we shall have the annual motion:
* Of **Saturn**: 347 degrees, 32 minutes, 3 seconds, 9 thirds, 4 fourths.
* Of **Jupiter**: 329 degrees, 25 minutes, 8 seconds, 15 thirds, 6 fourths.
* Of **Mars**: 168 degrees, 28 minutes, 30 seconds, 36 thirds, 4 fourths.
* Of **Venus**: 225 degrees, 1 minute, 45 seconds, 3 thirds, 40 fourths.
* Of **Mercury**: after three revolutions, 53 degrees, 57 minutes, 23 seconds, 6 thirds, 30 fourths. Of these...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

### Chapter 2. A demonstration of the uniformity and appearance of the stars according to the opinion of the ancients.

<note>Copernicus is here summarizing the Ptolemaic system—the prevailing geocentric model of his time—before he introduces his own heliocentric improvements.</note>

Having addressed their mean motions in this manner, let us now turn to their apparent inequality. The ancient mathematicians, who held the Earth to be immobile, imagined for Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus <term>eccentrepicycles</term> <note>A system combining an eccentric circle (a circle whose center is not the Earth) and an epicycle (a smaller circle carrying the planet that rotates on the larger circle).</note>, and furthermore another eccentric circle in relation to which the epicycle would move uniformly, as would the planet within the epicycle. For example, if there were an eccentric circle **a b** with center **c**, and a diameter **a c b** containing the center of the Earth **d**, so that the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> is at **a** and the <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> is at **b**; and if **d c** is bisected at point **e**, and with that center another eccentric circle **f g** is described equal to the first; and if on this circle a center **h** is taken anywhere, an epicycle **i k** is designated, and a straight line **i h k c** is drawn through its center, and similarly the line **l h m e**. 

Furthermore, let the eccentric circles be understood as inclined to the plane of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi", the circle of signs.</note>, and the epicycle to the plane of the eccentric, on account of the latitudes <note>The north-south deviations from the ecliptic path.</note> produced by the planet; but here they are treated as if in a single plane for the sake of the demonstration's convenience. They say, therefore, that this entire plane moves around center **d** of the circle of the signs, along with points **e** and **c** according to the motion of the fixed stars, by which they mean these have fixed seats in the sphere of the non-wandering stars. They also say the epicycle moves in the direction of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia", meaning eastward or following the order of the zodiac signs.</note> on the circle **f h g**, but according to the line **i h c**, in relation to which the star also revolves uniformly within the epicycle **i k**. 

However, it is established that the uniformity of the epicycle ought to occur in relation to **e**, the center of its <term>deferent</term> <note>The large circle that carries the epicycle.</note>, and the revolution of the planet in relation to the line **l m e**. They therefore concede that in this case, the uniformity of circular motion can occur around a foreign center and not its own. They claim a similar thing happens even more so in the case of Mercury. But this has already been sufficiently refuted in our discussion of the Moon. These and similar things provided us with the occasion to think about the mobility of the Earth and other ways by which uniformity and the principles of the art might be preserved, and the reason for apparent inequality be rendered more consistent.

<meta>catchword: General</meta>

<summary>Copernicus describes the complex Ptolemaic model of planetary motion involving eccentrics and epicycles, noting the mathematical inconsistency of the "equant" (moving uniformly around a foreign center). He cites these flaws as his primary motivation for proposing the Earth's motion as a more elegant solution.</summary>

<keywords>Ptolemaic system, epicycle, eccentric, equant, planetary theory, geocentrism, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, astronomical demonstration</keywords>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

## General demonstration of the apparent inequality caused by the motion of the earth. Chapter III.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two concentric circles centered at point C. The outer circle represents the Earth's orbit, with A at the bottom and B at the top. The inner circle represents a planetary orbit (Venus or Mercury), with E at the bottom and D at the top. From point A, two tangent lines are drawn to the inner circle, meeting it at points G on the left and F on the right. These lines extend to points M and L respectively. Point A represents the Earth, and the diagram illustrates the apparent motion and angular distance (elongation) of the planet as seen from Earth.</image-desc>

Therefore, since there are two causes by which a planet's uniform motion appears irregular—both because of the motion of the earth and because of its own proper motion—we shall explain each of them in general and separately with a visual demonstration, so that they may be better distinguished from one another. We begin with that motion which mixes with all of them because of the motion of the earth. First, we consider Venus and Mercury, which are contained within the circle of the earth.

Let circle AB be the eccentric <note>A circle whose center is slightly offset from the center of the universe (the Sun).</note> around the Sun, which the center of the earth describes in its annual circuit according to the method delivered above; let the center be C. Now, however, let us assume the planet has almost no other inequality <note>term: inequality (inæqualitas) — a technical term in Renaissance astronomy referring to any deviation from perfectly uniform circular motion.</note> except this one. This would be the case if we made a circle DE concentric to AB, representing either Venus or Mercury, which must be inclined to AB because of its latitude <note>The planet's north-south deviation from the ecliptic plane.</note>. But for the sake of a more convenient demonstration, let them be thought of as if they were in the same plane.

Let the earth be taken at point A, from which the lines of sight AFL and AGM are drawn, touching the circle of the planet at points F and G, with the diameter ACB being common to both circles. Let the motion of both—I mean the earth and the planet—be in the same direction, that is, in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" — moving eastward through the zodiac.</note>, but with the planet being faster than the earth. Therefore, point C and the line ACB itself will appear to be moved according to the mean motion of the Sun, as the eye is carried along in A.

The star <note>Copernicus uses "sidus" (star) to refer to planets.</note> on the circle DFG, as if on an epicycle, will pass through the arc FDG in the order of the signs in a longer time than the remaining arc GEF in the opposite direction <note>original: "in præcedentia" — westward or retrograde motion.</note>. In the former case, it adds the whole angle FAG to the mean motion of the Sun; in the latter, it subtracts the same. Therefore, where the subtractive motion of the star (especially around the perigee E <note>term: perigee — the point in the orbit closest to the observer (Earth).</note>) is greater than the additive motion of C by a prevailing amount, the star seems to move backward to the observer at A. This happens to these stars for which the ratio of the line CB to the line AB is greater than the ratio of the motion of A to the course of the planet, according to the demonstrations of Apollonius of Perga <note>A Greek geometer (c. 240–190 BC) famous for his work on conic sections and planetary models.</note>, as will be said later. But where the subtractive motion is equal to the additive, they compensate for each other...

N
<meta>catchword: each other</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains how the Earth's orbital motion creates the illusion of retrograde (backward) motion in the inner planets, Venus and Mercury. He uses a geometric model to show how the relative speeds and distances of the Earth and planets result in these apparent changes in direction.</summary>
<keywords>retrograde motion, Venus, Mercury, planetary theory, geometry, Apollonius of Perga, eccentricity, perigee</keywords>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS
Page 47

in turn, the planet will appear to stand still; all of these things correspond to the observed appearances. If, therefore, there were no other variation in the motion of the star <note>Copernicus uses "star" (stella) to refer to planets</note> as **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Perga, a 3rd-century BC Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections and epicycles</note> believed, these explanations might suffice. But the maximum elongations from the mean position of the Sun—which are understood through the angles FAE and GAE—of the morning and evening appearances of these stars are not found to be equal everywhere, neither one to the other, nor when joined together. By evident conjecture, it follows that their courses are not in circles concentric <note>original: "homocentris"</note> with the Earth's circle, but in certain others by which they produce a second variation. The same is also demonstrated in the three superior planets, **Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars**, which surround the Earth on all sides. Having repeated the previous circle of the Earth, let an exterior concentric circle DE be assumed, as if in the same plane, in which

->[Image: A geometric diagram showing the Earth's orbit (inner circle) and a planet's orbit (outer circle). Points D and E mark the planet's path, while A, B, C, F, and G mark points on the Earth's orbit relative to the planet's position.]<-

the position of the planet is taken at any point, such as sign D. From this point, straight lines DF and DG are drawn, tangent to the Earth's orbit at signs F and G, with DACBE as the common diameter. It is manifest that only from point A will the true position of the planet appear in the line DE of the mean motion of the Sun, being then at its "at-the-night-onset" <note>original: "acronyctus" (Greek: akronychos); referring to a planet rising at sunset, opposite the sun</note> position and closest to the Earth. For when the Earth is at the opposite point B, although it is in the same line, the planet will not be visible at all, having become "under-the-sun's-rays" <note>original: "hypaugus" (Greek: hypaugos); lost in the sun's glare</note> because of its proximity to the Sun. However, the course of the Earth being faster, by which it surpasses the motion of the planet, it will appear to add the entire angle GDF to the motion of the star through the apogeal arc FBG, and to subtract the same in the remaining arc GAF; but in a shorter time, according to the smaller arc GAF. And where the subtractive motion of the Earth surpasses the additive motion of the star, especially around A, the star will appear to be left behind by the Earth and to move into preceding signs <note>i.e., retrograde motion</note>, and to make a station there where the difference between these contrary motions is least according to sight. Thus it is again manifest that all those things happen through the single motion of the Earth, which the ancients sought to explain through the epicycles <term>epicycles: small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles</term> of individual planets. But since the motion of the star is not found to be uniform (contrary to the opinion of Apollonius and the ancients), even with a uniform revolution of the Earth relative to the star, the planets are therefore not carried in a concentric circle, but in another manner, which we shall also demonstrate immediately.

<meta>catchword: By which</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains that the apparent retrograde motion and stationary points of planets are optical illusions caused by the Earth's own movement, though he notes that simple concentric circles cannot fully account for all observed variations.</summary>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book V.

## The ways in which the proper motions of the wandering stars appear unequal. Chapter IV.

Since their proper motions in longitude follow almost the same pattern—with the exception of Mercury, who seems to differ from them—we shall treat those four together. A different place has been assigned to Mercury. Whereas the ancients assumed a single motion involving two eccentrics <note>An eccentric is a circular orbit where the center of the circle is offset from the center of the Earth or the Sun.</note> (as has been reviewed), we believe there are two equal motions from which the inequality of the appearance is composed, whether by an eccentric on an eccentric, or by an epicycle on an epicycle <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one.</note>, or even by a mixture of an eccentric-epicycle. These can produce the same inequality, as we demonstrated above regarding the Sun and the Moon.

<column-break/>

Let the eccentric be the circle AB around center C, with the diameter ACB passing through the mean position of the Sun and through the highest and lowest apsides <note>The points in an orbit farthest from (apogee) and closest to (perigee) the center of motion.</note> of the planet. Let D be the center of the Earth's orbit. With the highest apsis established at A, and at a distance of a third part of CD, let the epicycle EF be described, in whose perigee <note>The point in the orbit of the epicycle closest to the center.</note> (which is F) the planet is placed. Let the motion of the epicycle along the eccentric AB be in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" - moving forward through the zodiac from West to East.</note>. Likewise, let the motion of the planet on the upper circumference of the epicycle be in

->[Image: A large circular astronomical diagram illustrating a planetary model with eccentric and epicyclic components. A main outer circle is divided by a vertical diameter line labeled A (top) and B (bottom). The center of the large circle is labeled C, and a point D is located slightly below the center on the vertical axis. Small circles (epicycles) are drawn at the top (point A, containing points E and F), the bottom (point B, containing points K and L), and the left side (containing points G and H). Various lines connect point D to labeled points on the right arc of the main circle, including P, Q, R, S, and T. Additional points M, N, and O are labeled within the main circle.]<-

<margin>N ii</margin>
<meta>catchword: the order of the signs</meta>

<summary>Copernicus explains that the apparent irregular movements of planets (except Mercury) can be modeled using combinations of circular motions, such as epicycles and eccentrics, rather than the complex single-motion models of the ancients. He begins a geometric demonstration using a diagram to show how these circles interact to create observed planetary paths.</summary>

It will happen, therefore, that when the epicycle is at the highest point <note>the apogee</note> of the eccentric, and the planet is at the lowest point <note>the perigee</note> of the epicycle on the opposite side, they will be swapped to opposite parts when each has completed its half-circle. From this it will also be demonstrated that the star <note>the planet</note>, by this composite motion, does not describe a perfect circle according to the opinion of the ancient mathematicians, though the difference is imperceptible. For let the same epicycle be repeated at center B, which shall be KL; and having taken a quadrant of the circle AG, at point G let there be the epicycle HI; and with CD divided into three parts, let CM be one third, equal to GI; and let GC and IM be connected, intersecting at Q. Since, therefore, the circumference AG is similar to the circumference HI by prescription, and the angle ACG is a right angle, the angle HGI is also a right angle. And those angles at the vertex Q are also equal; therefore the triangles GIQ and QCM are equiangular, and also have equal sides to one another. Since the base GI is assumed equal to the base CM, the side QI is greater than GQ, just as QM is greater than QC. Therefore the whole IQM is greater than the whole GQC. But FM, ML, AC, and CG are equal to one another. Therefore, a circle described at center M through the points F and L, and thus equal to circle AB, will intersect the line IM. In the same way, it will be demonstrated from the opposite side and the other quadrant. The planet, therefore, through the equal motions of the epicycle on the eccentric, and itself in the epicycle, does not describe a perfect circle, but a "quasi-circle" <note>an oval or non-circular path</note>, which was to be demonstrated.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS Book V.

If the first epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> moves in the order of the signs, and the second moves just as much in the opposite direction, in which the planet is finally reflected by a doubled motion, the same effects which we have already described will occur. This is not much different than what was said regarding the Moon, or indeed through any of the other methods mentioned above. However, we have chosen the epicycle of the eccentric here, because while the distance between the Sun and the center remains constant, <term>D</term> <note>The center of the planet's orbit</note> is found in the meantime to have changed, as was shown in the appearances of the Sun. Since the other planets do not follow this change in an equal manner, it is necessary that some difference follows in them, which, although it is very small, is nevertheless perceived in <term>Mars</term> and <term>Venus</term>. Therefore, we shall now demonstrate from observations that these hypotheses are sufficient for the appearances; and we shall do this first for <term>Saturn</term>, <term>Jupiter</term>, and <term>Mars</term>. In these, the principal and most difficult task is to have found the location of the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth (or center of motion)</note> and the distance <term>CD</term>, since the rest are easily demonstrated through them. In these matters, we shall use almost the same method we used regarding the Moon. Namely, by making a comparison of three ancient solar oppositions to the same number of new ones—which the Greeks call <term>acronychial</term> <note>original: "acronychias"; referring to the planet's rising at sunset, when it is directly opposite the Sun</note> gleams, and we call the "extremes of the night"—specifically when the planet falls upon the straight line of the mean motion of the Sun, being opposite to the Sun. At this point, all that difference which the motion of the Earth introduces is stripped away. Indeed, such locations are captured from observations through astrolabic instruments, as was explained above, applying also the calculation of the Sun until it is established that the planet has reached the point opposite to it.

It was necessary for both to be known. But neither can the differences of the angles $AEN$, $BEO$, and $CEP$ be perceived unless the arcs $AF$, $FB$, and $FBC$—which are similar to those of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term>—are first established. Thus, these elements are so mutually dependent that they are either hidden or revealed together. 

Therefore, lacking the direct means of demonstration, they <note>referring to previous astronomers</note> have struggled from the effects backward and through circuitous routes toward those things to which a direct and prior approach was not open. Thus Ptolemy, in pursuing these matters, poured himself out into a vast multitude of numbers in a long-winded discourse, which I judge to be both tedious and unnecessary to recount, especially since in our own explanations which follow, we shall imitate nearly the same method. 

He found at last, through a recalculation <note>original: "retractatione"</note> of the numbers, that arc $AF$ was 57 degrees and 1 minute <term>minute: here called "scrupulis" or small parts of a degree</term>; $FB$ was 18 degrees and 37 minutes; and $FBC$ was 56 and a half degrees. ## Concerning three other oppositions of Saturn more recently observed. Chapter VI.

Since the calculation of Saturn's motion handed down by Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is updating.</note> differs not a little from our own times, and it could not be immediately understood where the error lay hidden, we were compelled to make new observations. From these, we have again recorded three of its "nightly extremes" <note>term: acronychijs (acronychal risings). This refers to a planet being in opposition to the sun, appearing at its brightest and visible all night.</note>. 

The first was in the year of Christ 1514, on the third day before the Nones of May <note>May 5th</note>, at one and one-fifth hours before midnight; at which time Saturn was found at 205 degrees, 24 minutes. The second was in the year of Christ 1520, on the third day before the Ides of July <note>July 13th</note> at noon, at 272 degrees, 25 minutes. The third was also in the year 1527, on the sixth day before the Ides of October <note>October 10th</note>, six and two-fifths hours after midnight, at 7 minutes of one degree from the horn of Aries <note>The "horn of Aries" refers to the first point of the zodiac constellation Aries, used as a reference point for celestial longitude.</note>. 

Therefore, between the first and second observations, there are six Egyptian years <note>term: anni Ægyptij. A year of exactly 365 days, used by astronomers for ease of calculation.</note>, 70 days, and 33 minutes <note>In this context, minutes refer to fractions of a day.</note>. During this time, the apparent motion of Saturn was 78 degrees and 1 minute. From the second to the third, there are seven Egyptian years, 89 days, and 46 minutes, and the apparent motion of the star was 86 degrees and 42 minutes. The mean motion <note>term: medius motus. The theoretical uniform motion of a planet, as opposed to its observed, irregular "apparent" motion.</note> in the first interval was 75 degrees and 39 minutes; in the second, 88 degrees and 29 minutes. 

Therefore, in the investigation of the highest absis <note>term: summæ absidis. The apogee, or the point in the orbit furthest from the center.</note> and the eccentricity <note>term: eccentrotetis. The measurement of how much the circular orbit is offset from the center.</note>, we must first proceed according to the rule of Ptolemy, as if the star moved in a simple eccentric circle. Although this is not sufficient, nevertheless, by being brought closer this way, we reach the truth more easily. 

Let the circle be A B C, in which the planet moves uniformly. Let the first opposition be at point A, the second at B, and the third at C. Let the center of the Earth be taken as D, to which A D, B D, and C D are connected. Let any one of these be extended in a straight line to the opposite parts of the circumference, such as C D E, and let A E and B E be joined. 

Since, therefore, the angle B D C is given as 86 degrees and 42 minutes (where two right angles at the center are 180 degrees), the remaining angle B D E will be 93 degrees and 18 minutes. But where 360 degrees represent two right angles <note>Copernicus is using a geometric convention where angles are measured relative to a circle of 360 degrees.</note>, it will be 186 degrees and 36 minutes; and the angle B E D, following the arc B C, will be 88 degrees and 29 minutes. And therefore the remaining angle, which is D B E...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

### On the Examination of the Motion of Saturn. Chapter VII.

It has been shown that at the time of the last of Ptolemy’s three observations <note>Ptolemy was a 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose work served as the foundation for astronomy for over a millennium.</note>, Saturn was at 174 degrees and 44 minutes according to its motion of commutation <note>term: motion of commutation: the apparent motion of a planet relative to the Sun's position</note>. The position of the highest apse <note>term: apse (apogee): the point in an orbit farthest from the center of motion</note> of the eccentric was at 226 degrees and 23 minutes from the head of the constellation Aries. It is clear, therefore, that in the intervening time between both observations, Saturn completed 1,344 equal revolutions of its commutations, minus a quarter of one degree. Now, from the 20th year of Hadrian <note>The Roman Emperor Hadrian; this refers to an observation made in 136 AD.</note>, on the 24th day of the Egyptian month Mesori, one hour before noon, until the year of Christ 1527, six days before the Ides of October, six hours [after midnight], the time of this observation consists of 1,392 Egyptian years, 75 days, and 48 minutes <note>In this context, "minutes" of a day refer to fractions of a day, not 60 seconds.</note>. If we wish to calculate the motion itself from the tables for this period, we will similarly find five times sixty degrees, plus 59 degrees and 48 minutes, which are the remainder beyond the 1,324 revolutions of the commutations. Therefore, what has been set forth concerning the mean motions of Saturn is correct. During this same time, the simple motion of the Sun is 82 degrees and 30 minutes; subtracting 359 degrees and 45 minutes from this leaves 82 degrees and 45 minutes as the mean motion of Saturn, which now amounts to its 47th revolution, consistent with the calculation. Meanwhile, the position of the highest apse of the eccentric has also advanced 13 degrees and 58 minutes under the sphere of the fixed stars. Ptolemy believed this point was fixed in the same way [as the stars], but it now appears that it moves by approximately one degree every hundred years.

### On the Commutations of Saturn, which proceed from the Earth's Annual Orbit, and how great its distance is. Chapter 9.

The equal motions of Saturn in longitude, together with its apparent motions, have been demonstrated in this manner. For the other appearances that happen to it are "commutations," as we have said, proceeding from the annual orbit of the Earth. Just as the size of the Earth creates parallaxes <note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from different positions</note> relative to the distance of the Moon, so too does the Earth's orbit, in which it revolves annually, produce effects regarding the five wandering stars <note>The planets</note>, but far more evident due to the magnitude of that orbit. However, such commutations cannot be understood unless the altitude <note>distance</note> of the star is first known. It is possible to apprehend this through any single observation of a commutation. We had such an observation regarding Saturn in the year of Christ 1514, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March <note>February 24th</note>, five equinoctial hours before the preceding midnight. For Saturn was seen in a straight line with the stars in the forehead of Scorpio—namely the second and third stars—which, having the same longitude, are at 209 degrees of the sphere of the fixed stars. Therefore, the position of Saturn was evident through these same stars. From the beginning of the years of Christ to this hour, there are 1514 Egyptian years and 77.25 days; and therefore, according to the calculation...

### On three other acronychal risings of Jupiter observed more recently. Chapter 11.

Having presented the three positions of the star of Jupiter from antiquity and evaluated them in this manner, we shall substitute three others, which we ourselves have observed with the greatest diligence at the acronychal rising of Jupiter. The first was in the year of Christ 1520, on the day before the Kalends of May <note>April 30, 1520</note>, 11 hours before the preceding midnight, at 200 degrees and 18 minutes of the sphere of the fixed stars. The second was in the year of Christ 1526, on the fourth day before the Kalends of December <note>November 28, 1526</note>, three hours after midnight, at 48 degrees and 34 minutes. The third, indeed, was in the year 1529, on the Kalends of February <note>February 1, 1529</note>, 19 hours after midnight, at 113 degrees and 44 minutes.

However, the mean motion <note>The "equal" or theoretical uniform motion, as opposed to the observed "apparent" motion</note> in the first time interval is 199 degrees and 40 minutes. In the second, it is 66 degrees and 10 minutes. 

Following this example, let an eccentric circle <term>eccentric circle: a circular path where the center of motion is offset from the physical center</term> ABC be described, in which the planet is understood to move simply and uniformly. Let three locations be designated according to the order of the letters A, B, and C, such that the arc AB has 199 degrees and 40 minutes, and BC has 66 degrees and 10 minutes. Consequently, the remaining arc of the circle, AC, is 94 degrees and 10 minutes.

### Chapter 12. Verification of the Uniform Motion of Jupiter.

Now, it was seen above that in the last of the three "all-night sightings" <note>original: "summae noctis fulsionum," referring to planetary oppositions where the planet shines all night</note> recorded by Ptolemy, the star of Jupiter was at 4 degrees and 58 minutes in its mean motion, with an anomaly of commutation of 182 degrees and 47 minutes. From this, it is established that in the time intervening between both observations, there passed—beyond full revolutions—1 degree and 5 minutes in the motion of commutation, and in its own motion approximately 103 degrees and 54 minutes. 

The time that elapsed from the first year of Antoninus, on the 20th day of the Egyptian month Athyr, five hours after the following midnight, until the year of Christ 1529, on the Calends of February <note>February 1st</note>, 19 hours after the preceding midnight, is 1,392 Egyptian years, 99 days, and 37 minutes of a day. To this time, according to the calculation set forth above, there likewise corresponds 1 degree and 5 minutes after the completed revolutions in which the Earth, by its uniform motion, overtook and passed Jupiter 1,237 times. Thus, the number is confirmed as certain and tested, agreeing with the visual evidence. During this time, it is also clear that the highest and lowest points of the orbit's arc <note>the apogee and perigee</note> have shifted 4 and a half degrees in the order of the signs. A proportional distribution allows for approximately one degree every three hundred years.

Let <term>FEV</term> be extended in a straight line through both circumferences of the Earth's orbit; then at <term>V</term> will be the true apogee of the planet. The angle of difference <term>REV</term>, equal to <term>DXE</term> itself, constitutes the entire arc <term>VRS</term> as 114 degrees and 26 minutes, and the remainder <term>FES</term> as 65 parts <note>degrees</note>.

In the intermediate positions, it follows accordingly. From these values, it is found that Jupiter at apogee produces a maximum <term>parallax</term> <note>original: "commutationem" - the apparent shift in position when viewed from Earth</note> of 10 degrees 35 minutes, while at perigee it is 11 degrees 35 minutes. The difference between them is one degree. Thus, the uniform and apparent motions of Jupiter have been demonstrated.

### On the star of Mars. Chapter XV.

Now we must examine the revolutions of Mars, taking three ancient oppositions <note>original: "extremæ noctis fulsionibus" - literally 'shining at the end of the night,' referring to when a planet is opposite the sun</note> of that planet, to which we shall also join the ancient evidence of the Earth's mobility. Of those observations which Ptolemy recorded, the first was in the 15th year of Hadrian, on the 26th day of the Egyptian month Tybi, one equinoctial hour after the following midnight. He says it was in the 21st degree of Gemini, but in comparison to the sphere of the fixed stars, it was at 74 degrees 20 minutes.

### Chapter 16. Concerning three other flashings at the end of the night, recently observed regarding the star of Mars.

To these observations of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is updating</note> concerning Mars, we have compared three others, which we recorded with no small diligence. angle <term>CEN</term> <note>The angle at the Earth between the center of the eccentric and the planet</note> is 50 minutes. Since, therefore, the star of Mars appeared in this location (as we have narrated) at 133 degrees and 20 minutes from the head of the constellation Aries, and angle <term>FEN</term> was shown to be nearly 13 degrees and 40 minutes: it is manifest, by counting backward, that the position of the apogee <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the Earth/Sun</note> of the eccentric in this last observation was at 119 degrees and 40 minutes in the sphere of the fixed stars.

In the time of Antoninus, Ptolemy found this position to be at 108 degrees and 50 minutes; therefore, up to our time, it has shifted 10 degrees and nine-tenths <note>original: "dextante"; a Roman fraction meaning ten-twelfths or five-sixths, here used for 50 minutes</note> in the order of the signs. We also found the distance between the centers to be smaller, at 40 parts (where the radius of the eccentric is given as 10,000). This is not because Ptolemy or we have erred, but is a manifest proof that the center of the great orbital circle of the Earth has approached the center of the orbit of Mars, while the Sun meanwhile remains immobile. For these things correspond to one another, as will appear clearer than light below.

Now let the annual orbital circle of the Earth be set out around center <term>E</term>, with its diameter <term>SER</term> parallel to <term>CD</term> on account of the equality of their revolutions. Thus we have it demonstrated here: that in the year of Christ 1523, on the eighth day before the Calends of March <note>February 22nd</note>, seven equinoctial hours before noon, the star of Mars was at 136 degrees and 16 minutes in its mean motion of longitude. Its uniform anomaly of commutation was at 177 degrees and 4 minutes, and the highest absis <note>The apogee</note> of the eccentric was at 119 degrees and 40 minutes. These were the things to be demonstrated.

### Proof of the Motion of Mars. Chapter XVII.

It was shown above that in the last of Ptolemy’s three observations, Mars was at a mean position of 244° 30' <note>original: "part. CCXLIIII. S."</note> and the anomaly of parallax <term>anomaly of parallax: the difference between the planet's actual position and its mean position caused by the Earth's own motion</term> was at 171° 26'. Therefore, in the intervening time, after completing full revolutions, there was an increase of 5° 38'. Now, from the second year of the reign of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; this refers to 139 AD</note>, on the twelfth day of the Egyptian month Epiphy, 9 hours after midday—that is, 3 equinoctial hours before the following midnight relative to the meridian of Krakow—until the year of Christ 1523, on the 8th day before the Kalends of March <note>February 22, 1523</note>, 7 hours before noon, there are 1,384 Egyptian years, 251 days, and 19 minutes. During this time, according to the calculation set forth above, the anomaly of parallax amounts to 5° 38' after completing 648 full revolutions. Furthermore, the Sun’s calculated mean motion is 257° 30'; when the 5° 38' of the motion of parallax is subtracted from this, there remains 252° 52' as the mean motion of Mars in longitude. All of these figures agree almost exactly with those just presented.

### Establishing the Positions of Mars. Chapter XVIII.

From the beginning of the years of Christ to the second year of Antoninus, the 12th day of the Egyptian month Epiphy, at 3 hours before midnight, there are 138 Egyptian years, 180 days, and 52 minutes. The motion of parallax during this interval is 293° 22'. When these are subtracted from the 171° 26' of Ptolemy’s last observation (by borrowing one full revolution), there remains 238° 4' <note>The text says 22', but the calculation suggests 4'</note> for the first year of Christ, at midnight on the Kalends of January <note>January 1st</note>. From the first Olympiad <note>776 BC, a standard epoch for ancient astronomers</note> to this point, there are 775 Egyptian years and 12 and a half days, during which the motion of parallax is 254° 1'. When these are similarly subtracted from the 238° 4', borrowing a full circuit, they leave the position for the first Olympiad...

### Chapter 19. How great the orbit of Mars is in parts, of which the annual orbit of the Earth is one.

To this end, we also observed the conjunction of Mars with the bright star of the first of the Claws <note>original: "Chelarum"; referring to the constellation Libra, formerly seen as the claws of Scorpio</note>, called the Southern Claw, which occurred in the year of Christ 1512, on the very Calends of January <note>January 1st</note>. For we saw, in the morning, six equinoctial hours before noon of that day, Mars distant from the fixed star by a quarter of one degree. But it was deflected toward the summer rising <note>the northeast</note>, which indicated that Mars was already separated from the star in longitude in the order of the signs by an eighth of a degree, but in latitude to the North by a fifth. Now, the position of the star from the first point of Aries is established at 191 degrees, 20 minutes, with a North latitude of 40 minutes. It was also evident that the position of Mars was at 191 degrees, 28 minutes, having a North latitude of 51 minutes. At this time, according to the calculation, the anomaly of commutation <term>anomaly of commutation: the angle representing the Earth's position relative to the planet's position in its orbit</term> is 98 degrees, 28 minutes.
