### Concerning the star of Venus. Chapter XX.

Having explained the motions of the three superior planets—Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars—which encompass the Earth, it now occurs to speak of those which the Earth itself circles. And first concerning Venus: which allows for an easier and more evident demonstration of its motion than the others, provided that the necessary observations of certain positions are not lacking. For if its greatest distances from the mean position of the Sun on either side, in the morning and evening, are found to be equal to each other, we then hold it as certain that the highest or lowest absis of the eccentric of Venus is in the middle of those two positions of the Sun. These are distinguished by the fact that such equalities of digression <note>The angular distance or elongation of the planet from the Sun</note> become smaller around the apogee and larger at the opposite point. Finally, in other locations, it is perceived without doubt through the differences by which they exceed one another how far the orbit of Venus is distant from the highest or lowest absis, and its eccentricity <term>eccentrotis: the degree to which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</term>, just as these things were most clearly handed down by Ptolemy. It would not be necessary to repeat these individually, except insofar as they are applied to our hypothesis of terrestrial mobility <note>The heliocentric theory where the Earth moves</note> based on those same considerations of Ptolemy. The first of these he took from the mathematician Theon of Alexandria, made in the 16th year of Hadrian, as he says, on the 21st day of the month of Pharmuthi, in the first hour of the following night; which was in the year of Christ 132, at twilight on the 8th day before the Ides of March. And Venus was seen at its greatest evening distance from the mean position of the Sun, being 47 degrees.

### Chapter 22. On the twofold motion of Venus.

HOWEVER, the motion of Venus is not a simple equality around center D, as evidenced by two specific observations of Ptolemy. One of these he took in the 18th year of Hadrian <note>Publius Aelius Hadrianus, Roman Emperor from 117–138 AD.</note>, on the second day of the Egyptian month Pharmuti; according to the Romans, this was the year 134 after the birth of Christ, at dawn on the 12th day before the <term>Kalends</term><note>The first day of the Roman month.</note> of March. For example, if we describe a small circle around center N with the distance DN, in which the orbit of Venus is carried and shifted, it follows this rule: whenever the Earth falls on the diameter ACB (where the highest and lowest apsides <note>The points in an orbit farthest from and closest to the center</note> of the eccentric are located), the center of the planet's orbit is always at the minimum distance, that is, at point M. But when the Earth is at the middle apsis, as when the center of the orbit is at G, it reaches point D and the maximum distance CD. From this, it is understood that in the time it takes the Earth to complete one circuit of its orbit, the center of the planet's orbit makes two revolutions around center N, moving in the same direction as the Earth, that is, in the order of the signs <note>Moving eastward through the zodiac</note>. For through such a hypothesis regarding Venus, the uniform motion and the observed appearances agree in all examples, as will soon be shown. Furthermore, all these things demonstrated so far concerning Venus are found to be consistent with our own times; whereas the total value was previously 416 parts, it is now 350, as many observations teach us.

Then, since the total angle **CEG** is 37 minutes <note>Copernicus is calculating the apparent distance of the planet from the mean Sun</note>, according to which the planet was seen to be distant from the mean position of the Sun, when **CEF** is subtracted from it, there remains the angle **FEG** of 35 degrees, 11 minutes. Furthermore, in the triangle **EFG** with the given angle **E**, the two sides are also given: **EF** is 10,034 parts, of which **FG** is 7,193. From this, the remaining angles are calculated as **EGF**, 53 and a half degrees, and **EFG**, 91 degrees, 19 minutes. By these amounts, the planet was distant from the true perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth</note> of its circle. But when **KFL**, the diameter parallel to **CE**, is drawn so that **K** is the apogee <note>The point furthest from the Earth</note> of mean motion and **L** is the perigee, and after subtracting the angle **EFL** (which is equal to **CEF**), there will remain the angle **LFG** and the arc **LG** of 89 degrees, 29 minutes. The remaining arc of the semicircle, **KG**, is 90 degrees, 31 minutes. This is the anomaly of commutation <note>term: anomaly of commutation; the angular distance of a planet from its apogee as seen from the center of its orbit</note> of the planet measured from the highest absis <note>The highest point of the orbit</note> of its mean circle, which we were seeking for this hour of our observation. However, in the observation of Timocharis <note>An Alexandrian astronomer, c. 320–260 BCE</note>, there were 252 degrees, 5 minutes. Therefore, in the intervening time, beyond the completed 1,115 revolutions, there are 188 degrees, 26 minutes. The time, moreover, from the year of Ptolemy...

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

<note>original: "REVOLVTIONVM LIB. V."</note>

from the first year of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Ptolemy II, ruler of Egypt 283–246 BCE</note>, at dawn on the 18th day of the month of Mesury <note>An Egyptian calendar month</note>, to the year of Christ 1529, on the 4th day before the Ides of March <note>March 12th</note>, 7 1/2 hours after midday, there are 1800 Egyptian years, 236 days, and approximately 40 minutes <note>scrupula, or sixtieths of a day</note>. Therefore, when we have multiplied the motion of 115 revolutions and 188 degrees 26 minutes by 365 days, and divided the sum by 1800 years, 236 days, and 40 minutes, we will have an annual motion of three sixty-degree units <note>180 degrees</note>, 45 degrees, 1 minute, 45 seconds, 3 thirds, and 40 fourths. These, again distributed over 365 days, leave a daily motion of 36 minutes, 59 seconds, and 28 thirds. From these values, the Table <note>Canon</note> which we set forth above was expanded.

### On the Positions of the Anomaly of Venus. Chapter XXIV.

Now, from the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE, a standard Greek chronological marker</note> to the 13th year of Ptolemy Philadelphus, at dawn on the 18th day of the month of Mesury, there are 503 Egyptian years, 228 days, and 40 minutes. In this time, the motion is calculated as 290 degrees and 39 minutes. If these are subtracted from 252 degrees and 5 minutes (after adding one full revolution), there remain 321 degrees and 26 minutes as the position for the first Olympiad. From this, the remaining positions are derived according to the ratio of motion and time already often mentioned: for Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> 81 degrees 52 minutes; for Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> 70 degrees 26 minutes; and for Christ 126 degrees 45 minutes.

### On Mercury. Chapter XXV.

The ways in which Venus is bound to the motion of the Earth, and under what ratio of circles its uniformity is hidden, has now been shown. There remains Mercury, which without a doubt will also reveal itself to us by adopting the same principle. However, it wanders with more complex windings <note>obuolutionibus</note> than Venus or any of the others mentioned above. It is certainly established by the experience of ancient observers that Mercury makes its smallest diversions <note>digressiones, or elongations</note> from the Sun in the sign of Libra, and larger ones in the opposite sign <note>Aries</note>, as is expected. Yet it does not make its greatest diversions in this latter place, but in certain others, namely in Gemini and Aquarius—especially in the time of Antoninus <note>Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius, during whose reign Ptolemy observed</note>, according to Ptolemy's opinion. This occurs in no other star. The ancient mathematicians, believing the cause of this thing...

<meta>The previous page likely discussed the motions of Venus or the general planetary theories of the ancients; the catchword "tuatur" (from "tueatur," meaning to maintain or uphold) connects to the opening argument regarding those who defend the Earth's immobility.</meta>

-># NICOLAUS COPERNICUS<-

Those who maintain that the Earth is immobile, and that Mercury moves in its great epicycle <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> along an eccentric path <note>A circular orbit where the Earth is not at the exact center</note>, realized that a single, simple eccentric could not satisfy these observed phenomena. Even after granting that the eccentric itself moved not around its own center but around a foreign one, they were further compelled to admit that this same eccentric moved on another small circle carrying the epicycle—similar to what they admitted regarding the Moon's eccentric. Consequently, with three centers existing—namely, one for the eccentric carrying the epicycle, a second for the small circle, and a third for that circle which more recent astronomers call the "equant" <note>term: Equant (a mathematical concept used to explain the observed speed changes in planetary orbits, though it violated the principle of uniform circular motion)</note>—they disregarded the first two and conceded that the epicycle moved uniformly only around the center of the equant. This was utterly foreign to the true center, to its logic, and to both pre-existing centers. Indeed, they believed the appearances of this star could be preserved in no other way, as is explained more diffusely in the Ptolemaic construction <note>Referring to Claudius Ptolemy’s *Almagest*, the standard astronomical text for over a millennium</note>.

However, so that this final star <note>Mercury</note> may be vindicated from the insults and opportunities of detractors, and so that its uniformity may be revealed no less than that of the preceding stars under the mobility of the Earth, we shall assign to it an "eccentric of an eccentric" in place of the epicycle imagined by antiquity. But this is done in a different manner than with Venus; nevertheless, a certain small epicycle moves within the eccentric itself, in which the star is carried not along the circumference, but up and down along its diameter. This can occur even from uniform circular motions, as was explained above regarding the precession of the equinoxes. Nor is this surprising, since Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his commentary on Euclid’s *Elements* admits that a straight line can be described by multiple motions.

By all these means, its appearances will be demonstrated. But so that the hypothesis <note>term: Hypothesis (the underlying geometric model or assumption)</note> may be more clearly understood, let the great orbital circle of the Earth be **AB**, its center **C**, and the diameter **ACB**. On this line, let center **D** be assumed between points **B** and **C**. With a distance of a third part **CD**, let a small circle **EF** be described, such that **F** is the greatest distance from **C**, and **E** is the least. Upon center **F**, let the orbit of Mercury be explained, which is **HI**. Then, with the center placed at the highest point of the orbit (the apogee) at **I**, let a small epicycle be added which the planet traverses. Let the orbit **HI** be an "eccentric-eccentric" or rather an "eccentric-epicycle" <note>original: "eccentrepicyclus"</note>. With the figure set out in this way, let all these points fall in order upon the straight line **AHCEDFKILB**, while the planet is positioned at **K**, that is, at the least distance from the center, which is **KF**.

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK V.

Now that the starting point for the revolutions of Mercury has been established, let it be understood that the center F performs two revolutions. One is synchronized with the Earth and moves in the same direction, which is in the order of the signs <note>original: "in consequentia" – meaning moving eastward, following the zodiacal sequence</note>. Similarly, the planet moves along the line KL, but moves up and down along that diameter with respect to the center of the orbital circle

<column-break/>

HI. For it follows from these arrangements that whenever the Earth is at point A or B, the center of Mercury’s orbit is at F, at its most distant position from C. However, when the Earth is in the middle quadrants, the center is at E, its closest position; in this regard, it acts in the opposite manner to Venus. By this same law, as Mercury traverses the diameter of the epicycle <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves along the circumference of a larger one</term> KL, it is at the point closest to the center of the orbit carrying the epicycle—which is point K—when the Earth falls on the diameter AB. In the middle positions on either side, the star reaches point L, its most distant location. In this way, two twin revolutions occur that are equal to each other: the center of the orbit moving on the circumference of the small circle EF, and the star moving along the diameter HK <note>The text likely intends KL as per the diagram</note>. These are both commensurable with the annual space of the Earth's movement. Meanwhile, the epicycle (or line FI) moves with its own proper motion along the orbit HI, and its center moves uniformly, completing one simple revolution relative to the sphere of the fixed stars in approximately 88 days. But in that motion by which it exceeds the Earth's motion—which we call the motion of commutation <term>motion of commutation: the relative motion between the planet and the Earth, determining the planet's phase and visibility</term>—it returns to the same position relative to the Earth in 116 days, as can be more exactly derived from the Table of Mean Motions. Accordingly, it follows

It follows that Mercury, by its own proper motion, does not always describe the same circular circumference, but one that differs greatly according to the ratio of its distance from the center of its orbit: the smallest indeed in the sign of κ <note>kappa</note>, the largest in ι <note>iota</note>, and a medium one through ι. This is observed in nearly the same manner as in the epicycle-on-epicycle <note>An epicycle is a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one; Copernicus uses this to explain complex planetary motions</note> of the Moon. But what the Moon does along a circumference, Mercury does along a diameter by a reciprocal motion, which is nevertheless composed of equal motions. How that occurs, we have shown above regarding the precessions of the equinoxes. However, we shall bring forth other and more numerous points concerning these matters below regarding latitudes. And this hypothesis suffices for all the appearances which are seen of Mercury, as will become manifest from the history of the observations of Ptolemy and others.

### Chapter XXVI. On the position of the highest and lowest apsides of Mercury.

For Ptolemy observed Mercury in the first year of Antoninus <note>Antoninus Pius, Roman Emperor; the observation dates to approximately 137 AD</note> after sunset on the 20th day of the month of Epiphi, while the planet was at its maximum evening distance from the mean position of the Sun. At this time, there had passed 137 years of Christ, 188 days, and 42.5 minutes at Krakow <note>Copernicus often calculated positions relative to the meridian of Krakow</note>, and therefore the mean position of the Sun according to our calculation was 63 degrees 50 minutes, and the star <note>planets were often called "wandering stars" in antiquity</note> was, as he says, at 7 degrees of Cancer by the instrument. But after subtracting the precession of the equinoxes, which was then 6 degrees 40 minutes, the position of Mercury was revealed to be 90 degrees 20 minutes from the beginning of Aries in the sphere of the fixed stars, and the maximum elongation from the mean Sun was 26.5 degrees. 

He took another observation in the 4th year of Antoninus, on the nineteenth day of the month of Phamenoth at dawn, when 140 years of Christ, 67 days, and nearly 12 minutes had passed from the beginning of the years of Christ, with the mean Sun being at 303 degrees 19 minutes. Mercury, however, appeared through the instrument at 13.5 degrees of Capricorn. But from the fixed beginning of Aries, it was at nearly 276 degrees 49 minutes. And therefore the maximum morning distance was likewise 26.5 degrees. Since, therefore, the limits of the digressions <note>The angular distance or elongation of the planet from the Sun</note> from the mean position of the Sun were equal on both sides, it is necessary that the apsides <term>apsides: the points in an orbit where a planet is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of motion</term> of Mercury were in the middle of those positions—that is, between 63 degrees 50 minutes and 110 degrees 20 minutes. These are 3 degrees 34 minutes and 183 degrees 34 minutes diametrically opposite, in which both apsides of Mercury had to be located.

For if **EF** were 10,000 parts, **FG** or **FH** would be 4054 parts, subtending an angle of 23 degrees and 52 minutes, by which the total angle **GEH** will be 47 degrees and 45 minutes. But at the lowest <term>apsis</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the center of motion; the perigee</note> only 46.5 degrees were observed, and similarly 46.5 degrees in the middle. This result is therefore greater than both by 1 degree and 14 minutes. This is not because the planet's orbit is closer to the Earth than it was at the perigee, but because the planet describes a larger circle here than there. All these findings are consistent with both present and past observations, and they flow from uniform motions.

### Examination of the Mean Motion of Mercury. Chapter 29.

For it is found in the more ancient observations that in the 21st year of Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>Pharaoh of Egypt, r. 285–246 BCE</note>, in the early dawn of the 19th day of the month of Thoth according to the Egyptians, Mercury appeared separated from a straight line passing through the first and second stars of Scorpio (located in its forehead) toward the following signs by two lunar diameters, and from the first star by one lunar diameter toward the North. It is clear, moreover, that the position of the first star is 209 degrees, a half, and a sixth in longitude <note>209° 40'</note>, and one and a third degrees in Northern latitude. The second star is at 209 degrees longitude, and one and a half plus a third—or five-sixths—of a degree in Southern latitude. From these, the position of Mercury was conjectured to be 210 degrees, a half, and a sixth in longitude <note>210° 40'</note>, and almost one and five-sixths degrees in Northern latitude. There were, moreover, 59 years, 17 days, and 45 minutes from the death of Alexander [the Great]. The mean position of the Sun according to our calculation was 228 degrees and 8 minutes, and the morning distance of the star was 18 degrees and 28 minutes, still increasing as was noted in the following four days. Thus it was certain that the planet had not yet reached its furthest morning limit, nor the point of contact with its orbit, but was still moving in the lower circumference and closer to the Earth. Since the highest apsis was at 183 degrees and 20 minutes, there were 44 degrees and 48 minutes to the mean position of the Sun. Let it be therefore again...

### On the more recent observations of the motions of Mercury. Chapter XXX.

The ancients indeed showed us this way of examining the course of this star, but they were aided by a clearer sky—namely where the Nile, as they say, does not breathe out such vapors as the Vistula <note>The river in Poland near Copernicus's home</note> does for us. For nature has denied that convenience to us who inhabit a more frigid region, where the tranquility of the air is rarer, and furthermore, due to the great obliquity of the sphere <note>The high latitude of Northern Europe</note>, it more rarely allows us to see Mercury. Even at its maximum distance from the Sun, if it is in Aries or Pisces, it does not rise into our view, nor does it set in Virgo or Libra. Neither does it show itself in Cancer or Gemini in any way when there is only twilight or dawn; it is never seen at night unless the Sun has moved well into Leo. For these reasons, this star has tortured us with many detours and labors so that we might scrutinize its wanderings. We have therefore borrowed three locations from those which were diligently observed at Nuremberg. The first was by Bernhard Walther, a disciple of Regiomontanus <note>A famous 15th-century German astronomer</note>, in the year of Christ 1491, on the 5th Idus of September <note>September 9th</note>, five equal hours after midnight. By means of astrolabe armillaries <note>term: armillas astrolabicas; a device of graduated metal rings used to determine the coordinates of celestial bodies</note> compared against the star Alpha Lyrae <note>original: "pallitium"; likely referring to the star Vega</note>, he saw Mercury at 13 and a half degrees of Virgo.

### On Establishing the Positions of Mercury. Chapter XXXI.

Since, therefore, from the beginning of the years of Christ until the final observation there are 1,504 Egyptian years, 87 days, and 48 minutes, during which the motion of Mercury's anomaly of commutation <note>The variation in the planet's position relative to the Sun as seen from Earth</note> is 63 degrees and 13 minutes (after rejecting the whole revolutions); when these are subtracted from 109 degrees and 38 minutes, there remain 46 degrees and 24 minutes as the position of the anomaly of commutation for Mercury at the beginning of the years of Christ. From there, going back to the beginning of the first Olympiad <note>776 BCE</note>, there are 775 Egyptian years and 12.5 days, in which 95 degrees and 3 minutes are counted after the whole revolutions. When these are deducted from the position at Christ's birth (by borrowing one full revolution), the position for the first Olympiad remains as 311 degrees and 21 minutes. From this, by a calculation made for the 451 years and 247 days until the death of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, 323 BCE</note>, the position arrives at 213 degrees and 33 minutes.

### On Another Method of Approach and Departure. Chapter XXXII.

Before we depart from Mercury, it was decided to review yet another method, no less credible than the previous one, through which that "approach and departure" <note>accessus et recessus: the apparent liberation or oscillation of the planet in its orbit</note> can be performed and understood. For let there be a circle divided into four parts, GHKP, with center F, in which a small homocentric circle LM is also inscribed. Again, with center L and at a distance LFO equal to FG or FH, let there be another circle OR. Let it be assumed that this entire configuration of circles...

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

<note>original: "NICOLAI COPERNICI"</note>

...is carried around center F in the order of the signs <note>moving eastward in the zodiac</note>, along with its sections G F R and H F P, daily by approximately 2 degrees and 7 minutes. This is specifically the amount by which the motion of the star's commutation <note>the planet's motion relative to the Sun</note> exceeds the Earth's motion in the zodiac, measured from the apogee <note>the point furthest from the center</note> of the star's eccentric. Meanwhile, the star completes the remaining motion from sign G through its own circle of commutation O R, which is nearly similar to the Earth's motion. Let it also be assumed that in this same annual revolution, the center of the orbit O R (which carries the star) is moved by a motion of libration <note>a back-and-forth oscillation</note> along the diameter L F M. This oscillation is twice as large as the one we previously established in its reciprocating motion, as stated above.

With these arrangements made, when we place the Earth in its mean motion opposite the apogee of the star's center, and at that time the center of the orbit carrying the star is at L, while the star itself is at sign O; then, being at the minimum distance from F, it will describe the smallest circle by the motion of the whole, the radius of which is F O. What follows thereafter is that when the Earth is near the mean apsis <note>the middle point between the furthest and nearest distances</note>, the star falls into sign H. According to its maximum distance from F, it will describe the largest circuits, namely according to the circle whose center is F. For then the carrying orbit O R will coincide with the circle G H because the centers unite at F. From here, as the Earth proceeds toward the perigee <note>the point closest to the center</note>, and the center of the orbit O R moves to the other extreme, which is M, the orbit itself is raised above G K. The star at R then falls again into the minimum distance from F, and the same things happen to it as in the beginning.

For here, three revolutions coincide as equals: the Earth's motion toward the apogee of Mercury's eccentric orbit; the libration of the center along the diameter L M; and the planet's motion from the line F G back to the same. The only difference from these is the motion of the sections G H and K P from the apsis of the center, as we have said. Truly, nature has played with such admirable variety around this star, yet she has confirmed it with a perpetual, certain, and immutable order.

But it must be noted here that in the middle spaces of the quadrants G H and K P, the star does not pass through without a difference in longitude. Since the intervening diversity of the centers will necessarily produce some <term>prosthaphæresis</term> <note>an astronomical correction used to calculate the difference between mean and true positions</note>, but the instability of that center stands in the way. If, for example, while the center remained at L, the star proceeded from O, it would admit the greatest difference near H according to the measure of the eccentricity... <note>original: "eccentrotetis"</note>

the eccentricity <term>FL</term> <note>FL refers to a specific line segment in Copernicus's geometric diagram of Mercury's orbit</note>. But from the assumptions made, it follows that the star <note>original: "stella"; here referring to the planet Mercury</note> indeed begins its progress from point O and promises the difference which the distance between the centers <term>FL</term> is supposed to produce. However, as the moving center approaches the midpoint <term>F</term>, more and more is subtracted from the promised diversity; it is frustrated to such an extent that around the middle sections <term>HP</term>, the difference vanishes entirely, exactly where it was expected to be greatest. And nevertheless—as we must admit—even when this small difference occurs, the planet is hidden under the rays of the Sun, and is not seen in the East or West as a morning or evening star, being completely lost within the windings of its circle. And we did not wish to pass over this method, which is no less reasonable than the previous one, and which will be most clearly useful regarding the deviations in latitude.

### On the tables of the corrections of the five wandering stars. Chapter XXXIII.

These matters concerning the uniform and apparent motion of Mercury and the other wandering stars <note>original: "errantium stellarum"; the planets</note> have thus been demonstrated and set forth in numbers. By following these examples, the path will be open to calculate the differences of motions for any other positions. For this purpose, we have prepared Tables <note>original: "Canones"</note> for each planet, consisting of six columns and thirty rows, arranged by three-degree intervals as is our custom. In the first part, two columns will contain the common numbers for both the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance of a planet from its furthest point on the eccentric circle</note> and the <term>commutations</term> <note>the parallax or apparent displacement caused by the Earth's motion</note>. The third column contains the total <term>eccentric corrections</term> <note>original: "prosthaphæreses"; the adjustments needed to find the true position from the mean position</note>—that is, the entire differences that fall between the uniform and the non-uniform motion of those orbits. The fourth contains the <term>proportional minutes</term> <note>original: "scrupula proportionum"; fractions used to scale the calculations</note>, which are sixtieths by which the commutations are increased or decreased due to the greater or lesser distance of the Earth. The fifth contains the <term>corrections</term> themselves, which are the commutations occurring at the highest apsis <note>the point in the orbit furthest from the center</note> of the planet's eccentric, caused by the Great Orbit <note>the Earth's orbit around the Sun</note>. In the sixth and last are the excesses by which those corrections occurring at the lowest apsis <note>the point in the orbit closest to the center</note> of the eccentric are greater. And these are the Tables.

### How the locations of these five planets are calculated in longitude. Chapter 34.

Through these Tables <note>original: "Canones"</note> thus set forth by us, we shall calculate the longitudinal positions of these five wandering stars <note>The "planets," from the Greek 'planētēs' meaning wanderer.</note> without difficulty. For in all of these, the method of computation is almost the same, though the outer planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note> differ somewhat from Venus and Mercury. Therefore, let us first speak of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars. Their calculation is such that, for any proposed time, the mean motions are sought—namely, the simple motion of the Sun and the commutation <note>term: commutation (the motion of the planet relative to the Earth's orbit)</note> of the planet—using the method delivered above. Then, the location of the highest absis <note>term: absis (the aphelion, or the point in the orbit furthest from the center)</note> of the planet's eccentric is subtracted from the simple motion of the Sun; from the remainder, the anomaly of commutation is subtracted; what then remains is the anomaly of the planet's eccentric. We seek the number of this anomaly among the common numbers in either of the first two rows of the Table, and from the opposite side in the third column, we take the equation of the eccentric and the following proportional minutes <note>original: "scrupula proportionum," used for interpolating between values.</note>. We shall add this equation to the anomaly of commutation and subtract it from the anomaly of the eccentric if the number we entered was found in the first series; and conversely, we subtract it from the anomaly of commutation and add it to the anomaly of the eccentric if it held the second row. What is collected or left over will be the equated anomalies of commutation and of the eccentric, while the proportional minutes are saved for a use soon to be mentioned. Furthermore, we seek the anomaly of commutation thus equated among the first common numbers, and in the fifth column, we take the prosthaphaeresis <note>term: prosthaphaeresis (the geometric correction needed to find the apparent position from the mean position)</note> of the commutation along with its excess placed at the end. From this excess, we take a proportional part according to the number of proportional minutes, which we always add to the prosthaphaeresis; this will yield the true commutation of the planet. This must be subtracted from the equated anomaly of commutation if it is less than a semicircle, or added if it is in the larger semicircle. In this way, we will have the true and apparent distance of the star from the mean position of the Sun in the preceding direction; when we subtract this from the Sun's position, the sought-after location of the star remains.

<summary>Copernicus provides a step-by-step mathematical procedure for calculating the longitudinal positions of the outer planets (Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars) using his tables and the concept of the Earth's motion.</summary>

is sought, relative to the sphere of the fixed stars. If the precession of the equinoxes <note>The slow wobbling of the Earth's axis that changes the position of the stars over centuries</note> is then added to this, it will determine the planet's position starting from the spring equinox. For Venus and Mercury, we use the eccentricity anomaly <note>The irregularity in a planet's orbit caused by it not being a perfect circle centered on the sun</note> which exists from the highest apse <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the center</note> to the mean position of the Sun; through this anomaly, we equalize the motion of commutation <note>The apparent change in a planet's position caused by the Earth's own movement</note> and the eccentricity anomaly itself, as has already been stated. But if the addition-subtraction <term>prosthaphæresis: a geometric correction used to find the true position of a planet from its mean or average position</term> of the eccentricity and the equalized parallax are of the same type or direction, they are added to or subtracted from the mean position of the Sun together. If, however, they are of different types, the smaller is subtracted from the larger, and with the remainder, one proceeds as just described, following the additive or subtractive property of the larger number; the result will be the apparent position of the planet being sought.

### On the Stations and Retrogradations of the Five Wandering Stars. Chapter XXXV.

It also seems relevant to the theory of longitudinal motion to understand the stations, regressions, and backward movements <note>original: "repedationum"</note>—where, when, and how great they are. Mathematicians have treated these extensively, especially Apollonius of Perga. But they did so as if there were only one inequality—that by which the stars move in respect to the Sun, which we have called "commutation" due to the motion of the Earth's Great Orb <note>The Earth's annual orbit around the Sun</note>. For if the circles of the stars were concentric with the Earth's Great Orb, in which all the stars are carried at unequal speeds in the same direction (that is, eastward), and some star in its own circle—and within the Great Orb, like Venus or Mercury—were faster than the Earth's motion, a straight line drawn from the Earth would cut the star's circle. If the ratio of half the segment intercepted within the circle to the line extending from our point of sight (the Earth) to the lower, receding arc of the cut circle is the same as the ratio of the Earth's speed to the star's velocity, then the point marked by the line so drawn onto the circumference near the planet's perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> distinguishes the backward movement from the forward progress. Thus, the star situated in that position gives the appearance of a station <note>The moment a planet appears to stand still before changing direction</note>. Similarly for the other three outer planets, whose motion is slower than the velocity

<note>Copernicus is explaining the "stationary point" where a planet appears to stop moving before reversing direction.</note> ...the speed of the Earth, a straight line drawn through our point of vision should intersect the great orbit <note>the Earth's orbital path</note> in such a way that the ratio of the half-section within the orbit to the segment extending from the star <note>planet</note> to our eye (positioned on the closer, convex surface of the orbit) is the same as the ratio of the planet's motion to the Earth's velocity. At that specific location, the star will present the appearance of standing still to our sight. 

If, however, the half-section within the circle has a greater ratio to the remaining outer segment than the Earth's velocity has to the velocity of **Venus** or **Mercury** (or the motion of any of the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> to the Earth's velocity), the star will move forward in sequence <note>prograde motion</note>. But if the ratio is less, it will move backward into the preceding signs <note>retrograde motion</note>. 

To demonstrate these points, **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Perga, a 3rd-century BC Greek mathematician known for his work on conic sections</note> adopts a certain lemma <note>a subsidiary proposition used to prove a larger theorem</note>, though he did so under the hypothesis of an immobile Earth. Nevertheless, it accords perfectly with our principles regarding the mobility of the Earth, and therefore we shall also employ it. We may state it in this form: 

If the longer side of a triangle is divided such that one of the segments is not less than the side adjacent to it, the ratio of that segment to the remaining segment will be greater than the ratio of the angles situated at the divided side, taken in reciprocal order. 

Let us say that in triangle **ABC**, the longer side is **BC**. If a point **D** is taken on it such that **CD** is not less than **AC**, I assert that the ratio of **CD** to **BD** will be greater than the ratio of angle **ABC** to angle **BCA**. 

It is demonstrated in this manner: Let the parallelogram **ADCE** be completed, and let the extensions of **BA** and **CE** meet at point **F**. Since **AE** is not less than **AC**, a circle described with center **A** and distance **AE** will pass through **C** or beyond it. Let it pass through **C**, and let it be **GEC**. Since triangle **AEF** is greater than the sector **AEG**, but triangle **AEC** is smaller than sector **AEC** <note>original: "sectori AEC"</note>, the ratio of triangle **AEF** to **AEG** is greater than the ratio of sector **AEG** to sector **AEC**. 

But as triangle **AEF** is to **AEC**, so is the base **FE** to **EC**. Therefore, the ratio of **FE** to **EC** is greater than the ratio of angle **FAE** to angle **EAC**. However, as **FE** is to **EC**, so is **CD** to **DB**. Furthermore, angle **FAE** is equal to angle **ABC**, and angle **EAC** is equal to **BCA**. Therefore...

<note>The diagram illustrates the geometric proof described above, showing the relationship between the segments of the triangle and the circular sectors used to establish the ratios of planetary motion.</note>

<summary>Copernicus adapts a geometric proof by Apollonius of Perga to explain why planets appear to stop or move backward from the perspective of a moving Earth. He uses a triangle-based lemma to establish the mathematical ratios required for these planetary "stations" and "retrogradations."</summary>

<keywords>planetary motion, retrogradation, stationary points, Apollonius of Perga, heliocentrism, geometry, ratios, Venus, Mercury</keywords>

And the ratio of CD to DB is greater than the ratio of the angle ABC to the angle ACB. It is evident, moreover, that the ratio will be much greater if CD is not assumed to be equal to AC (that is, AE), but is set as greater than it. Now, let the circle of Venus or Mercury be ABC around center D, and outside the circle let the Earth E be mobile around the same center D <note>Copernicus is describing the relative motion where the Earth is the observer, though both the Earth and the planet orbit the Sun at center D</note>. From our point of view, let the straight line ECDA be drawn through the center of the circle; let A be the place farthest from the Earth <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the observer</term>, and C the closest <term>perigee: the point in an orbit nearest to the observer</term>. Let it be assumed that the ratio of DC to CE is greater than the ratio of the motion of our sight to the velocity of the star.

It is therefore possible to find a line EFB such that half of BF has the same ratio to FE as the motion of our sight has to the course of the star. For as the line EFB moves away from the center D, it decreases in the segment FB and increases in EF until the required ratio is met. I say that the star, when positioned at point F, will create for us the appearance of a station <note>original: "stationis speciem"; a point where the planet appears to stand still in the sky before changing direction</note>. Furthermore, whatever small arc of the circumference we take on either side of F: if taken toward the apogee, we shall find the motion to be progressive; but toward the perigee, it will be regressive.

For let there first be taken the arc FG toward the apogee, and let EGK be extended, and let BG, DG, and DF be connected. Since in triangle BGE, the segment BF of the larger side BE is greater than BG, the ratio of BF to EF is greater than the ratio of angle FEG to angle GBF. Accordingly, half of BF to FE also has a greater ratio than angle FEG has to double the angle GBF—that is, to angle GDF. However, the ratio of half of BF to FE is the same as the ratio of the Earth's motion to the course of the star. Therefore, the ratio of the Earth's velocity to the star's velocity is less than the ratio of angle FEG to GDF. Consequently, the angle which has the same ratio to angle FDG as the Earth's motion has to the star's course is greater than FEG. Let that angle be FEL. Therefore, in the time in which the star has traversed the arc FG of its orbit, the line of sight will be thought to have [moved...]

### How the times, places, and arcs of retrogressions are distinguished. Chapter XXXVI.

Furthermore, if the orbits by which the wandering stars <note>The term "wandering stars" is a literal translation of the Greek *planētai*.</note> are carried were concentric to the Great Orbit, the things promised by the demonstrations would easily be established, as the ratio of the star's speed to the speed of sight would always remain the same. Our purpose is to find the circumference **F C**, which is half of the retrocession, or **A B F**, so that we may know how far the star has moved from its greatest distance at **A B** when it reaches its stationary point, as well as the angle contained under **F E C**. Furthermore, in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, the same mode of demonstration is evident; no less so in Venus and Mercury, provided that we take the sight for the star, and the star for the sight <note>A reference to the fact that for inner planets, the geometric relationship is inverted compared to outer planets</note>. These things happen conversely in the orbits which encompass the Earth from those which the Earth encompasses; and therefore, lest we repeat the same song over and over, let these things suffice. Nevertheless, since the variable motion of those stars according to sight and the ambiguity of the stations bring no small difficulty—from which the assumption of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga, a Greek geometer whose theorems on stationary points Copernicus is refining</note> by no means relieves us—I do not know if someone might not do better by entering upon the stations simply and from the nearest place, in the same way that we seek the conjunction of a star at opposition to the line of the mean motion of the Sun, or the meeting of any stars from the known numbers of their motions joining them; which we leave to the pleasure of anyone.

# THE REVOLUTIONS OF NICOLAUS COPER-
## NICUS
### BOOK SIX.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, holding a globe or circular object, surrounded by ornate foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

We have indicated, as clearly as we were able, what power and effect the assumed revolution of the Earth has regarding the apparent motion in longitude of the wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" or *planetae* refer to the planets known at the time: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, and into what certain and necessary order it compels them all. It remains for us to occupy ourselves with the transitions of those stars by which they digress in latitude, and to show how, in these matters as well, the same mobility of the Earth exercises its authority and has prescribed laws for them even in this part. Moreover, this part of the science is necessary because the digressions of these stars produce no small difference regarding their rising and setting, their appearances and disappearances, and other phenomena which were explained in general above. Indeed, their true positions are only said to be known when their longitude is established together with their latitude from the circle of signs <note>The "circle of signs" refers to the Ecliptic or the Zodiac.</note>. Therefore, what the ancient mathematicians believed they had demonstrated here by means of a stationary Earth, we shall perhaps accomplish with greater brevity and more appropriately by assuming the Earth's mobility.

### A general exposition on the digression in latitude of the five wandering stars. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' with intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

The ancients found a twofold expansion in latitude for all these stars, corresponding to the twofold inequality of longitude for each of them. One occurs by reason of the eccentric circles, and the other by means of the epicycles <note>In the Ptolemaic system, an epicycle was a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one (the deferent).</note>; in place of these epicycles, we have now frequently accepted the single Great Orb of the Earth. However, since the three superior planets—**Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars**—are carried in longitude by different laws than the remaining two <note>Venus and Mercury</note>, they also differ significantly in their motion in latitude. Therefore, [astronomers] first investigated where and how great the extreme limits of their northern latitude were. **Ptolemy** <note>The 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is updating</note> found these in **Saturn** and **Jupiter** near the beginning of **Libra**, but in **Mars** near the end of **Cancer**, almost at the apogee <note>The point in the orbit farthest from the center</note> of the eccentric. In our times, however, we have found these northern limits to be at 7° of **Scorpio** for **Saturn**, 27° of **Libra** for **Jupiter**, and 27° of **Leo** for **Mars**, just as the apogees have also shifted down to our time. For the inclinations and the hinges <note>cardines</note> of the latitudes follow the motion of those orbits. Between these limits, through the quadrants of the circles according to equal or apparent distances, they seem to make no departure in latitude at all, wherever the Earth happens to be at that time. Therefore, at these middle longitudes, they are understood to be in the common section of their orbits with the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signifero," the belt of the heavens containing the twelve signs</note>, not otherwise than the Moon in the ecliptic sections, which Ptolemy calls "nodes." The ascending node is where the star enters the northern parts; the descending node is where it passes over into the south. It is not that the Earth's great orbit, always remaining in the plane of the zodiac, brings any latitude to them, but every departure in latitude is from the planets themselves. This varies most in places other than these [nodes]; when the Earth approaches them—when they are seen opposite the Sun and rising at sunset <note>original: "acronycti," meaning the planet is visible all night</note>—they always move out with a greater departure than in any other position of the Earth. In the northern semicircle they move toward the North, and in the southern toward the South, and this with a greater difference than the approach and retreat of the Earth requires. By this occasion it was recognized that the inclination of those orbits is not fixed, but is changed by a certain motion of <term>libration</term> <note>A slow oscillation, like a swinging balance</note> commensurable with the revolutions of the Earth's great orbit, as will be said a little further below. **Venus** and **Mercury**, however, seem to move out in certain other ways, yet observing a certain law regarding the middle, highest, and lowest <term>apsides</term> <note>The points of greatest or least distance in an orbit</note>. For in the middle longitudes, namely when the line of the mean motion of the Sun is distant by quadrants from their highest or lowest apsis, and the stars themselves are distant from that same line of mean motion by quadrants of their orbits, whether in the evening or...

By this they understood that the planets were then at the common intersection of their orbits and the ecliptic, an intersection which passes through their <term>apogees</term> <note>farthest point from Earth</note> and <term>perigees</term> <note>closest point to Earth</note>. Therefore, whether they are at their highest or lowest points relative to the Earth, they then make their lateral movements manifest. Indeed, at their greatest distance from the Earth—that is, around their evening emergence or morning occultation—Venus is seen at her most Northerly, and Mercury at his most Southerly. Conversely, at the point closer to Earth, when they are hidden in the evening or emerge in the morning, Venus is Southerly and Mercury is Northerly. 

On the other hand, when the Earth is at the opposite location and at the other middle <term>apsis</term> <note>the turning point of an orbit</note>—namely, when the <term>eccentric anomaly</term> <note>the angular distance from the apogee</note> is 270 degrees—Venus appears Southerly at her greater distance from Earth, and Mercury Northerly; while near the point closer to Earth, Venus appears Northerly and Mercury Southerly. But during the Earth's transition toward the apogees of these stars, Ptolemy found a Northern latitude for the morning Venus and a Southern one for the evening Venus. Likewise, in turn, for Mercury: a Southern latitude when in the morning, and a Northern one in the evening. These are similarly reversed at the opposite location of the perigee, so that Venus as <term>Lucifer</term> <note>the Morning Star</note> is seen as Southerly, and as <term>Vesperugo</term> <note>the Evening Star</note> as Northerly; but Mercury in the morning is Northerly, and in the evening Southerly. 

And yet, in both of these locations, they found the Northern departure of Venus to be always greater than the Southern, and the Southern departure of Mercury greater than the Northern. On this account, they reasoned that there are two latitudes in this place, and three in total. The first, which occurs at the middle longitudes, they called **Inclination**. The second, which occurs at the highest and lowest apsis, they called **Obliquation**. And the remaining one, joined to this, they called **Deviation**—which is always Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. Between these four limits, the latitudes mix with one another, increasing and decreasing by turns and yielding to each other; for all of which we shall assign appropriate causes.

### Hypotheses of the circles by which these stars are carried in latitude. Chapter II.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a floral and scrollwork background.</note>

**A**ssumption must therefore be made regarding these five stars: that their orbits are inclined to the plane of the ecliptic, and that their common intersection is along the diameter of the ecliptic itself, with a variable inclination...

For in Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, the angle of the intersection <note>the angle where the planetary orbit meets the plane of the Earth's orbit</note> undergoes a certain oscillation <term>libration: a slow, swinging motion like a pendulum</term> around that intersection as if it were an axis, similar to what we demonstrated regarding the precession of the equinoxes. However, this is a simple oscillation, proportional to the motion of commutation <note>the relative motion between the Earth and the planet</note>, by which it increases and decreases over a fixed interval. Thus, whenever the Earth is closest to the planet—namely, at its nightly rising <term>acronycto: when a planet is in opposition to the sun and rises at sunset</term>—the greatest inclination of the planet's orbit occurs; in the opposite position, the least; and in the middle, a mean value. Consequently, when the planet is at the limit of its maximum Northern or Southern latitude, its latitude appears much greater when in proximity to the Earth than at its greatest distance. Although the unequal distance from the Earth could be the sole cause of this variation (since closer objects appear larger than distant ones), the latitudes of these stars increase and decrease by a greater difference than distance alone allows. This cannot happen unless the orbits themselves also oscillate in their tilt. But as we said before regarding oscillating bodies, it is necessary to assume a certain mean between the extremes.

Let the common section be $B E D$, which is extended into the straight lines $G B$ and $D L$. Indeed, let these four terms not change, except according to the motion of the apsides <note>the points in an orbit closest or furthest from the center</note>. Let it be understood, however, that the motion of the star in longitude is not carried under the plane of that circle $F G$, but under another circle $O P$ which is oblique to $F G$ and shares the same center <term>homocentro: having the same center</term>, and which intersects $F G$ along the same lines $G B$ and $D L$ re-

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS BOOK VI.

GB and DL are straight lines. Therefore, while the star <note>The term "star" here refers to a planet.</note> is carried along the orbital circle OP, and occasionally coincides with the plane FK through a motion of oscillation <term>libration: a back-and-forth or swinging motion, like a pendulum</term>, it moves across into both directions, and because of this, it makes the latitude appear to vary. For let the star first be at its maximum Northern latitude under the sign O, closest to the Earth, which is located at A; the latitude of the star will then increase according to the angle OGF of the maximum inclination of the orbit OGP. 

Because the motion of this approach and retreat is, by hypothesis, proportional to the motion of parallax <term>commutation: the apparent displacement of a planet caused by the Earth's own movement</term>, if the Earth is then at B, O will coincide with F, and the latitude of the star will appear smaller in that same place than before. It will appear much smaller still if the Earth is at the sign C. For O will then move to the extreme and opposite part of its oscillation, and will leave only as much as remains after the oscillation has subtracted from the Northern latitude—namely, from an angle equal to OGF. 

Thereafter, through the remaining semicircle CDA, the Northern latitude of the star (located around F) will increase until it returns to the first sign from which it departed. The same process and manner will apply to a Southern star positioned around the sign K, taking the starting point of the Earth's motion from C. But if the star is at either of the nodes G or L, whether it is in opposition to the sun <term>acronyctus: rising at sunset or visible all night</term> or hidden beneath the Sun's rays, no latitude of the star will be perceived, even though the orbits FK and OP are then at their greatest inclination to one another, because the star occupies the common intersection of the orbits. 

From these points, I believe it is easily understood how the Northern latitude of a planet decreases from F to G, and the Southern latitude increases from G to K, which then vanishes entirely at L and passes back to the North. And the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.</note> behave in this manner. 

Venus and Mercury differ from these not a little in their latitudes, just as they do in longitude, because they have the common intersections of their orbits located through their apogees <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> and perigees <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</term>. Their maximum inclinations, however, are shifted toward the middle apsides <term>apsides: the points of greatest or least distance in an orbit</term> and are changeable by an oscillation, like those of the superior planets mentioned above; but these planets undergo an additional oscillation unlike the first. Both oscillations, however, are proportional to the revolutions of the Earth, but not in the same way. For the first oscillation has this property: when the Earth has revolved once to their apsides, the motions of oscillation themselves have revolved twice, having a permanent axis at the intersection I mentioned through the apogees and perigees. Thus, whenever the line of the mean motion of the Sun is in their perigee or apogee, the greatest angle of intersection occurs; but in the middle longitudes, it is always the smallest.

<summary>Copernicus explains the geometric model for planetary latitude using "libration" (oscillation) to account for observed changes in a planet's distance from the ecliptic. He distinguishes the behavior of the superior planets from the more complex double-oscillation seen in Venus and Mercury.</summary>

<keywords>planetary latitude, libration, orbital inclination, superior planets, Venus, Mercury, apogee, perigee, parallax, celestial mechanics</keywords>

--- Page 384 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the complex orbital motions of the inner planets, specifically addressing the "deviation" or second oscillation that affects their latitude relative to the Earth's path.</meta>

# NICOLAUS COPERNICUS

The second **oscillation** <note>original: "libratio"; a back-and-forth motion like a swinging scale</note> occurring in addition to the first differs from it in this respect: because it has a movable axis, it ensures that when the Earth is positioned at the middle longitudes—whether of Venus or Mercury—the planet is always on the axis, that is, in the common section of this oscillation. However, the planet is at its maximum deviation when its **apogee** <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> or **perigee** <note>the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> faces the Earth. At that time, Venus is always toward the North <note>original: "Boream"</note>, as has been said, and Mercury is toward the South <note>original: "Austrum"</note>; even though, due to the first and simple inclination, they ought to have lacked any latitude at that point.

For example: when the mean motion of the Sun is at the apogee of Venus, and Venus herself is in the same place, it is clear that according to the simple inflection and the first oscillation, she would have admitted no latitude, being in the common section of her orbit with the plane of the **zodiac** <note>original: "signiferi"; the path of the Sun</note>. But the second oscillation introduces its maximum deviation upon her, having its section or axis along the transverse diameter of the **eccentric** <note>a circular orbit where the center is not the Earth</note> orbit, cutting at right angles the line that passes through the highest and lowest **apsides** <note>the points of greatest or least distance in an orbit</note>.

If, however, at the same time she is in either quadrant and near the middle apsides of her orbit, then the axis of this oscillation will coincide with the line of the mean motion of the Sun. Then Venus herself will add the maximum deviation to her Northern reflection, while she will subtract it from the Southern reflection, leaving it smaller. In this way, the oscillation of the deviation is made commensurate with the motion of the Earth.

Their common section is FG, passing through the apogee of the orbit, which is F, and the perigee, G. <margin>G</margin> Let the common section <note>The line where two orbital planes intersect</note> be shifted according to the motion of the perigee and apogee <note>The points in an orbit closest to and farthest from the Earth</note>. When the Earth is situated on this line, namely at *a* or *c*, and the planet is on the same line, it is clear that it would then produce no latitude, since all latitude is measured from the sides. In the semicircles *G K F* and *F L G*, the planet makes its approach toward the North or the South, as has been said, according to the degree of inflection of the circle *F K G* to the plane of the zodiac. Astronomers call this departure of the planet "obliquation," while others call it "reflexion." However, when the Earth is at *b* or *d*—that is, at the middle apsides <note>The points halfway between the highest and lowest points of the orbit</note> of the planet—there will be the same latitudes above and below *F K G* and *G L F*, which they call "declinations." Thus, these differ from the former more in name <term>than</term> in reality, and at the intermediate positions, the names are used interchangeably. But since the angle of inclination of these circles is found to be greater in obliquation than in declination, they understood this to happen through a certain <term>libration</term> <note>A slow oscillation, like the swinging of a balance scale</note>, bending itself on the section *F G* as an axis, as was stated above. Therefore, since we have the known angle of such a section in both cases, we could easily understand from their difference how great that libration was from the minimum to the maximum.

Now, let another circle of deviation be understood, oblique to *G K F L*. This is concentric <note>Sharing the same center</note> in the case of Venus, but eccentric to the eccentric <note>An orbit whose center is itself moving on another circle</note> in the case of Mercury, as will be said later. Let their common section be *R S*, acting as the axis of this libration, which moves in a circuit. This is done in such a way that while the Earth is at *A* or *B*, the planet is at the extreme limit of deviation, wherever it hits at sign *T*. As far as the Earth has progressed from *A*, so far is the planet understood to be removed from *T*, while the obliquity of the circle of deviation meanwhile decreases. Thus, when the Earth has measured out a quadrant *A B*, the planet is understood to have arrived at the node of this latitude, that is, at *R*. But with the planes then coinciding at the middle moment of the libration and then striving in the opposite direction, the remaining semicircle of deviation, which was previously Southern, breaks out into the North. Entering this, Venus leaves the South behind and seeks the North again, and will now seek the South through this libration. In the same way, Mercury, by following the opposite parts, remains Southern; he also differs in this: that he does not librate in the center of the eccentric, but in the eccentric of the eccentric. For this, we used an <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</note> regarding the motion in longitude in the demonstration of inequality. But because in that case there was longitude without latitude, and here latitude...

### Chapter 3. How great the inclination is of the orbits of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars.

After explaining the hypotheses for the diversions <note>original: "digressionum," meaning the deviations in latitude</note> of the five planets, we must descend to the facts themselves and distinguish the individual details. First of all, we must determine how great the inclinations of the individual circles are. We calculate these by means of a great circle which passes through the poles of the inclined circle and at right angles to the circle through the middle of the signs <note>The Ecliptic or Zodiac</note>, according to which the transitions in latitude are observed. For once these are understood, the way to knowing the latitudes of each planet will be opened. Beginning again with the three superior planets <note>Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note>, we find that at the extreme southern limits of their latitudes, according to Ptolemy's exposition, the deviations of Saturn when at opposition <note>original: "acronychi," meaning the planet is rising as the sun sets</note> are 3 degrees and 5 minutes; for Jupiter, 2 degrees and 7 minutes; and for Mars, 7 degrees. However, in the opposite positions—namely, when they are in conjunction with the Sun—the deviations are 2 degrees and 2 minutes for Saturn; 1 degree and 5 minutes for Jupiter; and for Mars, only 5 minutes, so that it almost touches the circle of the signs, as far as could be noticed from the latitudes observed during their disappearances and emergences.

With these things proposed, let there be a plane at right angles to the circle of the signs, and let the common section of the zodiac be AB. Let CD be the section of the eccentric orbit of any of the three superior planets through the greatest Southern and Northern limits. Let E be the center of the zodiac, and FBG be the diameter of the great orbit of the Earth. Let D be the Southern latitude and C the Northern, to which are joined the lines CF, CG, DF, and DG. Now, the ratios of EG (the Earth's great orbit) to ED (the planet's eccentric orbit) have been demonstrated above for any of their proposed locations. But the locations of the greatest latitudes are also given from observations. Therefore, since the angle BGD of the greatest Southern latitude is given, being the exterior angle of the triangle EGD, the interior and opposite angle GED—the inclination of the greatest Southern eccentricity to the plane of the zodiac—will also be given by the demonstrations of plane triangles. Similarly, by means of the minimum Southern latitude, we shall demonstrate the minimum inclination, namely by the angle...

Regarding the triangle EFD: since the ratio of the sides EF to FD is given, along with the angle EFD, we will determine the exterior angle DFE <note>The angle of the smallest southern inclination</note>. We shall provide an example using Mars, because it exceeds all others in the extent of its latitude. And since the ratio of EF to CE is as 1 to 1, 39 minutes, and 57 seconds, and the angle CEF is equal to DEG (1 degree and 51 minutes), it follows that the exterior angle we mentioned, CFA, is 4 and a half degrees when the planet is at its <term>acronyctos|the 'night-rising' or opposition, when a planet is opposite the sun and visible all night</term>. 

Similarly, in the opposite position, while it moves with the Sun, if we take the angle DFE as 5 minutes from the given sides DE and EF, with angle EFD, we will have angle EDF and the exterior angle DEG as nearly 9 minutes of minimum inclination. This also reveals to us the angle CGE of Northern latitude as nearly 6 minutes. Therefore, when we subtract the minimum inclination from the maximum—that is, 9 minutes from 1 degree and 51 minutes—there remains 1 degree and 42 minutes. This is the oscillation of this inclination, and its half is nearly 50 and a half minutes. 

In a similar manner, the angles of inclination and the latitudes of the other two, Jupiter and Saturn, have become clear. Namely, the maximum inclination of Jupiter is 1 degree and 42 minutes; the minimum is 1 degree...

In order that these matters may be distinguished individually, we shall begin with that which they call **declination** <note>original: "declinationem"; here referring to the tilting or inclination of the planetary orbit relative to the ecliptic</note>, as it is a simpler treatment. Indeed, it happens to the Sun <note>Copernicus refers to the Earth's motion relative to the Sun in his heliocentric model</note> that it is sometimes separated from the others, because when the Earth is positioned at the middle longitudes and near the nodes—according to the examined motions of longitude through the quadrants of the circles—away from the **apogee** <note>the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</note> and **perigee** <note>the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note> of the planet, they found the parts of southern or northern latitude in **Venus** to be 6 degrees 22 minutes, and in **Mercury** 4 degrees 5 minutes.

However, at the greatest distance of the Earth, they found for **Venus** 1 degree 2 minutes, and for **Mercury** 1 degree 45 minutes. From these, the angles of the inclinations in this position become manifest through the set out tables of equations. For **Venus** in that place, at the highest distance from the Earth, 1 degree 2 minutes, and at the lowest, 6 degrees 22 minutes agree, such that in both cases the circumference of the orbit is approximately 2 degrees 30 minutes. For **Mercury**, indeed, 1 degree 45 minutes at the top and 4 degrees 5 minutes at the bottom requires a circumference of its orbit of 6 degrees and one quadrant <note>6 degrees 15 minutes</note>.

Thus, the angle of inclination of the orbits is 2 degrees 30 minutes for **Venus**, and for **Mercury** 6 degrees and a quadrant, of which 360 make four right angles. ### On the second transition in latitude of Venus and Mercury according to the obliquity of their orbits in apogee and perigee. Chapter VI.

These things concern the transition of the latitude of these stars which happens around the middle longitudes of their orbits, which latitudes we have said are called "declinations." at the greatest distances from the sun in the morning and evening, as we have said. For because of the equal angles they subtend, HD, KE, and LF are proportional to HM, KN, and LO. And since the same ratio of these to their excesses remains, it follows that the excess of EK and KN has a greater ratio to EA than the others have to lines similar to AD. From this it is also manifest that whatever ratio the maximum longitudinal prosthaphairesis has to the maximum transit of latitude, the longitudinal prosthaphaireses of the segments of the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circular orbit where the center is not the Earth</note> will have the same ratio to the transits of latitude. Since as KE is to EN, so are all those similar to LF and HD to those similar to FO and DM, which were the things proposed to be demonstrated.

In the case of Mercury, the demonstration proceeds in the same way: for where the radius of the orbit is 3573 parts, the greatest distance of the orbit from the Earth is 10,948, and the minimum is 9052; the mean between these is 10,000. Since the ratio of line AB to BD is as 10,000 to 3573, we will have the third side of the same, AD, as 9340 parts. And since as AB is to AD, so BD is to DF, then DF is 3337 of such parts in length. And since the angle of latitude DAG is set at 2 degrees and 30 minutes <note>original: "part. II. S." where S stands for semis, or half</note>, then DG will be 407 parts where DF is 3337. Thus, in the triangle DFG, with the ratio of these two sides given and the angle G being a right angle, we will have the angle at DFG as approximately 6 degrees. This is the angle of inclination or slant of Mercury's orbit from the plane of the zodiac <note>original: "signiferi"</note>. But around the middle longitudes or quadrants, the angle of inclination itself was shown to be 6 degrees and 15 minutes; therefore, 45 minutes have now been added by the first motion of oscillation.

Similarly, for the sake of examining the angles of correction and their difference, one may observe—after it has been shown that the line DG is 407 parts where AD is 9340 and DF is 3337. If, therefore, we subtract the square of DG from the squares of AD and DF, the squares of AG and FG will remain. We will then have the length of AG as 9331 and FG as 3314, from which the angle of correction GAF is elicited as 20 degrees and 48 minutes, while the angle DAF is 20 degrees and 56 minutes, from which the angle according to the slant is deficient by about 8 minutes.

In this way, we will have explained each particular latitude of the <term>obliquations</term> <note>the "slanting" or tilting of the planetary orbits relative to the Earth's path</note> occurring when the Earth is at their highest and lowest <term>apsides</term> <note>the points in an orbit closest to or furthest from the center</note>, just as we previously set forth the latitudes of the <term>declinations</term> at the middle quadrants and middle longitudes. What happens between these four limits could indeed be explained with the subtlety of the mathematical art from the proposed hypothesis of circles, though not without great labor. However, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer whose geocentric model Copernicus is updating</note>, being as concise as possible everywhere, saw that both types of these latitudes increased and decreased proportionally throughout all their parts, similar to the lunar latitude. Therefore, by taking any of its parts twelve times (because its maximum latitude is five degrees, which is the 12th part of 60), he established "proportional minutes" from them. He thought these should be used not only for these two stars, but also for the three superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, as will be shown below.

### On the third type of latitude for Venus and Mercury, which they call deviation. Chapter 8.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or astronomer, holding a book or instrument.</image-desc> Having explained these matters, it remains to say something about the third motion of latitude, which is the **deviation**. Those predecessors who keep the Earth in the center of the universe <note>the geocentric or Ptolemaic school</note> believe this occurs through the tilting of the <term>eccentric</term> along with the <term>epicycle</term> <note>the small circle on which a planet moves, which itself moves along a larger circle</note> around the center of the Earth, especially when the epicycle is located at the <term>apogee</term> <note>furthest point from Earth</note> or <term>perigee</term> <note>closest point to Earth</note>. For Venus, this is by a sixth of a degree, always toward the North; for Mercury, it is by three-quarters of a degree, always toward the South, as we said before. Yet it is not sufficiently clear whether they intended such an inclination of the orbits to be always equal and the same, for their numbers indicate this when they command that a sixth part of the proportional minutes always be taken for the deviation of Venus, and three-quarters for Mercury. This cannot take place unless there remains the same...

The angle of inclination remains the same, just as the ratio of those minutes <note>original: "scrupulorum," referring to small units of angular measurement</note> requires, upon which they are based. Furthermore, if the angle remained the same, it could not be understood how the latitude of these stars could suddenly spring back from the common section <note>the intersection of the orbital planes</note> into the same latitude it had just left, unless you were to say it happens by the refraction of light, as in optics. Now let the Earth be at any distance from the apogee or perigee of the planet's eccentric; according to this motion, let a similar arc of the small circle be taken, which shall be <term>F G</term>. The circle described from <term>G C</term>, which carries the planet, will also intersect the small circle's diameter at <term>E</term>. 

Let the planet be at <term>K</term>; the arc <term>E K</term> will be similar to <term>G F</term> according to the hypothesis. Also, let <term>K L</term> be drawn perpendicular to the circle <term>A B C</term>. The goal is to find the magnitude of <term>K L</term> (that is, the distance of the planet from the circle <term>A B C</term>) from <term>F G</term>, <term>E K</term>, and <term>B E</term>. Since from the arc <term>F G</term>, <term>B G</term> will be given as a straight line differing very little from a circular one, and <term>E F</term> likewise in parts where <term>B F</term> is the whole, the remainder is <term>B E</term>. However, <term>B F</term> is to <term>B E</term> as the chord of the double quadrant is to the chord of the double <term>K</term>, and <term>B E</term> is to <term>K L</term>. Therefore, if we set both <term>B F</term> and the radius <term>C E</term> to the number 60, we will also have <term>B E</term> in those same units. When <term>B E</term> is multiplied by itself and the product divided by 60, we will have the <term>proportional minutes</term> of <term>K L</term> from the sought circumference. These we have also assigned to the fifth and last place of the Table, as follows.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating planetary deviation. It features a large arc labeled A and C at the nodes, with a smaller circle at the top labeled with points D, F, G, B, and E. A line extends from the center toward an arc on the left labeled L and K.</image-desc>

<summary>Copernicus explains the geometric method for calculating the "deviation" of Venus and Mercury using a small circle of libration. He provides a mathematical basis for the proportional minutes used in his astronomical tables to determine a planet's distance from the ecliptic.</summary>
