# Nicolaus Copernicus

### On the calculation of the latitudes of the five wandering stars. Chapter 9.

The method for calculating the latitudes <note>The angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic, the sun's apparent path.</note> of the five wandering stars <note>The planets known in the 16th century: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.</note> by means of these tables is as follows. For Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, we shall compare the adjusted or equated anomaly of the eccentric <note>The "anomaly" refers to the planet's position in its orbit; "eccentric" refers to the circular path whose center is offset from the Earth.</note> to the common numbers—taking that of Mars exactly as it is. For Jupiter, however, a subtraction of 20 degrees must first be made, and for Saturn, 50 degrees must be added. We shall then note down the sixtieths, or proportional minutes, placed in the last column which correspond to these values.

Similarly, by using the adjusted anomaly of commutation <note>The planet's position relative to the Sun, reflecting the Earth's motion.</note>, we shall take the latitude adjacent to each planet's specific number: the first and Northern latitude, if the proportional minutes are in the upper part of the table (which happens when the anomaly of the eccentric is less than 90 or more than 270 degrees). But we take the Southern and following latitude if the proportional minutes are in the lower part—that is, if the anomaly of the eccentric used for entry was more than 90 or less than 270 degrees. If, therefore, we multiply one of these latitudes by its respective sixtieths, the result will be the distance from the zodiac circle <note>original: "circulo signorum"</note> toward the North or South, according to the designation of the chosen circles.

But in the case of Venus and Mercury, three latitudes must first be taken by means of the adjusted anomaly of commutation: the declination, the obliquation, and the deviation <note>These are three distinct components of latitudinal motion used in the Copernican model to account for the complex tilting of the inner planets' orbits.</note>. These should be noted separately, except that in the case of Mercury, a tenth part of the obliquation is rejected if the anomaly of the eccentric and its number are found in the upper part of the table, or the same amount is added if in the lower part; the remainder or the sum of these is then kept.

Their designations, whether they be Northern or Southern, must be distinguished. For if the adjusted anomaly of commutation is in the apogee <note>The point in the orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> semicircle—that is, less than 90 or more than 270 degrees—and the anomaly of the eccentric is also less than a semicircle: Or again, if the anomaly of commutation is in the perigee <note>The point in the orbit closest to the Earth.</note> circumference—namely, more than 90 <note>original: "XV", likely a typo for "XC" (90) in the Latin source text.</note> and less than 270 degrees—and the anomaly of the eccentric is greater than a semicircle, then the declination of Venus will be Northern, and that of Mercury Southern. If, however, while the anomaly of commutation is in the perigee circumference, the anomaly of the eccentric is less than a semicircle...

<summary>Copernicus explains the mathematical steps for calculating the latitudes of the five planets using astronomical tables, distinguishing between the outer planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars) and the inner planets (Venus, Mercury).</summary>
<keywords>Nicolaus Copernicus, planetary latitude, anomaly of the eccentric, anomaly of commutation, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, astronomy, trigonometry</keywords>

--- Page 407 ---
<meta>This page concludes Book VI of Copernicus's "On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres," focusing on the final calculations for the latitudes of Venus and Mercury and providing the publication colophon.</meta>

# ON THE REVOLUTIONS, BOOK VI.

is smaller, or if the anomaly of parallax <note>original: "commutationis anomalia"; the apparent shift in position due to the Earth's motion</note> is in the apogeal part <note>the point furthest from Earth</note> and the eccentric anomaly is more than a semicircle, then conversely the declination of Venus will be Southern, and that of Mercury Northern. In the case of obliquation <note>the second component of latitude, related to the inclination of the orbital planes</note>, if the anomaly of parallax is less than a semicircle and the eccentric anomaly is apogeal, or if the anomaly of parallax is greater than a semicircle and the eccentric anomaly is perigeal <note>the point closest to Earth</note>, the obliquation of Venus will be Northern and that of Mercury Southern; these also swap. However, the deviations <note>the third component of latitude</note> always remain Northern for Venus and Southern for Mercury. Furthermore, when the eccentric anomaly is determined, the proportional minutes <note>term: "scrupula proportionum"; small fractions used to scale the maximum latitude based on the planet's current position</note> should be taken—which are common to all five planets, although assigned to the three superiors—and these are assigned to the obliquation, and the last ones to the deviation. After this, by adding 90 degrees to the same eccentric anomaly, the common proportional minutes that occur with that sum are applied to the latitude of declination. With all these values placed in order, each of the three explained latitudes is multiplied by its own proportional minutes, and they will emerge fully calculated for that specific place and time. Finally, to obtain the sum of the three latitudes for these two stars, if they are all of the same name <note>i.e., all Northern or all Southern</note>, they are added together; if not, at least the two that share a name are joined, and depending on whether they are larger or smaller, the third latitude of a different name is subtracted from them, and the prevailing latitude sought will remain.

<margin>fixed</margin>
Another miracle of Saint Augustine.
<note>original: "Otro ſe ſant agustin"</note>
...that he should lay his hand upon him and heal him of his sickness. And there came to him a sick man <note>The text describes a healing miracle performed by the saint</note> who asked that they might read his psalms and perform his prayer. And ten days before he died, he ordered that no one should enter to see him, so that they would not hinder him from reading his psalms and making his prayer. And ten days before he died, he saw them very often, weeping greatly from his eyes. And understanding that he was to die, he had the seven penitential psalms written down; and he had them placed before him. In the time of the three hundred and forty-fourth era <note>The Spanish "Era" system often differs from AD dates; this refers to the 5th century AD</note>, the Vandals destroyed the province of all Africa with great ferocity, and they spared neither creature great nor small. They came to besiege the city, and after three months, Saint Augustine fell ill with a fever. And in this tribulation, Saint Augustine found his life in his old age more bitter and more tearful than all other things. And instead of bread, he ate tears day and night, seeing some killed and others exiled; the church without clergy, and the city without people. The houses were destroyed. And with all these evils, he consoled them with a word he had heard from a wise man who said: "Do not think it a great thing that wood and stones fall and man dies." And he called his brothers and others to him. "Pray to our Lord that He may take you out of these dangers: either give you patience, or take me from this grief, so that I may no longer see more miseries and wretchedness." And they gained the third thing they asked for <note>meaning his death</note>. He said that many times the honor and power that a man has kills him; and he said that the good must have many tribulations in this world, while the wicked have their consolation. And he told of a bishop named Liberius who was very ill and prayed to God to give him holiness, and there appeared to him a very beautiful youth. And being very angry with him, the youth said: "You are afraid of the pains, and therefore you do not want to know what I will do with you." And he told great things and highly praised those who desired to die. He spent his time day and night in the scripture of God and in his deeds. He did not involve himself in building houses or palaces, so that they would not hinder him from reading. However, if anyone wanted to build them, he did not forbid it, unless he himself wanted to do it.

<column-break/>

...he prayed to God for him, and immediately he was healed. And Saint Augustine healed many who were possessed by demons and performed many other miracles. And after his death, the unbelieving people <note>referring to the Arian Vandals</note> took all the land and defiled the churches and holy places. And the Christians took his body and carried it to Sardinia.
¶ A monk guarding the body of Saint Augustine: a poor man came with devotion and offered much money to the monk so that he might give him one of Saint Augustine's fingers. And the monk took the money and gave him a finger from another dead man wrapped in a piece of silk, or perhaps it was from a dried-up man. And the man took it with great honor and great solemnity, and honored it with great devotion, and placed it over his eyes many times. And God, seeing his faith, granted him a miracle through mercy. And it became known that he had one of Saint Augustine's fingers. And when the fame of this reached Pavia, to the Abbot of that monastery where the body of Saint Augustine lay, they affirmed what the said monk had done—that it was the finger of a dead man. They came to open the tomb of Saint Augustine and found that he was indeed missing a finger. And the Abbot, seeing that it was true, removed that monk from his office and gave him many punishments.
¶ In Burgundy, there was a monastery called Frontaluro; and in it was a monk who had a very great devotion to Saint Augustine and begged him very earnestly that he should not let him leave this world except on his feast day. And twenty days before his feast, that monk fell ill in such a way that on his vigil they laid his body on the ground as if dead. And then many beautiful men came in white <note>original: "claros," meaning bright or shining</note> with their procession, and they entered the church; and behind them came one very honored like a bishop in pontifical vestments. And a monk who was in the church saw all this; he asked them who they were or where they were going, and they said they were Saint Augustine with his canons who go to fetch his devotee who wishes to die to take him to paradise. And after this, they buried him in the infirmary; and while he was there a little while...

<meta>This page continues the biographical account of Saint Augustine of Hippo, focusing on his conversion, his relationship with Saint Ambrose and Bishop Valerius, and his personal conduct as a bishop.</meta>

the pain: that he had, for he lost the tablet: and therefore he wrote on a tablet that everyone should pray to God for him: and as soon as he knelt down, he was immediately healed. And Saint Augustine being thirty years old, through the merit of his mother: and through the preaching of Saint Ambrose, he had himself baptized along with a son he had <note>Augustine's son, Adeodatus</note> and a [companion]. Saint Ambrose and he composed the *Te Deum laudamus* <note>original: "Te Deum laudamus" - We praise thee, O God; a famous Christian hymn</note>: Ambrose speaking: and Augustine responding: and from then on he was greatly confirmed in the faith of Jesus Christ: and he abandoned whatever hope he had in the world and said against God <note>likely "unto God" or "concerning God"</note>. Lord, I have fixed your words in my heart and the examples of your servants whom you made from dark to bright: and from dead to living. And thus he reasoned with God concerning the deeds of his life, and afterwards he took his mother: and all his friends: and left [his property] and surrendered it: and they returned to Africa by the coast: and there his mother died in Ostia: and Augustine returned to his land and fasted and kept vigil and prayed to God. And his fame spread through all the land: and he did not want to go to any city where there was no bishop, so that they would not make him a bishop. And then there was in Hippo <note>original: "ypo"</note> a bishop named Valerius: and he ordained Saint Augustine to the mass: although it grieved him: and he wept for not wanting to be [a priest]. But the bishop consoled him: saying that he was worthy of greater honor. And because the bishop of Hippo was Greek and did not know the Latin language and letters well, he gave his power to Augustine so that he might preach in the church before him. And in this time Augustine defeated many heretics which would be long to tell. And Valerius was afraid that they would demand Augustine for a bishop in another place: and other times they had demanded him: except that he hid him: and therefore he obtained from the Archbishop of Morocco <note>likely referring to the Primate of Numidia/Carthage</note>: that they should make Saint Augustine bishop of Hippo: in his place: and Augustine not wanting to take it, he had to do it by force: however, later he [regretted] it: and wrote that such a thing should never be done as this: and of another. There is nothing in the world that grieves me as much as this: because I am not fit to rule the realm: and they put me at the govern[ment]

<column-break/>

but they were of good manner. And he said of himself: I tell you in truth that I have great shame of precious and noble clothing. And when they give it to me, sell it: because I cannot give the garment to everyone. And let the price be common to all. His table was not meager: but moderate. And by reason of the guests and the sick: sometimes among the cabbages and vegetables he ate meat. And being at the table he loved disputation or reading more than hearing ill of others. At one time some bishops—many of them—his familiars spoke ill of others. And he said that they should be silent, otherwise: they should rise from the table: and he said that he had learned three things from Saint Ambrose. The first, that he should never arrange a marriage for anyone: for if afterwards they lived a bad life together, they would give him their curse every day. The second, that if anyone wished to be a knight <note>or soldier/nobleman</note> that he should not praise it to him. [For] if the knights had some battles they would say that he was at fault. The third, when they invited him to eat that he should not go there: for by chance he would eat more than was necessary for him. And so great was his cleanliness and humility that the sins which we consider to be nothing or small, he excused them before God and confessed them: such as when he was a boy and played ball: and when he had to go to school: that he did not want to learn or read: except by force from the master and the father: and from the relatives and friends, and he willingly heard jokes that were told, and that he stole money from his father: and that he gave it to those with whom he played: and in the games he deceived the boys: and that he stole a tree <note>referring to the famous "theft of the pears" in his Confessions</note> that was near a vineyard when he was fifteen years old. And how he delighted in eating and drinking. And this holy man confounded the heretics: in such a way that they said it would be no sin to kill him like a wolf. And he always remembered the poor in doing them as much good as he could, in such a way that he had the chalices of the church broken: and melted: and gave what they were worth to the poor: and he did not want to take houses or estates that they gave him.

<meta>This page continues the hagiography (lives of the saints) of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux and begins the account of Saint Symphorian. The text is translated from Early Modern Spanish, maintaining the pious and instructional tone of a medieval or early Renaissance devotional work.</meta>

do not dare to touch that woman. And after they had done so, he never again dared to approach her. ¶ Saint Bernard performed many other miracles that would be long to recount. And when this blessed man felt that death was drawing near, he called all the monks and said to them: "Guard yourselves against three things that I guarded myself against while I lived in this world. The first, that I never wished to cause grief to anyone; if any scandal occurred, I appeased and extinguished it as much as I could; and I always trusted my own judgment less than that of others. And if anyone did me harm, I never took revenge for it; and I leave to you charity, humility, and patience." And after Saint Bernard had written many books and many treatises and performed many miracles, and established one hundred and sixty monasteries—being sixty-three years of age—he departed from this world in the hands of his monks and went to Paradise. And after his death, his glory was revealed to many. He appeared to an abbot of a monastery in Lebanon <note>original: "libano"</note>. And [the abbot said], "I shall ascend there, and you shall remain on earth." And that abbot asked him why he wished to ascend there. And he said: "Once more I wish to go and learn, for there is no poor man in the world who sees you and hears you who can surpass you in knowledge." And Saint Bernard said: "There is no knowledge here, nor any understanding of truth. These things are in heaven." And saying this, he disappeared. And the abbot marked that day and that hour, and found that at that very hour Saint Bernard had departed from this world. And God performed many other miracles for the love of this his <unclear>servant</unclear> Bernard.

### ¶ The Life of Saint Symphorian.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration depicting a saint (likely Symphorian) being led by soldiers or officials. The saint is in the center, and there are architectural elements in the background.</image-desc>

<margin>These crowns you shall take from my hands.</margin>

¶ Saint Symphorian was born in a city called Autun <note>original: "Augustinens", the Roman name for Autun, France</note>, and being a youth, he possessed such good character that it seemed he had adopted the life of the elders, anticipating it in his youth. And the pagans were holding a festival for Venus, and bringing the image before the governor <term>adelantado</term> <note>A high-ranking official or provincial governor</note>, Symphorian was there. And they saw that he would not worship the idols, and he refused to do so. And the governor ordered him to be seized and put in prison. And the next day they took him out of prison and told him to worship, and that they would give him many jewels. And he said: "My Lord Jesus Christ knows how to give good jewels and a good reward to all those who suffer pains for His love; and for this reason we must fear God, because on the Day of Judgment His jewels shall be rewarded, and yours—"

<column-break/>

<margin>Seeing this, a man named Apollinaris was immediately baptized; and therefore the governor ordered them to be beheaded because they stood firm in the faith of Jesus Christ.</margin>
